Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

PRIVATE & PUBLIC BIKE 
PARKING & STORAGE
Based on marketability of the 1, 2 and 3 bedroom 
condos at 114-122 Harvard Street building has 16 
units and 1 commercial space, we have provided 8 
first-come first-serve off-street parking spaces. 
18-24 Standish Street is a mix of 3-bedrooms
and 1-bedrooms and we are providing 3 off-street
parking spaces for the 6-unit building. Family units
prefer off-street parking. Our real estate agents
advised against combining the parking for both
sites for marketability.
Our landscape plans show new raised planting 
beds and grade changes that screen the parking. 
All drive aisle use existing curb cuts to access off-
street parking.
The Project will offer many benefits to the City of 
Boston and more specifically the community of 
South Dorchester. 
- Creation of 22 new, affordable, sustainable 
homeownership condos with access to public 
transit and green space.
- Opportunity for a local small business to 
purchase 1,245 SF of commercial space.
- Common and individual green space for 
homeowners.
- Offering additional space to abutters of the 
property for setbacks and drive aisles.
Bike parking for visitors has been provided at both 
parcels parallel to the curb on the sidewalk between 
street trees. 6 are provided at 114-122 Harvard 
Street and 4 are provided at 18-24 Standish Street.
Indoor bike parking for 114-122 Harvard Street 
is located off the common areas to contain 16 
bike parking spots for retail and residential (1 per 
residential unit and 1 per 3,000 SF of commercial 
space).
Enclosed bike parking for 18-24 Standish Street 
includes space for 6 bike parking spots (1 per unit).

Project Summary 
The Proposed Project consists of the re-development of a 22,233 square-foot existing industrial 
commercial site located at 1188-1200 Bennington Street in East Boston. The site currently 
includes a 2 story, 13,172 square foot industrial/commercial building that served as the 
corporate headquarters of GVW, Inc., a Boston based Construction company that has been in 
business for over thirty (30) years. The project will include construction of two (2) new residential 
buildings, containing a total of forty (40) residential units, two (2) ground level retail spaces, 
twenty (20) accessory off-street parking spaces, bike storage and a dog wash all located in the 
building’s at grade level. Parking will be entered and exited via Bennington Street, which has 
access to Revere (North) and Orient Heights (South). The site is within walking distance (less than 200 
yards) from the MBTA’s Suffolk Downs Rapid Transit Station and within 1/4th of a mile from the Orient 
Heights Rapid Transit Station. The site is also within a 6 minute walk to the Belle Isle Reservation and 
a 10 minute walk to Constitution Beach. 
The Proposed Project would create a transit oriented residential development combining market-
rate and affordable housing opportunities in an aesthetic appropriate in scale, massing and design 
to this particular Orient Heights Neighborhood of East Boston, providing additional high density 
housing for the area. 
In planning the building, which maintains more than 400 feet of frontage along Bennington Street, 
consideration was given to abutting properties, which share boundaries with the Site including the 
commercial building to the right and the MBTA Right of Way to the rear as well as modifications 
made during the community outreach and Article 80 process as well as design modifications as 
recommended by the Urban Design Staff at the BPDA so as to ensure that the project meets the 
goals and objectives of PLAN: East Boston. As a result, the proposed building has been designed 
and scaled to compliment other current and future potential developments in the general area and 
including Walley Street, Suffolk Downs, the approved project at 1181 Bennington Street and the 
proposed project at 1141 Bennington Street. 
Community Benefits 
The Proposed Project will offer many public benefits to the neighborhood and to the City of Boston, 
including the following: 
•
The creation of forty (40) new transit oriented residential units, including seven (7) units (17.5%), which
will be subject to the City of Boston Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) as well as [1200+] square
feet of new ground level retail spaces.
•
Improvements to the property boundaries including landscape buffering and associated streetscape
improvements as well creating approximately 4,200+/- square feet of open space on site (18.9%);

Project Description 
The Project Site will include 22,233 Ft2 of land area, comprising the parcel situated at 1188-1200 
Bennington Street, East Boston. The City of Boston Assessor’s Parcel Numbers is 010567000. 
The Parcel is the site of an existing commercial/industrial building containing approximately 13,000 square 
feet of floor area. 
Proposed Program, Data and Dimensions 
Lot Area: 22,233 Ft2
Maximum Building Height/Stories: 62 feet (6 stories) 
Number of Residential Units Proposed: 40 
Number of Retail Spaces Proposed: 2 
Total Building Square Footage: 49,992Ft2 
Floor Area Ratio: 2.25:1 
Parking Spaces: 20 (18 full size; 2 Handicap Accessible) 
Design Approach 
The Proposed Project would consist of two buildings ranging from 4 to 6 stories. The residential 
program for the building will contain a total of 49,992 +/- square feet, which includes 33,368 +/- 
square feet of residential space, 3,672 square feet of space lobby/amenity space, and an 
additional 9,023 square feet of core/circulation. A covered parking garage at the grade level will 
accommodate the needs of the building’s residents through the provision of 20 parking spaces 
and a total of 40 bicycle storage racks plus 8 visitor racks (48 Total). The 40 residential units will 
have a mix of 4 studios (70%) (478 s.f. per unit average), 18 one bedroom (45%) (745 s.f. per 
unit average), 15 two bedroom (37.5%) (969 s.f. per unit average), and 3 three bedroom (7.5%) 
(1162 s.f. per unit average) units. There will be additional ground level areas for bicycle parking, 
a gym, mechanical, trash handling and recycling facilities. 
The building’s massing is derived from the neighboring context including the approved project at 
1181 Bennington Street (approved for 44 residential units), the recently completed project at 11-
19 Walley Street (38 residential units), and the proposed project at 1141 Bennington Street 
(proposal for 200+ residential units) as well as the unique lot size and frontage along Bennington 
Street. A mix of masonry, fiber cement hardi board, metal panels and other design elements 
which are consistent with the design standards set forth by the BPDA will provide a continuation 
of the strong identity along Bennington Street. The design will present a unique appearance as it 
relates to it’s immediate context and will serve as a compelling precedent for the area’s future 
development.

Traffic, Parking and Access 
The project’s 20 on-site parking spaces will be accessed via multiple independent entrances on 
Bennington Street, which is bi-directional and leading to Revere and points north and Orient Heights 
Square to the south. Vehicles will both enter and discharge from their separate garage entrances to 
an area which has been designed to minimize the building’s impact on adjoining neighboring 
properties. The garage and lobby will have direct elevator access provided to all floors in the 
building. Ample secure space for bicycle racks will be provided within the building’s garage.

2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new five-story residential building situated at 118 B Street in 
South Boston’s St. Vincent neighborhood. The project site is a 12,367 square foot parcel currently 
occupied by a one- to three-story commercial building with surface parking. The applicant 
proposes a new of thirty-seven unit residential apartment building, with twenty-six accessory 
garage parking spaces, and bicycle storage in accordance with Boston Transportation 
Department policy requirements. 
 
 

118 B Street Residential Project 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of thirty-seven new dwelling units in an attractive low-rise building, 
including six affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy; 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
• the expected creation of approximately sixty construction industry jobs to complete the 
proposed project; 
• a bikeshare contribution to the Boston Transportation Department in the amount of 
$10,175, in accordance with Boston’s Bike Parking guidelines; 
• a community benefits package to be determined in conjunction with the BPDA and City 
agencies, and upon input from neighbors, the local civic association, and local elected 
officials. 
 
4. 
Project Financing and Developer Pro Forma 
 
The developer enjoy an extensive record of development success in Boston, enjoy a strong 
working relationship with several local lenders, and intend to finance the project using traditional 
institutional financing. 
 
Total Development Cost (soft/hard costs): $20,000,000 
Construction Cost (hard cost): $15,000,000 
 
Estimated Constructions Start: 
Second Quarter 2024 
Estimated Construction Completed: 
Third Quarter 2025 
 
5. 
Urban Design Overview, Building Massing & Design, Materials 
 
The corner lot at 118 B Street is located across East Third Street from a popular playground, 
Flaherty Park. Breaking down the massing of the building was critical to its relationship with not 
only the park but also with the surrounding buildings. By creating a collection of smaller building 
elements with softer edges–instead of a single mass with harder edges–the residential building 
would be more appealing visually and cast shorter and irregular shadows. 
 
The massing of the building follows the tripartite division of base, shaft and capital. The brick 
veneer of the ground floor is followed by three floors of square bays separated by recessed 
balconies and topped by a fifth floor that is recessed on all sides. 
 
The grand framed opening with angled bays highlights the main entrance. This feature alludes to 
the prominent brick window surrounds of the building across B Street, the former Lawrence 

118 B Street Residential Project 
School, now a residential condominium. Lastly, the building’s main entrance and area of most of 
the social interaction is located near the corner of B Street and West Third Street, and the street 
from Flaherty Park. 
 
6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The proposed project’s thirty-seven dwelling units will be served by twenty-six motor vehicle 
parking spaces located in an at-grade garage to be accessed by a single existing curb cut on B 
Street, which is to be slightly relocated horizontally. A second twenty-foot wide curb currently 
serving the site will be closed, with the sidewalk and curbing restored, as part of the project. The 
new building will also feature secure interior resident bicycle storage, and outside visitor post-
and-ring assemblies, in compliance with the City of Boston’s bicycle parking requirements. The 
site is located approximately 1,000 feet from the MBTA’s Broadway Red Line rapid transit station, 
and also within easy walking distance of bus stops on MBTA bus routes 9, 11, and 47.

PROJECT SUMMARY
1.1
Introduction
Holocaust Legacy Foundation, Inc. (the “Foundation” or the “Applicant”) respectfully
submits this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”) in accordance with the requirements of
Article 80E of Chapter 665 of the Acts of 1956, the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code” or “BZC”)
for the development of New England’s first Holocaust Museum and Educational Center to be
located, at 125 Tremont Street, in the Midtown Cultural District of Downtown Boston.
The Foundation was formed in 2019 when project co-founders Jody Kipnis and Todd
Ruderman created and fully funded the Foundation's hallmark program – Holocaust Legacy
Fellows – a Holocaust education and travel program to Germany and Poland for high school
seniors. Jody and Todd believed that with the right knowledge and understanding of the past,
young people can be the agents for change. After the 2020 fellowship was canceled due to the
pandemic, and with former Govenor Baker’s 2021 signing of the of S.2557, An Act Concerning
Genocide Education, Jody and Todd knew they had to find a way to make a larger impact. The
universal lessons of humanity that can be learned from the Holocaust and other genocides
depended on future generations to carry the message forward, underscoring the need for a
Holocaust Museum and Educational Center in Boston.
In April 2022, the Foundation purchased the former Merchant’s Cooperative Bank
building at 125 Tremont Street with the intention of building a museum dedicated to preserving
and perpetuating the memory and lessons of the Holocaust for future generations. Situated,
appropriately, along Boston’s historic Freedom Trail, this vital and timely project will tell the
story of the dangers of intolerance, discrimination, and the consequences of unchecked state
power. By examining the causes and factors that enabled the Holocaust to occur, visitors will be
able to apply those lessons to contemporary issues and work towards creating a more inclusive,
tolerant, and just society. The Holocaust Museum and Educational Center – which has not yet
been formally named – will connect the past to present-day human rights issues, fostering
dialogue and encouraging visitors to actively engage in the fight against prejudice and injustice.
With President Biden’s recent announcement of the first ever U.S. National Strategy to
Counter Anti Semitism – the most ambitious, comprehensive effort in U.S. history to counter
antisemitism – the Holocaust Museum and Educational Center is an extraordinary gift to the City
of Boston. Accessible to the public, the vision is for the Museum and Educational Center to serve
as a hub for Holocaust and genocide education, as well as educate on the dangers of Anti-
semitism, and all forms of prejudice and hate. The museum will be designed to be an interactive
educational center that is meant to raise awareness in visitors about their responsibility as
participants in a democratic society today.
9
To preserve and perpetuate the memory and lessons of the Holocaust for future generations

Through the museum exhibits, the Foundation is dedicated to enhancing the New
England Holocaust Memorial and other significant sites along Boston’s Historic Freedom Trail,
and is expected to bring hundreds of thousands of visitors to the Boston area each year. Most
importantly, the Foundation desires to see every New England student visit the museum before
they graduate.
1.2
Project Description
The development proposal contemplates the demolition of the existing three-story
structure at 125 Tremont Street and building in its place a new, six-story, 84.5 foot tall, 32,696
square foot DLT and steel, sustainably designed building that will serve as a first of its kind
Holocaust Museum in Boston. The original 1880s granite foundation was retained in 1955 and
will remain in place, maintaining the original 1880s foundational footprint and preserving the
historical street-wall envelope of the original structure. Given the nature and use of the proposed
Project, the physical building will be strategically developed with materials designed to protect
its occupants and visitors, the surrounding neighborhood, and the sensitive and irreplaceable
contents within.
The Proposed Project has been specifically designed to reflect the building height, design,
massing, and architecture of the surrounding infrastructure, while also emphasizing its
importance as a new element to Boston’s community. The exterior of the building is constructed
of materials such as steel, stone, and wood, designed to be hopeful and inspiring. The building’s
most prominent feature is the decorative architectural mesh screen that wraps the facade. This
screen could have many interpretations from the passersby such as: a curtain pulled back to
witness and document the atrocities of the Holocaust; fences that separated Jews within ghettos
or concentration camps; and barriers torn down during liberation. The consistent metal fabric
curtain is purposely drawn back at two critical moments on the facade. One, at the fifth floor
where the visitor will begin their journey through the museum with a view of the State House
and Freedom trail, serving as a reminder of the freedoms of living in a democratic society. The
other opening is at the bay window on the fourth level, to reveal the visitors walking into an
authentic railcar. The European rail system played a crucial role in the implementation of the
“Final Solution” to the “Jewish Problem.” The passersby will see that moment in the history of
the Holocaust when freedom was lost and Jews were brought to killing centers in
German-occupied Poland.
The majority of the building will serve as the permanent gallery space of the Museum
and Educational Center. As visitors circulate through the interactive and immersive gallery
spaces, they will be brought back in time to learn about the history and lessons of the Holocaust,
as well as other genocides. One essential element is the Dimensions in Testimony Theater on the
second floor. Partnering with the USC Shoah Foundation, the opportunity to engage with
holographic Survivors allows the visitor to be an active participant in a real-time conversation
with a Survivor, enabling the visitors to be agents of their own learning. In addition to the highly
curated galleries, the building will also feature a temporary changing gallery space that will
explore relevant current events and other genocides. To truly harness the impact of these galleries
10
To preserve and perpetuate the memory and lessons of the Holocaust for future generations

and to align with the framework of the mandatory genocide education act in Massachusetts, two
classrooms are located in the museum offering students the opportunity to dive deeper into
learning to gain a more meaningful understanding of genocides in their historical context with
their teacher or museum staff. An expansive event space located on the sixth floor will be
utilized for speaker events, or gatherings such as programs for educators, law enforcement,
religious leaders and city leaders to learn and reflect on their role in a democratic society today.
This space features views of the Boston Common, the Massachusetts State House, and the Park
Street Church. The views from this event space will offer a unique venue for the city of Boston.
In addition, the sixth floor will also include office space and a conference room.
It is culturally, historically, and geographically significant that the Museum and
Educational Center will be situated along Boston’s historic Freedom Trail, along with other
notable locations, such as the Massachusetts State House; the Boston Common, inclusive of The
Embrace statue; King’s Chapel; the Park Street Church; the Old South Meeting House; and
more. In contrast to the building it replaces, the proposed new Museum and Educational Center
provides a visible open lobby on Tremont Street which will engage passersby, more
appropriately adding to the civic dialogue already present along the Freedom Trail.

8.0
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION
8.1
Building
The structure of the building is designed to be a sustainable and low carbon system.
Rather than structuring the building with a high carbon and heavy system such as concrete, the
system used is a dowel laminated timber (DLT) and steel hybrid. The efficient steel frame will be
used with DLT floor slabs to minimize the building’s carbon footprint. DLT is a renewable
resource with low embodied energy and a more sustainable cradle-to-gate life cycle. When
constructed, DLT requires no nails and does not contain any glue or VOC’s. This ensures that
there is no off-gassing to improve the air quality in the building. This innovative floor slab also
provides acoustical absorption which will limit the use of added acoustical material.
To mitigate heat island effect, the white membrane roof provides a high Solar Reflective
Index (SRI) for heat island reduction. The thermal envelope is to be efficient and includes a R-31
roof, R-15 walls and U-0.25 triple glazing. The window-to-wall ratio of 17% will aid in the
reduction of energy consumption and solar heat gain. The high performing envelope and
strategically placed glazing minimizes the heating and cooling demand of the project, allowing it
to meet the Stretch Code and minimize GHG emissions. A stormwater retention system is being
included in the design to aid in the handling of rainwater from major storm events.
The primary design strategy to meet the Stretch Code is replacing the current fossil-fuel
system to an all-electric, heat pump based heating system. The air source VRF has a coefficient
of performance (COP) advantage over the baseline furnace heating, resulting in a significant
reduction in heating energy. In addition to these reductions, the new ERV system can
dramatically reduce the ventilation heating load compared to the baseline. Other energy end uses
that experience savings are interior lighting, space cooling, fans and domestic hot water heating.
The energy savings in lighting are due to an overall reduced lighting power density compared to
ASHRAE 90.1-2019 (See Appendix G of ASHRAE document). Space cooling savings are due to
the higher cooling efficiency of the VRF compared to the baseline direct expansion (DX)
cooling. Fan energy savings are from decoupling ventilation from space conditioning. The ERV
will provide only the necessary amount of outdoor air to ventilate all the spaces, while fan coil
units will provide heating and cooling. This arrangement can significantly reduce energy
consumption. They also take up significantly less space, allowing for smaller ducts in the ceiling
plenum. Domestic hot water savings are from low flow water fixtures.

of debris. The General Contractor will take an active role in managing the processing and
recycling of construction waste and will have in-place a Construction Waste Management Plan
(CWMP) for the entirety of the project. The CWMP will require the General Contractor to
contract with a licensed waste hauler that has off-site sorting capabilities. All construction debris
will be taken off-site by the waste hauler, sorted as either recycled debris or waste debris and sent

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

of carbon-neutrality by 2050 the performance of new buildings will need to progressively improve to carbon net zero and net
positive.

For this filing - describe how building energy performance has been integrated into project planning, design, and
engineering and any supporting analysis or modeling:
The team explored and assessed different design options (ECMs) regarding envelope performance and service hot
water. Since the HVAC system is all-electric, it already meets the Stretch Code and BPDA intent for high-performance
buildings. The ECMs are not effective in significantly reducing EUI because the proposed is already optimized in design
and further improvements will only have a small impact on the overall EUI.

and systems:
The thermal envelope includes a R-31 roof, R-15 wall and U-0.25 triple glazing. The window-to-wall ratio is 17%. The
high performing envelope minimizes the heating and cooling demand of the project, allowing it to meet Stretch Code
and minimize GHG emissions.
Describe building specific load reduction strategies including on-site renewable energy, clean energy, and storage
systems:
The primary design strategy to meet Stretch Code is fuel switching from a fossil-fuel baseline to a heat pump based
heating system in the proposed design. The air source VRF has a coefficient of performance (COP) advantage over the

Project Summary
Project Summary
The Proposed Project consists of the redevelopment of a 17,120 square-foot lot at 1274 
Massachusetts Avenue in the McCormack neighborhood of Dorchester (the “Proposed Project”). 
The Proposed Project is a mixed-use development consisting of a 6 story building containing 45 
residential units, approximately 1,000 square feet of ground floor commercial space, a public 
landscaped plaza space, 46 bike storage spaces, and 25 accessory off-street parking spaces located 
in the building’s basement level enclosed parking garage. The garage will be entered and exited 
through the existing ramp at 1258 Massachusetts Avenue. The Proposed Project is adjacent to 
multiple MBTA bus routes.
In designing the building, great care was given to respecting the character and scale of the 
residential area along Boston Street. As a result, the Proposed Project has been designed to scale 
down and knit into the existing neighborhood fabric. Using a similar language and palette, the 
building will offer a larger, glassier massing at the Massachusetts Avenue frontage as a response the 
industrial character of the area.
Community Benefits
The Proposed Project will offer many public benefits to the neighborhood and the City of Boston, 
including the following:
•	 The creation of 45 new residential units. The Project will meet the income-restricted units 
required under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
•	 The creation of approximately 2,850 square feet of landscaped public open space on 
Massachusetts Avenue, enhancing sidewalks and creating a plaza space for an improved 
pedestrian experience adjacent to the new retail entry.
•	 Creating a more pedestrian friendly Massachusetts Avenue and Boston Street by enhancing the 
streetscape with improved sidewalks and landscaping.
•	 The addition of new commercial space on the site, enhancing the streetscape	
	
	
	
	
connecting to Edward Everett Square.
•	 The future generation of hundreds of thousands of dollars in new property and sales tax revenue 
annually to the City of Boston.

Design Approach
The proposed Project will consist of a new six story residential building. The Project site straddles two 
contrasting urban contexts: a larger, more industrial zone from Newmarket along Massachusetts 
Avenue and denser, residential neighborhood made up of triple-deckers and row homes along 
Boston Street. The Project negotiates these different scales through a stepped massing, taking 
influence from proportions of its immediate context. The stepping creates visual continuity along 
the street edge and transitions the massing from six stories to four. The street level site plan 
activates Massachusetts Avenue through the creation of new commercial space and an adjacent 
public plaza. Boston Street is enhanced by the new sunken private patios and walk-up entries. The 
two edges are connected by a private path through the site, lined with ground-level entries.
The lobby and residential bike room will be at-grade, fully accessible, and accessed from 
Massachusetts Avenue. Enclosed parking will be located in a basement-level garage with access via 
the existing ramp at 1258 Massachusetts Avenue. Floors one through six will contain 45 residential 
units, with a mix of one-and two-bedroom units.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

1. Project Summary / Overview
1.1 Introduction
This application is being submitted on behalf of 129 Portland Street LLC (the “Proponent”) for an office
to residential use conversion development of the existing 30,800 Sq ft existing structure at 129 Portland
street. The proposed conversion would include 25 residential units occupying floors 2-6. The proposed
ground level Use will be retail as well as residential lobby.
The existing building is approximately 30,800 gross square feet of vacant office space. The proposed
project consists of the redevelopment of the existing building, with an interior fit out for residential. The
current estimated construction cost of this project is approximately $4,000,000.
The vision of the project is to revitalize this section of the neighborhood by replacing the existing office
space with a residential building that will add new housing units to the increasingly popular Bulfinch
Triangle community. As part of the community benefits related to the proposed project, the existing
and unsightly commercial buildings will be renovated, and will be replaced with a new residential
building. The development seeks to activate the ground level, thereby bringing more much needed
retail space to the neighborhood.
The proposed project requires filing under Small project review regulations, pursuant to Article 80 of
the boston Zoning Code as the proposed 25 units will exceed 15 units requirement for article 80. The
proponent has also applied to participate in the Downtown Boston Office to residential conversion
Program.
Additionally, the proponent will be seeking relief from the Board of appeal, since residential is a
conditional use in the Bulfinch Triangle District.
1.2 Detailed Project Description
The proposed project will be contained in the existing 6 story building on the roughly 4,400 Sq ft corner
Site. The location lies within a commercial of the neighborhood, but alsoabutts a large residential
building. The neighborhood is a home to a unique mix of commercial and Residential uses. The building
has been used as an office building for many years, with even the ground floor most recently being used
as office space. The developers are proposing a project that fits well in the neighborhood, and are filling
a large need by providing residential apartments. The Portland Street site is positioned in the Genera
Area subdistrict of the Bulfinch Triangle Zoning District (article 46). As part of the community benefits
related to this project, the commercial building will be renovated, and new market rate residential
3

housing will be developed. The proposed project will serve to invigorate this section of the Bulfinch
triangle area and bring residential foot traffic to the neighborhood.
The proposed project will be comprised of the redevelopment of the existing six-story building and a
conversion to residential apartments. The building is ideally situated for commuters, steps to multiple
train stations, & bus lines. Additionally the proposed bike room with storage for 25 bikes should allow
for an environmental & economically friendly transportation option for residents. Ideally located
walking distance to multiple local restaurants, shops and retail, the additional residents should had a
positive contribution to the local economy.
The proposed project will provide a unique mix of apartment sizes, including five three bedroom homes,
five two bedroom homes, ten one bedroom homes, and five studios. A bike room will allow for bike
storage for each resident. The project is also a very short walk to multiple Train lines, as well as MBTA
bus stops.
In addition to Small Project Article 80 Review, the proponent will need to seek relief from the board of
appeal for Conditional Use as well as GCOD and CFROD overlay districts.
A dynamic site located at the edge of the district, the new uses for the building should help to
activate this side of the neighborhood.

the Downtown Boston neighborhood. The proposed project provides for:
●Revitalizing underutilized building and office space.
●Creating much needed market rate residential housing in the neighborhood.
●Creating four on-site affordable IDP units, which will meet the Boston Planning and
Development Agency’s affordable housing standards
●Creating one much needed Voucher unit
●Encouraging alternative modes of transportation through the use of bicycling and

encourage bicycling as a mode a transportation, allowing for less vehicular traffic.
●Adding revenue in the form of property taxes to the City of Boston.
●Creating temporary construction and labor jobs.

3. Design And Sustainability_____________________________________________
3.1 Site and Surroundings
The project site is located at the edge of the Bulfinch Triangle District on the Corner of Portland street
and valenti way. . The proposed sit is roughly 4400 Sq feet with existing 6 Story brick structure. The
buildings current use is office space, and currently sits as a vacant underutilized structure. The proposed
development will be contained to the existing building, which fits very well in the neighborhood, which
is made up of commercial and warehouse buildings both similar in height and building materials. For
existing site pictures see Appendix B.
3.2 Urban Design Concept
The proposed design is a mixed use re-development of the existing building prominently sitting on the
corner of Portland and Valenti Way. The existing Lobby is at ground level, and will be reconfigured as
the Residential lobby. The rest of the Ground level would serve as retail for the neighborhood,
whereas floors 2-6 would be home to 25 Residential apartments, with 5 apartments on each floor.
3.3 Materials and Finishes
129 Portland is a brick structure in excellent condition. The exterior needs little to no work. The majority
of the project will include restoration of the existing facades with little to no changes from the current
configuration.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

On behalf of the Project Developer and Property Owner, Joseph Federico, we are pleased 
to submit this letter as Notice of our Small Project Review Application submission under 
Article 80E of the City of Boston Zoning Code, in connection with the proposed 
development at 1305 Hyde Park Avenue in Hyde Park, MA. 
 
The project site consists of an approximate 11,998 square feet lot fronted by Hyde Park 
Avenue at the corner of Dana Avenue near Cleary Square. The parcel currently has 2 
vacant structures. The 2 story buildings are non descript residential structures that do not 
add vitality to the neighborhood shopping context. Landmarks Commission has already 
approved the demolition of this structure. The redevelopment of this site will compliment 
the existing neighborhood and recent newly developed sites in the Cleary Square Area. 
 
The Proposed Project is a four story building comprised of forty two (42) residential units 
on floors two through 4. Level one consists of the residents lobby, bike storage and 
parking for 42 vehicles. There is also a loading/drop off area to service the building. 
 
The development team is led by Joseph Federico. Mr. Federico has over 10 years’ 
experience developing and owning various properties in Nubian Square and Jamaica 
Plain. He will lead a team of Architects and Engineers who all have significant 
experience developing similar scale residential projects. The team has presented to 
several neighborhood groups receiving positive feedback. In addition, there have been 
several design meetings with BPDA staff and other associated city agencies led by BPDA 
Project Manager Dan Polanco. 
 
We intend to pursue the Article 80E Small Project Review Process for this proposed 
project and we look forward to continuing our strong working relationship with the 
BPDA, the community, and the elected officials in the months ahead. 
 
Very truly yours,

i.
Proposed Project
The site located at 1305 Hyde Park Avenue, on two (2) parcels of land, totaling approximately 
11,998 square feet (the “Project Site”). The Project Site sits at the intersection of Hyde Park 
Avenue and Dana Avenue in Hyde Park, MA. Currently the site has two – 2 story residential 
structures that are vacant with an adjacent surface parking that occupies approximately 75% of 
the total Project Site area. The Project Site is mostly impervious. 
The proposed development calls for razing the current structures, removing the asphalt parking 
lot and creating a new, attractive and energy efficient building that will enliven and visually 
enhance this vital intersection on Hyde Park Avenue. The revitalization of the Project Site 
consists of a four-story residential building, containing forty two (42) dwelling units and forty 
two (42) parking spaces. The forty two (42) units will consist of thirty six (36) studio units and 
six (6) one bedroom units. All of the forty two (42) parking spaces are located internally to the 
building, at grade, concealed behind an active street wall and accessed via an existing curb cut 
off Hyde Park Avenue. (Collectively, the “Proposed Project”). 
The Proponent of the Proposed Project is Joseph Federico. Federico has redevelopment 
numerous sites in Nubian Square and Jamaica Plain over the past 10 years. 
ii.
The Neighborhood and Project Location
The Proposed Project is located on Hyde Park Avenue at the western corner of the intersection of 
Hyde Park Avenue and Dana Avenue in the Hyde Park Neighborhood of Boston. The Proposed 
Project is located just south of Cleary Square. The site is within walking distance of Cleary 
Square and the MBTA Commuter Rail Station. The site has direct access to all that Cleary 
Square has to offer. 
iii.
Development Context
The Proposed Project will contain forty (42) residential units of housing, consisting of thirty six 
(36) studio units and six (6) one bedroom units. The studio units average approximately 450
square feet, the one bedroom units average approximately 710 square feet of Floor Area.
As indicated on the Hyde Park Neighborhood Zoning Map, the Proposed Project is located 
within the NS-2 Neighborhood Shopping District. Based on the attached design the proposed 

project is designed in accordance with the zoning bylaw and does not require any variances from 
the City of Boston’s Zoning Board of Appeals. 
iv.
Urban Design Context
The project has been designed to be consistent with the intent of the Neighborhood Shopping 
District. The 42 residential units will provide added vitality to a neighborhood. The parking is 
located on site with the all of the spaces under the proposed building. The project site will be 
developed with appropriate design and site improvements to provide proper public safety and 
functionality. The building has been designed responding to a more commercial level of detail 
versus a residential “gabled” structure. We designed the building to fit within the context of the 
neighboring industrial designed buildings. 
v.
Proposed Project Benefits
a.
New Housing Units. These units will be very attractive to those seeking the
diverse neighborhood within the urban context of Boston. Additional housing is
a priority in the city and the Proponent seeks to modestly fill this need with a
project that builds upon the other redevelopment projects that have begun re-
shaping this Cleary Square.
b. Site Enrichment – the Proposed Project will transform the current use into an
eighteen hour residential use, enlivening the retail uses in Cleary Square and
adding to the overall fabric of the district.
c.
Enlivened Edge – the Proposed Project will enliven the corner of Hyde Park
Avenue and Dana Avenue with a new edge of attractive architecture.
d. Job Creation & Taxes – the Proposed Project will be a job creator both during and
after construction. In addition to jobs, the Proposed Project will be increasing the
city’s tax base with the inclusion of forty two (42) units of housing.
vi.

2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new five-story building containing 52 residential units, 
primarily market rate, with 7 affordable units in accordance with the City of Boston’s Inclusionary 
Development Policy, situated at 13 Norwood Street in Dorchester. Fifty garage parking spaces 
will be provided, as well as ample bicycle storage space. The lot size is approximately 18,409 
square feet, comprises one assessing parcel (#1602411000), and is currently used for outdoor 
storage of rental vehicles. 
 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
2

13 Norwood Street Residential Project 
• the creation of 52 new apartment units in an attractive low-rise building, including 4 
affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy; 
 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
 
• the expected creation of approximately 60 construction industry jobs to complete the 
proposed project; 
 
• contributions in amounts to be determined by the BPDA committed to improvements 
to the pedestrian realm around the project site, including new sidewalks, street trees, and 
bicycle parking; 
 
• contributions to be determined to support the activities of local community 
organizations. 
 
4.

Under the direction of Fred Starikov and Stephen Whalen, City Realty Group, LLC, specializes in 
local and regional projects that maintain community character, build value, and enhance quality 
of life. City Realty has a track record of success and enjoys a strong working relationship with 
several local lenders, and intends to finance the project using traditional institutional financing.

5. 
Building Program Details, Massing, and Materials 
 
The proposed project is located in a transitional area of the Dorchester’s Pope’s Hill 
neighborhood. The site’s location on Norwood Street is nestled between Morrissey Boulevard to 
the southwest and the MBTA Redline and Commuter Rail to the northeast. This stretch of 
Norwood Street houses multiple uses and typologies from large scale commercial storage 
facilities, hotels, construction support services, and parking as well as multiple scales of 
residential development. Most recently several multifamily developments have been proposed 
and constructed on Norwood and Tolman Streets providing context and massing influences on 
this proposal. 
 
The program of the building has been developed to respond to the site context, locating the lobby 
and additional amenity spaces including ample bike facilities along Norwood Street to facilitate 
and activated streetscape. Parking has been located to the rear of the site away from the street 
as to not impact the public realm while also providing multimodal transportation options for 
3

13 Norwood Street Residential Project 
building residents. The ground floor has also been raised almost five feet from existing grade to 
meet resiliency requirements for this area of the city. A comprehensive landscape plan has been 
developed for the project to navigate this proposed grade change as well as providing new street 
plantings and sidewalks along Norwood Street meeting the City’s Complete Streets guidelines. 
Fifty-two residential dwelling units are located on second through fifth floors, as well as 
additional amenity space, including a fitness room, a common room, and a roof deck facing the 
Neponset River and Boston Harbor to the northeast. In addition to the common roof deck, most 
of the units have been designed to have private outdoor space on inset exterior decks. 
 
The massing of the building is designed as a series of interlocking volumes facilitating step backs 
on upper levels to minimize the scale of the project from the street. The building massing also 
accommodates the stacked inset decks, providing additional open space as well as helping to 
create a rhythm and delineation to the façade. Materially, the proposal incorporates a strong 
masonry base with a series of large format panels and horizontal clapboard siding on upper levels 
to further break up the scale of the building and provide texture to the façade. Large format 
casement windows will provide ample access to light and air for residences. 
 
6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The project will include 50 on-site garage parking spaces accessed via a garage entrance on 
Norwood Street. The replacement of the current commercial use and its associated vehicular 
traffic will allow for the closure of approximately 34 feet of existing curb cut on Norwood Street, 
making for a better and safer pedestrian environment and also reducing the opportunity for 
vehicular conflicts. Direct elevator access will be provided from the garage to all floors. Ample 
secure storage for resident bicycles will be provided on the first floor, with direct access to 
Norwood Street. Visitor bike parking spaces will also be provided in compliance with the City of 
Boston’s requirements for new development. Additionally, the site is located within short walking 
distance to the MBTA bus routes 202 and 210, providing service to the Fields Corner, North 
Quincy, and Quincy Center MBTA Red Line rapid transit stations.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

1.1 Introduction 
This application is being submitted on behalf of DND Homes (“Proponent”) for a ground-up, residential 
development project at 140 Wachusett Street in Boston’s Jamaica Plain neighborhood in accordance with 
the Article 80E requirements of the Boston Zoning Code (“Code”). 
 
The development proposal is for a new residential building comprising of 28 units and 20 parking spaces. 
Included in this proposal is to raze the existing, vacant structure on the lot. The proposed three-story 
building will be situated on an 18,591 square foot lot that is bordered by Patten Street, Wachusett Street, 
and Walk Hill Street. The project has been designed to incorporate the lot’s existing rock ledge, maintain 
the existing right of way off Walk Hill Street, and revive the lot with new residential housing and carefully 
designed landscape and outdoor space for residents. This project also includes a spacious bike room 
capable of housing 38 bicycles. 
 
This project will exceed the 20,000 square foot total build-out requirement for a project in a Boston 
neighborhood, and therefore the proponent is required to file under the Small Project Review regulations 
pursuant to Article 80 of the Boston Zoning Code (“Code”). Additionally, the Proponent will be seeking relief 
from the terms of the Code from the Boston Zoning Board of Appeal. In addition to this application, the 
proposed project will seek zoning relief from the Code at the Zoning Board of Appeal.

housing to the Jamaica Plain neighborhood. This project will revive this sizeable lot along Wachusett Street 
that is one of the largest lots in the area with a ground-up residential development with 28 units and 20 
parking spaces. The proposed unit breakdown and allocation of square footage was carefully considered 
to account for Jamaica Plain’s diverse community and allows for a variety of household sizes to reside in 
these units. 
 
The proposed building has a total gross square footage of 30,114 SF and is three stories tall with a partially 
below-ground garage level for parking and bike storage. The garage is accessed via a curb cut on Walk Hill 
Street that runs parallel to the existing right-of-way driveway. The garage additionally houses a bike storage 
room capable of storing up to 38 bicycles. The first floor consists of 6 one-story units and the lower level of 
4 townhouse style units. The second floor consists of 8 one-story units and the upper level of 4 townhouse 
style units. The third floor consists of 10 one-story units. 11 of the units have direct access to an outdoor 
deck space. While this lot does abut residential buildings in the rear, the development team feels that this 
lot also abuts non-residential buildings on the other three sides, this height, scale, and mass are 
appropriate. Specifically, regarding building height, the proposed building is 38’-0” tall, while the Boston 
Teachers Union School across Wachusett Street is 36’-0” tall, Bethel AME Church across Walk Hill Street 
is 38’-0” tall, and Young Achievers Middle School across Patten Street is 38’-0” tall.

units.

Methodist Episcopal Church on the other side of Walk Hill Street. While this lot falls in a one-family 
subdistrict, the proposed structure for this project is 38’-0”, which stands in harmony with the three

2.3 Design Concept 
The project has been designed to be consistent with the scale of the neighborhood. The 28 residential units 
have been designed to fit into the sloping site with outcroppings of puddingstone. The parking garage is 
located on site with all the spaces under the proposed building. The project site will be developed with 
appropriate design and site improvements to provide proper public safety and functionality. The building 
has been designed to respond to a more residential structure. We designed the building to fit within the 
height of the neighboring buildings. 
 
2.4 Materials and Finishes 
The color and texture of the outcroppings of puddingstone have been incorporated in the façade ground 
level. The stone base will tie in with the puddingstone. We are also proposing a light gray brick to tie into 
the adjacent school and clapboard siding and mansard oof to tie into nearby residences. The site slopes 
from front to back and Walk Hill to Patten Street. The massing has been designed to limit the height at the 
lower area and tie into the height of nearby structures at the Patten Street side.

The proposed project will include an interior garage partially underground due to the lot’s topography with

as possible to incorporate the lot’s unique features into the new design. The garage will be accessed via a 
ramp off Walk Hill Street that runs along the existing right of way.

Project Summary
Project Summary
The Proposed Project consists of the redevelopment of a 19,745 square-foot lot at 1420 Dorchester 
Avenue in the Field’s Corner neighborhood of Dorchester (the “Proposed Project”). The Proposed 
Project is a mixed-use development consisting of a 4 story building containing 41 residential units, 
approximately 2,000 square feet of ground ﬂoor commercial space, a public landscaped plaza space, 
33 accessory oﬀ-street parking spaces, and 50 bike storage spaces. The Proposed Project will utilize 
numerous alternative transit options including close proximity to the Fields Corner Red Line MBTA 
station, numerous bus routes as well as ample bicycle amenities.
In designing the building, great care was given to respecting the area’s distinct conditions and 
location along Dorchester Avenue within the vibrant Fields Corner neighborhood. As a result, the 
Proposed Project has been designed and scaled to ﬁt into the commercial streetscape, surrounding 
residential fabric, and bustling intersection of Dorchester Avenue and Adams Street. The building will 
oﬀer a contemporary aesthetic appropriate in massing and design to the surrounding neighborhood 
context.
The Proposed Project is located entirely within the area of PLAN: Glover’s Corner, a comprehensive 
planning initiative conducted by the BPDA in partnership with the Dorchester community in 
contemplation of the future re-zoning of the PLAN area. Located within Zone 3, which provides for 
maximum building heights of 40 feet and a maximum ﬂoor area ratio of 2.5, the Proposed Project 
has been judged by BPDA planning and urban design staﬀ as being consistent with the PLAN’s goals 
and requirements.
Community Beneﬁts
The Proposed Project will oﬀer many public beneﬁts to the neighborhood and the City of Boston, 
including the following:
• The creation of 41 new residential units. The Project will meet the income-restricted units required 
under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
• The creation of approximately 1,500 square feet of landscaped public open space on Dorchester 
Avenue, enhancing sidewalks and creating a plaza space for an improved pedestrian experience 
on the busy commercial thoroughfare. This plaza, adjacent to the residential entry, will serve as a 
space to host public art installations.
• The enhancement of Dorchester Avenue by reducing an existing oversized curb cut, making the 
sidewalk experience safer for pedestrians.
• Encouraging alternative modes of transportation, such as bicycling and walking, owing to 
the close proximity of the Fields Corner MBTA station and the large quantity of on-site bicycle 
storage.
• Continuation of ground-ﬂoor commercial space at the site, enhancing the active streetscape 
 
 
within Fields Corner.
• The future generation of hundreds of thousands of dollars in new property and sales tax revenue 
annually to the City of Boston.
• The expected creation of more than 90 construction jobs over the length of the project.

Design Approach
The proposed Project will consist of a new residential building four stories in height. The street-level site 
plan activates Dorchester Avenue and the Fields Corner neighborhood area through the creation of a new 
commercial space and south-facing public plaza featuring ornamental trees, public seating, and an area 
to host public art installations. The building’s massing folds and curves along Dorchester Avenue to provide 
ample setbacks at the public realm level as well as visual orientation to the building’s various ground-ﬂoor 
functions. This articulation forms the plaza space directly adjacent to the main lobby, as well as providing 
access to the commercial space and parking garage. The rear of the building is set back from the rear 
abutters, creating a south-facing landscaped backyard serving as an outdoor accessible green space 
amenity for residents. 
The lobby and residential bike room will be at-grade and accessed from Dorchester Avenue. Enclosed 
parking will be located in a basement-level garage with ramp access via the existing curb cut on Dorchester 
Avenue. Floors one through four will contain 41 residential units, with a mix of one- and two-bedroom units. 
The site will adhere to Dorchester Avenue’s designation as a “Neighborhood Main” typology under the 
Boston Complete Street guidelines. The pedestrian zone will be a continuous 5’ wide minimum path. The 3’ 
furnishing zone will include one new street tree.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

On behalf of Big Dot Realty Trust (the “Proponent”), as developer of the real property situated at 
1444-1446 Dorchester Avenue in the City’s Dorchester neighborhood (the “Property Site”)1, we are 
pleased to submit this enclosed application for Article 80 Small Project Review. The Property Site 
consists of two (2) contiguous parcels of land of approximately 26,635 total square feet located at the 
corners of Dorchester Avenue, Adams Street, and Leonard Street in the Fields Corner section of 
Dorchester. It consists of an existing four (4) story mixed-use commercial building of approximately 
39,950 square feet of Gross Floor Area (“GFA”) with retail stores, a bank, and a Post Office on the 
ground floor, along with offices and old warehouse storage on the upper floors. The Property Site also 
includes the historic Clap-Field House built in the late 1700s, which was later converted into a brick 
cladded storage facility with the rest of the Property Site in the early 1900s as the O’Hearn’s Warehouse, 
although the Clap-Field House has no state or federal historic designations and is not a Boston 
Landmark. 
 
The Property Site is located in the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning District and the Adams 
Street Neighborhood Shopping Commercial Zoning Subdistrict and is subject to Article 65 of the City of 
Boston Zoning Code. It is also located within the Dorchester Neighborhood Design Overlay District. 
 
 
The Proponent proposes the revitalization of this underutilized Property Site with the renovation 
and reconfiguration of the existing commercial building of approximately 15,800 square feet of GFA of 
commercial and storage and approximately 21,200 square feet of GFA of residential living space, along 
with proposed new construction (rear and fifth story addition) of approximately 28,000 square feet of 
GFA of residential with a total of 47 new residential units, including the renovation of the existing Clap-
Field House into an additional two (2) units, while maintaining the existing Post Office and ground floor 
commercial at the Property Site (the “Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project will also provide for 21 
parking spaces, primarily underground, compliant bicycle room, and a variety of open space 
programming, including a ground level interior courtyard with paved accessible walkways, green open 
space and seating areas of approximately 6,750 square feet, a third floor common roof deck of 
approximately 222 square feet, a fifth floor common roof deck of approximately 1,738 square feet, and 
two (2) fifth floor private unit roof decks of approximately 421 square feet for a total of approximately

SITE AND PROJECT SUMMARY 
 
This Small Project Review Application (the “Application”) is being submitted by Big Dot Realty Trust 
(the “Proponent”), in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code” or “Zoning Code”). 
 
The project site at 1444-1446 Dorchester Avenue in the City’s Dorchester neighborhood includes 
two (2) contiguous parcels of land of approximately 26,635 total square feet located at the corners of 
Dorchester Avenue, Adams Street, and Leonard Street in the Fields Corner section of Dorchester (the 
“Property Site” or “Site”).2 It consists of an existing four (4) story mixed-use commercial building of 
approximately 39,950 square feet of Gross Floor Area (“GFA”) with retail stores, a bank, and a Post 
Office on the ground floor, along with offices and old warehouse storage on the upper floors. The Site 
also includes the historic Clap-Field House built in the late 1700s, which was later converted into a brick 
cladded storage facility with the rest of the Site in the early 1900s as the O’Hearn’s Warehouse, 
although the Clap-Field House has no state or federal historic designations and is not listed as a Boston 
Landmark. 
 
The Proponent envisions the revitalization of this underutilized Site with the renovation and 
reconfiguration of the existing commercial building of approximately 15,800 square feet of GFA of 
commercial and storage and approximately 21,200 square feet of GFA of residential living space, along 
with proposed new construction (rear and fifth story addition) of approximately 28,000 square feet of 
GFA of residential with a total of 47 new residential units, including the renovation of the existing Clap-
Field House into an additional two (2) units, while maintaining the existing Post Office and ground floor 
commercial at the Site (the “Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project will also provide for 21 parking 
spaces (three (3) at grade and 18 underground), compliant bicycle room, and a variety of open space 
programming, including a ground level interior courtyard with paved accessible walkways, green open 
space and seating areas of approximately 6,750 square feet, a third floor common roof deck of 
approximately 222 square feet, a fifth floor common roof deck of approximately 1,738 square feet, and 
two (2) fifth floor private unit roof decks of approximately 421 square feet for a total of approximately 
9,130 square feet of open space. 
 
Additionally, the Proposed Project will include converting entirely paved space into landscaping, 
pedestrian connectivity, and related public realm improvements in and around the Site, such as bike 
racks, street trees, and sidewalk improvements, consistent with the character and housing needs of the 
surrounding community. The scale, design and programming of the Proposed Project has been carefully 
shaped and designed to be complementary to, and consistent with, the ongoing Fields Corner Squares 
and Streets Planning Initiative. In this regard, the Proposed Project will revitalize this vastly 
underutilized Property Site with a residential component of market-rate and on-site affordable housing, 
with a building aesthetic and renovation appropriate in scale, massing, and design for this section of the 
Dorchester neighborhood.

c). Building Design and Programming 
 
The Proposed Project consists of a five (5) story building of approximately 49,089 square feet of GFA. 
Eighteen (18) indoor covered parking spaces are provided on the lower level and three (3) are provided 
at grade. The building will consist of 47 residential units of which nine (9) units, or approximately 18%, 
will be allocated as affordable units. There are accessible entrances on Adams Street and Leonard Street. 
The vehicular parking area will be primarily in the lower level and will also provide 56 indoor bike 
storage spaces with 25% of the parking spaces wired for EV chargers to encourage commuting via 
bicycle and to promote Electric Vehicles. The guest bike parking will be provided along Leonard Street 
and consists of 16 bike parking spaces. One elevator is provided at the Leonard Street entrance. The first 
floor consists of the building entrance and residential units. The building will be 100% electric and will 
apply for Passive House Certification. Loading and unloading will be achieved from Leonard Street. 
Trash collection and a disposal area will be located on the north side of the courtyard, adjacent to the 
Bank of America parking lot, and be contained within a trash enclosure. 
 
The design concept for the Proposed Project draws inspiration from the Site’s unique history and 
architectural legacy, particularly the adaptive reuse of the existing four (4) story storage building, which 
originally functioned as a theater. The intent is to respectfully restore and celebrate the building’s 
historic character while introducing a new residential addition that complements and enhances the urban 
fabric of the surrounding area. One of the key features of the existing structure is a series of large arched 
windows, which, though long since infilled with brick, remain visible from the interior. These windows 
will be fully restored as part of the design, reactivating the building’s historic façade and re-establishing 
its visual connection with the street and neighborhood. 
 
The new five (5) story residential addition is physically and architecturally linked to the historic 
structure through a thoughtfully designed lobby element. This transitional space references the geometry 
and scale of the arched windows, serving as a contemporary interpretation that harmonizes with the 
historic architecture while establishing a clear sense of entry. The design language of the lobby, 
characterized by a balance of modern material expression and contextual sensitivity, extends across the 
new building’s frontage and is mirrored on the opposite end and in the courtyard entrance, reinforcing a 
cohesive visual identity throughout the development. Brick, as the primary cladding material, has been 
selected for both the restored and new construction elements to ensure material continuity and resonance 
with the character of adjacent buildings. 
 
The Site design further supports the architectural intent through the integration of green spaces and 
pedestrian-oriented improvements. The central courtyard, anchored by the historic Fields Mansion, will 
be revitalized as an accessible landscaped amenity that respects the mansion’s scale and presence while 
introducing much-needed open space. Sidewalk enhancements along Leonard Street, including new tree 
plantings and bike racks, strengthen the project’s contribution to the public realm. A resident roof deck 
atop the existing structure offers additional amenity space and activates the roofscape, completing a 
design that is both historically grounded and forward-looking.
