(e) Vehicular Access, Parking and Transit-Oriented Programming 
 
Passenger vehicles will enter and exit the garage from the driveway on Leonard Street. Loading and 
unloading will be internal to the Proposed Project from the same location. The Proponent is exploring 
ways to reduce traffic by hiring locally and encouraging public transportation by implementing 
discounted MBTA Charlie Cards, unbundled parking, providing 56 onsite bicycle parking spaces (above 
city requirements), promoting bicycle usage, and widening sidewalks for pedestrian traffic. 
 
(f) Historic 
 
The Site is currently occupied by two (2) buildings, the original Dorchester Music Hall/former O'Hearn 
Storage warehouse at 1444 Dorchester Avenue and, to its rear, an originally residential building 
understood to be the former home of the locally prominent Field family, from which this Dorchester 
neighborhood takes its name. The Music Hall building, much the larger of the two, is a four-story brick 
structure whose angled façade has frontages on Dorchester Avenue, Adams Street and Leonard Street. 
 
The building's location at this prominent Site lends it a significant visual presence within the context of 
the Fields Corner business district. In its exterior expression, 1444 Dorchester Avenue has the 
appearance of a massive red-brick box, largely without fenestration above its second floor. Above that 
level, the silhouettes of double-height window openings are discernible despite the fact that the windows 
themselves are no longer exposed, having been sealed when the building was converted from a 
performance space to a storage warehouse. The original two-story volume of the historic auditorium was 
also subdivided horizontally at that time. 
 
Although sealed with brick long ago, the round arches of these original windows continue to 
demonstrate a strong affinity to the Romanesque Revival style. This aesthetic is confirmed within the 
interior, from which it is evident that the original windows were not removed during the warehouse 
conversion but rather encapsulated in situ. 
 
The Renaissance Revival architectural idiom was popular at the time of the building's initial 
construction, circa 1886, and was frequently employed by its architect, Edwin J. Lewis, Jr. (1859-
1937). A Roxbury native and MIT graduate (1881), Lewis was a prolific designer of residential, 
commercial and ecclesiastic buildings in Massachusetts and elsewhere in New England. Lewis's works 
are particularly well represented in Dorchester, where he resided for many years. The Music Hall is 

 
 
 
1444-1446 Dorchester Avenue│Dorchester, MA 
believed to be among his earliest independent efforts, dating from shortly after he left the employment 
of Peabody & Stearns (Boston's most nationally prominent architectural firm of the day), in order to 
establish his own practice. 
 
To the rear of the 1444 Dorchester Avenue building stands a two-story, hip-roofed building whose 
sparsely fenestrated brick exterior appears to be contemporaneous with the infill of the Music Hall 
windows. Though heavily altered, this structure appears to be the ca. 1795 original dwelling of the Field 
family, or possibly a remnant thereof. Surviving historic images and insurance maps demonstrate that 
the Field house (or "mansion," in the local parlance) was a frame building originally located on the 
approximate site of 1444 Dorchester Avenue. It was evidently moved to its present position and 
veneered in brick as a fireproofing measure as part of the latter building's storage warehouse 
conversion. Like those of the former Music Hall, the Field dwelling's window openings were also sealed 
with brick at that time. Nevertheless, the window sash, mantelpieces and cornices that survive within the 
interior are broadly consistent with a construction date within the Federal period. 
 
With regard to the Boston Landmark Commission (“BLC”), although the existing buildings on the Site 
have been heavily altered and are undesignated, they are understood to represent significant chapters in 
the development of Dorchester. As such, the Proponent and team have consulted the BLC, who has 
encouraged the retention and appropriate rehabilitation of both buildings. A recent site visit conducted 
by BLC staff has confirmed both the historic nature of both buildings and the survival of significant 
original interior features which will guide their exterior rehabilitation. 
In addition, because the Proponent intends to seek State and Federal historic tax credits (“HTCs”), the 
BLC, in its capacity as a Certified Local Government, has been asked to provide an opinion of the 
properties' eligibility for the National Register of Historic Places (“NR”). The anticipated favorable 
finding will represent the first step in the HTC process. Moreover, confirmation of the properties' NR 
eligibility (and their eventual NR inclusion) will also extend the BLC's role within the local review as an 
interested regulatory entity.

The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

As counsel to Lincoln Avenue Capital, the proponent of a Multifamily Residential 
development project at the above-referenced property in Mattapan (“Proponent”), I am pleased 
to submit the enclosed application for Article 80 Small Project Review. 
Situated on approximately 27,164 square feet of vacant land located at the corner of Blue 
Hill Avenue and Culbert Street (the “Property”), the Property includes two unsightly billboards 
within a fenced-in overgrown lot; and within Mattapan Square’s Community Commercial 
Subdistrict, which allows for a 4.0 Floor Area Ratio and 55-foot Building Height under the City 
of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). 
The Proponent’s proposed project contemplates the improvement and revitalization of 
this underutilized and vacant Property with the construction of a new, five (5) story residential 
building including 48 affordable rental units, onsite parking for 12 vehicles, and community art 
space/work room, on a uniquely-constrained and topographically-challenged property site, in an 
appropriately designed building along with related improvements in landscaping, site design and 
pedestrian access that is consistent with the character and housing needs of the surrounding 
community (the “Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project will revitalize this underutilized 
Property with a building aesthetic appropriate in scale, massing and design for this section of the 
Mattapan neighborhood and this specific location. Additionally, the Proponent is proposing both 
broader and deeper affordability than the City of Boston’s Inclusionary Development Policy 
requirements by designating all of the units as affordable, serving households with income 
ranges at 30% of the Area Median Income (“AMI”) with Project-Based Section 8 vouchers, 60% 
of AMI, and 70% of AMI (workforce units), throughout the building.

Project Summary
The proposed project will redevelop a vacant 27,164 
square foot parcel of land, at the corner of Blue Hill 
Avenue and Culbert Street, into an all-affordable 
housing building. This newly constructed building of 
approximately 49,900 gross square foot and five 
stories will include 48 rental apartment style flats 
(the “Proposed Project”). 
1471 Blue Hill Ave is bounded by Blue Hill Avenue to 
the east, Culbert Street to the southwest, and Almont 
Street to the north (the “Property”). Rows of triple-
deckers surround the Property to the north along 
Blue Hill Avenue, with single family homes west along 
Culbert Street. Hunt Almont Park is located within a 
two-minute walk directly west of the Property with a 
developed trail connecting Culbert Street to the park 
entrance. Blue Hill Avenue is a four-lane road with 
heavy traffic linking locations from south Roxbury all 
the way to Mattapan Square, directly south of the 
Property, while Culbert Street is a quieter street that 
terminates with a trail to the park entrance.
The Property is located just outside Mattapan Square, 
Mattapan’s commercial center, in a neighborhood 
which benefits from being just a ten-minute walk to 
the MBTA’s Mattapan station, which links Mattapan 
Square to Dorchester’s Ashmont Red Line station via 
the Ashmont-Mattapan High Speed Line. The 
Property is also located just a six-minute walk from 
the Fairmount commuter rail station, which links

8

Mattapan to South Station in Downtown Boston, and 
is located directly between two MBTA bus stops, 
within a one-minute walk, that will connect Blue Hill 
Avenue to Ruggles Orange Line station. The Property 
will also benefit from its location near the recently 
completed Neponset River Greenway, a bicycle-
pedestrian path which connects Mattapan Square to 
John Paul II Park in Dorchester, five miles to the east. 
The Property is within a 6-minute walk to Mattapan 
Square that includes a new 50,000 square foot
health center and recently improved streetscapes. 
The Property is also a short drive to Interstate
93, a major north-south roadway and, as detailed 
herein, in walking distance to life’s everyday 
necessities such as grocery stores, banks, 
pharmacies, parks, and schools at all levels.
The first floor will have outdoor amenity space 
including a pocket park with a community focused 
mural. The lower entry will have a gym, lobby, bike 
parking, amenity space, work station/classroom and 
a cultural anchor. The upper entry will have 
residential units and 12 covered parking spaces. The 
top floor will have lounge space and a community 
garden deck, in addition to residential units. The 
apartment flats will be a mix of studio, one bath; one 
bedroom, one bath; two- bedroom, one bath; and 
three-bedroom, two bath units. The building will have 
solar panels and be an all-electric building. 
The area has traditionally been home to single family 
homes and affordable rental housing and there are 
few middle-income and market rate rental housing 
choices nearby. Therefore, the variety of housing that 
will be offered by the Proposed Project at the 
Property will reach many different populations in 
need of quality housing at a variety of price points. 
Community Benefits
The Proposed Project was guided by the community 
plans and vision of Mattapan residents as included in 
PLAN: Mattapan, the Blue Hill Avenue Transportation 
Action Plan, the Boston Climate Action Plan, and 
many other neighborhood and city initiatives. The 
Proponent utilized valuable feedback from these 
plans, and as a result, the Proposed Project aims to 
provide many community benefits that align closely 
with the vision for PLAN: Mattapan, such as providing 
quality, energy-efficient affordable housing, creating 
opportunities for local businesses, strengthening 
existing local culture, and enhancing transportation 
connections and pedestrian safety. 
Affordability
The Proposed Project will include forty-eight (48) 
rental apartments, consisting of studios, 
one-bedrooms, two-bedrooms and three-bedrooms 
that will be affordable to households earning 60% of 
the Area Median Income (AMI) and below, in addition 
to four units of affordable workforce housing. This 
income limit is equal to individuals making an annual 
salary of $58,900 and below, and a 4-person family 
making $84,100 and below. For comparison, the 
HUD-defined median annual income for the Boston 
metro area is $98,150 for an individual and $140,200 
for a 4-person family.
Energy-Efficient Design
Article 37 requires all projects achieve at minimum 
the ‘certifiable’ level utilizing the most appropriate 
US Green Building Council Leadership in Energy and 
Environmental Design (LEED) Rating System. The 
Proposed Project will meet this requirement, seeking 
a LEED-Silver certifiable standard. The Proposed 
Project will retain existing old-growth trees on the 
9

Property, provide bioswale stormwater treatment, 
high-efficiency irrigation, community planters and 
permeable paving/landscaping. The building itself 
will be designed to the passive house standard, 
utilizing enhanced indoor air quality strategies such 
as unit compartmentalization, local exhaust and 
energy recovery ventilation, and no/low VOC 
materials and finishes. The building will be 
all-electric including the heating and cooling systems. 
Electric demand will be offset by solar power 
generation using photovoltaic panels on the roof and 
building envelope and potential battery storage to 
capture excess supply. Additionally, community 
garden space provided for tenants on the roof deck 
will help to reduce the heat island effect and allow for 
sustainably sourced produce.
Street-Level Amenities
The Property is located on a prominent corner lot and 
will provide ground-level space for local business, 
the community as well as opportunities for art 
installations. The focal point and building entry will 
be centered by a cultural anchor space. Tenants and 
the community will benefit from a pocket park along 
Blue Hill Avenue and that will showcase a painted 
mural from a commissioned local artist. There will be 
a fitness center overlooking the terrace/green space 
in the rear of the building. Visitor bike racks, outdoor 
seating, planting areas with trees, and a rain garden 
with native grasses will create an inviting and 
aesthetically appealing streetscape for residents and 
the surrounding community. 
Central Location
The Proposed Project is located between two 
"Gateway Development Areas" that have been 
identified within the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood 
District: the Mattapan Gateway Area and the 
Cummins Highway Gateway Area. The Mattapan 
Gateway Area is located within the Neighborhood 
Shopping Subdistrict along the east side of Blue Hill 
Avenue between Landor Road and Frontenac Street 
and along the west side of Blue Hill Avenue between 
Deering Road and Rhoades Street. The Cummins 
Highway Gateway Area is located along Cummins 
Highway, bordered by the MBTA tracks to the north 
and Regis Road to the south. The purpose of the 
Gateway Development Area Overlay Districts is to 
provide zoning regulations that allow for the 
development of buildings that serve as distinctive 
visual cues to signify the entrance to the commercial 
areas of Mattapan.

Transit-Oriented Design
Located within 500 feet of the Blue Hill Avenue MBTA 
train station (Fairmount commuter line) and three bus 
stops, the Proposed Project design will accommodate 
multimodal transportation by providing safe, 
inclusive connections to public transit. This includes 
working closely with the City to improve the sidewalk 
and pedestrian experience, at the corner of Culbert 
Street and Blue Hill Avenue, with clearly marked 
crosswalks, providing adequate seating and shading 
for bus-stop users, siting visitor bike racks for public 
use, and providing space for a potentially relocated 
Blue Bike station near the intersection to coordinate 
with the City’s Blue Hill Avenue Transportation Plan. 
Limited podium-style parking will be provided to 
tenants on-site to reduce the impermeable surfaces 
while encouraging residents to utilize other forms of 
transportation. Within the parking spaces, spots will 
be set aside for ride-sharing vehicles for building 
tenants and electric vehicle charging stations. 
Overall, the Proposed Project anticipates changes to 
Blue Hill Avenue, with dedicated bus and bike lanes, 
through the design of sidewalks that comply with The 
Boston Complete Streets Initiative and enhance the 
overall experience of walking around the site.
Employment Opportunities
The Proposed Project is expected to bring 
approximately 50-60 new residents to the 
neighborhood, whose spending power and economic 
contribution are expected to support numerous local 
jobs and infrastructure. As a part of the construction 
process, it is estimated that the Proposed Project will 
create more than seventy (70) temporary construction 
jobs over the length of the project and approximately 
5 new permanent jobs in property maintenance, office 
staff, and the cultural anchor space. The Proponent 
will work closely with local community leaders to 
ensure that the Proposed Project fosters 
opportunities for employment available to 
neighborhood residents. 
New Property Tax Revenue
The Property is currently vacant and produces little to 
no property tax revenue. Once completed, the 
Proposed Project will generate tens of thousands of 
dollars of property tax revenue annually for the City.
From conception through construction and future 
occupancy, the Proponent has placed particular 
emphasis on benefits sought after by the Mattapan 
community and the City, including affordability, 
economic opportunity, urban connectivity, reduced 
carbon footprint, and occupant well-being, among 
other priorities.

DETAILED PROJECT INFORMATION

Site Description
The Property consists of a single, vacant parcel 
comprised of 27,164 square feet of land area situated 
on Blue Hill Ave. in Mattapan. The site is bordered by 
Blue Hill Ave. to the East, Culbert Street to the South, 
and residential properties to the North and West. 
Although the site is currently vacant, it does contain 
a billboard sign, which will be removed, as well as 
existing vegetation and an urban tree canopy, some 
of which is being maintained as part of the proposed 
development.
The topography of the site is quite dramatic, sloping 
20’ from the high point in the center of the site to the 
low point along Blue Hill Ave. The site contains 
exposed ledge, and previous surveys show bedrock 
is close to the existing topography. The proposed 
building steps with the existing grading to minimize 
the need for disruptive construction activities and to 
create a harmonious design with the landscape.
Abutting properties to the site are composed of 
mostly multifamily residential uses, including triple 
decker building types which are common in the area. 
There are commercial uses along Blue Hill Avenue 
including a car wash and repair shop directly across 
from the Property, and the Blue Hill Church of Christ 
and their associated surface parking lot located 
south of the Property. 
There are a variety of public park spaces in the area, 
most notably Hunt Almont park which is located west 
of the Property. The park contains playgrounds, 
sports fields, walking trails, and community gardens 
accessible to the neighborhood. Pedestrian access to 
this park is provided at the end of Culbert Street, 
making it easily accessible to building residents and 
the overall community.

Design Approach
Mattapan is made up of an eclectic mix of 
architectural types and styles, in fact the site is at the 
confluence of residential neighborhoods, commercial 
areas, and transportation routes. The design team’s 
main goal was to stitch together this varied urban 
fabric, while reinforcing the existing community. The 
proposed massing has been shaped to retain as 
many of the existing trees as possible, maintaining a 
green buffer between the proposed building and the 
adjacent neighbors. The building height steps down 
from the more public corner on Blue Hill Avenue 
towards the residential neighborhood on Culbert 
Street, to relate to the scale and height of homes 
along Culbert Street. Furthermore, the building has 
been carefully planned around the existing grading to 
integrate the building design into the landscape and 
the existing urban fabric. 
Engagement with the community is a key feature of 
the proposed design, the corner of the building is 
activated by a cultural anchor: a flexible community 
space which invites the public to participate in the 
creation of a vibrant and active residential 
neighborhood. The landscape design reinforces this 
goal, creating a public pocket park along Blue Hill

The proposed façade was inspired by a desire to 
break down the scale of the building to better relate 
to the existing context. Striving to achieve our energy 
and sustainability goals, we have proposed that 
Building Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) panels be 
used where they receive the most sun along Blue Hill

electricity for the building while creating an attractive

design that relates to the colorful and varied 
architectural style of the neighborhood. The ground 
level of the building will be clad in masonry, 
providing a durable and beautiful material at the 
pedestrian level.
Sustainability
Sustainability is a key consideration in the building 
design. The proposed project is targeting Passive 
House certification as well as LEED Silver certifiability. 
Some of the sustainable strategies include:
•	
An advanced building envelope meeting the 
stringent passive house requirements
•	
On-site renewables from solar arrays on the roof 
and integrated BIPV solar panels
•	
An all-electric building, without fossil fuel 
sources
•	
Reduced parking ratio, to encourage use of public 
transportation
•	
Indoor and outdoor bike parking for building 
residents and guests
•	
Materials with reduced embodied carbon and low 
VOCs
•	
Bioswale stormwater treatment & permeable 
paving

Transportation, Parking, and Loading
The Property has excellent access to public 
transportation, including several bus stops and a 
commuter rail station within a quarter mile radius. 
See Exhibit 5 for a transportation map of the area. 
Future residents of the building will be able to easily 
walk to public transportation. In addition to public 
transit, the site has easy access to a nearby blue bike 
station one-block away at the corner of Almont and 
Blue Hill Avenue, which will allow residents to take 
advantage of the newly planned bike lanes as part of 
the Blue Hill transportation action plan. 
The project proposes the addition of 12 off-street 
parking spaces for residents in a covered area 
beneath the building. In addition, the project will 
provide 58 total bicycle parking spaces, 48 of these 
bicycle spaces will be indoor bike parking for building 
residents. A loading zone for the building will be 
provided along Culbert Street, as the building is 
entirely affordable residential, the rates of move-ins 
and move-outs are minimal, and we do not anticipate 
frequent loading use.
Public Review Process
The Proposed Project has already benefited from 
initial agency and public review as the Proponent has 
worked nearby and abutting property owners, area 
residents, local elected and appointed officials, the 
Department of Neighborhood Development (“DND”), 
the Woodhaven Culbert Regis Neighborhood 
Association, the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood 
Council, and the Mattapan Square Main Streets, as 
well as with agency staff to seek and integrate input 
on its development program. As a result of the initial 
input received and continued community outreach, 
as well as reviewing previous project scopes from 
unaffiliated and previous developers, the Proponent 
has incorporated responsive revisions to the 
Proposed Project, including with regard to 
affordability, design, landscape, vehicular and 
pedestrian access. The Proponent looks forward to 
continuing to work with the DND, the BPDA, and the 
community during the remainder of the design review 
and permitting process for the Proposed Project.
The Proponent will meet all of the public review 
requirements pertaining to the Article 80 Small 
Project Review.

Public Outreach
Working closely with community members and 
stakeholders is central to not only inform the concept 
and design of the Proposed Project, it is also at the 
core of Lincoln Avenue Capital’s mission. We work 
thoughtfully and strategically to maximize value for 
all stakeholders – including residents, nonprofit

sustainable, affordable homes is clear. Our focus

B – Greenhouse Gas Reduction and Net Zero / Net Positive Carbon Building Performance 
 
Reducing GHG emissions is critical to avoiding more extreme climate change conditions. To achieve the City’s goal of 
carbon neutrality by 2050 new buildings performance will need to progressively improve to net carbon zero and positive. 
B.1 – GHG Emissions - Design Conditions
For this Filing - Annual Building GHG Emissions:
TBD
For this filing - describe how building energy performance has been integrated into project planning, design, and 
engineering and any supporting analysis or modeling: 
Energy eﬀiciency is a primary consideration of the building design. The building will be modeled as soon as possible 
during design to allow the energy models to inform the decisions of the architects and engineers. High performance 
envelope details and systems are planned, in line with our passive house target.
Describe building specific passive energy efficiency measures including orientation, massing, envelop, and systems: 
The massing of the proposed building is oriented to increase the southern façade frontage, and minimize exposure on 
the east and west. The planned residential units have operable windows in all bedrooms and living spaces to facilitate 
natural ventilation, in addition to the exterior balconies provided at many of the units. The building envelope will be 
made up of high-performance window systems, which meet the stringent passive house rating, and an exterior 
rainscreen system that features 2” of continuous exterior insulation. 
Describe building specific active energy efficiency measures including equipment, controls, fixtures, and systems:
The heating and cooling system under consideration for the project is an all-electric VRF air source heat pump system. 
This heating and cooling system will be decoupled for the ventilation system, which will consist of energy recovery units 
which provide air supply to the building. Hot water will either be provided by a central DHW plant, or individual unit water 
heaters.
Describe building specific load reduction strategies including on-site renewable, clean, and energy storage systems:
The building has been designed to have two mechanisms for on-site power generation; roof mounted photovoltaics and 
a building integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) system within the exterior cladding on the south and east façade of the 
building. In addition, the proponent is considering the feasibility of a battery power storage system, which would allow 
the building to take advantage of fluctuations in the power grid, and provide additional resilience to building residents. 
Describe any area or district scale emission reduction strategies including renewable energy, central energy plants, 
distributed energy systems, and smart grid infrastructure:
N/A
Describe any energy efficiency assistance or support provided or to be provided to the project:
The proponent will pursue Mass Save energy rebates where possible.
B.2 - GHG Reduction - Adaptation Strategies 
Describe how the building and its systems will evolve to further reduce GHG emissions and achieve annual carbon net 
zero and net positive performance (e.g. added efficiency measures, renewable energy, energy storage, etc.) and the 
timeline for meeting that goal (by 2050):
The Project is designed to be all-electric with a high performing envelope. The goal is to minimize the building loads
such that future eﬀiciency upgrades can be limited to HVAC equipment and not involve cost-prohibitive strategies such 
as added insulation or a major retrofit to reduce loads.

The massing of the building has been shaped to preserve existing trees and 
maintain the urban tree canopy. New street trees continue this canopy, along with 
a planting strip on Blue Hill Ave. and a bioswale / rain garden at the corner of 
Culbert Street. The building features a roof terrace with planting, which will help to

meet LEED standards for the reduction of urban heat islands. 
C.2 - Extreme Heat – Adaptation Strategies
Describe how the building and its systems will be adapted to efficiently manage future higher average temperatures, 
higher extreme temperatures, additional annual heatwaves, and longer heatwaves:
The Project design parameters will be optimized for both heating and cooling.
Strategies include continuous insulation, insulated operable windows with Low-E 
coating and optimum solar heat gain coeﬀicient (SHGC), natural ventilation 
strategies, and added cooling capacity by using higher design temperatures. 
Describe all mechanical and non-mechanical strategies that will support building functionality and use during extended 
interruptions of utility services and infrastructure including proposed and future adaptations: 
On-site power generation from rooftop PVs and a façade integrated BIPV system 
will provide power during interruptions of utilities. A battery system is being 
considered which would further insulate the building from interruptions and allow 
the building to better align power use to off-peak times. 
 
 
D - Extreme Precipitation Events 
 
From 1958 to 2010, there was a 70 percent increase in the amount of precipitation that fell on the days with the heaviest 
precipitation. Currently, the 10-Year, 24-Hour Design Storm precipitation level is 5.25”. There is a significant probability 
that this will increase to at least 6” by the end of the century. Additionally, fewer, larger storms are likely to be accompanied 
by more frequent droughts.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

PROPONENT 
 
In 1863, the Massachusetts House and Senate passed an Act to incorporate a new school 
rooted in the sixteenth century teachings of St. Ignatius and fashioned on the European 
model- a seven-year program combining college and secondary school. Twenty-two 
pioneering students ranging in age from 11 to 16 years of age enrolled that first year in a 
curriculum of rudiments (Latin and Greek) and humanities (philosophy and theology) in 
what was called “Boston College.” The school was founded to educate a burgeoning 
population of Irish Immigrants during a period of bitter racial and religious hatred in the 
City of Boston. Rev, John Bapst, SJ, was selected as the first president of the school and its 
first home was on Harrison Avenue and James Street in Boston's South End. 
 
In 1913, the schools separated and Boston College relocated to its present site in Chestnut 
Hill. Boston College High School (“BC High”) remained in the South End and in 1948 
Rev. Robert A. Hewitt, SJ, purchased 70 acres on Columbia Point to serve as the new 
home of BC High. 
 
In 1950, McElroy Hall opened its doors to 600 juniors and seniors and the entire student body 
moved to the new campus by 1954. In 1957, Loyola Hall, the Jesuit residence, was completed 
and in 1965 the Walsh Hall Science Center was dedicated. Ten years later, the Student Training, 
Athletic and Recreation Complex (S.T.A.R.) was dedicated and in 1988, the school dedicated 
the 37,000 square foot multi-use McNeice Pavilion. The Corcoran Library followed in 1997. In 
2005, President William J. Kemeza- the school's first lay president- opened the school's newest 
building, the largest in the school's history, a 63,000 square foot addition, including a student 
commons, science center and cafeteria, named McQuillan Hall. On September 7, 2007, BC 
High’s Arrupe Division for seventh and eighth graders opened its doors in the fully renovated 
Walsh Hall. Named after Rev. Pedro Arrupe, SJ, the former superior general of the Society of 
Jesus, the Arrupe Division extends the rigorous Jesuit educational experience offered at BCHS 
to a younger generation of students.

In 2014, BC High opened Cadigan Hall, an approximately 28,000 sq. ft. addition that features 
student activity areas, fine arts areas, lecture hall, music and art classrooms, offices and a main 
lobby. BC High is currently reconstructing the football grandstand and making other 
landscaping and signage improvements.

DESIGN CONCEPT 
 
The design concept for the Cadigan Wellness Complex is grounded in the following objectives: 
 
• Development of a site strategy that minimally displaces existing parking and maintains 
the existing north side of campus vehicular circulation path. In addition, create a new 
view visual focus when entering from the North side of campus. 
• Transform what is now considered the East Rear of the campus into a new East Front of 
campus. 
• Create a new East Campus Entry that completes the main internal east west campus 
circulation spine and establishes a stronger connection between the Arrupe program and 
the main campus. 
• Develop a new face for BC High Athletics by enveloping the existing McNeice 
Gymnasium into the new Cadigan Wellness Complex building footprint. 
• Integrate the facades of the new Cadigan Wellness Complex into the existing campus 
exterior material fabric, to create a seamless campus addition in material use and 
massing. 
• Create interior and exterior visual transparency throughout the Cadigan Wellness 
Complex, to reinforce a sense of the BCH community, for students and visitors. 
 
Exterior Building Envelope 
 
The exterior building envelope will be constructed of masonry, brick, with glass 
windows and is designed to blend in with the existing brick in size, color and texture. 
The Proposed Project will be visible from William T. Morrissey Boulevard from the 
northerly entrance of the Site.

Sustainability 
 
The Proposed Project has been designed to be energy efficient and sustainable. 
Attached as Exhibit C is a summary of the Energy Efficiency and Sustainability 
Strategies for the Proposed Project. It should be noted that the Proposed Project is 
located outside of the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District and will be 
constructed at elevation 23 feet (Boston City Base). 
 
Landscaping 
 
The landscape design concept for the Cadigan Wellness Complex has the following 
objectives: 
 
• Create a legible vehicular and pedestrian circulation route around the west, north, and 
east sides of the natatorium building. 
• Provide inviting exterior entrance spaces at the main -west - public entrance to the 
natatorium and the existing Bulger Theater. 
• Provide a team bus drop off/pick up along the north side of the natatorium. 
• Provide tree screening on the north edge of the access road adjacent to the proposed 
Martin Richard Dorchester Field House. 
• Transform the existing site on the east side of the natatorium building into a multi-use 
plaza defined by canopy and understory trees and pedestrian unit paving that extends 
across the surface of the tree lined access roadway. This plaza connects the east entrances 
of the new building and the Arrupe program with the new grandstand of the athletics 
stadium on the other side of the access road. 
• Adjacent to the east side of the building tree groupings define intimate exterior spaces 
that can accommodate outdoor classroom activities. 
• The site landscape will include a total of 92 new trees. The trees are a mix of 7 species 
and all are native to the Boston region. The species variety and native provenance will 
provide resilience against disease. All new trees will be planted in modified soils to 
provide optimum growing conditions. 
 
 
 
 
Parking 
 
The area of the Proposed Project currently contains 372 parking spaces. Portions of 
the existing parking areas will be relocated elsewhere on the Site to make way for the 
Proposed Project. Approximately 12 parking spaces will be removed permanently, 
resulting in 360 parking spaces. The proposed parking relocation is shown on the 
Project Plans.

ZONING: 
 
Zoning Area. The BC High property at 150-160 William T. Morrissey Boulevard 
(the “Site”) is located within the Dorchester Neighborhood District, shown on Zoning Map 
5A/5B and is regulated by Article 65 of the Boston Zoning Code (“Code”). The Site is 
located within the Community Facilities subdistrict (“CF”). A portion of the Site is located 
with the Greenbelt Protection Overlay District (“GPOD”) of Morrissey Boulevard and a 
portion of the Site along Morrissey Boulevard is located within the Coastal Flood Resilience 
Overlay District (“CFROD”). The portion of the Site on which the Proposed Project will be 
constructed is located well outside of the CFROD as shown on the Project Plans. The Site 
is also within the Restricted Parking District. Portions of the existing parking affected by the 
Proposed Project will be relocated and there will be no increase in the amount of parking 
spaces (372) as a result of the Proposed Project. 
 
Use Regulations. BC High and the Proposed Project are allowed uses in the CF 
Subdistrict as delineated in Table B of Article 65. 
 
Dimensional Regulations. The Proposed Project meets the dimensional regulations 
contained in Table D of Article 65. Section 65 sets FAR at a maximum of 2.0; the proposed 
FAR of 0.2 meets that requirement. Maximum height is set at 65’ and the height of the 
Proposed Project will be 37’. The rear yard requirement of 20’ is not impacted by the 
Proposed Project. 
 
GPOD Permit. As noted above, the Site is impacted by a portion of the Morrissey 
Boulevard Greenbelt Protection Overlay District. ISD has determined that the Proposed 
Project will require the issuance of GPOD Permit even though the Proposed Project is located 
outside of the GPOD area. BC High has applied to the Board of Appeal for such GPOD 
Permit (BOA Application Number BOA1392224; ISD Permit Application Number 
ALT133426). 
 
Article 80 Review. Article 80B Large Project Review does not apply to the Proposed 
Project because the square footage (42,000 sf) is less than 50,000 square feet. The Proposed 
Project is subject to the provisions of Article 80E, Small Project Review, as the square footage 
is greater than 20,000 square feet, but less than 50,000 square feet. It is anticipated that, if 
approved, the Board of Appeal will require BPDA Design Review.

ENERGY EFFICIENT AND SUSTAINABLE STRATEGIES 
 
SITE: 
SOILS 
• 
Implemented soil design -soils suited to each plant type in order to ensure long-term plant 
health and avoid unnecessary soil amendments in the future. 
• 
Landscape Maintenance Program will be implemented to fertilize only after soil testing has been 
conducted to ensure minimal application of phosphates and nitrogen. 
HYDROLOGY 
• 
Proposed stormwater infiltration system for 100% of roof runoff and runoff from paved parking 
at north/west of Wellness Complex per BWSC and BPDA requirements. The system will collect 
and filter run off and return back to existing hydrologic process. 
• 
Proposed design/build irrigation system which harvests water for irrigation purposes. Roof drain 
leaders connect to surface runnels and/or underground pipes leading to tree planting areas or 
to rain garden/stormwater detention areas 
• 
Proposed pervious precast unit paving systems to ensure recharge of existing hydrologic 
processes. 
• 
Proposed design build irrigation system will specify moisture sensors and the system will be 
zoned based on orientation to minimize water use. 
VEGETATION 
• 
Selected existing invasive trees will be removed. These trees are invasive Norway Maple trees. 
New native species will be planted in excess of those trees removed 
• 
Native and naturalized plant material to the New England area is proposed to improve success 
of plant longevity and reinforce/sustain the local ecosystem. 
• 
Variety of plant species are proposed to minimize potential disease effects that can affect a 
monoculture. 
MATERIALS 
• 
environmentally responsible forested wood products specified in accordance with the Forest 
Stewardship Council’s (FSC) Principles and Criteria. 
• 
‘dark-sky’ luminaires specified. Dark Sky refers to exterior lighting that has no upward light 
spillage into the sky. All the illumination is directed down to the ground. light fixtures will 
comply with BC High Dark Sky 
HUMAN WELL-BEING 
• 
Universally accessible outdoor spaces. 
• 
Variety multipurpose spaces that may be used for either formal or informal gatherings of large 
and small groups proposed in east plaza 
• 
Reduce pollution from automobiles by providing alternative transportation opportunities by 
creating bicycle storage locations. 
 
 
 
BUILDING and BUILDING SYSTEMS: 

• 
All light fixtures are energy efficient LED and dimmamble with high efficiency controls 
• 
All new proposed roofs are white roofs to reduce heat island effect 
• 
All new proposed roofs are PV array ready 
• 
All roof-top units provided for space heating/cooling are all-electric heat pump style, 
contributing to lower emissions and avoiding reliance on limited natural energy source- gas. 
• 
The boilers (CONDENSING BOILERS) that are required for the Natatorium heating and 
condensation control are ultra-high efficient condensing units operating at low water 
temperatures. 
• 
The domestic hot water heaters for the gym and pool locker rooms are electric with high-
efficiency storage, using heat exchanger, 90% efficient 
• 
All plumbing fixtures specified are at the minimum low and ultra-low flow style. Project uses 
dual flush sensory toilets and sensory faucets. 
• 
The Natatorium conditioning unit utilizes full air-side energy recovery Conditioning (cooling) all 
year round 
o It also utilizes a hot-gas heat exchanger to capture the waste heat from the compressors 
to pre-heat the pool water. 
• 
State-of-the-art controls are utilized to perform night set-back operation, day-time temperature 
re-set, economizer monitoring and occupancy control. Perimeters are set at the building 
opening and than operate automatically. 
• 
Air-side energy recovery is provided on locker room ventilation units and McNeice gym RTU to 
reduce outdoor air heating and cooling loads. 60-75% energy recovery lowers energy bills by 
70% 
• 
All-electric variable refrigerant volume (VRF) heat pump system with simultaneous 
heating/cooling serving multiple small spaces (training rooms, offices, etc.). Individual Fancoil 
unit in each small space. 
 
AQUATICS: 
• 
Pool recirculation pumps will utilize variable frequency drives (VFDs). The pumps are required 
to be sized based on maximum system head pressure which occurs when the filters are dirty, 
but is only experienced for a small percentage of time during actual operations. VFDs will 
ensure that the pumps operate at peak design efficiency during all operating conditions, 
whether the filter is clean or dirty. This can lower the associated electrical costs by 30-40% and 
recover capital cost investment within 18-24 months. 
 
• 
The pool will use regenerative media filtration (RMF). Compared to traditional high-rate sand 
(HRS) filter systems, RMF will save 85-90% on water consumption for the pool. This will not 
only save dramatically on the potable water demand, but it will also be a substantial savings on 
heating and chemical costs since more water is being retained within the pool recirculation. The 
RMF system is anticipated to have a payback on the initial capital investment after 8-10 years of 
use. The filter is anticipated to last 30 years and over that time, more than 6 million gallons of 
water are expected to be saved. 
 
• 
Rejected heat from the natatorium’s dehumidification system will be used as the primary heat 
source for the pool water. In most competition pool applications, this rejected heat can meet 
100% of the daily demand for water lost due to evaporation, filter cleaning, and splash-out from 
swimmers. 

 
• 
A medium pressure UV system will dramatically improve the indoor air quality within the 
natatorium. Chloramines are off-gassed from the pool and generate the familiar “swimming 
pool smell.” They lead to respiratory issues and asthma for swimmers and “lifeguard lung” is 
common for staff. UV will destroy chloramines as the filtered pool water passes through the 
treatment chamber. This system will be able to maintain aggressive chloramine levels to 0.2 
parts per million on a 24 hour average. 
 
• 
To further improve the indoor air quality, a source capture system is being designed into the 
perimeter gutter around the pool to strip chloramines from the water and off the surface as 
their being emitted, and exhausted to the exterior. Most chloramines will reside low and close 
to the water surface. A source capture system will be integrated either into the pool’s gutter 
trough which will have an exhaust fan that continually pulls this chloramine-laden air off the 
water surface and the swimmer’s breathing zone. Chloramines are also what is destructive to 
uncoated ferrous metals and equipment systems within the natatorium. So, building materials 
and equipment systems like the natatorium’s dehumidification unit, should expect longer 
functional life. 
 
• 
The Myrtha pool system will utilize less energy over its lifecycle than a conventional pool 
constructed of concrete, reinforcing steel, and ceramic tile. Typical pools require periodic 
draining for maintenance events such as acid washing or re-grouting. Most Myrtha pools 
maintain water in the pool for 10 years or more without having to be drained. And should there 
be an issue with the PVC membrane, most servicing can be done while water remains in the 
pool. Since the BCH pool is nearly 280,000 gallons, this equates to a significant utility saving in 
addition to minimizing programmatic and facility-use impact. 
 
• 
Utilize waste heat from the natatorium dehumidification system as the primary heat source for 
the pool. The rejected heat can often get close to meeting 100% of the daily heat demands of 
the pool. A back-up heater will still be needed for initial pool heating and possibly during larger 
make-up water events, such as filter backwash.

This firm represents EJS Investments, Inc. (“EJS” or the “Applicant”), the developer of 156 Wellington

Application pursuant to Article 80, Section 80-E-2 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). The 
Applicant proposes to construct, for residential condominium ownership, a five (5) story, twenty-seven

The Property is located at the intersection of Wellington Hill Street and Greendale Road, along Morton 
Street in Mattapan. The Proposed Project will front along Wellington Hill Street, with the retail entrance 
at the intersection of Wellington Hill Street and Greendale Road. The Proposed Project seeks to revitalize 
the Property, combining two (2) existing lots under common ownership consisting of approximately

In planning the Proposed Project, a great deal of care and attention was paid to the existing and proposed

PROJECT SUMMARY 
 
Introduction 
The Applicant respectfully submits this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”) in accordance with 
the requirements of Article 80E of Chapter 665 of the Acts of 1956 for the development of 156 
Wellington Hill Street, Mattapan, MA 02126. 
The project is led by Sathuan Sa the Principal of EJS Investment Inc., a privately held and minority 
owned development and investment firm with over twenty (20) years of experience in delivering the 
highest quality residential and commercial projects. EJS has partnered with Eric Zachrison of Context, a 
collaborative architectural workshop that believes in cultivating deep relationships with community 
stakeholders and centering the community in its designs. Additionally, EJS has paired with TJD 
Construction Services LLC, a Black woman owned Boston based construction firm to serve as the 
Project’s general contractor. 
 
Existing Conditions 
The Proposed Project is located within the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Zoning District near the 
intersection of Morton Street and Blue Hill Avenue. The Property consists of two (2) existing parcels 
under common ownership comprising a total of approximately 8,160 square feet of land, currently 
improved by the former Mount Sinai Baptist Church building. 
This area is populated with a mixture of single, two (2), and three (3) family dwellings on Wellington Hill 
Street and Greendale Road and four (4) and five (5) story, multi-family apartment buildings on 
Wellington Hill Street. The Property is approximately one-half (0.5) mile away from the larger Olmstead 
Green Apartments and the recently completed homes at Harvard Commons. 
 
Project Description 
The Proposed Project consists of approximately thirty-six thousand, three hundred and sixty (36,360) 
square feet divided into one thousand, one hundred and seventy- one (1,171) square feet of retail space 
and twenty-seven (27) one (1) and two (2) bedroom condominium units. One- and two- bedroom units are 
needed in this section of Boston, as illustrated in the City of Boston Planning and Development Agency’s 
Housing and Household Composition Community Profile tool, 42% of households in the project area 

contain one or two persons; however, the project area has only 34.2% housing stock as studios, one-
bedrooms, or two-bedrooms, as compared to 66.3% citywide. In other words, the project area needs 
additional one- and two-bedroom units. Four (4) of the units will be designated as affordable, giving the 
project an affordability rate of 14.8%. Additionally, there will be twelve (12) off-street parking spaces, 
and an enclosed bicycle storage room offering twenty-seven (27) tenant bicycle parking spaces on the 
ground level. 
The Proposed Project will incorporate three (3) levels of the existing structure into the new four (4) to five 
(5) story building, which has been specifically designed to reflect the architecture of the surrounding 
community, particularly the larger scale multi-family structures in the vicinity. The massing of the 
Proposed Project blends in with that of the surrounding community as it provides a balance between the 
smaller two (2) and three (3) family dwellings and the larger residential buildings. The design team has 
intentionally activated pedestrian access along the building’s periphery on both Wellington Hill Street and 
Greendale Road by prioritizing landscaping and moving the parking entrance to the rear of the building 
on Greendale Road. In addition, the Proposed Project will be removing an existing billboard location, the 
height of which is approximate to that of the Proposed Project. 
The Proposed Project has been modified from its originally proposed plans and has gradually been 
reduced in size through the community process. The most recent plans reflect a more animated and 
cohesive façade along Greendale Road, better distinguish between the historic and new exterior features, 
and provide a safer pedestrian and traffic concept for the intersection of Wellington Hill Street and 
Greendale Road.

Public Benefit: Affordable Housing and Job Creation 
In the face of Boston’s rising real estate prices and the well documented wealth gap, the Applicant 
recognizes the importance of homeownership as a tool to build wealth and seeks to increase the number 
of homeownership opportunities available to middle and low-income individuals and families. According 
to the City of Boston Planning and Development Agency’s Housing and Household Composition 
Community Profile, 68% of housing units in the Proposed Project area are renter occupied. As such, the 
Proposed Project will further contribute to the ongoing revitalization of the Morton Street Corridor by 
creating twenty-seven (27) units of homeownership. 
In keeping with the mayor’s initiative to bring additional market rate housing to the city, the Applicant 
has designated four (4) of the units will be designated as affordable, giving the project a 14.8% 
affordability rate. 
Additionally, the Proposed Project will create between five (5) and ten (10) construction jobs and will 
result in approximately seven (7) to ten (10) full-time jobs. 
Community Outreach and Engagement 
As of the date of this Application, the Applicant has engaged the local community through meetings with 
elected officials and community leaders to introduce and discuss the project. 
The Applicant held its initial community outreach meeting with the Wellington Hill Neighborhood 
Association on February 14, 2022. The Applicant then held its first Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (the “BPDA”) prefile meeting regarding this project on October 27, 2022, and took the BPDA’s 
recommendations into consideration and incorporated them into the design presented and the same at its 
second BPDA prefile meeting on February 9, 2022; subsequent changes were made to the project’s plans 
and were presented at the third BPDA prefile meeting on March 22, 2023, and again for a subsequent 
meeting on April 14, 2023. Additionally, the Applicant met with State Representative Russell Holmes on 
October 26, 2022, and with City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo on November 11, 2022. 
The Applicant looks forward to continued outreach with local organizations, elected officials, and 
residents as the process advances.

PROJECT COMPONENTS 
 
Traffic and Parking Management 
Due to its proximity to public transportation, the Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to 
minimize vehicular traffic by encouraging and accommodating alternate modes of transportation, such as 
public transportation, transportation services, bicycles, and pedestrian traffic. 
As previously mentioned, the Project site is located less than a quarter (0.25) mile from five (5) MBTA 
Bus Routes. This area is easily accessed on-foot and via bicycle, additionally the Proposed Project offers 
twelve (12) off-street parking spaces and twenty-seven (27) indoor tenant bicycle spaces located on the 
ground floor. 
The Proposed Project has, in consultation with BPDA and BTD, reviewed the flow of traffic at the 
intersection of Wellington Hill Street, Glendale Road and Moron Street and as a result the Proponent 
proposes the construction of several traffic islands and neckdowns at the intersection of to better 
accommodate vehicular traffic and pedestrian safety. Additionally, the Proposed Project proposes 
enhancements to the public realm with the inclusion of striped guidelines at the intersection of Wellington 
Hill Street, Greendale Road, and Morton Street; new crosswalks on Wellington Hill Street and Greendale 
Road; new concrete walkways; public groundcover with granite curbs; a retail plaza area with a retaining 
wall and fixed seating; and guest bike racks. BTD and BPDA are currently reviewing said enhancements. 
The Proponent, along with BTD and BPDA, shall engage directly with the Massachusetts Department of 
Transportation (“MassDOT”) with regard to proximate road changes. 
Construction Management 
 
The Applicant will engage a professional traffic engineer to provide the required Construction 
Management Plan that shall be submitted to the City. 
 
Project Impact and Mitigation, Monitoring 
The Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to minimize the impact on the surrounding 
neighborhood and community before, during and after construction. The Applicant has intentionally 
incorporated into the Proposed Project’s design to minimize the Proposed Project’s impact. The Applicant 
will have a dedicated staff person who will establish consistent, ongoing procedures for evaluating and re-
evaluating the effectiveness of any and all mitigation measures related to the Proposed Project, including, 
but not limited to construction management, traffic management, parking management, and post-
construction aspects. The Applicant will work with the City and the community to regularly intake 
feedback and recommendations to improve upon and revise any and all mitigation measures. 

DESIGN 
 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of this portion of the Morton Street corridor and 
more specifically the intersection of Wellington Hill Street and Greendale Road by transforming the 
existing, vacant structure into a mixed- use residential building that will match the surrounding 
neighborhood at an urban scale. In fact, the Proposed Project will be similar in height to the existing five 
(5) story apartment building located directly across the street from the development site and will 
complement the other multifamily buildings in the vicinity. 
Although the Proposed Project has been designed with a modern aesthetic, the original structure will be 
incorporated in into its design. Additionally, the building’s massing, setbacks, and carefully curated 
landscaping all lend towards a streetscape that is both cohesive with the existing architecture and 
welcoming to pedestrians. 
As previously mentioned, the Proposed Project has evolved to blend into the existing neighborhood, the 
exterior façade has been redesigned to include additional open space by way of increasing the number of 
units with private balconies and adding a common roof deck, accessible by stairs and/or elevator, with a 
seating area and grilling area that can be enjoyed by the building’s residents. The retail entry at the 
intersection of Wellington Hill Street and Greendale Road provides a welcoming combination of 
landscaping and hardscaping between the building and sidewalk, new trees will be planted along the 
periphery of the building which will offer residents greater privacy and pedestrians a visually stimulating 
sidewalk. 
The Proposed Project will further enhance pedestrian and vehicular safety with the inclusion of striped 
guidelines at the intersection of Wellington Hill Street, Greendale Road, and Morton Street; new 
crosswalks on Greendale Road and Wellington Hill Street; new concrete walkways; and public 
groundcover with granite curbs.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

1.3 Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project offers the following benefits: 
•PROVIDES NEW HOUSING UNITS - Dorchester has seen an influx of new people moving in 
because of its close proximity to Downtown Boston, and accessible public transportation, and 
herefore there is a strong need for new affordable residential housing. The Project will create 26 
affordable units of housing. 
•PROVIDES AFFORDABLE HOUSING - As Dorchester rental unit prices continue to rise, there 
is a strong need to keep longtime residents, and new families from being out priced. This Project will 
create affordable units that will meet the Boston Redevelopment Authority housing requirement of 
two affordable units. 
•REVITALIZATION OF SITE - The Project will tear down a vacant building and also utilize an 
adjoining vacant lot that will provide new infrastructure and landscaping. 
•ON-SITE PARKING - This Project will create 6 on-site parking spaces for residents of the 
building. The Project is not only within walking distance to public transportation, but will also hold a 
1-1 bike storage space which will encourage less need for vehicular travel. 
•COMMUNITY SPACE - The Project will create a 2,000sq ft community space with a view of the 
park across on Waumbeck St. This Community space will be available for the residents as well as 
the people of the community. 
•ELIMINATE BLIGHT - Over the years the building and land of the lots has deteriorated, the land 
itself is becoming uneven. This Project will clean up this parcel and create a visually aesthetic 
building and landscape that will complement the surrounding residential community. 
•JOB CREATION - This Project will create temporary construction and labor jobs during the 
development process. It will also create permanent jobs in the form of property management of the 
building and grounds. 
 
 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The Nehemiah Development Project is a transformative endeavor aimed at revitalizing a vacant 
building and neighboring vacant lot in the Dorchester neighborhood by providing much needed 
decent, safe, and affordable family housing. 

 
Since purchasing the property in 1989, Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church has envisioned 
the future development of this property. With the many development efforts taking place in 
the city, the church is looking to respond to the call of the community to develop this site. To 
do that, the church sought an experienced development partner to help move this project 
forward and make the vision of the church and community a reality. The Nehemiah 
Development Project is a collaboration and joint venture between two dedicated entities: 
Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church; Nehemiah Committee and Nuestra Comunidad 
Development Corporation. Together, we are committed to enhancing the quality of life for the 
Dorchester community. 
 
The team has considered several development scenarios include full and partial 
homeownership and have found the proposed program of 100% affordable, family rental 
described below to be the most feasible.

The proposed project will occupy two adjacent lots owned by Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist 
Church that surround the church. These lots include a vacant structure at 157 Humboldt 
Avenue that has been unused for over three decades and vacant land at 64 Waumbeck Street. 
The project site sits across the street from an active playground and is north of Boston’s 
Franklin Park. The William Munroe Trotter Elementary School is one block south of the 
development and Boston’s Latin Academy is two blocks away from the development. Other 
neighborhood amenities include convenience stores, hair and barbershops, locally owned take 
out restaurants, churches, and public transportation. There are MBTA bus stops just outside the 
proposed building that will transport commuters to and from the MBTA’s Orange Line’s Jackson 
Station and Ruggles Station via Nubian Square. 
 
 
2.3 Development Context 
 

The Nehemiah Development Project consists of a newly constructed, 4-story, L-shaped building 
that will provide 26 affordable, family rental units with a mix of 8 one-bedrooms, 14 two-
bedrooms and 4 three-bedroom units. The building will also include an elevator, laundry room, 
bike storage, 6 off-street parking spots, and 2,000 sq. ft. of community space for resident and 
community use. 
 
 
2.4 Urban Design Approach – Building Program, Massing and Materials 
 
For the design and materials, we will be using the guidance of Section 5-39 #17: New residential 
construction shall respect certain standards of scale in order to maintain the subdistrict's 
special qualities. Overall building height and massing, relationships of primary Buildings to 
secondary Buildings, and landscape elements all shall be consistent with the surrounding 
architecture and environment. 
 
2.5 Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
Access to the site by vehicle will be off of Humboldt Avenue utilizing the current existing curb cut from 
the existing driveway. This driveway would lead to the parking lot which will hold 6 parking spots

PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
 
The proposed Project at 15 Supertest Street represents an exciting evolution of the 2019 PDA Master Plan, moving 
forward the “North Block” of the 20 +/- acre Hood Park campus in the West Rutherford area of the Charlestown 
neighborhood of Boston, with an anchor retail component and added affordable, family-sized residential housing. 
The original 15 Supertest building, as approved in the 2019 Master Plan, was a 12,000 square foot, one level, “general” 
retail building with a green roof, immediately adjacent to the proposed “Hood Green” one-acre community open space, 
bounded by Supertest Street on the south, Rutherford Avenue to the east, and a proposed community multi-use 
pedestrian and bicycle path along the northern Hood Park property boundary, adjacent to the former freight rail line and 
D Street. The concept anticipated a recon<gured Rutherford Avenue with fewer vehicle lanes, signalized crossings at D 
Street / Mishawum Street and Hood Park Drive, and a reduced volume and speed of traf<c, as part of a network of 
connected intersections in lieu of the current Sullivan Square rotary condition. 
Today, the 15 Supertest Project is proposed as a more robust and community-focused program, addressing two high-
priority neighborhood needs: 1) a +/- 23,000 sf ground floor retail space for a grocery store; and 2) an eighteen (18) 
unit housing program of two, three, and four bedroom affordable, family-sized, rental units. Both uses will be supported 
by a below grade structured parking level with approximately +/- 69 parking spaces, shared between residential and 
retail uses based on differing hours of need. The retail tenant will have a primary entrance fronting on Rutherford 
Avenue, providing high visibility, easy access, and ultimately, when recon<gured, a direct signalized pedestrian crossing 
at the corner of the site, providing strong pedestrian access to the grocery store for residents in the northern half of the 
Charlestown neighborhood, including those residents in the Mishawum Park and General Warren Senior Housing units. 
The residential program will have a vestibule and entrance on Supertest Street, providing suf<cient separation from both 
the retail activity and the traf<c on Rutherford Avenue, providing a strong and separate identity for the residents. The 
residential units will be developed as “off-site” affordable IDP housing from the 25 Supertest proposed hotel / residential 
tower being concurrently but separately proposed and permitted. The units will comply with all Mayor’s Of<ce of 
Housing standards and requirements for two-, three-, and four-bedroom family rental units, with AMI values to be 
reviewed with the community and City of Boston as part of the permitting review process. 
The Project is located within the Coastal Flood Resiliency Overlay District and is designed with <nish floor elevations 
elevated well above the existing Rutherford Avenue elevation, at 18’-0” FFE for the retail program and 19’-0” FFE for the 
residential vestibule. The project will incorporate dry floodproo<ng to an elevation of 20’-6” FFE to meet the 
requirements for this part of the city, given the proximity to the Mystic River. The parking access will be further elevated 
to ensure flood water does not enter down into the below-grade parking level.

In addition to the above noted resiliency design features, the project is targeting LEED Gold and the residential portion is 
proposed as Passive House compliant, and all-electric. Given the need for natural gas service to support the cooking 
and food preparation involved in groceries, the project will include approximately 8,000 square feet of rooftop solar 
panels, on the grocery roof, to offset the mixed-fuel use within the retail area of the project. 
P. 7
The Project will be designed to be fully accessible and all program and use areas will meet ADA / MAAB requirements. 
Further, the project will convert a driveway to surface parking into the formal “Supertest Street” with a complete street 
design and installation including sidewalks, planting zones, shared travel lanes, and new accessible curb cuts and 
sidewalk transitions along Rutherford Avenue. Finally, the project will also include indoor and outdoor café seating areas 
to encourage activation and community use along the retail storefront area, continuing the evolution from former 
industrial land to an active, seven-day-a-week live, work, play neighborhood.

Community Benets 
 
The proposed 15 Supertest Project, as one of the individual Projects anticipated by the 2019 Master 
Plan approval, continues Hood Park’s commitment to the Community Benets program outlined and 
dened by the Amended and Restated Planned Development Area Master Plan for Planned 
Development Area No. 51 and its associated Cooperation Agreement. The Community Benets dened 
in the approved PDA documentation include community nancial resources, transportation nancial 
and infrastructure commitments, education and activation commitments, and community open space 
commitments. Of the various specic benets outlined within the approved Master Plan PDA 
documents, the following is specically noted as being related to the 15 Supertest Project: 
1) Hood Park will make a nancial contribution of $2.00 per square foot for the retail and hotel 
gross floor area square footage (“GFA SF”)…to support public realm improvements and 
neighborhood based initiatives in Charlestown, such as non-prot youth / teen education and 
recreation programs. The increase of retail square footage at 15 Supertest from 12,000 GFA SF 
to 24,500 GFA SF will increase the nancial contribution by $25,000. 
2) The Applicant shall fully fund and install a new Bluebikes or other bicycle sharing system to be 
located on or around the Hood Park campus which shall be operational or fully funded prior to 
or upon issuance by ISD of the Certicate of Occupancy for the Project. 
 
In addition to these specically relevant sections of the Master Plan PDA Community Benets package, 
the 15 Supertest Project will provide the following associated Benets: 
• The Project continues the transformation of the former Hood Dairy plant from an obsolete 
industrial plant to a state-of-the-art 21st century mixed-use development. 
• The signicant landscaping program will provide the neighborhood with a new outdoor 
softscape area which will improve the water quality and reduce runoff in and around the Site by 
replacing the current expanses of asphalt on the Site with new pervious areas. 
• The proposed uses of the Development will result in a reduction in trafc impacts (i.e., noise, 
road infrastructure damages, air quality) by the elimination of uses relying upon trucks and

The proposed 15 Supertest Project is well positioned within the Hood Park property for the proposed 
uses. The proposed Project is in the northeast corner of the Hood property. It replaces a surface level 
parking lot rendered unnecessary by the development of 100 Hood Park Drive structured parking. 
The Project is bounded by Supertest Street on the south and Rutherford Avenue on the east, with 
direct access for traf/c from Rutherford Avenue southbound lanes to Supertest Street and immediately 
into the parking garage entrance at the southwest corner of the structure. The current “U-Turn” 
condition between Mishawum and D Streets allows for easy access for northbound Rutherford traf/c to 
access the site on the same pathway until the signalized intersection is developed as part of the 
Rutherford Avenue recon/guration project. 
The Project’s creation of Supertest Street connecting Rutherford Avenue and the interim Stack Street 
con/guration will formalize the current parking lot drive lane condition and create a safer and more 
well-de/ned transportation access condition with formal sidewalks, curbs and street lighting conditions. 
This will improve pedestrian and bicycle safety along 500 Rutherford North where the current loading 
and trash compactor equipment is located, and will remain, opposite the proposed loading and trash 
compactor equipment for the new 15 Supertest building. Loading, and trash service for the new grocer 
will be off Supertest, set back from the sidewalk and fully enclosed and screened with an overhead 
door, concealing loading and service vehicles during operations. 
Supertest Street has been redesigned, from the former Master Plan layout plans, to narrow the ROW by 
eliminating separated bike lanes in favor of shared drive and bike lanes and eliminating parallel parking 
on the south side of Supertest. This reduction in width will allow for 15 Supertest to accommodate the 
dimensional requirements for a market standard Urban Grocery tenant. Given the robust bicycle 
infrastructure on Hood Park Drive and the proposed /fteen (15) foot multi-use bicycle and pedestrian 
path immediately adjacent to 15 Supertest, on the north boundary of the Hood Parcel, from Rutherford 
Avenue to Spice Street, the reduced bike infrastructure dimension on Supertest will have no negative 
impact on accessibility to the various campus facilities and eliminate potentially unsafe crossings of 
loading and parking garage access points by encouraging use of the de/ned path and separated lanes

The above noted multi-use path will include two (2) /ve foot bicycle lanes with a parallel adjacent /ve

the BPDA) conducted a substantial community process as part of review and approval of PLAN: 
Charlestown rezoning effort. The approved PLAN: Charlestown master plan con7rmed the Hood Park 
master plan dimensional and height conditions for additional parcels along the entire west side of 
Rutherford Avenue and increased the FAR density from Hood’s approved 2.0 to a more standard 3.0 
along the same corridor. 
Both processes noted above involve substantial public review and community engagement and have 
educated the neighborhood on planning principals, zoning obligations, and the statutory approval 
process for PDAs, Development Plans and Article 80 Large and Small project review efforts. 
As such, and given the general consistency with the Hood Park Master Plan PDA, and compliance with 
all aspects of the PLAN: Charlestown rezoning effort, the Applicant anticipates a robust and supported 
public review process for the 15 Supertest Project. As an Article 80 Small Project 15 Supertest is 
subject to less agency review than prior Hood developments going through Article 80 Large Project 
review, speci7cally noting the lack of jurisdiction for BCDC review. However, as a Development Plan 
within the Hood PDA and given the need for amendment of the PDA Master Plan to accommodate the 
increased retail area and added residential component, the 15 Supertest Project review process will 
include requirements for IAG review and approval, a Public Meeting for both the Development Plan and 
Master Plan PDA Amendments, a Planning Department Board vote and Zoning Commission review and 
approval of the Development Plan and Master Plan PDA Amendments, making for a robust community 
engagement opportunity.
