COASTAL FLOOD RESILIENCY OVERLAY DISTRICT (CFROD) 
COMPLIANCE AND RESILIENCY NARRATIVE 
 
The Hood Park Master Plan PDA includes a commitment to a phased resiliency solution whereby each 
Development Plan will include site plan details and designs that allow for elevating 1nished grade 
above the FEMA 2070 100-year Flood Elevation and Coastal Storm Flood Elevation levels for the West 
Rutherford portion of Charlestown. 
The current topography of Charlestown allows for storm surge and coastal flooding to inundate the low 
lying areas at the northern end of Charlestown through the Sullivan Square area via the low banks 
along the Mystic River channel at Ryan Playground, Schrafts parcels, and the MBTA repair facility on 
the north side of the Alford Street Bridge. Rising coastal waters can surge through this low area, at the 
intersection of Bunker Hill Street, Main Street, and Rutherford Avenue and move into Hood Park along 
the Rutherford Avenue corridor, which is currently at BCB Elevation 16.0 feet. 
The current proposed remediation for this issue involves elevating Ryan Playground and the Flatley 
redevelopment parcels around Schrafts to restrict water flow at the shore line. There are gaps in this 
solution and the full implementation may be decades in the future. A reasonable alternative with a 
speci1c, consolidated timeline would be to elevate Rutherford Avenue as part of the recon1guration of 
that roadway, which would provide a comprehensive solution for the West Rutherford neighborhood. 
However, for economic reasons this comprehensive solution is not incorporated into the current design 
plans for Rutherford Avenue and Sullivan Square. 
Absent those options, Hood Park has committed to localize flood resiliency by developing each project 
with a site plan which requires elevating 1nished grade at the perimeter of existing building and new 
buildings to meet the CFROD requirements with base elevation values of 20.5 feet for all commercial 
and residential structures built on campus. Further, storm water management practices are being 
implemented as the site is developed to recharge storm water and provide detention and retention 
swales and basins to improve coastal flood and storm resiliency capacity at Hood Park. 
Unfortunately, as a result of the decision to leave Rutherford Avenue at its current low elevation of 16.0 
feet to 16.5 feet BCB, the 15 Supertest Project will be unable to achieve the desired goal of setting

A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Hood Park Grocer Building 
Sustainability Development / High Performance Green Buildings Narrative 
 
Summary 
This project will be designed with consideration to energy efficiency, water conservation, waste 
management, environmental stewardship, and healthy indoor environment for occupants. To comply with 
Article 37 of the Boston Zoning Code, the project shall demonstrate that it is able to meet LEED (Leadership 
in Energy and Environmental Design) certification. 
The following is a detailed summary of the LEED compliance strategy of the project, demonstrating the 
LEED v4 BD+C categories and credits that are expected to be met through the integration of a range of 
sustainable features planned for the building and site. A LEED Scorecard is attached at the end of this 
summary. Based on this strategy, the project expects to achieve a total of 63 points, which would meet 
LEED Gold level certification. 
Category: Integrative Process (1 point) 
The project will perform simple box energy modeling as well as water balance calculations early in the 
project in order to analyze the design, assess energy and water reduction strategies, and inform 
sustainable design choices. This preliminary analysis will earn the project 1 point for this credit and 
category. 
Category: Location & Transportation (14 points) 
LTc1 Sensitive Land Protection. The project site is not located on prime farmland or a greenfield site. By 
locating the project on a previously developed site, 1 point for this credit is earned. 
LTc2 High Priority Site. The project anticipates soil contaminants that will require remediation. By 
identifying any soil contaminants present on site and remediating contamination to the local standard, the 
project will earn 2 points for this credit. 
LTc3 Surrounding Density and Diverse Uses. The project will pursue the LEED v4.1 version of this credit, 
under which points are earned by the Walk Score of the project location. Based on a Walk Score of 89 for 
the project site, the project earns 4 points for this credit. 
LTc4 Access to Quality Transit. The project is located within 0.25 mile of the Sullivan Square MTBA subway 
station, which also serves the 89, 90, 91, 92, and 93 bus lines. The number of public transit rides available 
through these public transit options earns the project 5 points for this credit. 
LTc6 Reduced Parking Footprint. The project is anticipated to include 53 parking spaces, which is a 37.6% 
reduction from the 85 spaces required by the ITE Standard. By reducing parking over 30% compared to the 
ITE Standard, the project earns 1 point. 
P. 73

LTc7 Green Vehicles. By providing. The project will pursue the LEED v4.1 version of this credit, under which 
the project is required to provide electric vehicle charging for 5% of total parking spaces. By providing 3 
electric vehicle chargers in the parking area, the project will earn 1 point for this credit. 
Category: Sustainable Sites (8 points) 
SSp1 Construction Activity Pollution Prevention. An Erosion & Sedimentation Control (ESC) Plan will be 
developed and implemented during demolition and construction to ensure that the construction activities 
comply with all applicable measures outlined in the 2012 EPA Construction General Permit and do not 
result in air or water impacts on the surrounding area. 
SSc1 Site Assessment. The project will conduct a site survey and analyze the potential design impacts of 
the typography, hydrology, climate, vegetation, soils, human use and human health impacts of the site. The 
project will complete a Site Assessment Worksheet documenting how these impacts have shaped the 
project design to earn 1 point for this credit. 
SSc2 Protect or Restore Habitat. The project will include landscaping on site, and will use native/adapted 
vegetation. The project will pursue the LEED v4.1 version of this credit, which requires the landscaping area 
to constitute a minimum 15% of the project site to earn 1 point. If the landscaping area is insufficient to 
meet this requirement, the project will provide a donation to a land trust equal to $0.20 per square foot of 
site area. 
SSc4 Rainwater Management. The project is anticipated to manage 1.25” of stormwater on site through 
groundwater recharge in order to meet local building requirements. By doing so, the project will manage the 
90th percentile of rainfall events on site, which earns 3 points for this credit. 
SSc5 Heat Island Reduction. The project will use high albedo (light colored) roof and paving materials. 
Doing so will earn 2 points for this credit. 
SSc6 Light Pollution Reduction. The project will design exterior lighting to minimize uplighting, and will 
select exterior and site light fixtures which minimize backlight, uplight and glare ratings in order to meet the 
BUG lighting limits for Lighting Zone 3. This will earn 1 point for this credit. 
Category: Water Efficiency (6 points) 
SSp1 / SSc1 Outdoor Water Use Reduction. The project will not include any permanent irrigation beyond 
the initial plant establishment. Plants that are drought tolerant and/or water efficient will be selected for 
the landscaping design. This meets the prerequisite and will earn 2 points for the credit. 
SSp2 / SSc2 Indoor Water Use Reduction. The project will select water efficient plumbing fixtures which will 
result in a 35% water use reduction compared to a baseline calculated using the EPAct 1992 flow rates. 
Fixtures will be Water Sense labeled. In addition, plumbing and HVAC equipment and appliances will meet 
the LEED requirements for efficiency and will not include once-through cooling. This will meet the 
prerequisite and earn 3 points for the credit. 
Water Metering. The project will install water submeters to monitor water usage for at least 2 end uses. This 
will earn 1 point for the credit. 
P. 74

Category: Energy & Atmosphere (11 points) 
EAp1 Fundamental Commissioning. Third party commissioning services will be contracted to review design 
and oversee the installation, startup and testing of MEP systems during construction. 
EAp2 / EAc1 Minimum/Optimize Energy Performance. The project will be designed to maximize energy 
efficiency and will select high performance envelope, lighting fixtures and HVAC systems. The project will 
perform energy modeling analysis of the building in order to compare energy performance to the ASHRAE 
90.1-2010 Appendix G baseline. The project anticipates exceeding the 10% energy cost reduction and 
earning 4 points for the credit. 
EAp3 / EAc3 Building Level Energy Metering / Advanced Energy Metering. The project will have a whole 
building meter for each energy source in order to determine and track whole building usage. In addition, the 
project will submeter all energy end uses which constitute 10% or more of the total usage. This will earn 1 
point for the credit. 
EAc5 Renewable Energy. The project is expected to install photovoltaic panels on the roof. It is anticipated 
that this system will offset at least 1% of the annual energy usage which will earn 1 point for this credit. If 
the capacity of the system is insufficient to achieve this threshold, the project will pursue the LEED v4.1 
version of the credit and purchase energy offsets from an off-site system equivalent to 35% of the building 
annual energy usage. 
Green Power. The project will contract for renewable energy sources or purchase energy offsets for a 
minimum of 50% of the annual project usage, which will earn 1 point for this credit. 
Category: Materials & Resources (6 points) 
MRp1 Storage & Collection of Recyclables. The project will include a dedicated and accessible space for 
the collection and storage of recyclables, including batteries and e-waste, that is adequately sized to meet 
the needs of the building. 
MRp2 Construction & Demolition Waste Management Planning. The project will develop and implement a 
Demolition & Construction Waste Management Plan for the management of construction waste. Waste will 
be tracked throughout demolition and construction. 
MRc1 Building Lifecycle Impact Reduction. The project will perform building lifecycle analysis and prioritize 
the selection of design and materials for the envelope and structure of the building to minimize greenhouse 
gas emissions. This is anticipated to earn 2 points for the credit. 
MRc2 Environmental Product Declarations. The project will select building materials with Environmental 
Product Declarations for at least 20 products, which will earn 1 point for this credit. 
MRc4 Material Ingredients. The project will select building materials with the required disclosure 
documentation (such as HPDs, Declare labeling or Cradle to Cradle certification) for at least 20 products, 
which will earn 1 point for this credit. 
P. 75

MRc5 Construction & Demolition Waste Management. The project will target diverting a minimum of 75% of 
construction and demolition waste through on site separation and recycling. Requirements will be 
included in specifications and in the Construction Waste Management Plan. This will earn 2 points for this 
credit. 
Category: Indoor Environmental Quality (9 points) 
IEQp1 Minimum IAQ Performance. The project will design ventilation systems to comply with ASHRAE 62.1-
2010 requirements. Airflow monitors will be installed to verify ventilation rates are provided as designed. 
IEQp2 Environmental Tobacco Smoke Control. The project building will prohibit smoking in the grocery 
store and within 25 feet of the building. If smoking is not specifically prohibited in the residential units, the 
project will perform blower door testing to confirm air sealing i 
IEQc1 Enhanced IEQ Strategies. The project will include entryway systems at all regularly used entrances 
to prevent contaminants from entering the building. All spaces used for the storage and use of chemicals 
will have exhaust to create negative pressurization, deck to deck partitions and self-closing doors. The 
HVAC system will include MERV 13 filtration. The project will either achieve 30% increased ventilation 
beyond the ASHRAE 62.1-2010 requirements or install CO2 sensors in densely occupied spaces. These 
measures will achieve 2 points for this credit. 
IEQc2 Low Emitting Materials. The project will select low-VOC products for all products in the following 
categories: flooring, ceilings, adhesives & sealants, paints & coatings, and insulation. Requirements will be 
included in specifications. This will achieve 3 points for this credit. 
IEQc3 Construction IAQ Management Plan. The project will develop and implement a Construction IAQ 
Management Plan for the construction phase of the project to mitigate and control air contaminants 
generated by the construction process. Measures will be maintained monthly and photographed for record. 
This will earn 1 point for this credit. 
IEQc4 Indoor Air Quality Assessment. The project will conduct air testing after the installation of finishes 
and prior to occupancy to verify air quality. This will earn 1 point for this credit. 
IEQc9 Acoustic Performance. The project will be designed with consideration for the acoustic separation of 
spaces, particularly between the grocery store and residential portions of the building. HVAC background 
noise and sound transmission will be addressed. It is anticipated that 1 point for this credit will be earned. 
Category: Innovation (5 points) 
IDc1.1 Exemplary Performance. The project anticipates exceeding the requirements of credit MRc2 
Environmental Product Declarations. By sourcing 40 products with the required EPD disclosure 
documentation, the project will achieve 1 point for this credit. 
IDc1.2 Innovation. The project lighting design will include LED lighting, which will minimize the mercury 
content of connected lighting fixtures. Based on the lighting design, the project anticipates meeting 1 point 
for the Purchasing-Lamps innovation credit. 
P. 76

IDc1.3 Innovation. The project site design will promote pedestrian access. The project anticipates having 
the pedestrian pathways, building elevations and walkability of the site required to meet the Walkable 
Project Site innovation credit, worth 1 point. 
IDc1.4 Innovation. The project will consider the Green Building Education innovation credit, which will 
require incorporating signage on the project to inform occupants and visitors of the sustainability features 
of the building, and creating a case study of the project to inform industry peers of the methods and 
success of the project. 
IDc2 LEED Accredited Professional. The sustainability consultant retained for this project is a LEED AP 
BD+C, which earns 1 point for this credit.

SUBJECT: 
Hood Park – 15 Supertest Street 
 
The Hood Park Master Plan PDA that was approved in 2019 envisioned a 12,000 square foot retail 
building at 15 Supertest Street. As part of the Small Project Review Applications (SPRA), 15 
Supertest Street is now proposed to consist of a 23,130 square foot grocery store and 18 residential 
units. 
Howard Stein Hudson has reviewed the modifications and investigated the transportation impacts of 
the proposed changes. These modifications include parking and loading accommodations, 
dimensional changes to Supertest Street and the shared use path along the northern edge of the 
property, and a trip generation comparison. 
15 Supertest Street 
The residential lobby will be located with pedestrian access from Supertest Street. As part of the 
proposed changes to this site, below grade parking will now be included with the ramp located along 
Supertest Street. The one level below grade parking will consist of approximately 83 parking spaces. 
Adjacent to the garage ramp will be the off-street grocery loading area. 
The 15 Supertest Street site will also include bike parking in conformance with the BTD Bike 
Parking Guidelines. This will include 26 private secured and covered bike parking spaces for 
residents (18 spaces) and employees (8 spaces). In addition, the site will also include 5 visitor bike 
racks for public use. 
PDA Site Layout 
Due to the change in uses, the Master Plan PDA site plan has been slightly modified. Four parallel 
parking spaces are proposed to be located on the north side of Supertest Street between the 
residential lobby and grocery store entrance. These spaces can be used for pickup drop off activity, 
as well move-in and move-out operations for the residential units. 
In order to facilitate a wider open space (known as Hood Green) between 15 Supertest Street and the 
future 25 Supertest Street (hotel and residential building), the unprotected five foot wide bike lanes 
on Supertest Street in the Master Plan PDA have been removed. Similarly, the 20 foot wide shared 
use path along the northern edge of the Hood Park site has been narrowed from 20 feet to 15 feet

Trip Generation Comparison 
For the purpose of evaluating the transportation impacts of the proposed modification, the trip 
generation estimates for both the approved Master Plan PDA and proposed building programs were 
calculated. To estimate the number of trips expected to be generated by all of the different uses 
within Hood Park (both existing and future), data published by the Institute of Transportation 
Engineers (ITE) in the Trip Generation Manual (11th Edition, 2021) were used. Based on the 
building program of the entire Project, the following Land Use Codes (LUC) were utilized: 
 
LUC 221 (Multifamily Housing Mid-Rise); 
 
LUC 310 (Hotel); 
 
LUC 710 (General Office Building); 
 
LUC 820 (Shopping Center); and 
 
LUC 850 (Supermarket). 
The ITE trip generation rates produce vehicle trip estimates, which are then converted to person 
trips using vehicle occupancy rates (VOR) based on the 2022 National Household Travel Survey data 
and other local data. Using travel mode split information for this area of Boston provided by the 
Boston Transportation Department (BTD), the total person trips are then allocated to vehicle, 
transit, and walk/bicycle trips. 
It is important to note, the trip generation totals shown below include trips that are already 
occurring and visiting Hood Park. This comparison is NOT an estimate of additional future trips 
expected, but a comparison of the total transportation activity to Hood Park. 
The walk/bike mode share for this area is estimated to be 15% for residential, hotel, and office land 
uses; 40% for retail uses, and 35% for supermarket uses. The transit mode share for this area is 
estimated to be 35% for residential, hotel, and office land uses; 40% for retail uses, and 15% for 
supermarket uses. The vehicle mode share for this area is estimated to be 50% for residential, hotel, 
office and supermarket land uses, and 20% for retail uses. Table 1 shows a comparison of the trip 
generation for the currently approved program and the proposed program for each of the mode

streetscape and improve the pedestrian experience. This project includes a 
total of eighteen parking spaces, potential for a permanent public bike parking 
facility, and approximately fifty bike parking spots. The Proposed Project will 
completely revitalize these lots and will serve to help invigorate this section of 
Roxbury, which has been underdeveloped.

1.8 Affordable Housing 
 
The Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) was created to ensure access to 
affordable housing within the City of Boston. The IDP requires the housing 
developments with ten or more proposed units and requiring zoning relief are 
subject to the creation of affordable housing opportunities. These opportunities 
are usually satisfied through the creation of on-site affordable units or monetary 
contributions to the Inclusionary Development Policy Fund. Typically, projects 
are required to contribute a minimum of thirteen percent of the Project’s units at 
an affordable level. The IDP is continuing to evolve to increase the overall level 
of affordability within Boston, but as currently constituted, this Project would 
create at least a minimum of five affordable units.

The surrounding sites along Blue Hill Ave contain a variety of three- and four-story 
buildings housing three-family dwellings, multi-family dwellings, and commercial 
uses. The property at 197 Blue Hill Ave abuts a parcel to the rear owned by 
Boston Edison Company. Other abutting properties along Southwood Street 
and Edgewood Street contain two and three family dwellings as well as condo 
buildings. The building on the corner of Edgewood Street and Blue Hill Ave, 
located at 233 Blue Hill Ave, contains a large four-story, mixed-use building. 
Finally, the building directly across the street from 197 Blue Hill Ave contains a 
four-story, mixed-use building. 
The proposed multi-family residential project will not alter the character of this 
neighborhood and will blend in with some of the recent developments and 
existing housing and commercial stock along this major thoroughfare. The 
development will play a role in this neighborhood’s ongoing transformation and 
development. This project will continue to add high-density residential housing 
in former commercial locations around this area of Boston, providing some 
much-needed affordable housing. Additionally, the lots close proximity to 
numerous public transportation opportunities and the proposed permanent 
Bluebike station will help further the City’s initiative to reduce reliance on private 
motor vehicles and encourage alternative modes of transportation. 
 
3.2 Urban Design Concept 
 
This project is unique in that it owns frontage along three streets in a busy mixed-
use area. Although Blue Hill Ave will be the front facing predominant street, the 

29 | P a g e 
191-203 Blue Hill Ave – Small Project Review Application 
 
additional frontage along Southwood Street and Edgewood allows for nearly 
every unit of the Proposed Project to have unobstructed views and access to 
sunlight. The buildings have been designed to fit within the context of the newly 
developed three- and four-story buildings in the surrounding area. Special 
attention was paid to enlivening the streetscape and improving the pedestrian 
experience along Blue Hill Ave, Southwood Street and Edgewood Street. 
Specifically, plantings and individualized unit entries work to make the structures 
feel more inviting and residential in nature. The Proposed Project also provides a 
variety of transportation options including ample parking, bike parking, public 
bike use via the Bluebike Station and access to multiple modes of public 
transportation, making it convenient for commuting professionals. Along with the 
access to transportation, this Project provides two distinct open spaces for 
residents to gather in and make use of. 
 
3.3 Landscape Plan 
 
The Proponent is proposing a project that incorporates new and improved open 
space features. Currently, the lots contain the existing structure, and the 
remainder of the site is predominantly paved and serves as parking lots. The 
Development Team is working on landscape plan which includes sidewalk 
improvements, street trees, lawn areas, and opportunities for future residents to 
congregate. Private decks are also being proposed to allow for future residents 
to take full advantage of usable outdoor living space. The Proponent is also 
proposing to maintain as many of the existing trees on the property as possible 
to preserve the existing tree canopy as well as provide screening and buffering 
to abutting properties. 
 
3.4 Building Design 
 
The proposed project is the redevelopment of a former church use and 
associated parking. The proposed design features three residential buildings on 
the two lots totaling 36 units. The sites provide parking, accessed via one curb 
cut along Southwood Street and a separate curb cut from Edgewood Street. 
 
The three buildings are 4-stories each. Building A, located at 191-197 Blue Hill 
Ave is shaped as fairly symmetrical rectangle with predominate frontage on 
Blue Hill Ave. Building B is also rectangular in shape but is perpendicular to the 
building at 191-197 Blue Hill Ave and has a small presence on Blue Hill Ave and 
significant frontage and access from Southwood Street. The building at 2-4 

30 | P a g e 
191-203 Blue Hill Ave – Small Project Review Application 
 
Edgewood Street, has a more distinct shape and works with curve of Edgewood 
Street and the property. This building fronts on Edgewood Street and its rear 
abuts the rear of the proposed building at 70-74 Southwood. 
 
The buildings are set back from the sidewalks to provide additional space for 
wider sidewalks or additional landscaping and shade. 
 
The design focuses on addressing residential scale in this multifamily 
development. Materials are used to break up the massing of the building and 
present the buildings in more of a residential scale. Balconies are provided in the 
Blue Hill Ave building to provide some private outdoor space but they have 
been strategically placed so as not to interrupt the façade along Blue Hill Ave. 
The first floor features direct access to a number of units to help enliven the 
streetscape. 
 
3.5 Materials and Finishes 
 
The proposed exterior materials are hardiplank clap board, brick veneer, and 
hardiplank panels. The windows and aluminum/clad wood and French doors 
are proposed at the entries for a welcoming feel. The materials provide a 
combination of an inviting feel and durability. The design is reflective of some of 
the similarly sized projects and buildings in the area and serves to blend the new 
residential use with the prior commercial building and surrounding properties. 
 
3.6 Shadow Study 
 
A shadow study was conducted to demonstrate the impact of the proposed 
development to the abutters and surrounding properties. The study was 
conducted at 9 AM, 12 PM, and 3 PM during the Spring, Summer, and Winter. 
The study was completed with three different conditions. The first shows the 
proposed structures with the existing surrounding structures to reflect actual 
future conditions. The second shows only the proposed buildings without the 
abutting structures to show which specific shadows are cast but the new 
structures, and the third shows the existing conditions without the newly 
proposed structures. For the full Shadow Study please see Appendix D.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in Boston’s built 
environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, rather than after a design is 
completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment 
which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to provide specific 
detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout Boston's built 
environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing. 
 
Accessibility Analysis Information Sources: 
 
1.

https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/download?fid=6623&nid=3496

Massachusetts State Building Code 780 CMR 
http://www.mass.gov/eopss/consumer-prot-and-bus-lic/license-type/csl/building-codebbrs.html 
5. 
Massachusetts Office of Disability – Disabled Parking Regulations 
http://www.mass.gov/anf/docs/mod/hp-parking-regulations-summary-mod.pdf

MBTA Fixed Route Accessible Transit Stations 
http://www.mbta.com/riding_the_t/accessible_services/

12. LEED – Pilot Credits for Social Equity and Inclusion 
 https://www.usgbc.org/articles/social-equity-pilot-credits-added-leed-nd-and-leed-om 
 
Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth by MAAB 521 
CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth by MAAB 521 
CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the specific functional 
needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary requirements set 
forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in the City. For more 
information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more information visit: 
https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community benefits, particularly for 
persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors openings, hallways, 
bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Dear Chief Shen: 
 
 
On behalf of my client, Glenshane Properties, it is my pleasure to submit this application 
for Small Project Review pursuant to Article 80, Section 80E, of the Boston Zoning Code, for the 
1954 Commonwealth Avenue historic preservation and development of a new multi-family 
residential project in Brighton. 
 
The proposed project is to consist of 26 new residential units, primarily market rate, with 
4 affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy. The project site 
comprises 13,364 square feet at 1954 Commonwealth Avenue in the Brighton neighborhood, and 
is currently occupied a 2 ½ story three-family unoccupied house. The proposed project is bounded

Proposed Project Summary 
 
2.1 Project Identification 
 
Glenshane Properties (“the Proponent”), submit this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”) 
to initiate review by the Boston Redevelopment Authority, d/b/a Boston Planning & 
Development Agency (the “BPDA”) under the provisions of Article 80E of the Boston Zoning 
Code (the “Code”) for the historic preservation and development of a new multi-family 
residential project (the “Project”) located at 1954 Commonwealth Avenue in the Brighton 
neighborhood of the City of Boston. 
 
This SPRA provides comprehensive analysis of the relevant features and impacts of the Project 
that are subject to Small Project Review. This Project is located in a Conservation Protection 
Subdistrict and a Greenbelt Protection Overlay District on a lot containing less than one (1) acre 
of land. Consequently, the Project is subject to the Site Plan Component of Small Project Review 
pursuant to Sections 80E-2(2) and 80E-4(2) of Article 80 of the Code. Furthermore, as detailed 
below, the Aberdeen Architectural Conservation District Commission has jurisdiction over the 
Design Review for this Project and has approved its design. Thus, the Design Review component

of Small Project Review does not apply even though the Project otherwise concerns a net 
increase of 15 or more dwelling units as part of a Project not subject to Large Project Review. 
See Code Art. 80 sec. 80E-2(1) (Design Component of Small Project Review “shall not apply to 
any Proposed Project that is subject to the jurisdiction of the Boston Landmarks Commission or 
any other architectural board of commission having design review authority . . .”). This SPRA 
informs reviewing agencies and the community about the Project, its potential impacts, and the

2.2 Project Site and Surroundings 
 
The Project site is located at 1954 Commonwealth Avenue (Parcel ID: 2102470000) on a parcel 
of land consisting of approximately 13,364 total square feet (0.31 acres) (the “Site”). The Site is 
within the Aberdeen Architectural Conservation District (“District”) and a Greenbelt Protection 
Overlay District. The Site’s current use is an unoccupied, 2 1/2 story three-family house 
(“Historic Residence”). The house was constructed in approximately 1910 and is one of the few 
extant examples of a Mission Style home in the District. Mission Style architecture became 
popular in various areas of the City of Boston, including Brighton, between 1895 and the 1920s. 
This style’s popularity may be due to the design of the California Building at the City of 
Chicago’s Columbian Exposition in 1893. Characteristic of the Mission Style design are stucco 
covered walls, wide pyramidal red terra cotta tile roofs, arched openings, and curvilinear roof 
gables. The house at 1954 Commonwealth Avenue—designed by Boston architect Frank H. 
Dillaby and built for Erastus C. Gaffield—is an example of the Mission Style, having stucco 
parged, curvilinear treatment of the entrance porch’s pediment, and terra cotta title roofing. 
 
The Site is zoned MFR-2, multifamily residential, but is subject to a variance from the City’s 
Board of Appeal which currently permits the change in occupancy from a 3-family dwelling to a 
16-unit dwelling with the erection of a 6-story new building connected to the existing structure 
including one (1) level below-grade parking beneath the rear building. The current Project 
reflects a project change from the existing variance and conditional use permit. 
 
The Site is bounded by Commonwealth Avenue to the North, a 5 to 6 story multifamily masonry 
residential building to the East, the 6-story Parklake Apartments masonry building to the West 
(containing a 150 unit mix of studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom apartments), and the 
Chestnut Hill Reservation and Reservoir to the South. Across Commonwealth Avenue from the 
Site are 6-story+ masonry apartment buildings. At the Site’s western lot line, among the hedges 
in that location, are side-by-side 6” dia. and 10” dia. maple trees, while an unplanned, dual 
trunked 8” dia. oak tree has grown to obscure a street view of the western side of the Historic 
Residence’s front entrance. South the Site on Reservation land, a 46” dia. oak tree is about 5’ 
from the rear lot line, a 24” dia. oak tree is about 14’ away, and a 12” dia. oak is about 18’ 
distant. Small-stemmed shrubs are at the rear, front and side of the Site.

2.3 Project Description and Design 
 
The Proponent proposes to develop a 26-unit multi-family residential development by 
relocating closer to Commonwealth Avenue and preserving the Site’s existing historic 
residence, relocating a reconstructed porte coch.re, installing a new driveway, modifying the 
existing stone wall, re-landscaping, and constructing behind the house a new 6-story building 
with connected central lobby including one (1) level parking beneath the rear building. The 
Project will reconfigure the interiors of both the existing house and the rear building to align 
the unit mix with community demand and market realities, by increasing the units in the 
existing house from 3 to 6, increasing the 13 units currently permitted in the rear building to 20 
units, and preserving the exterior dimensions of those structures. An elevator will serve all 
floors of the rear building, including the parking level. As well as all the unit entries in the 
Existing Building. 
 
The Project will contain of mix of 1 studio unit, 2 one-bedroom units, and 23 two-bedroom 
units as follows: Existing House: 1 studio unit (453 sq. ft.), 2 one-bedroom unit (596 to 618 sq. 
ft.), and 3 two-bedroom units (625 tom988 sq. ft.) New Building: 20 two-bedroom units (748 to 
765 sq. ft.). The Project’s 49 total bedrooms encompass 29,788 sq. ft. The Project also will 
ensure that 4 units are dedicated Affordable Housing Units under the City’s Inclusionary 
Development Policy (“IDP”). 
 
The parking area is fully screened below grade. The parking area will be accessed from 
Commonwealth Avenue. The original parking area plan, which allowed for 19 parking spaces of 
narrower width (including a wide HP-van accessible space), has been revised at the request of 
the BPDA to permit 10 parking spaces (including a wide HP-van accessible space) so that each of 
the parking spaces will be completely covered by the New Building the Project provides storage 
for 32 bicycles including 6 Visitor bicycle spaces. 
 
The Project will relocate the current curb cut easterly on Commonwealth Avenue and will 
relocate the existing streetlight. As a result, there will be no net loss of public parking spaces on 
Commonwealth Avenue that run the length of the Site. Moreover, in accordance with BPDA 
feedback, the relocated residential driveway and curb cut will be narrowed to 12’ wide, a street 
tree will be added at the former driveway location, and there will be no dedicated pick-up or 
dropoff area alongside the driveway itself. The existing break in the cobble wall will be 
maintained and reused for the Project’s handicap accessible ramp with handrails. The existing 
stairs adjoining the sidewalk will be restored and preserved. 
 
The plan for the Historic Residence, its stucco facade, which currently suffers from extensive 
staining, mildew, and cracks, will be replicated and replaced. Intact clay roof tiles will be 
preserved and reinstalled as part of the relocation of the Historic Residence. Broken or missing 
tiles will be replaced with tiles saved from the garage or, if there are not enough, with new tiles 
to match the existing. Painted Aluminum clad wood windows will be installed at the Historic 
Residence with custom sizing to match existing. Basis-of-Design is Pella Architect Series. 
 

 
1954 Commonwealth Avenue Small Project 
The New Building has been designed to read as differentiated from, but complementing, the 
Historic Residence, respecting the existing building in material, form, and siting, as well as the 
existing landscape and streetscape of which it is a part, while being sensitive to the height, 
scale, massing, rhythm, and materials of the adjacent apartment buildings. The Basis-of-Design 
of the New Building windows is Inline Fiberglass Series 325, although actual windows will be as 
permitted by the AACDC. It will have a mixture of through-color, high density, fiber cement 
panels, in sand hues and Stucco. A raised parapet to hide from street-level or park-level view, 
and muffle noise from, the Project’s rooftop mechanicals, including ventilation and condensing 
units, which are not oriented to public open spaces. 
 
Loading and delivery, residential move-in and move-out loading, and trash and recycling pick-up 
will take place from the on-Site parking area beneath the New Building or at curbside. 
 
The landscape design will include native plant materials that require less maintenance once 
established and other plant materials that are hardy in New England. Plantings will offer four 
seasons of landscape interest to the historic site. Plantings will highlight and enhance the 
building’s architectural features. Ornamental flowering understory trees will provide planting 
focal points from within the building and evergreen screen planting will be provided where 
necessary. Upright, red maple street trees will line Commonwealth Avenue and the existing 
stonewalls will be rebuilt along the property line. 
 
A handicap accessible route is provided from Commonwealth Avenue to the Main Building 
Entrance, located at the side where the historic building and new five story, plus parking 
garage, building connect. A pleasant circulation corridor with layered plant massing and 
terraced planter walls along the rear property line will run from Commonwealth Avenue to the 
Chestnut Hill Reservation and the Chestnut Hill Reservoir. 
 
Pedestrian walks and patio terraces will be scored concrete and/or concrete pavers and steps 
will be solid granite steps that coordinate with the building materials. A bituminous driveway 
will lead to the below grade parking garage. 
 
There will be building mounted light fixtures and low voltage pathway lighting at the stairs and 
ramps. All light fixtures will be Dark Sky compliant.

PROJECT SUMMARY 
The proposed project consists of a new six-story building with an underground parking 
garage. There will be fourty residential units on floors two through six. The first floor will 
contain three retail spaces, a bike storage room and building amenities. 
1.1 
Project Site and Area Context 
The project will be situated at 1 Taber Street in Roxbury. The lot size will be 10,696± 
square feet being City of Boston Assessor’s Parcel No. 0802547000, Main Facade fronts 
along Warren Street with residential entrance at Taber street. The site is currently occu-
pied by a one-story commercial building. 
1.2 
Proposed Project Narrative 
The proposed new building will consist of a six-story building with Commercial entrance/
egress on Warren Street and residential entrance/egress on Taber Street as well as an 
egress at the rear of the building. The garage entrance will be located on Taber Street. 
The first floor will contain the 2,735 +/-square foot commercial space and as part of build-
ing amenities a private lounge room as well as a private storage bike room with space for 
60 +/- bicycles. In the underground level there will be a private garage with 19 parking 
space. The second through sixth floors would contain eight dwelling units on each floor. 
Floors two through six will have three two-bedroom dwelling units and five one-bedroom 
dwelling units.

4.0 DESIGN COMPONENT 
4.1 
Introduction 
The proposed project in its current form, addresses the comments received during the 
profile meetings. 
It will consist of a new 6-story mixed use building. A commercial and retail space will oc-
cupy the ground floor along with the various building services, bike room storage and 
utility rooms. A private parking garage entrance and residential lobby entrance will be 
accessible through Taber Street. The parking level will be underground providing 18 car 
spaces. Floors two through six will contain 40 residential units. 
The Project’s design intention is to integrate the building with the scale and materiality of 
existing neighborhood structures and the forthcoming buildings. 
Discussion of design elements for the proposed new building is provided in the sections below, 
and is illustrated on the plans, perspectives, and photographs that are included in the Design 
Component. 
4.2 
Building Program 
The building program includes a residential lobby located on Taber Street, eighteen (18) space 
parking garage, and forty (40) residential units, located from the second floor level through the 
sixth level. At the first floor level, the building contains three (3) commercial spaces, a lounge 
room for the residential use amenities. Building mechanical equipment are housed at roof level 
and the associated utility room is appropriately located with enough distance from the roof 
parapet that will have minimum visibility and noise impact. The program also includes private 
outdoor roof deck area for the tenants use with the installation of solar panels being a green 
and sustainable design component. 
4.3 
Design Concept 
The design development of the two primary facades at Taber Street, and Warren Street place 
emphasis on its position as a corner lot building. The retail storefront develops along the main 
commercial street facade on Warren Street while the building’s parking garage will be ac-
cessed through Taber Street. 
The placement of the residential entry creates a pedestrian friendly residential Street along 
Taber Street while improving the pedestrian experience along Warren Street creating a wide r 
sidewalk in compliance with the Complete Street Guidelines of the Neighborhood Connector 
Street. 

1 TABER STREET • SPRA
24
4.4 
Height and Massing 
The massing of the Project has been designed to maintain the scale of the existing and 
future Taber Street structures as well as the buildings along Warren Street. 
4.5 
Façade Design, Fenestration, and Building Materials 
The façade treatment and fenestration concept for the Project is intended to create a dialog 
between the existing Taber Street building as well as the character of the buildings along War-
ren Street. 
The use of vertically and horizontally articulated cladding, will create a stylistic differentiation 
and contrast to architectural vocabulary of the surrounding neighborhood while maintaining a 
uniform aesthetic with the existing contemporary and future developments. 
The street level commercial façade will be glazed with retail storefront and a durable masonry 
treatment composed from a mix of arriscraft and brick veneer with a granite base treatment. 
The upper residential floors will be constructed as a rainscreen with a composition of ceramic 
panel and composite metal panel and fiber cement panel configuration 
4.6 
Exterior Signage 
The Project will allow for the integration of appropriately scaled retail signage above the 
retail storefront and entrance by future retail tenants. Building address signage will be 
incorporated at the residential entrance. Any necessary exterior way finding signage relat-
ed to the garage entrance and adjacent mechanical and trash rooms will be designed to 
be compatible with exterior building materials and the graphic identity of the Project. 
4.7 Pedestrian Circulation - Parking and Vehicular Circulation 
The Proposed Project has given special care in the location of the tenant bicycle storage room 
as well as the parking garage.These spaces are strategically located parallel to the building en-
trance on Taber Street. Tenants who park their car in the garage level will have direct access to 
the elevator. A pedestrian alert safety, visual/audio system will be provided in vicinity to the 
garage entrance. 
Bike parking storage will be designed as per city’s bike parking guidelines, providing 6 short 
term bike spaces along Taber Street. 
Recycling and trash disposal area is located at the First Floor level, with direct access to the 
rear of the building. 
Adopting the principles of transit-oriented development and supporting the decreasing trend 
in neighborhood auto ownership described above, the Project will provide 19 parking spaces 
and 60 +/- bike spaces for the proposed 40 residential units.

Article 80 – Accessibility Checklist 
 
 
A requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities strives to reduce architectural, procedural, attitudinal, and 
communication barriers that affect persons with disabilities in the City of Boston. In 2009, a Disability Advisory Board was 
appointed by the Mayor to work alongside the Commission in creating universal access throughout the city’s built 
environment. The Disability Advisory Board is made up of 13 volunteer Boston residents with disabilities who have been 
tasked with representing the accessibility needs of their neighborhoods and increasing inclusion of people with 
disabilities. 
 
In conformance with this directive, the BDPA has instituted this Accessibility Checklist as a tool to encourage developers 
to begin thinking about access and inclusion at the beginning of development projects, and strive to go beyond meeting 
only minimum MAAB / ADAAG compliance requirements. Instead, our goal is for developers to create ideal design for 
accessibility which will ensure that the built environment provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of their 
abilities. As such, any project subject to Boston Zoning Article 80 Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional 
Master Plan modifications and updates, must complete this Accessibility Checklist thoroughly to provide specific detail 
about accessibility and inclusion, including descriptions, diagrams, and data. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, advancing best practices, and learning about progressive approaches 
to expand accessibility throughout Boston's built environment. Proponents are highly encouraged to meet with 
Commission staff, prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1. Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional and 
inclusionary requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. Accessible Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional 
and inclusionary requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
3. Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional and 
inclusionary requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
4. Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing 
opportunities, in the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
5. Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way. For 
more information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
6. 
Visitability – A place’s ability to be accessed and visited by persons with disabilities that cause functional 
limitations; where architectural barriers do not inhibit access to entrances/doors and bathrooms.

2. PROPOSED PROJECT SUMMARY 
The proposed project includes the demolition of an existing three-story residential structure and 
the construction of a six-story, twenty-five (25) unit multi-family building. The new building will 
include thirteen (13) one-bedroom units, three (3) two-bedroom units and nine (9) three-bedroom 
units. The site is approximately 9,600 square feet and located within a 3F-4000 three-family 
residential zoning sub-district but lies directly adjacent to a CC-1 community commercial sub-
district. 
The development will replace an existing parking area at the rear of the site with shared open 
space for building residents, reducing impervious surface and increasing usable green space. 
The proposed building conforms with the required rear yard setback and side yard setback 
along the east side while the front yard aligns with existing modal setbacks. 
 
3. SITE AND SURROUNDINGS 
The project site is located near Union Square in the heart of the Allston neighborhood, at the 
beginning of North Beacon Street once it transitions from Brighton Avenue. Both the immediate 
and broader contexts of the site have witnessed significant development in recent years that has 
reshaped the neighborhood. The largest of these developments include the Boston Landing and 
ongoing Allston Yards projects just north of the site with additional development planned along 
the south edge of the Turnpike, to the north of North Beacon and Cambridge Streets. Closer to 
the site, numerous smaller projects have replaced single-story commercial and light industrial 
uses with mid-rise residential and mix-use buildings along North Beacon and Cambridge Streets. 
This growth has begun to define and emphasize these major commercial corridors and 
encourages continued infill development of the remaining parcels. A key contributor to this 
recent evolution is the transit rich nature of the area with the Green Line to the south, the 
Commuter Rail Boston Landing station to the north and multiple key bus routes along North 
Beacon and Cambridge Streets all within a short walk. 
 
4. URBAN DESGN 
The proposed project seeks to infill one of the remaining underdeveloped sites at the east end 
of North Beacon Street. The project site is a deep and narrow parcel that supports a single-
loaded corridor with an exposed vertical circulation core and residential units facing the 
opposite direction. The abutting property to the east at 15 North Beacon Street contains an 
existing curb and driveway along the shared property boundary, while the abutting project to 
the west at 21 North Beacon Street (One Everett) is orientated toward the corner of North 
beacon and Everett Streets, utilizing the east side of the building for utility program along the 
shared property line. The siting of the proposed building responds to these conditions and 
justifies the footprint of the building toward the west property boundary, with the circulation 
core facing the rear of the adjacent building. This placement allows for a larger setback from 
23-25 N BEACON ST | AUGUST 14, 2024 | 6

the east property boundary that mirrors the setback of the adjacent building and creates a 
significant buffer between the two buildings that benefits the east facing units. The rear of the 
site has a significant grade change, leading to a rear yard populated by numerous mature 
trees. This vegetation and the grade change create a natural buffer between the project site 
and the rear abutting residential properties along Clevemont avenue to the North. The siting of 
the proposed building respects this buffer and maintains an adequate setback to preserve the 
existing trees and grading. At the front of the site, the proposed setback at the ground floor and 
southwest corner will match the modal setback of the west abutting building and the primary 
massing at the residential floors will protrude and transition to the east abutting building which 
directly fronts the North Beacon Street sidewalk with no setback. This protruded massing 
reinforces the four-story datum established by both abutting buildings and steps back at the fifth 
floor and again at the sixth. This setback at the sixth floor is carried around the building with a 
setback at the east façade and a significant setback at the rear as well. The narrow shape of 
the site and resulting single-loaded corridor plan create a narrow building frontage and minimal 
presence along North Beacon Street that allow for increased height and density to fully utilize 
the site’s development potential. 
 
5. BUILDING DESIGN, MASSING AND MATERIALS 
The massing of the building is simultaneously a response to the site’s context, a reflection of the 
building’s program and a tool to visually reduce the scale of the building. The circulation core 
and elevator overrun create a vertical column that anchors the building to the site. The east 
façade is folded to ensure the walls and windows are not parallel to the adjacent building at 
15 North Beacon Street, creating privacy for both building residents and neighbors. This 
geometry also provides greater daylighting to the residents as windows from every unit are 
oriented towards the street and south. In terms of the building massing, the folds in the façade 
occur at the scale of the individual rooms and units. This ensures each unit contains south-
orientated windows and visually reduces the scale of the massing without the introduction of 
additional bays or arbitrary changes of material. The folded geometry creates a simpler form 
that enhances the design, simplifies construction and reduces costs. The front setback is 
programmed with a small patio for building residents adjacent to the lobby entry, with the 
remainder planted with ground cover and shrubs to soften the urban streetscape. The ground 
floor is occupied by a residential lobby and bike storage room at the front that are highly 
transparent and inviting from the street. The rear of the building provides a pair of ground floor 
units, each with private exterior access. The rear of the site behind the building and before the 
existing tree growth and slope will be utilized as a shared resident lawn and patio space. 
The proposed material treatment is a combination of masonry, fiber cement and wood shiplap 
that enhances the building geometry and reflects the surrounding context. The primary material 
at the street frontage and main building volume is a neutral-toned, Norman brick that grounds 
the building with weight and provides a visual juxtaposition to the buildings’ verticality with 
strong horizontal texture. The brick blends with the masonry façades of the adjacent buildings 
23-25 N BEACON ST | AUGUST 14, 2024 | 7

on each site, further reinforcing the four-story datum along North Beacon Street. Above the 
datum, the secondary building volume is setback at the front and clad in a dark gray fiber 
cement that complements the masonry as the two volumes intersect and overlap along the east 
façade. Where the secondary volume is broken by unit balconies or vertical reveals, a wood 
shiplap accent is introduced to contrast the dark fiber cement and provide warmth and a finer 
scale. The penthouse level and vertical circulation core are each covered in a light gray, large-
format, fiber cement that visually recedes from view. At the residential lobby and bike room at 
the front, storefront glazing provides transparency and creates a welcoming and engaging 
space for building residents approaching from the sidewalk. 
 
6. TRAFFIC, PARKING AND ACCESS 
The project leverages its superior walkability and access to public transit by providing no on-
site parking. To minimize congestion on North Beacon Street, the project provides a dedicated 
off-street loading area beneath the building for passenger drop-offs/pickups as well as short 
term deliveries. This area is accessed via the existing curb cut off North Beacon Street. 
Bicycle parking spaces are provided in the building and are accessed both internally from the 
residential lobby and from an exterior door at the driveway. Space is provided for 24 bicycles 
in conformance with the City of Boston’s Bike Parking Guidelines. In addition, visitor bicycle 
parking is provided along the front sidewalk for an additional 6 spaces. 
 
7. ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS 
Each unit will be conditioned with individual heat pumps. Domestic hot water will be provided 
with electric hot water heaters and all appliances within each unit will be electric. 
As noted above, the project will provide no parking. In addition to deterring dependence on 
cars within the city, this has several benefits to the building itself, including a significant 
reduction in building materials and energy use. To accommodate parking requires the 
construction of a garage that occupies a large footprint on the ground floor, must be ventilated 
and creates challenges to insulating the units above.

8. COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
The proposed project will provide many benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, they include: 
• 
Creation of 25 units of new rental housing, in furtherance of the City’s housing 
production goals. 
 
• 
Creation of 4 new affordable housing units, including one 3-bedroom unit. 
 
• 
Generation of thousands of dollars in annual revenue to the City in the form of new real 
property tax payments upon completion. 
 
• 
Creation of numerous construction period jobs. 
 
• 
Improvements to the public realm through robust urban landscaping plan. 
 
• 
Incorporation of significant sustainability measures, including all-electric systems and 
efficient building envelope.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

ii. 
Proposed Project 
The 231-245 Grove Street proposed development consists of the redevelopment of two 
parcels, 231-239 Grove Street (3,470 square feet) and 241-245 Grove Street (10,016 square 
feet). The parcels combine to create a 13,486 square foot project site. Both parcels 
currently contain one (1) story commercial buildings. The proposal is to construct a five 
(5) story building containing 6,140 square feet of ground floor retail and thirty (30) 
residential units. Parking is provided at-grade and will be accessed from Washington 
Street, through an existing project the Proponent has come into ownership of (5205 
Washington Street). Eleven (11) motor vehicle parking spaces will be provided, all 
internal to the building. Additionally, forty-six (46) bicycle parking spaces are provided 
for residents, as well as up to ten (10) visitor bicycle parking spaces on site. 
 
 
iii. 
Design Process 
The design of the proposed building has been shaped by prefiling input from the 
BPDA. During the prefiling process, meetings were held on September 14, 2022, 
November 15, 2022, and July 13, 2023. The meetings were attended by the project team 
and representatives of the BPDA.

The Proposed Project will contain thirty (30) units of housing, with units ranging in size 
from 755 square feet to 1,446 square feet, averaging approximately 955 square feet per 
unit. The building will be a total of 40,641 Gross Square Feet 
Per Map 11E of the West Roxbury Neighborhood District, the Proposed Project is

vi. 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will replace two (2) existing single-story commercial retail 
buildings with a mixed-use development. The Proposed Project is located within a 
Neighborhood Shopping subdistrict and abuts a residential subdistrict. The Proposed 
Project can update the retail spaces within the existing buildings, increase the number 
of those spaces, and create new residential opportunities to create a point of transition 
from a commercial subdistrict to a residential subdistrict. 
 
vii. 
Building Design 
The Proposed Building has been designed to respond to the curved transition between 
Grove Street and Washington Streets. The ground level retail provided transparent 
facades with ground level commercial space and the residential lobby entry. The right 
side of the ground level façade was inspired by the existing brick and concrete façade. 
The upper levels have been designed to be cohesive yet not just a redundant elevation. 
We broke up the massing to provide relief between the ground level and second floor 
and also stepped back the fifth level so the main elevation would match the building at 
5205 Washington Street. 
 
viii. 
Site Design 
The Proposed building site design has responded to the curve transition between Grove 
and Washington Streets. The entry to the parking area will be accessed from an existing 
curb cut and parking area located at 5205 Washington Street. 
 
ix. 
Landscape Design 
The proposed landscape design includes public realm improvements along Washington 
Street and Grove Street following Boston Complete Streets guidelines. The design will 
provide 3 new street trees, plus the removal and replacement of 1 existing (dead) street 
tree and preservation of 1 existing street tree, for a total of 5 street trees along the 
frontage of 231-245 Grove Street and 5205 Washington Street. Permeable paving will be 
added in the furnishing zone to support drainage and tree health. 5 bicycle racks will be 
added providing parking for 10 bicycles. The proposed streetscape design also includes 
ornamental plantings and a small seating area with a bench and bike repair station.

including a dog run and roof deck with planting and furnishing. 
 
x. 
Traffic and Parking 
Parking is provided at-grade and will be accessed from Washington Street via a 12’ curb 
cut. Eleven (11) motor vehicle parking spaces will be provided, including two (2) 
handicap spaces, with an access drive aisle of 22’. Proposed standard parking space 
dimensions are 9’ wide x 18’ deep; ADA stalls are 8’ wide x 18’ deep with a 22’ drive 
aisle. Additionally, up to forty-six (46) bicycle parking spaces are provided for 
residents, as well as up to ten (10) visitor bicycle parking spaces on site. 
 
xi. 
Proposed Project Benefits 
 
a. New Housing Units - Additional housing is a priority in the city and the 
Proposed Project seeks to provide ample residential opportunities with a 
project that bridges two distinct subdistricts. 
 
b. Site Enrichment – The Proposed Project will serve to update and enhance 
the current retail opportunities existing on this site, while adding 
additional retail storefronts to improve the current commercial fabric of 
the Neighborhood Shopping subdistrict it resides in. The housing units 
provided by the project will also serve to enliven existing local retail uses 
within the area by providing a new group of potential customers. 
 
c. Job Creation – The Proposed Project will be a job creator during and after 
construction. The ground floor retail spaces will also provide 
opportunities for jobs upon their completion.

accessibility in Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at

minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment which provides equitable 
experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability.

Checklist to provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project 
plans change significantly.

Situated at a mid-block location along Notre Dame Street in Roxbury, near the 
intersection of Columbus Avenue and Washington Street, the project site consists of 
approximately 11,900 square feet of land at four (4) contiguous parcels (the “Project Site”). Its

significance, surrounded by narrow and inaccessible public sidewalks.

1.2 Project Introduction and Summary 
This Small Project Review Application is being submitted by Notre Dame Development LLC (the 
“Proponent”) in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Zoning Code”) regarding the development of an approximately 11,900 square‐foot property at 
24‐34 Notre Dame Street (Parcel Nos. 1100980000, 1100979000, 1100978000 and 1100977000) 
in the Roxbury neighborhood of the City of Boston (collectively, the “Property Site” or “Site”). 
The Site includes an existing non‐descript single family dwelling of no historic/architectural 
significance.  Situated at a mid‐block location along Notre Dame Street in Roxbury, near the 
intersection of Columbus Avenue and Washington Street, the Site consists of approximately 
11,900 square feet of land on four (4) contiguous lots numbered 24‐34 Notre Dame Street.  It is 
regulated by the Multifamily Residential (“MFR”) Zoning Subdistrict of the Roxbury 
Neighborhood Zoning District, which Allows the project’s proposed Multifamily Residential Use 
but restricts its dimensional, off‐street parking and loading requirements under Article 50 and 
other applicable sections of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”).  The context of 
the immediate area includes several existing multifamily uses along Notre Dame Street and 
certain mixed‐use commercial buildings of larger‐scale and size at the intersection of Columbus 
Avenue and Washington Street. 
The proposed project includes the construction of a new five (5) story multifamily residential 
building of approximately 28,357 gross square feet, with 26 units of homeownership, 15 on‐site 
parking spaces, roof decked, terraced, and ground level open spaces, residential amenity areas 
and related sidewalk, landscaping, pedestrian and vehicular access improvements at the Site (the 
“Proposed Project”).   
The Proposed Project will create a residential development of both market‐rate and income‐
restricted housing opportunities, with a contemporary design that is appropriate in scale, 
massing, and programming for the future growth of the Roxbury neighborhood. As a result, the 
proposed building has been designed and scaled to complement its specific location while also 
responding to the Site’s unique challenges and characteristics.  
The Proposed Project also includes over 5,550 square feet of open space in a combination of 
ground level open space, unit balconies and a common 5th floor deck, including a community

2.2 Urban Design and Building Design Approach  
The Proposed Project is located on a residential side street in the Roxbury neighborhood, 
between the busy thoroughfares of Columbus Avenue and Washington Street and within walking 
distance to both Egleston Square and the public transportation node at Jackson Square.  The 
Proposed Project will replace a currently vacant lot and dilapidated house along Notre Dame 
Street. The Site itself is a rarity in the area for its size and lack of development, and the Proposed 
Project will contribute to the housing needs of the community by revitalizing and transforming 
its underutilized and oversized Project Site. The building’s mass is predominantly a five (5) story 
building that has been broken down in scale using projecting bays, balconies, and varying 
materials. The Proposed Project will also provide new home ownership opportunities with much‐
needed public realm improvements at this deficient and inaccessible section of Notre Dame 
Street, including a new widened sidewalk, street trees and public bike racks (in front of the Site).  
Its on‐site parking facility will be accessed from a garage entry via a vehicular alleyway that runs 
along the rear of the Site, to enhance pedestrian safety and mitigate vehicular impacts along 
Notre Dame Street.   
 
The Proposed Project will combine the Site’s four (4) contiguous parcels into a single 
consolidated lot with frontage on Notre Dame Street and its adjacent side alleyway. The facade 
along Notre Dame will be public facing, housing the main residential lobby, mail, and resident 
bike room. Vehicular entrance and egress will be off the quieter alley to the rear of the Site.  
 
The main façade along Notre Dame Street is broken up using a rhythmic series of bays which 
provide visual interest and a nod toward classic New England window bays. An emphasis has 
been placed on using colors and hues that are blended with the visual fabric of the existing 
buildings, which range in size, material, and age. Predominantly clad in brick, the façade has a 
familiar appearance to those of the four‐ and five‐ story masonry buildings behind it. The 
proposed mix of grey and black bricks is a contemporary take on the traditional material. Cedar 
is used at the punched windows and balconies to provide warmth and contrast to the masonry. 

 
24‐34 Notre Dame Street, Roxbury 
 
7 
The enclosure will be assembled using modern technologies and materials that are in scale with 
the surrounding brick and siding buildings.  
 
The new building’s 26 unit residential program features a variety of unit types for 
homeownership, including the following:  one (1) studio, five (5) one‐bedrooms, eighteen (18) 
two‐bedrooms and two (2) three‐bedrooms.  The Proposed Project will also provide a mix of 
affordable, handicap accessible and market rate housing, while enhancing the pedestrian 
friendly nature of the street in the surrounding Roxbury neighborhood.  
The building’s amenities will include 15 garage parking spaces located at grade and a secure 
bicycle storage area for 26 bicycles, with its own direct access to the main residential entry 
walkway and area out to the street, along with over 5,550 square feet of open space in a 
combination of ground level open space, unit balconies and a common 5th floor deck, along with 
an amply sized community room (adjacent to the common deck on the top floor).   A large and 
welcoming common front lobby area and vestibule is pulled back from the street, to enliven the 
front of the building while providing direct access to mail area, bike room and central elevator to 
the upper floors.  
2.3 Traffic, Parking and Access   
The Proposed Project is located within a half mile of the Jackson Square MBTA Orange Line 
Station, walking distance to many bus routes on Columbus Avenue/Washington Street and 
within close proximity to the Southwest Corridor Park bike paths, all providing convenient access 
to downtown Boston and beyond. The Site is also within walking distance to the Washington 
Street and Egleston Square commercial areas, which includes easy access to grocery markets, 
pharmacies, banks, restaurants, shopping, retail, and other amenities in the area, such as the 
Egleston Square YMCA. As stated above, the building will also feature a secure bicycle storage 
area for 26 bicycles of various sizes with convenient and direct access to the street, along with 
six (6) additional exterior bike racks for visitors. The building is intended to connect people to 
every means of transportation easily.   
The pedestrian entrance is located prominently at the corner of the building along Notre Dame 
Street with bicycle parking directly adjacent. The vehicular entrance is positioned off the alley to 
the rear of the Site, so that pedestrian conflicts with vehicular access will be minimized, as will 
any traffic build‐up. Fifteen (15) parking spaces are provided on the ground floor with direct 
access to the lobby and elevator. Trash will be handled by a dedicated walkway directly from the 
building garage to Notre Dame Street. 
The Proponent will work with the BPDA, Public Improvement Commission (“PIC”), and BTD to 
restructure the curb configuration to help protect and enhance the pedestrian experience.

COMMUNITY BENEFITS   
The Proposed Project will provide substantial public benefits to the City of Boston and the 
Roxbury neighborhood including: 
 Revitalizing and transforming an underutilized, oversized, and distressed property site in 
a residential section of the Roxbury neighborhood, with new home ownership 
opportunities and much‐needed public realm improvements to a deficient and 
inaccessible section of the public way, including a new widened sidewalk, street trees 
and public bike racks (in front of the Site).  Specifically, the Proposed Project would 
upgrade the existing sidewalk widths and enhance pedestrian accessibility in front of the 
Site, by reconstructing the unimproved asphalt surface areas with a new ADA‐compliant 
public sidewalk, the planting of new street trees, installation of public bike racks and 
new ground level landscaping to buffer vehicular access to its on‐site parking garage.  
 Creating expanded market rate and affordable homeownership opportunities in the 
Roxbury neighborhood, with an increased allotment of on‐site income restricted units 
for family‐sized housing than otherwise required by the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy (“IDP”). This includes over 15% of on‐site income‐restricted units, with greater 
bedroom sizes and Group 2 accessible accommodations in accordance with MAAB 521 
CMR. 
 Introducing new neighborhood residents who will provide support to the local 
community and utilize local businesses. 
 Providing a project scope and scale that is intended to further the residential policy 
goals of the City of Boston.  
 Encouraging alternative modes of transportation through the use of bicycling, walking, 
and public transportation by adding a bicycle storage space for the building’s residents 
and providing other transit oriented amenities and services.  
 Generating property and sales tax revenue for the City of Boston.  
 Creating construction jobs throughout project development.
