ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new five-story mixed-use building at 243-245 
Dorchester Street in South Boston. The new building will contain twenty dwelling units 
intended to be condominium units for sale, with six accessory off-street garage parking 
spaces, in light of the site’s close proximity to Red Line rapid transit, as well as ground 
floor commercial space. The residential units are planned to be smaller in size, thus 
providing a more naturally affordable home ownership opportunity for first-time buyers 
looking for an alternative to renting. The unit sizes will also be ideal for empty-nesters 
giving up larger homes in favor or more economical living in the city. Fourteen of the 
units are proposed one-bedroom units, and six would be bi-level two-bedroom units. 
 
The project will include three affordable units pursuant to the City of Boston’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy, representing 17% affordability, per the requirements 
of PLAN: South Boston Dorchester Avenue. The lot size is approximately 4,576 square 
feet, and comprises three parcels of land, Assessor’s Parcels 070051200, 070051300, 
and 070051400, and is located partially within an L-1 Local Business District under the 
Base Code, and partially within an MFR Multifamily Residential Subdistrict under Article 
68, the South Boston Neighborhood District. The site is currently occupied by a three-
story mixed-use building with a ground-floor restaurant with take-out, a single-story 
commercial building, and a two-story two-family dwelling.

243-245 Dorchester Street Mixed-Use Small Project 
Total development cost is estimated at approximately $10,000,000, with a projected 
commencement of construction in the first quarter of 2025 and a projected completion 
date of the second quarter of 2026. 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood 
and to the City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of 20 new dwelling units in an attractive and energy-efficient 
building, including 4 affordable units in accordance with the City of Boston’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy, as well as modern new commercial space; 
 
• generation of tens of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of 
Boston once the project is completed in the form of new real property tax 
payments; and 
 
• the expected creation of approximately 45 construction industry jobs to 
complete the proposed project; 
 
• a community benefits package to be determined by the BPDA which will provide 
financial commitments to improving public infrastructure in the area and also to 
one or more South Boston non-profit community service organizations.

Project Summary
Project Summary
The proposed project consists of the redevelopment of a 16,564 square-foot lot at 247 Hancock 
Street in Dorchester (the “Project”). The Project is a multifamily residential development comprised 
of a six story building that will contain 47 residential units, approximately 1,500 square feet of public 
open space, 18 accessory off-street parking spaces and 57 bike storage spaces. The Project will utilize 
numerous alternative transit options including a building-dedicated on-site electric vehicle share and 
ample bicycle amenities.
In designing the building, great care was given to respecting the area’s as-built conditions and 
location on Hancock Street, at the foot of Meeting House Hill and across the street from the new 
Dot Block development. As a result, the proposed Project has been designed and scaled to fit into the 
unique topography, the busy thoroughfare of Hancock Street, and the area’s ongoing residential and 
mixed-use development. The building will offer a contemporary aesthetic appropriate in massing and 
design within the changing neighborhood.
Community Benefits
The proposed Project will offer many public benefits to the neighborhood and the City of Boston, 
including the following:
•	 The creation of 47 new residential units; the Proponent is actively working to secure subsidies 
to add additional affordability to the Project above the minimum required under the BPDA 
Inclusionary Development Policy. At a minimum, the Project will exceed the seven (7) income-
restricted units as required under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
•	 The creation of approximately 1,500 square feet of landscaped public open space on Hancock 
Street, creating additional open space and an improved pedestrian experience on the busy 
commercial thoroughfare abutting the new Dot Block development.
•	 The enhancement of Hancock Street by removing a 76-foot curb cut and carwash in the middle 
of a residential block, creating new sidewalk, and adding hardscaping, which will make the 
experience safer for pedestrians.
•	 Encouraging alternative modes of transportation such as bicycling and walking, due to the close 
proximity of the Savin Hill MBTA station and the large quantity of on-site bicycle storage.
•	 The future generation of hundreds of thousands of dollars in new property and sales tax revenue 
annually to the City of Boston.
•	 The expected creation of more than 90 construction jobs over the length of the project.

Project Description
The project site is located at 243-255 Hancock Street, Dorchester, Massachusetts (Parcel ID: 1502984000), designated 
as Lot B on the plan dated October 2, 2005, and entitled “#247-255 Hancock Street, Proposed Subdivision Plan of Land 
in Boston (Dorchester District) MA, Suffolk County,” John A. Hammer, II, PLS, which plan is recorded with the Registry as 
Plan 626 of 2006 (the “Proposed Subdivision Plan”). The Property consists of approximately 16,564 square feet of land 
and an existing car wash building and constitutes a portion of the land described in a Deed from Edward F. McGourty, 
Trustee of 247 Hancock Street Trust, dated March 31, 2000 and recorded with the Registry in Book 24824 Page 78.
The proposed Project will replace the existing car wash which contributes to significant traffic along Hancock Street. By 
removing the existing structure, the Project will have the opportunity to revitalize the streetscape and create a far more 
walkable environment.

Design Approach
The proposed Project will consist of a new residential building with three and five stories along the street wall, 
stepping up to six stories at the rear of the site. The street level site plan activates and enhances Hancock 
Street through the creation of additional public space, which features ornamental trees and seating under 
the building’s canopy. The building’s massing is carefully folded on the Hancock Street facade to ensure visual 
continuity between the Proponent’s adjacent multifamily building at 233 Hancock Street and the lower, 
three story buildings to the east. This folding movement forms the open space adjacent to the sidewalk, 
as well as the roof deck , which will serve as an outdoor, accessible amenity for residents. The lobby and 
residential bike room will be at grade, fully accessible, and accessed from Hancock Street. Enclosed parking 
will be located at street level and tucked away at the rear of the site. Floors two through six will contain 47 
total residential units with a mix of studios, one, two, and three bedroom residential units. The architecture 
along the northeastern portion of the site steps back from the lot line, creating an entry plaza for additional 
public green space. Building access walks through the plaza and follows the natural pedestrian desire lines 
from both the north and south. Raised planters, ornamental trees and seat walls are used to define the 
space and provide buffers from Hancock Street. Pavers and flush granite banding help to differentiate the 
entry from the public realm. Four additional bike spaces are located within the plaza, totaling ten for the site. 
The site will adhere to Hancock Street’s designation as a “Neighborhood Main” typology under the Boston 
Complete Street guidelines, and continues the current design at the Proponent’s adjacent 233 Hancock 
Street building. The existing public sidewalk width of 8’ will be maintained along Hancock Street while 
reducing the number of curb-cuts. The new concrete sidewalk will feature a continuous granite curb. All 
street signage and lighting will remain. The pedestrian zone will be a continuous 5’ wide path. The furnishing 
zone will be 3’ in width and will include four new trees (open tree pits) and six new bike spaces.
To minimize curb cuts, vehicular access and movement will be limited to the northern edge of the site via an 
existing shared driveway with The Meeting House (233 Hancock).

Parking and Transportation
While the proposed Project contains 18 accessory off-street parking spaces, to take a progressive 
approach to development, the Project will adopt the guideline of MAPC’s Metro Boston Perfect Fit 
Parking Initiative which finds that the provision of abundant parking is counterproductive to local 
transportation goals for traffic and sustainability. If demand necessitates, additional off-site parking 
spaces can be utilized at Arx Urban’s other projects, 233 Hancock Street (abutting) and 200 Hancock 
Street (one block away), which have parking availability. The Project will utilize numerous methods to 
encourage alternative modes of transportation, including bicycle amenities, and an electric vehicle 
car-share. Bicycle parking will be secure, with direct elevator access provided to all floors of the 
building from the central lobby.

Proponent Track Record
Arx Urban is an innovative real estate firm focused on creating attainable housing in the Greater Boston 
area. Founded in 2014, Arx Urban has acquired or developed over 25 multifamily and mixed-use projects 
valued over $300M and has used various capital sources to fund these projects including traditional bank 
financing, subsidies, grants, crowdfunding, social impact equity and syndication.
Case Study 1: The Meeting House:
In September 2020, Arx Urban completed The Meeting House, a 36-unit mixed-income housing development 
in Dorchester. Arx Urban acquired the 15,000 square foot site (which abuts the proposed Project) in 2017, 
which previously consisted of two auto body shops. After completing a robust community engagement 
process, Arx Urban procured public subsidy to add additional affordability to the project through the 
MassHousing Workforce Housing Initiative and the City of Boston Community Preservation Act Fund (for 
which Arx Urban was the first ever project to receive funding).
The project is 100% electric with solar power on the roof and also contains ground-floor retail space, ample 
bike-parking and an art installation called The Meeting House Doors Project that was created to support 
local artists impacted by the COVID pandemic.
Case Study 2: Dorchester Workforce Portfolio:
In 2015, Arx Urban completed its first major redevelopment project in Boston with the redevelopment of 
200 Hancock Street (one block away from the proposed Project) and 90 Wrentham Street, 49 units across 
two buildings that were previously on the Boston Problem Property list. Over three years, Arx Urban worked 
hand-in-hand with the City’s Inspectional Services Division, Boston Police Department, local neighborhood 
organizations and socially-minded financing sources to create a private market solution for renovating the 
buildings without displacing tenants in good standing. Arx Urban then piloted a program, in tandem with 
City Life/Vida Urbana, that provided for the stability of tenants by capping rent increases at 3% per year, 
regardless of how their rent compares to current market rents.
In 2022, Arx Urban partnered with Boston’s Mayor’s Office of Housing to income-restrict the building under 
the Acquisition Opportunity Program (for tenants earning between 30-90% of AMI). The program aims to 
increase the share of Boston’s affordable rental housing stock protected from market forces and to prevent 
displacement of tenants threatened by rapidly increasing rents.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in Boston’s built 
environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, rather than after a design is 
completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment 
which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to provide specific 
detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout Boston's built 
environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth by MAAB 521 
CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth by MAAB 521 
CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the specific functional 
needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary requirements set 
forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in the City. For more 
information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more information visit: 
https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community benefits, particularly for 
persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors openings, hallways, 
bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will be an addition to the rear of an existing three (3) story, six (6) 
unit multi-family dwelling. The Proposed Project is located within a 2F-6000 zoning 
subdistrict. The existing structure will undergo a renovation which includes moderate 
façade changes and construction to allow for basement bicycle parking, but otherwise, 
the exterior façades will remain as currently constructed in order to maintain street line 
context of the neighborhood. 
 
vii. 
Building Design 
 
The building design has two main components. 
 
1. Preservation and restoration of a wonderful example of Second Empire 
architecture in the existing structure at 24 Mt Everett Street. The character 
and detail of the original building will be preserved, repaired and restored 
as result of this project. Ownership and the design team view the project 
not only as a renovation but an investment in sustainable design. The 
proposal will provide new life for a sound and attractive structure. 
Restoration and reuse are primary forms of recycling, by making optimal 
use of already present on-site materials. The restoration preserves the 
carbon embodied in the existing structure and conserves the energy and 
materials required had the project proposed demolition and 
reconstruction of this handsome structure vs. restoration and adaptive 
reuse. 
a. The major work proposed for the existing exterior façades include:

double-hung clad wood windows. 
ii. Repair and painting of the existing siding, trim and 
architectural details. 
iii. Preservation and enclosure of the existing side porch as new 
living space. 
iv. Activation of the basement to create an accessible front 
entrance, which allows for the preservation and restoration 
of the existing, inaccessible front porch. 
v. Construction of a limited use limited access (LULA) lift in 
the basement to provide access to the first floor. 
vi. Construction of a Lobby, Mail Room and Bike Parking area 
in the basement. 
2. The new addition, which consists of 16 dwelling units in a 4-story 
building, is designed to reflect and complement the Second Empire 
architecture of the existing building. 
a. Design components of the addition include: 
i. Centering the addition massing behind the existing building, 
minimizes views of the addition from the public way, and 
makes the addition secondary to the Second Empire 
architecture of the existing building. 
ii. The new fourth floor, is designed as a modern interpretation 
of a mansard roof, by recalling the color, scale and form of 
the existing mansard roof. 
iii. The placement of a new egress stair and LULA to serve as a 
“break” between the restoration of the existing Second 
Empire architecture and the new addition. 
iv. A fenestration pattern which reflects, recalls and 
compliments the fenestration of the existing building. 
v. Resident outdoor space will be provided through the use of 
private balconies. 
An accessible second means of egress and access to the first floor is provided through a 
rear porch, which will recall the scale and detailing of the existing front porch

The design of the landscape is based on three objectives:

with the site’s program and mitigate tree removals where possible, 
 
2. To support residential living by creating shared amenity spaces, new

3. To maintain and enhance buffers to abutters including privacy fencing,

URBAN FOREST 
 
Architectural and landscape improvements are aimed to minimize the amount of 
disturbance to the existing tree canopy. Due to a generous percentage of open 
space, there are twenty significant trees existing on site. We are proposing five 
trees to be removed (all of which are invasive) and fifteen to remain. In addition, 
we are proposing to add to the Urban Forest by planting five deciduous trees 
and thirty-four (34) evergreen trees across the property. 
 
RESIDENTIAL LIVING 
 
Residential living is supported through accessible pedestrian circulation design 
and with ample open space. An outdoor amenity is proposed in the rear yard to 
support outdoor entertainment, play and relaxation. The amenity space features 
retaining seatwalls, a flexible lawn space as well as a pervious unit paver patio. 
The front and rear access points into the building are fully accessible, and a 
sideyard connection between the front and rear is also ADA accessible via sloped 
walkways, ramps, handrails and cheekwalls. 
 
ENHANCED BUFFERS 
 
The existing site has minimal fencing to provide privacy for abutters. We are 
proposing a 6’ height solid wood board fence around the majority of the site to

The site has a Walk Score of 80 and Transit Score of 61. It is a 14-minute walk to both the

a. Housing for At-Risk Individuals – Working with Economic Mobility 
Pathways (EMPath), a Boston-based non-profit organization, the 
Owner/Developer for 24 Mt. Everett, Diarmaid McGregor, plans to offer 
the units within the building to at-risk women and their children. 
McGregor has worked with EMPath since 2010, housing women from

The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

Dear Mr. Harvey:
TLee Development LLC (TLD) is pleased to submit this Notice of Project Change for 270 Talbot
Avenue (a previously approved Article 80 Small Project). This application includes the proposed
development of eighteen residential condominium units affordable to households earning between
80% and 100% of the area median income (AMI) in a newly constructed four-story elevator building
on City-owned land at 270 Talbot Avenue in Dorchester, MA (Proposed Project). The Project also
includes about 3,117 square feet of ground floor retail space and nine (9) off-street parking spaces.
This application proposes a change to the project as formerly approved by the BPDA Board. In lieu of
21 units of rental housing, TLD now proposes a project with 18 affordable condo units. The ground
floor retail space and off-street parking spaces will remain as originally proposed.
In January 2022, TLD determined the original rental project to be financially infeasible as a result of
challenges imposed by labor shortages and construction material pricing increases related largely to
the pandemic. After substantial engagement with civic associations abutting the site, as well as the
Mayor’s Office of Housing and the BPDA, TLD is now proposing an affordable homeownership project
with proposed financing through the MassHousing CommonWealth Builder program. Key changes
between the original and proposed project include (1) the conversion of residential rental units to
homeownership condominiums; (2) the reduction of units from 21 to 18 in order to enlarge unit sizes;
(3) the inclusion of three-bedroom units; and (4) the conversion of ground floor retail spaces from
rental to ownership.
The Proposed Project will revitalize an underutilized, tax foreclosed property to create an
aesthetically pleasing building appropriate in massing, scale and design in this neighborhood of
Dorchester. Further, it will help to facilitate the goals of the Housing a Changing City: Boston 2030
Report by creating 18 new units of affordable homeownership housing including three studio units,
nine one-bedroom units, three two-bedroom units, and three three-bedroom units. The building will
include three handicap accessible units, a common / community space, indoor bicycle storage, as well
as open space to the rear of the building and nine off-street parking spaces.
The redevelopment of 270 Talbot Avenue (Site) has been in the works for many years. The City of
Boston Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) first issued an RFP for the Site in 2015. No
developer was selected at that time due to neighborhood concerns. When DND re-issued the RFP in
2018, TLD met with the community and crafted a joint response with Codman Square Neighborhood
Development Corporation (CSNDC) whereby TLD would develop workforce rental housing on the

portion of the Site. On January 28, 2019, CSNDC and TLee Development were awarded Tentative

Project Summary
This Small Project Review Application is being submitted by TLee Development LLC (TLD or
Proponent) in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). The
project consists of the development of a portion of parcel # 1700593000 located at 270 Talbot
Avenue and parcel #1700592000 located on Spencer Street in the Codman Square neighborhood of
Dorchester (the “Site”) to create eighteen affordable condominium units in a four story building with
3117 SF of retail space and nine parking spaces, including one handicap accessible parking space.
270 Talbot Avenue consists of two adjoining parcels of land totaling approximately 0.6 acres, or
24,714 square feet, situated at the intersection of Talbot Avenue and Spencer Street. The Site is
currently owned by the City of Boston and contains three attached single-story structures with three
garages, a central parking area, and smaller parking areas to the north and west. On January 28,
2019, CSNDC and TLee Development were designated by the City of Boston as the redevelopers of
270 Talbot Avenue and Spencer Street through a Request for Proposals process. The proposal
submitted by CSNDC and TLee Development included the development by TLD of the Proposed
Project on the Talbot Ave portion of the Site (Talbot Ave Building) and the development by CSNDC of
an affordable housing multi-family building on the Spencer Street portion of the Site.
TLD proposes to develop the Talbot Ave Building to create three studio units, nine one-bedroom
units, three two-bedroom units, and three three-bedroom units for a total of 18 new affordable
residential homeownership units (Proposed Project). The Proposed Project will include three
handicapped accessible units, 3117 SF of ground floor retail space, a common / community room and
bicycle storage. Open outdoor space will be shared by the residents directly behind the building. The
parking lot will be accessed off of Spencer Street and will be connected with parking for the CSNDC
development on Spencer Street.
The Proposed Project will offer studio, one-, two-, and three-bedroom units to households earning

II.
Detailed Project Information
Project Site Description
The project consists of a portion of two adjoining parcels of land, parcel # 1700593000 and parcel
#1700592000, totaling 24,714 square feet. Both parcels are currently owned by the City of Boston.
The site is an irregular shaped lot with an address of 270 Talbot Avenue and Spencer Street. The lot
has frontage on both Talbot Avenue and Spencer Street.
The Site is currently improved by a former single-story structure with three automobile repair
garages, a large central parking area, and smaller parking areas to the north and west. The Site is
currently used to store equipment used by a local landscaping business.
To the east of the Site, along Spencer Street, there are two- and three-family homes. To the south
and west of the site, along Talbot Avenue is a mix of commercial and multi-family residential uses. To
the north is a residential neighborhood of a mix of housing types.
The Site is close to a variety of amenities, many that are along or just off of Talbot Avenue,
Washington Street or Norfolk Street. These include, but are not limited to, America’s Food Basket,
Walgreens, the Codman Square Branch of the Boston Public Library, a Post Office, a dry cleaner,
several churches, salons/barber shops, convenience stores, small shops, and restaurants. The Site is
also located in close proximity to parks and recreation areas, including Elmhurst Park and Harambee
Park.
Residents of the Proposed Project will enjoy proximity to public transportation. There is a covered
bus stop served by MBTA bus routes 22 and 45 at the front of the site along Talbot Avenue, and the
Talbot Avenue Commuter Rail Station on the Fairmount Line is less than a three minute walk down
Talbot Avenue. These transportation amenities provide access to employment centers in Greater
Boston.
The Site is currently classified as a Tier 2 disposal site. The City of Boston became the owner of the
Site due to tax foreclosure. The City carried out certain assessment and remedial work under the
Massachusetts Contingency Plan to make sure there were no Imminent Hazard conditions or impacts
to abutters. As of the most recent filing with the Department of Environmental Protection in
September 2018, the recommendation is that any further remediation work should be conducted at
the time of redevelopment of the Site. The Proponent has contracted with Goldman Environmental
Consultants, Inc. to carry out response actions in conjunction with the Proposed Project and has
initiated groundwater sampling and other assessment activities. A MassDevelopment’s Brownfields
Grant was awarded to the Proponent to carry out the environmental assessment and remedial
activity.

Design Approach
270 Talbot Ave is a proposed development consisting of 18 income-restricted residential
condominium units and 2 retail spaces. The site comprises an irregularly shaped lot, bounded by
Spencer St on the North and East and by Talbot Ave at the South. The Project Site consists of a
vacant existing 1-story building. The Proposed Project consists of a 4-story wood-framed building
which will offer approximately 3117 SF of retail space and 17,007 SF of residential space distributed
through 18 condominiums, ranging in size from studios to three-bedroom units.
The Proposed Project retains the streetscape by placing the parking area to the rear of the site.
Located at the North of the building, this area will consist of 9 parking spaces. Along both Talbot and
Spencer streets, the parking spaces are set back to allow for a landscape buffer with outdoor space
and bench seating for the residents. The building footprint includes a triangular wedge, chamfered at
the Talbot Ave / Spencer St corner. This enlarges the sidewalk at the intersection, creating a
welcoming public front for the building in close proximity to the retail entries.
Located on a street which is home to both residential and light industrial uses, the Proposed Project
makes a contemporary contribution to, and reinforces, the residential character of the street and
neighborhood. The building deploys two different facade treatments. The Talbot Ave facade wraps
around the chamfered corner and consists of a series of protruding vertical bays, which relate directly
to the character and proportions of surrounding residences. The Spencer St facade adds a horizontal
element between the third and fourth floors to visually reduce the scale of the building massing and
incorporates lap siding, a similar material found on surrounding residences.
9

Sustainability
The Proposed Project will be constructed to meet zero carbon emission standards that consider both
operational performance, EUI (energy use intensity) and cost measures. To achieve these standards
of sustainability, the Proposed Project will be modeled in WUFI passive and will use Passive House
design criteria as a baseline metric.
Transportation, Access and Parking
The Proposed Project will provide 9 on-site uncovered parking spaces, located at the North side of
the building. The parking driveway will connect to Spencer St via a new curb cut.
Secure and covered bicycle racks with the capacity to store 21 bicycles will be provided in the new
building, with an additional bicycle rack for 7 bicycles to be provided outside the building.
The Project Site is a five-minute walk (approximately 0.2 miles on foot) from the Talbot Ave MBTA
Station, which serves the Commuter Rail Line and numerous bus lines; as such the Proposed Project
represents a transit-oriented development opportunity.

Public Review Process
In 2015, the City issued a Request for Proposals for 270 Talbot Avenue to which CSNDC responded
with a proposed project to create affordable housing. The community expressed concern about the
proposal, primarily because an all affordable housing development would take too long to get
approved and into construction. The City re-issued the RFP in 2018. This time, CSNDC responded to
community feedback by partnering with TLD to create a unique proposal that addressed concerns
regarding the speed with which the project could be developed and the levels of affordability. On
March 28, 2018, CSNDC and TLd jointly submitted a proposal that creates a mix of workforce
housing units and affordable rental housing units. The community supported this proposal because it
enables part of the site, the Talbot Avenue portion, to proceed more expeditiously due to the fact that
10

it does not rely on public affordable housing funds to complete the project. Further, the proposal as a
whole offers a greater range of affordable housing. On January 28, 2019, the City designated CSNDC
and TLD as the redeveloper of 270 Talbot Avenue, with TLD constructing a new multi-family mixed
use building on the Talbot Avenue portion of the site, and CSNDC constructing a new residential
multi-family building along the Spencer Street portion of the site
Since the designation of CSNDC and TLD as the redevelopers of 270 Talbot Avenue, TLD has been
working with its architect (Studio Luz) and the CSNDC team to establish a Master Site Plan for the
project. On April 12, 2019, CSNDC and TLee Development jointly met with the BPDA and DND design
review staff to further develop the master plan of the 270 Talbot Avenue site. After several iterations
of the plan, and a subsequent meeting on July 22, 2019, the BPDA and City approved the master site
plan.
On September 24, 2019, CSNDC and TLD presented the Master Site Plan as well as individual plans
for each building at a neighborhood community meeting held by the Talbot-Norfolk Triangle
Community Improvement Association (TNT-CIA). The community held a vote at the TNT meeting to
approve the Talbot Ave Building. Meanwhile, TLD continued its dialogue with the community
regarding the Talbot Ave Building through the Article 80 review process and the Zoning Board of
Appeals process and obtained approvals in 2020.
Labor shortages and material price increases related to the COVID-19 pandemic made the rental
housing project, as planned, infeasible.
In January 2022, TLD sent a memo to the Mayor’s Office of Housing (MOH) describing the financial
challenges facing the project and requesting approval to convert the workforce rental component of
the project to affordable condominiums. MOH staff advised TLD to share the proposed change with
community members to determine the extent of community support for the change.
In February, TLD met with leaders of key civic organizations abutting the Site—including TNT-CIA, the
West of Washington Coalition (WoW), and Erie-Ellington Neighborhood Association—to gauge their
interest in the change. After receiving affirmative responses from these leaders, TLD presented the
proposed changes at the March meeting of the West of Washington Coalition, which had been
advertised to members of TNT-CIA as well as other nearby residents outside of WoW’s catchment
area. Following the meeting, both the WoW and TNT-CIA board members voted to support the
project change, and provided signed letters of support to TLD in late March. District 4 City Councilor
Brian Worrell was also represented at the WoW meeting and provided a letter of support in early
April 2020.
TLD will continue to provide periodic updates to community members as the project moves through
the Notice of Project Change review process.

Exhibit 8: Proposed Building Program
Design Approach
270 Talbot Ave is a proposed development consisting of 18 income-restricted residential
condominium units and 2 retail spaces. The site comprises an irregularly shaped lot, bounded by
Spencer St on the North and East and by Talbot Ave at the South. The Project Site consists of a
vacant existing 1-story building. The Proposed Project consists of a 4-story wood-framed building
which will offer approximately 3,117 SF of retail space and 17,007 SF of residential space distributed
through 18 condominiums, ranging in size from studio to three-bedroom units.
The Proposed Project retains the residential scale by maintaining a large backyard that creates an
entry plaza from the parking area. Located at the North of the building, this area will consist of 9
parking spaces. The building footprint includes a triangular wedge, chamfered at the Talbot Ave /
Spencer St corner. This enlarges the sidewalk at the intersection, creating a welcoming public front
for the building in close proximity to the retail entries.
Located on a street which is home to both residential and light industrial uses, the Proposed Project
makes a contemporary contribution to, and reinforces, the residential character of the street and
neighborhood. The building deploys two different facade treatments. The Talbot Ave facade wraps
around the chamfered corner and consists of undulating panels that visually reduce the scale of the
building massing. The Spencer St facade expresses a residential character by emphasizing vertical
bays, relating directly to proportions of the surrounding residences.
Sustainability
The Proposed Project will be constructed to meet zero carbon emission standards that consider both
operational performance, EUI (energy use intensity) and cost measures. To achieve these standards
of sustainability, the Proposed Project will be modeled in WUFI passive and will use Passive house
design criteria as a baseline metric. The following baseline criteria will be met; air-tight envelope that
meets 0.06 cfm / sf air tightness requirement, a thermally broken envelope with continuous
insulation; triple-glazed windows (min. 0.22 U-value); a rain screen wall assembly, 75% of clear roof
area to support solar PV arrays; high-efficiency heating/cooling system (3.0 C.O.P), heat recovery
ventilation system for fresh air (min. 57% efficiency); air-tight compartmentalized residential units;
low water consumption fixtures; LED lighting; low/no VOC finishes.
Transportation, Access and Parking
The Proposed Project will provide 9 on-site uncovered parking spaces, located at the North side of
the building. The parking driveway will connect to Spencer St via a new curb cut.
Secure and covered bicycle racks with the capacity to store 21 bicycles will be provided in the new
building, with an additional bicycle rack for 7 bicycles to be provided outside the building.
The Project Site is a five-minute walk (approximately 0.2 miles on foot) from the Talbot Ave MBTA
Station, which serves the Commuter Rail Line and numerous bus lines; as such the Proposed Project
represents a transit-oriented development opportunity.

This building will contain two retail areas on the ground floor, classified as Use Group M. The Bicycle

Building Area:
The proposed building area for 270 Talbot Ave. of 5,985 s.f. is well within the 36,000 sf allowance

31

Aggregate Building Area:
The maximum allowed aggregate area is three times the maximum allowed Building Area.
36,000 x 3 = 108,000 sf. The actual aggregate building area is 22,399 sf, and therefore compliant.
Building Height:
IBC defines “Building Height” as “the vertical distance from the grade plane to the average height of
the highest roof surface.” Mechanical penthouses occupying one-third or less of the roof surface
below do not contribute to the calculation of building height in either feet or stories.
Construction Type:
Construction Type VA requires a fire-resistant primary structural frame of 1 hour. Also please see
discussion of fire separation distance below.
Frame Hourly Rating:
In addition to 1 hour of fire-resistance on the primary structural frame, any building component
required to be rated, such as shafts and dwelling unit separations, must be supported by construction
of an equivalent fire-resistance.
Shafts:
Whether for mechanical ducts, elevators or stairs, shafts must be separated from adjacent spaces to
prevent fire spread between stories. As vehicles for stack effect, the taller the shaft, the more
potential for air movement, and therefore for spread of smoke and fire. For this reason a shaft that
exceeds three stories in height must be rated to achieve a 2 hour fire-resistance, whereas shafts that
are three stories or less are only required to provide 1 hour.
Fire Separation Distance:
Fire separation distance regulates exterior wall ratings and the allowed percentage of exterior
openings based on distance to the centerline of a public way, an interior lot line, or an imaginary line
between two buildings on the same lot. Fire separation distance for the proposed building is
sufficient to not require exterior wall ratings and to allow unlimited openings on all exterior walls.
Dwelling Unit Separations:
A fully sprinkled dwelling unit in construction type VA is required to have 1 hour of fire-resistance for
unit separations (780 CMR 708.3). As mentioned above, all supporting construction must be
equivalent.
Fire Protection:
The building will be provided with sprinklers throughout in conformance with NFPA-13. The alarm
system will sound upon sprinkler waterflow. Standpipes will be required if the floor level of the
highest story is located more than 30 feet above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access.
A manual fire alarm system that activates the occupant notification system is not required if the
notification appliances will automatically activate upon a sprinkler water flow. Single- or
multiple-station smoke alarms shall be installed and maintained on the ceiling or wall outside of each
separate sleeping area and in each room used for sleeping. Carbon monoxide detection is required
outside of each separate sleeping area. Emergency responder radio coverage is required in all new
buildings.
32

Egress:
The remoteness of proposed egress from all floors meets the minimum requirement of 1/3 the
maximum overall diagonal distance. Exit signs and means of egress emergency lighting will be
provided with emergency standby power.
Elevator:
The elevator will meet the cab size requirement for movement and transportation of stretchers. The
elevator is not required to be provided with emergency standby power as it does not serve four floors
above the level of exit discharge.

2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new four-story residential building situated at 27 Farragut 
Road in South Boston’s City Point neighborhood. The project site is a 9,401 square foot site 
currently occupied by a single-story commercial building with surface parking. The applicant 
proposes a new of twenty-one unit residential apartment building, with twenty-one accessory 
garage parking spaces, and bicycle storage in accordance with Boston Transportation 
Department policy requirements. 
 
 

27 Farragut Road Residential Project 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of twenty-one new dwelling units in an attractive low-rise building, 
including three affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy; 
 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
 
• the expected creation of approximately fifty construction industry jobs to complete the 
proposed project; 
 
• a bikeshare contribution to the Boston Transportation Department in the amount of 
$5,775, in accordance with Boston’s Bike Parking guidelines; 
 
• a community benefits package to be determined in conjunction with the BPDA and City 
agencies; 
 
4. 
Project Financing and Developer Pro Forma 
 
The owners and developers enjoy an extensive record of development success in Boston, enjoy 
a strong working relationship with several local lenders, and intend to finance the project using 
traditional institutional financing.

5. 
Urban Design Overview, Building Massing & Design, Materials 
 
The redevelopment of 27 Farragut Road will transform an underutilized single-story commercial 
structure into a residential centerpiece on a street corner with direct views to water and access 
to public open space. In a rapidly transforming area, the development will add 21 new residential 
rental units to the neighborhood, with accompanying amenities and ancillary support spaces. The 
site is on the corner of Farragut Road and East Second Street, with the proposed development 
capping the contiguous block of housing along Farragut Road. With two street frontages, the 
proposed building will have well-considered and thoughtfully-located access points and 
openness, with a proposed curb extension at the street corner providing a safer and more com- 
 

27 Farragut Road Residential Project 
 
fortable pedestrian experience connecting East Second Street to the public amenities of the 
skating rink, fields, and courts located on the side of Farragut Road. 
 
27 Farragut Road is proposed as a four-story building with a ground-level podium of enclosed 
parking, residential support, and amenity spaces, and streetscape and rear yard improvements. 
There are three proposed floors above the ground floor with 21 metro size units consisting of a 
mix of studio, two-bedroom, and three-bedroom units. Back at grade, the building’s lobby, 
lounge, and indoor bike parking will be featured along the Farragut Road streetscape. 
 
The building’s footprint and massing take dimensional cues from its abutting context, matching 
existing modal setbacks, massing, and heights. Along Farragut Road, the proposed front setback 
matches the modal setback of its neighbors at 35 and 37 Farragut Road, maintaining and 
continuing the rhythm of bays and decks above ground floor that provide views and outdoor 
access for the units above. Streetwall continuity is kept rounding the corner onto East Second 
Street, with setbacks again matching the abutting twenty-one unit apartment building at 933 East 
Second Street. The proposed building is similar in height to its abutters, matching the number of 
stories of its 933 East Second Street neighbor, while being a story below the building at 35 
Farragut Road. 
 
The exterior character of the proposed design is a contemporary interpretation of classic 
materials and cladding methods vernacular to New England housing. A variated vertical board 
and batten cladding adorns the main façade; with insets, reveals, and other modulations to the 
main façade clad in a wood-look vertical siding. A durable stone skirt surrounds the building at 
grade, providing a solid base to the building, punctured by large expanses of storefront glazing 
providing an open and welcoming streetscape presence. Generously sized window openings 
provide ample light and view for the units, with Juliet guardrails in select areas adding scale and 
detail while offering another layer of exterior access for tenants. 
 
6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The proposed project’s 21 dwelling units will be served by 21 motor vehicle parking spaces 
located in an at-grade garage to be accessed by a single new curb cut on East Second Street. The 
building will also feature secure interior resident bicycle storage, and outside visitor post-and-
ring assemblies, in compliance with the City of Boston’s bicycle parking requirements. The site is 
located within walking distance of bus stops on MBTA bus routes 7 and 9, both of which provide 
easy direct access to Red Line rapid transit.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

Dear Director Jemison: 
 
 
It is my pleasure to submit this application for Small Project Review pursuant to Article 
80, Section 80E, of the Boston Zoning Code, for the 281 Franklin Street Office to Residential 
Conversion Project in downtown Boston (the “Proposed Conversion Project”). 
 
 
The Proposed Conversion Project consists of the conversion of the six-story building 
located at 281-285 Franklin Street in downtown Boston from its present occupancy of a 
restaurant with take-out and a shoe repair store on the ground floor, and upper-story offices, to 
the same ground-floor uses with fifteen (15) new dwelling units on floors two through six. The 
building in question is the historically significant Henry Gustavus Dorr Building, an 1878 brick and 
sandstone mercantile building designed by architects Abel C. Martin and William M. Rumney for 
Henry Gustavus Dorr, a Boston merchant. 
 
 
The applicant, and my client, is Boston Pinnacle Properties and its principal, Adam Burns. 
Architectural services are being provided by Balance Architects and Philip Sima, with engineering 
and building code compliance services being provided by the Sullivan Code Group/R.W. Sullivan 
Engineering. Attorney Deborah A. Ryan is providing expertise with respect to compliance of the 
conversion with state and local accessibility requirements. MEP services are being handled by 
Zade Associates LLC, and structural services by Forest Structural Engineering. 
 
 
The Proposed Conversion is intended to take advantage of, and comply with, the 
provisions of the Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive Pilot Program (the “Conversion 
Program”) for unused downtown office building space. This will include a PILOT agreement with 
the City of Boston and the BPDA, fulfillment of the Conversion Program’s affordable housing 

281 Franklin Street Office to Residential Conversion 
requirement of 17% of all newly created units being submitted to the provisions of the 
Inclusionary Development Policy, compliance with the requirements of the Stretch Energy Code, 
and a fast-tracked Article 80 approval and Inspectional Services Department permitting process. 
 
A set of schematic design architectural plans depicting the details of the building 
conversion, as well as a site plan, are submitted herewith. It is noted that the interior renovation 
work, as well as the change of legal occupancy, are intended to be fully compliant with the 
requirements of the Boston Zoning Code and, as such, will not require review and approval by 
the Zoning Board of Appeal. The estimated cost of work is $1,599,000. 
 
On behalf of Boston Pinnacle Properties and Adam Burns, and the entire development 
team, I wish to thank the BPDA for its guidance and assistance to date in this matter, in particular 
John Weil, Matt Donovan, Dylan Norris, and Michael Sinatra. We look forward to continuing to 
work closely with the BPDA and relevant City of Boston departments and agencies in order to 
complete this exciting conversion proposal. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Very truly yours, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
George Morancy, Esq.

Re: APPLICATION FOR ARTICLE 80 SMALL PROJECT REVIEW AND 
REVIEW PURSUANT TO THE DOWNTOWN RESIDENTIAL CONVERSION 
INCENTIVE PILOT PROGRAM 
 
Dear Director Shen: 
 
This office represents the legal interests of Franklin Holdings Group, LLC (the 
“Applicant”) with respect to the above reference matter. 
 
It is my pleasure to submit this application for Small Project Review pursuant to 
Article 80, Section 80E, of the Boston Zoning Code, for an Office to Residential 
Conversion Project in downtown Boston located at 295-297 Franklin Street (the 
“Proposed Conversion Project”). 
 
The Proposed Conversion Project consists of the re-use of a pre-existing five 
(5) story building located at 295-297 Franklin Street in downtown Boston from its 
present occupancy of commercial space on the ground floor, and upper-story offices, 
to approximately 744 square feet of ground floor retail and eighteen (18) new 
dwelling units on floors one through five. Located in the B-10 Zoning Subdistrict, the 
site consists of a 2,430 square foot lot with existing gross floor area of 14,580 square 
feet, which includes a basement to be re-purposed for bike storage and other 
building services. 
 
The subject building, which is being preserved, is a historically significant 
structure known as the Bowker Building (See Inventory No. BOS.1749) located within 
the National Register Custom House District. It was originally constructed as a four 
and one half story Queen Anne, four (4) bay structure combining 2nd Empire and 
medieval stylistic vocabulary, which was constructed c. 1870 by John Bates, Jr. 
However, it has been substantially rehabilitated since the 1980 MACRIS Inventory 

 
 
was competed including the addition of a fifth story to the rear half of the building 
(See MACRIS Abstract attached). 
 
The applicant is Franklin Holdings Group, LLC and its principals are Jiahoa Chi 
and Dong Chi. Architectural and building code compliance services are being 
provided by DMS Design, LLC and Daniel M. Skolski, AIA, NCARB, with structural 
engineering to be provided by H+O Structural Engineers, and MEP services are 
being handled by BLW Engineers, Inc.

ADDITIONAL ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
The building has been substantially rehabilitated since the 1980 inventory form was completed. An inappropriate in-fill storefront 
has been replaced with a more compatible installation. Window sash have been replaced and false shutters added to the 
Franklin Street façade. A fifth story had already been added to the rear half of the building. 
 
ADDITIONAL HISTORICAL NARRATIVE 
By 1883 the two lots comprising what is today 295-297 Franklin Street were combined under the name of merchant John D. 
Bates, Jr. and the extant building erected. Bates was the son and heir of John D. Bates, a wealthy Boston merchant, whose 
house on the corner of Commonwealth and Arlington streets overlooking the Public Garden was a local landmark. (A marble 
statue of Venus in the midst of fountains in the Public Garden was presented by Bates to the city in celebration of the new water 
system.) The elder Bates was born in 1805 in Concord where his father, Caleb Bates, was a merchant. Caleb had been a ship 
captain having made many trips to Europe, and he sent his young son to apprentice in a mercantile house in Holland.1 John D. 
Bates returned to Boston in 1820 and became a clerk in the Central Wharf trading house of Nathan Bridge. When Bridge died in 
1830, Bates and another clerk, Adam W. Thatcher, took over the business, later renaming it John D. Bates & Co.2 Bates further 
assured his fortune when he married Mary Bordman around 1834. She was the daughter of China trader William H. (Beau Bill) 
Bordman. Her sister, Elizabeth, was the young widow of Harrison Gray Otis, Jr., the eldest son and namesake of Boston’s 
legendary mayor, and “ruled in elegant society.”3 John D. Bates, Jr., his parents’ only child, inherited his father’s business and 
fortune. He has the notoriety of having married his young Irish cook in 1895, just before he died, making her one of the 
wealthiest women in Boston.4 The building at 295-297 Franklin Street remained with the heirs of John D. Bates well into the 20th 
century.

3 Richard Hildreth, Our First Men, A Calendar of Wealth, Fashion and Gentility, Iss. 1 (1846), p. 33. 
4 Bruce D. Heald , Around Squam Lake (2002), p. 46.

The “B” carved in the sandstone medallion at the top of the central gable dormer on the Franklin Street façade probably does not 
represent Bates’s ownership; rather it likely denotes his first tenant, Dr. Horace L. Bowker, manufacturing chemist, city vinegar 
inspector, state assayer, city councilor, and state representative. Bowker was born in Phillipston, Massachusetts, in 1832 and 
arrived in Boston in 1861, where he commenced the practice of medicine. About eight years later, he went into business as a 
manufacturing chemist at 132 Milk Street. Bowker advertised various pharmaceutical remedies and flavored soda. The 1883 
city directory locates his business at 195 Franklin Street. Bowker was elected a member of the City Council of Boston in 1864, 
and served in the Legislatures of 1873, 1875 and 1878. He was appointed State Assayer for Massachusetts in 1877.5 An 
advertisement in an 1883 issue of American Druggist carried the following advertisement (see illustration below). 
 
The finest flavors; the largest variety; the best-selling drinks in the world. Cold, sparkling and delicious. 
Established in 1864. They can be drawn at any soda fountain at a cost of one and one-half cents per glass. Out of 
several hundred different varieties, the most popular beverages have been Dr. Bowker's birch beer, root, bitter 
beer, ginger ale and fruit flavors. For any and all soda water preparations, new or old, send direct to us; ask as 
many questions as you like, and get the best of everything. Beware of imitations of our goods, which have been 
extensively counterfeited. Order from wholesale druggists, our local agents, or direct from the house. Send for our 
fifty-page catalogue. No drummers.6 
 
By 1904 Bowker had moved his business to 58 Eastern Avenue and the National Coal Tar Company; another chemical 
manufacturing firm took occupancy of the premises. In 1913 the building was occupied by the Boston office of the Barrett 
Manufacturing Company, a chemical firm based in Everett, Massachusetts. By 1921 two electrical supply houses were at the 
address: the Boston branch office and warehouse of the Arrow Electric Company, makers of electrical wiring in Hartford, 
Connecticut and S.B. Condit, Jr. & Co., who represented Garland Manufacturing Company, of West Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, 
makers of armored cables and metal conduit. Condit Electrical Manufacturing Company occupied the building at 76-78 
Batterymarch Street, around the corner, between 1908 and 1913. The building has been assessed as commercial since 1984. 
The first floor houses retail businesses, while the upper floors are devoted to office use.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

29 High Street Residential Project 
2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new three-story residential building situated at 28 High Street 
in Dorchester’s Meeting House Hill neighborhood. The project is located on a vacant 32,663 
square foot parcel and proposes the creation of thirty-one residential condominium units, with 
twenty-three accessory garage parking spaces, and bicycle storage in accordance with Boston 
Transportation Department policy requirements. The three-quarter acre site will benefit from 
expansive landscaped open space, with approximately 56% of the site being left unoccupied by 
the new building’s footprint. 
 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of thirty-one new condominium units in an attractive low-rise building, 
including five affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy; 
 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
 
• the expected creation of approximately fifty construction industry jobs to complete the 
proposed project; 
 
• a bikeshare contribution to the Boston Transportation Department in the amount of 
$8,525, in accordance with Boston’s Bike Parking guidelines; 
 
• a community benefits package to be determined in conjunction with the BPDA and City 
agencies; 
 
4. 
Project Financing and Developer Pro Forma 
 
The owners and developers enjoy an extensive record of development success in Boston, enjoy 
a strong working relationship with several local lenders, and intend to finance the project using 
traditional institutional financing.

29 High Street Residential Project 
5. 
Urban Design Approach 
 
The proposed project is located within the Meeting House Hill neighborhood and will consist of 
a new three-story multi-family building with a below-grade garage. There will be 31 residential 
condominium units, a rear communal patio, 23 garage parking spaces, and 44 bicycle parking 
spaces. The site is a short walk away from multiple MBTA bus stops as well as the Savin Hill and 
Fields Corner rapid transit stations on the MBTA’s Red Line. The proposed design is a 
contemporary expression of a townhouse that breaks down the scale of the massing by 
incorporating two uniquely designed façades along the High Street frontage with a central access 
to the residential lobby. The mansard roof, 2-over-1 windows, decorative columns, covered front 
porch, and the proposed materiality not only blend with the vernacular of the local architecture, 
but also with the historical nature of the neighborhood. A majority of the landscaping, rock 
outcroppings, and trees in the rear yard will be incorporated into the new design to maintain the 
natural shaded beauty of the site and to provide pleasant communal space for residents and their 
guests. Well over half the site will remain unbuilt, with the majority of the resulting open space 
being landscaped recreation space. 
 
6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The proposed project’s 31 dwelling units will be served by 23 motor vehicle parking spaces 
located in a below-grade garage to be accessed by a single new curb cut on High Street. The 
building will also feature secure interior resident bicycle storage, and outside visitor post-and-
ring assemblies, in compliance with the City of Boston’s bicycle parking requirements. The site is 
located approximately 12 minutes’ walking distance from the Savin Hill Red Line station, and 
approximately 16 minutes from the Fields Corner Red Line Station, with additional easy access to 
numerous MBTA bus stops.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in Boston’s 
built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, rather than after 
a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a 
built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

communities

Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in the

A. 
INTRODUCTION 
NFLSRE 2 Financial LLC (the “Proponent”) is pleased to submit this Small Project Review 
Application (“SPRA”) for the proposed renovation and partial conversion of portions of a building 
in the Leather District located at 60 South Street, also known as 2 Financial Center (the “Property” 
or the “Project Site”), to accommodate research laboratory use by life sciences tenants (the 
“Project”). The partial change of use, which is allowed under the City of Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”), is expected to provide much-needed space for life sciences tenants in support of 
economic development within the Leather District, consistent with the Boston Planning and 
Development Agency’s Life Sciences Action Agenda for encouraging growth in the life sciences 
industry in the City. 
The Proponent is an affiliate of Nan Fung Life Sciences Real Estate (“NFLSRE”), a real estate 
investment and development platform focused on acquiring, developing, and managing life 
sciences related properties in innovation-driven markets across the U.S. and U.K. NFLSRE is a 
subsidiary of Nan Fung Group, a Hong Kong based holding company focused on real estate 
investment and development. The NFLSRE team is based in Boston, and led by an experienced 
management team that collectively has spent more than 75 years in the local Boston and 
Cambridge life science industry and has developed 5.0 million square feet of life sciences real 
estate.

PROJECT SUMMARY 
The Property is currently improved by a 12-story, approximately 218,000 square foot (“sf”) office 
building, constructed in 2007, with ground floor retail space and three subsurface parking levels 
containing approximately 200 parking spaces (the “Building”). The Project’s conversion of space 
in the Building to life sciences use, which is an allowed use, involves: 
1. Conversion and renovation of four floors of the Building from the current office use 
to a mix of office and Bio-Safety Level 2 (BSL-2) research laboratory use; and 
2. In conformance with the Leather District’s guidelines for rooftop structures, 
installation of mechanical equipment on the roof to serve the research laboratory 
uses; and 
3. In conformance with the Leather District’s guidelines for rooftop structures, redesign 
the existing roof deck to allow for the new mechanical equipment. 
The total space converted to research laboratory use (rather than renovated for continued office 
use) is approximately 21,535 sf of Gross Floor Area (GFA). The Project contemplates no material 
changes to parking or loading. 
As further described below, Small Project Review is required for the Project pursuant to the 
design regulations set forth in Article 44-8 of the Code, which governs certain rooftop 
improvements within the Leather District. 
D. 
ARTICLE 80E REVIEW THRESHOLD 
Section 44-8 of the Code requires the Design Component of Small Project Review for any project 
within the Leather District that includes a rooftop addition (such as rooftop mechanical units) 
that is not visible from a street within the Leather District. As noted above, the Project will add 
mechanical equipment on the roof to serve the research laboratory uses, and will redesign the 
existing roof deck. As such, Small Project Review is required to confirm the Project’s consistency 
with the design guidelines in Section 44-8. The Project has been designed to be consistent with 
these guidelines. The local Architect and Engineering teams have designed and located the 
proposed rooftop mechanical units and redesigned roof deck so as not to be visible from a public 
way within the Leather District. 
E. 
DETAILED PROJECT INFORMATION 
The Project will convert approximately 40% of the existing office space across four floors to 
research laboratory uses. The floor plates range from 16,357 to 16,517 sf; the current office use
