is 13,621 sf to 13,461 sf per floor, with the remaining square footage being building services and 
corridors. The Proponent expects that 21,535 sf across the four floors will be converted to 
research laboratory space. 
F. 
ANTICIPATED ZONING RELIEF 
The Property is located in the Leather District zoning district governed by Article 44 of the Code. 
The Property is also located in the Greenway Overlay District (GWOD) governed by Article 49A, 
the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD) governed by Article 32, the Coastal Flood 
Resilience Overlay District (CFROD) governed by Article 25A, and the Restricted Parking Overlay 
District (RPOD) regulations. The regulations of the GWOD, GCOD, CFROD, and RPOD do not apply 
to the Project, which involves only the renovation and change of use of certain floors within the 
Building, and the changes to the rooftop structures described herein. 
The Building’s current office and retail uses are allowed as of right in the Leather District, as is 
the planned research laboratory use. 
Section 44-6 of the Code requires a conditional use permit to erect or enlarge a roof structure 
designed or used for human occupancy, access, mechanical systems, or storage. Roof structures 
are required to be designed so as not to be visible from any public way within the Leather District. 
The Project’s screened or enclosed mechanical equipment on the roof serving the proposed 
research laboratory uses have been designed to comply with the visibility standard in Section 44-
6, and will be constructed with metal exteriors as specified in Section 44-6. Likewise, the 4,000 sf 
roof deck will be redesigned to run along the south and west sides of the roof and will be below 
all site lines within the Leather District. The roof deck will be redesigned to the same size (4,000 
sf) with similar materials and finishes to the existing roof deck, and will comply with all Leather 
District design and code requirements. 
G. 
DESIGN APPROACH 
 The Project, which is primarily an interior renovation of the Building, is designed to embrace the 
character of the Building and increase its usefulness. Internally, the research laboratory and 
office spaces are laid out to take advantage of the shape of the Building, focused on maximizing 
daylight and views from occupied spaces, and re-using the Building’s existing core elements for 
minimum disruption. Upgrading elevators and building infrastructure will increase future 
tenants’ experience and utility of the existing structure for the Project’s uses. 
The renovation project is supported by the minor modification to the rooftop mechanical 
systems. The Building footprint and overall Building envelope will not change. There will not be 
any visible exterior renovations to the building. 
The Project’s new mechanical, electrical and plumbing (“MEP”) equipment will be more 
environmentally friendly than the existing equipment which is 15 years old. The new MEP 
equipment is also designed to support the City’s sustainability initiatives, including BERDO 3.0. 
The design plans for the Project’s rooftop mechanical equipment contemplate air handling units, 
chillers, an emergency generator, and the like. This equipment will be below the sight lines from 
all public ways in the Leather District. During the equipment design process, the appropriate low-
noise mechanical equipment will be selected and potential noise mitigation measures will be 
employed. Overall, the sound levels associated with the Project’s rooftop mechanical equipment 
are expected to be minimal and will comply with the City of Boston’s noise standards.

Project Summary 
 
The Proposed Project consists of the development of two (2) sites in Orient Heights Square: (a) a 
9,409 square-foot site situated at 2 Ford Street in East Boston, which will consist of a proposed 
new four story, mixed use multifamily residential/retail building, containing twenty seven (27) 
residential units, 1,593 square feet of ground floor retail, eighteen (18) accessory off-street 
parking spaces and bike storage, trash and recycling, and building amenities all located within 
the building’s at 3,538 square-foot at grade garage. The garage for 2 Ford Street will be entered 
and exited via Boardman Street, which has direct access to McLellan Highway and Saratoga Street; 
and (b) a 6,090 square-foot site located across from 2 Ford Street and situated at 970 Saratoga 
Street, which will also consist of a proposed new four story, mixed use multifamily 
residential/retail building, containing fourteen (14) residential units, 2,815 square feet of ground 
floor retail, bike storage, trash and recycling, and building amenities all located at grade. 
 
The Proposed Project would transform two underutilized sites in Orient Heights Square from 
commercial industrial use by creating a mixed use residential/retail development combining both 
market-rate and affordable housing opportunities in an aesthetic appropriate in scale, massing and 
design to the Orient Heights Neighborhood of East Boston, which has considered preliminary 
proposed recommendations for squares and corridors as developed through the ongoing PLAN: East 
Boston initiative. Further, as the sites are located within 900 feet of public transportation with 
access to the MBTA’s Orient Heights Blue Line Rapid Transit station, the Proposed Project will 
provide an additional unique high density housing opportunity for the area with access to public 
transportation. 
 
In planning the buildings, great care was given to respecting the abutting properties, which share 
boundaries with the Site as well as modifications made during the community outreach process and 
discussions with BPDA Staff. As a result, the proposed buildings have been designed and scaled to 
compliment other current and future potential developments in the area and the surrounding streets 
including Saratoga and Boardman Streets, Orient Heights Square and the proximity to public 
transportation.

Boston Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) along with additional ground floor retail opportunities for 
the Orient Heights Square;

Design Approach 
The Proposed Project at 2 Ford Street would consist of a new four-story building. The at grade 
floor will contain 3,395 +/- square feet of an enclosed parking garage intending to accommodate 
the needs of the building’s residents through the provision of 18 parking spaces (8 stackers, 1 
Accessible Space and 1 compact space) and at least 25 bicycle racks along with building 
amenities such as trash storage, lobby space and mechanical space. In addition, there will be 
1,593 square feet of ground level retail space. Floors two, three and four will contain 27 total 
residential units, with a mix of one bedroom two bedroom units. 
As for 970 Saratoga Street, the site will also include a new four-story building to be located on a 
6,090 square-foot site directly across from 2 Ford Street. The program for 970 Saratoga will also be a 
mixed use multifamily residential/retail building, containing fourteen (14) residential units on 
floors two through 4, 2,815 square feet of ground floor retail, bike storage, trash and recycling, 
and building amenities all located at grade. 
Each building’s massing is derived from an assessment of it’s site context and urban conditions. 
A mix of cement fiber board, metal panels and other design elements which are consistent with 
the design standards set forth by the BPDA will provide a strong identity along Orient Heights 
Square and serve to have the building become a focal point. The design will present a unique 
appearance as it relates to its immediate context and will serve as a compelling precedent for the 
area’s future development. 
The design and approach to each site has also taken into account the preliminary 
recommendations of the BPDA with respect to the guidelines for Squares and Corridors as set 
forth under PLAN: East Boston including recommendations regarding height, density and 
streetscape. In addition, 3 of the 4 curb cuts on Boardman Street servicing both 970 Saratoga 
and the vacant lot at 7 Boardman will be retired with only one curb cut remaining to service the 
garage at 2 Ford Street. 
Lastly, the project has taken into consideration the design requirements of Article 25A to address 
the requirements of the Coastal Flood Resiliency Overlay District (“CFROD”). 
Traffic, Parking and Access 
The project’s 18 on-site parking spaces located in the garage of 2 Ford Street will be accessed via a 
single entrance on Boardman Street, which is a two way street leading to Mclellan Highway (Route 
C1 – North and South), Saratoga and Bennington Streets. Vehicles will both enter and discharge 
from the garage on the Boardman Street side of the building. The garage and lobby will have direct 
elevator access provided to all floors in the building. Ample secure space for bicycle racks will be 
provided within each building’s lower level.

Re: 2 Ford Street, East Boston, MA – Article 25A  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
To whom it may concern, 
 
The proposed project at 2 Ford Street offers the following to address Article 25A Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District 
Requirements.  The proposed first floor will be approximately +16.0’. See Level Rise – Base Flood Elevation (SLR‐BFE) is at +19.5’ 
and Sea Level Rise‐ Design Floor Elevation (SLR‐DFE) is at +20.5’ as there is no residential use on the ground floor.  
The Residential units and accessory uses will be located on the second floor and above.  
The Lobby and Elevator are located at approximately +16.0’, flush with the sidewalk in compliance with MAAB requirements. 
The elevator Machine room is located on the second level, above the SLR‐DFE.  
The Retail components will be located at approximately +16.0’, flush with the sidewalk in compliance with MAAB requirements.  
All critical electrical equipment will be located in the Main Electrical Room, above the SLR‐DFE.  
The Parking Area will be located at grade, flush with the sidewalk in compliance with MAAB requirements. An accessible path 
connects the parking area to the Residential Lobby and Elevator.   Electrical equipment related to the parking stackers will be 
located above the SLR‐DFE.  
All portions of the building which are located below the SLR‐DFE will utilize flood‐damage resistant materials per ASCE 21‐14 
and FEMA guidelines.  Material includes concrete and Masonry, metal, cement‐fiber board and tile. No basement is proposed. 
And, removable metal flood barriers will be utilized at the retail and lobby entrances on Boardman St and Ford St.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms:

by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

PROJECT SUMMARY
Project Overview 
This application for Small Project Review is being submitted by Caribbean Integration Community 
Development (the “Proponent”) in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning 
Code (the “Code”). 
The Proponent is submitting this Small Project Review application to develop an elderly affordable 
rental complex. This Article 80 Small Project Review application (the “Application”) with the City of 
Boston Planning Department Agency (BPDA) will utilize the project site to help meet the demand for 
the creation of affordable rental housing for elderly households ages 62 and older. 
Project Description: The Proposed Project consists of one building at the corner of Blue Hill Avenue and 
Gaston Street in Dorchester. The Subject Property is bound by Gaston Street to the north, Blue Hill 
Avenue to the east, a one-story commercial building with a laundromat to the south, and three-story 
homes to the west. The site consists of four vacant parcels. The Proposed Project is a new five-story 
elevator building with 51 income- and age-restricted rental housing units and parking at grade. The 
building will be 48,340 gross square feet. The flat-style units will be age-restricted to households 62 
years old and older. There will be 4 studio units and 47 one-bedroom units. The building will include 
covered parking for 5 vehicles. Residents will have access to a Resident Services Coordinator. Additional 
amenities will include a common room, terrace, landscaped courtyard, leasing office, management 
office, mail and package room, fitness center, and individual meeting rooms. There will be laundry 
rooms on every other floor.
The Proposed Project is consistent with the community goals as defined in the Blue Hill Avenue Action 
Plan, of the Greater Grove Hall and Quincy/Geneva neighborhood, and makes an important 
contribution to the senior housing goals of the City of Boston’s Imagine Boston 2030. 
Design Vision 
The overall design of the Proposed Project responds to community goals for lively, affordable 
housing to accommodate all generations of Dorchester residents. The building has been positioned 
onsite to provide density in the appropriate location and to preserve as many existing trees as 
possible. Vehicular access to the site is provided by a new curb cut at Blue Hill Ave. The new 
driveway abuts the City parcel and provides access to the off-street parking. 
7

Community Vision 
The Proponent met with the HGGOB in April and May 2025, and plans to continue to meet with a range 
of neighborhood association groups, elected officials, and individual abutters to solicit feedback on the 
Proposed Project. The Proposed Project is responsive to the community vision as outlined in the Blue 
Hill Avenue Action Plan, as well as responsive to direct feedback from the HGGOBA. 
Residential Building 
The proposed building form is ‘L’-shaped in plan, and provides appropriate density and massing 
along Blue Hill Avenue. The building’s massing and materials also reflect the proportions and 
typology of the surrounding residential structures. The building is 5 stories and approximately 60’ tall. 
The height allows for 12’ ceilings at the first floor, consistent with other existing and recently 
constructed buildings along Blue Hill Avenue. The first floor will include approximately 1,000 square 
feet of common space divided among a community room, lobby, Management Office, CICD Office, a 
wellness room, and package room. The building will also include two elevators for redundancy 
purposes providing access to all floors. The flat roof will accommodate storage of mechanical 
equipment and will also have the capacity for roof top solar panels. 
Sustainability / Green Building Narrative 
The development team will implement design principles that create a healthier, more resilient 
building, promoting sustainability while achieving energy savings for residents. Our project aims to 
incorporate a variety of sustainable strategies for building operations, including resilient site design 
(such as reducing heat islands, utilizing native or naturalized plantings that are largely drought-
tolerant, and managing rainwater onsite. It will also encourage alternative 
8

transportation options, such as promoting neighborhood walkability and bikeability, as well as 
providing convenient access to public transportation. The Proposed Project will meet the 
maximum heating and cooling efficiency by achieving PassiveHouse certification. The design will 
comply with BERDO and will incorporate many best practices from USGBC and Energy Star 
guidelines and will be solar-ready. The Proposed Project will also be fossil-fuel-free, meeting the 
City of Boston’s Zero-Net Carbon New Construction Guidelines. 
The building has been positioned to be the least impactful to the site, as such we will be able to 
preserve a number of existing trees on the site. The project site will also be designed in 
accordance with the City of Boston Complete Streets Guidelines. 
Public Benefits 
A.
Affordability – Approximately 30% of the units will be designated with a preference to former
homeless individuals. All 51 units will be deed-restricted affordable between the income ranges of 30%
and 60% of Area Median Income (AMI.
B.
Senior Housing – The City of Boston’s Imagine Boston 2030 Comprehensive Plan calls for the
development of an additional 2,000 dedicated senior housing units. Between 2014 and 2020,
production of senior housing units has proceeded at only 75% of that pace. Seniors will continue
to make up a growing proportion of Boston’s population for several years to come, and the
Covid-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical importance of high-quality management in all
senior facilities. The development team has a track record and experience in managing senior
housing properties.
C.
Community Vision – The Proposed Project is responsive to the community vision as outlined in
the Blue Hill Ave Action Plan, and also responsive to direct feedback from community members,
who met with the project team in April and May 2025. The community is pleased that the project
includes retail space at the corner of Blue Hill Avenue and Gaston Street to re-activate this key
intersection.
D.
Minimal Parking & Traffic Impact – Senior housing units have been shown to have a significantly
lower trip-generation and parking demand rate than other types of residential development, and
that the peak parking demand is generally mid-day when service provision occurs.
9

(Source: Institute of Transportation Engineers.) While zoning allows for no parking, the 
Proponent received feedback from neighbors and neighborhood groups that providing parking 
was an important issue to them. In response, the Proponent proposes to provide 10 parking 
spaces, 2 of which will be HC van-accessible. The project will also allow passenger loading off-
street for vans and other vehicles, and parking for residents and visitors will be 
accommodated in a covered parking area. The parking ratio is sufficient to accommodate the 
anticipated peak demand at 25%, limiting congestion and mitigating the project’s impact on 
extremely-limited on-street parking in the vicinity. Bicycle parking is also provided in a 
covered, first-floor space with one bicycle space for every two units. 
E.
Project Development Program
The Proposed Project consists of a single 48,340 gross square foot (GSF) five-story building 
consisting of four-studio and forty-seven one-bedroom senior housing units.
Accessibility-The Proponent seeks to offer a safe and healthy home for seniors to age in place. The 
Proposed Project includes support spaces to serve the specific needs of seniors and will exceed 
minimum accessibility requirements by providing 6 accessible units: (3 Group 2, 3 CBH, and 1 
sensory impaired unit.) The remaining units will be Group 1, and all units will be visitable. All 
common amenities will be located along an accessible route and building entries are at-grade.
F.
Project and Resident Amenities
The Proposed Project will also include the following on-site amenities:
❖A 3,000 square foot green space area
❖A 900 square foot Community Room
❖A 600 square foot on-site Management Office
❖A 400 square foot on-site CICD Office
❖A 400 square foot Wellness Center
❖Five on-site parking spaces
❖A 3,000 square foot ground floor retail space
G.
Community Benefits
The new construction of 329-341 Blue Hill Avenue will benefit the local community in the following 
ways:
10

❖Neighborhood Revitalization- The new building will contribute to the continued revitalization of the
Blue Hill Avenue Corridor. The addition of retail and housing will further activate the resurgent
neighborhood as a place to live, work, and shop.
❖Affordable Housing- Approximately 30% of the units will be designated with a preference for 
formerly homeless individuals. The levels of affordability for all 51 rental units will be deed-
restricted affordability between the income ranges of 30% and 60% of Area Median Income 
(AMI).
❖Re-Activating a Vacant Site-The Proposed Project will re-develop a formerly active and now dormant
parcel of land and further enliven the streetscape.
❖Sustainable Design/Green Building-The 329 Blue Hill Avenue development will meet the maximum
heating and cooling efficiency by achieving PassHouse certification. The design will comply with
BERDO and incorporate many best practices from USGBC and Energy Star Guidelines. The flat roof
will accommodate future photovoltaic panels.
❖Increased Employment-The Proposed Project will generate permanent jobs , and temporary 
construction jobs during the construction phase.
❖Expanding Affordable Housing Opportunities for Seniors- The Proposed Project will increase the
number of high-quality affordable housing for seniors in the Quincy-Geneva neighborhood. The
addition of these housing units is consistent with the goal of providing residents with close proximity
to public transit and access to jobs.
❖Maximizing Public Community and Open Space-The 3,000 square foot green space will provide
opportunities for residents and friends to gather and socialize in a relaxing public gathering space.
❖Creating Transportation Choices-The Proposed Project’s location near reliable public transit will
provide access to employment and basic services.
❖Creating Economic Opportunity-The Proposed Project will generate construction jobs, and an
extensive outreach process will be implemented to maximize opportunities for a diverse
construction workforce, along with a key goal to maximize the diversity of Minority and Women-
Owned Business Enterprise subcontractors on the project.
11

H. Community Engagement
The Proponent has held several meetings with key neighborhood groups, including the Holborn,
Gannett, Gaston, Otisfield Betterment Association (HGGOBA) to get their feedback on the Proposed
Project. 
I.
Response to BPD and MOH Pre-File Comments
Feedback received from the Boston Planning Department (BPDA) and the Mayor’s Office 
of Housing (MOH) at an October 2024 Article 80 Pre-File meeting resulted in several 
design improvements including:
❖Relocate parking to not be visible from Blue Hill Ave
❖Curb cut on Blue Hill Ave
❖Reposition and reshape the building footprint
❖Save as many existing trees as possible in accordance with the Urban Forest Plan
❖Set back entry to increase clearances at the sidewalk for improved access
Project Financing Approach 
Overview of Financing Plan 
At the present time, the estimated cost of this development is $30, 000,000. The financing sources to
support this cost consist of a combination of Federal and State Low Income Housing Tax Credits, the City 
of Boston, the Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities and permanent 
financing. 
The development team has received a Letter of Interest from Bank of America for construction financing 
and a Letter of Interest for permanent financing from the Massachusetts Housing Partnership. 
Based on the anticipated timing of the next City and State funding rounds, we expect the project to start 
construction in early 2028 and be completed eighteen months later.

DETAILED DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM 
Site Description 
The project site is currently vacant and includes four existing, contiguous parcels that will be 
consolidated into one lot totaling 23,000 square feet. The lot has been vacant for over 20 years, but at 
one time was developed for a dry cleaning shop. The Proposed Project seeks to reactivate an under-
utilized parcel on the Blue Hill Avenue Corridor. 
The overall design of the project responds to community goals for lively, safe, and affordable housing to 
accommodate all generations of Dorchester residents. In response to community feedback, the building 
will provide an outdoor space for residents to enjoy. The building is positioned close to Blue Hill 
Avenue, continuing the street wall and activating the street with common spaces located on the lowest 
floor. The apartments are located on first and upper floors. Given the density and traffic in this 
neighborhood and concerns we heard from neighbors about limited parking, we are pleased to provide 
5 off-street parking spaces and a dedicated loading area. The off-street parking is accessed via from 
Blue Hill Avenue. 
Project Development Description 
The proposed development of 329 Blue Hill Avenue is envisioned as a 51-unit affordable rental 
apartment building designated for seniors (62+). The site is on the northern side of Blue Hill Avenue 
between Otisfield and Gaston streets. The site includes 4 existing parcels that will be consolidated into 
one lot totaling 23,000 square feet. The lot has been vacant for over 20 years, but at one time was 
developed as a dry-cleaning facility. The Proposed Project seeks to reactivate an under-utilized parcel 
on the Blue Hill Avenue Corridor. The proposed development is also in keeping with community goals 
for the Blue Hill Avenue Action Plan, and makes an important contribution to the senior housing goals of 
Imagine Boston 2030. The Proposed Project will provide safe, healthy housing, and support for seniors .

Environmental Site Assessment 
GZA GeoEnvironmental performed a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment of 329, 337, and 339 Blue 
Hill Avenue and 2R Otisfield Street, in Boston, Massachusetts (Subject Property) in April of 2024 in 
general conformance with the scope and limitations of ASTM International’s Standard Practice for 
Environmental Site Assessments: Phase I Environmental Site Assessment Process-E1527-21 (ASTM 
E1527-21. In GZA’s opinion, this Phase I ESA revealed evidence of the following Recognized 
Environmental Conditions (RECs) in connection with the Subject Property. 
From the 1940s to the 1960s, Golden Bell Cleaners, a dry cleaner, occupied a retail unit at the 329 Blue 
Hill Avenue parcel. Also, in the 1940s, House of Liederman, cleaner and a dyer, occupied a retail unit at 
the 339 Blue Hill Avenue parcel. It is likely that typical chemicals for dry cleaning were used and stored 
at the Subject Property. The historical use of the Subject Property as a dry cleaner is considered a REC. 
A limited subsurface investigation conducted in 20c15 confirmed the presence of a UST at the 329 Blue 
Hill Avenue parcel. Since documentation of either the UST removal or its decommissioning was not 
provided, this is considered a REC. 
To assess the environmental conditions identified by ESS in 2015, the RECs identified by GZA in the 2024 
Phase I ESA, and the Subject Property in consideration of future development by the Proponent, GZA 
conducted a Limited Phase II Environmental Site Assessment. The assessment included the 
advancement of borings, the installation of groundwater monitoring wells, a well elevation survey, and 
the collection of groundwater monitoring wells, a well elevation survey, and the collection and analysis 
of soil and groundwater samples. The concentrations of compounds in soil samples collected during this 
assessment were generally consistent with the prior site assessment activities by others, are indicative 
of anthropogenic conditions attributable to the presence of coal and coal ash in soil; and are not 
considered a reportable condition under the MCP. Certain compounds were detected in groundwater 
samples collected during the Phase II activities. The detected concentrations did not exceed the 
applicable Massachusetts Contingency Plan (MCP), and did not trigger reporting requirements to the 
Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP), and were likely present due to 
historic Subject Property or vicinity property usage. Based on the results of the limited Phase II 
Environmental Site Assessment, no further assessment was recommended with respect to the RECs 
previously identified during the 2024 Phase I ESA.

Introduction 
This package is being submitted on behalf of Angelo Gianakis (the “Proponent”) 
for a new six-story residential building comprising of approximately 43,029 gross 
square feet, thirty-nine dwelling units, and a 5,004 square foot garage. This 
Proposed Project is being designed with green space and common areas in mind 
with a focus on creating a community environment for the residents. This project 
includes a total of eleven parking spaces, approximately forty bike parking 
spaces in a dedicated bike room, which will accommodate different types of 
bikes and bike storage, and a proposed future connection to the “People’s Pike”. 
The Proposed Project will completely revitalize these lots and will serve to continue 
to help invigorate this section of Allston, which has experienced a recent boom 
in development including projects such as Allston Square, Allston Green, 22-24 
Pratt Street, and 76 Ashford Street.

Detailed Project Description 
Angelo Gianakis proposes a new residential development containing a six-story 
structure which will include thirty-nine dwelling units and eleven parking spaces in 
an interior, at-grade garage. The Proposed Project site sits on three separate 
parcels containing 13,904 square feet along Pratt Street in the Allston section of 
Boston. The current addresses of these parcels per the City of Boston Assessing 
Department are 34 Pratt Street (Parcel ID 2100451000), 34 R Pratt Street (Parcel ID 
2100450000), and 36 Pratt Street (Parcel ID 2100449000). 
The Proposed Project site is located in a Two-Family Residential Zoning Subdistrict 
(2F-5000). However, the site directly abuts a Linden Street LI-1 Zoning Subdistrict 
to the back left and an Allston Landing South EDA Zoning District to the rear. 
Currently, two of the lots contain buildings and the remaining area is comprised 
of largely compacted surfaces for parking. 
The Proposed Project will completely revitalize these lots and will serve to 
invigorate this section of Allston, while creating much needed residential rental 
opportunities, as well as providing various amenities, parking, and commuting 
options for residents that will reside at the property. 
 
The Proposed Project will consist of a six-story building comprising of 43,029 square 
feet. The building will front on Pratt Street and provide pedestrian and vehicular 
ingress and egress from Pratt Street. The site is bounded by residential structures 
to the right, front left, and across the street. Additionally, the site abuts the 22-24 
Pratt Street development to the back left, a strip of land owned by Harvard 
University to the rear and beyond that, Massachusetts Bay Transportation 
Authority railroad tracks. 
 
The proposed structure will contain thirty-nine dwelling units along with eleven 
parking spaces and approximately forty bicycle parking spaces in a dedicated 
and easily accessible bike room. The bike storage room will provide a safe and 
secure area to store and maintain various types of bicycles. The bike storage 
room will have direct access outside providing residents with convenient ingress 
and egress from the pedestrian pathway leading from Pratt Street towards the 
rear of the property. 
 
The developer is proposing a wide variety of unit sizes and styles for the building, 
which will help to accommodate Allston’s diverse and growing population. The 
units will be comprised of a mixture of one-bedroom, two-bedroom units, and 
three-bedroom units. Based on the current plans, the Project includes twelve (12)

The Proposed Project is ideally situated within walking distance to multiple bus

The Proposed Project is subject to Small Project Review under Article 80E of the

and structures, access to stores, restaurants, and other commercial activity along 
Cambridge Street, Harvard Ave, Brighton Ave, and Commonwealth Ave, recent 
similar development within this neighborhood, and the Site’s proximity to public 
transportation. 
 
The Proposed Project will enliven this section of Allston by developing necessary 
residential housing, while improving the overall infrastructure of this corridor, and 
providing necessary access to public transportation for future commuters.

1.8 
Affordable Housing 
Inclusionary Zoning (IZ) under Article 79 was created to ensure access to 
affordable housing within the City of Boston. IZ promotes the public health, safety 
and welfare of the residents of Boston by helping to ensure a range of housing 
options with sizes, types, and levels of affordability to support a diverse populace. 
The purpose of inclusionary zoning is to generate affordable housing through 
conventional market-rate housing development. The IZ requires that housing 
developments with seven or more proposed units are subject to the creation of 
affordable housing opportunities. These opportunities are usually satisfied through 
the creation of on-site affordable units or monetary contributions to the 
Inclusionary Development Policy Fund. Typically, projects are required to 
contribute a minimum of seventeen percent (17%) of the Project’s units at an 
affordable level. As currently constituted, this Project would comply with the IZ 
requirements and create at least seven affordable units.

3.1 
Site and Surroundings 
The Proposed Project site encompasses three separate parcels consisting of 
13,904 square feet along Pratt Street in the Allston section of Boston. The current 
addresses of these parcels per the City of Boston Assessing Department are 34 
Pratt Street, 34 R Pratt Street, and 36 Pratt Street. The existing buildings at 34 and 
36 Pratt Street contain residential houses, and the third lot is vacant. 
The surrounding sites along Pratt Street contain a variety of residential uses. Pratt 
Street contains a number of single-family and two-family homes to the right and 
across the street from the Site. To the left of the Site there are a number of different 
projects in various stages of development. Directly to the left abutting the rear 
portion of the Site is a large project containing hundreds of units and spanning 
between seven and sixteen stories. Further to the left is a project known as Allston 
Green, which contains multi-family residential housing structures along Linden 
Street and Pratt Street. Other larger developments are either proposed or in 
process including a multi-parcel project known as Allston Square, a large 
development at 76 Ashford Street, and several other developments throughout 
the neighborhood. The Site abuts railroad tracks to the rear and provides a 
strategic opportunity to connect to the proposed West Station in the future. The 
Site is also in close proximity to a number of commercial uses including 
commercial corridors along Brighton Ave, Cambridge Street, and Harvard Ave. 
The Site is in close proximity to numerous forms of public transportation including 
the green line, the commuter rail at Boston Landing, and several bus stops 
accommodating multiple bus routes. Several institutional uses including Saint 
Elizabeth’s Medical Center and numerous educational uses are located within 
approximately a one-mile radius. 
The proposed multi-family residential project represents a larger building and 
higher use than what currently exists, however, it has been designed to blend in 
with some of the recent developments and represents a step-down approach 
from the larger developments to the left and the existing housing stock to the

right. The Pratt Street corridor and the surrounding neighborhood are 
experiencing positive growth due to the proximity to surrounding commercial 
opportunities as well as the variety of public transportation options. The 
development will play a role in this neighborhood’s ongoing transformation and 
development. This project will continue to add high-density residential housing, 
providing some much-needed affordable housing. Additionally, the lots close 
proximity to numerous public transportation opportunities will help further the 
City’s initiative to reduce reliance on private motor vehicles and encourage 
alternative modes of transportation. 
 
3.2 
Urban Design Concept 
This project is unique in that it fronts on Pratt Street and has an expansive 
undeveloped area to the rear, which allows for many of the units of the Proposed 
Project to have unobstructed views. The buildings have been designed to fit within 
the context of both the recently approved developments and the existing 
buildings and uses in the surrounding area. Special attention was paid to 
enlivening the streetscape and improving the pedestrian experience along Pratt 
Street. Specifically, the building design, which includes set back upper floors, a 
minimized curb cut, trees and plantings work to make the structures feel more 
inviting and residential in nature. Although the proposed structure is taller than 
some of the surrounding buildings, special attention was paid to including building 
setbacks which align with abutting properties setbacks. The Proposed Project also 
provides a variety of transportation options including parking, bike parking, public 
bike use, a connection to the future People’s Pike, and access to multiple modes 
of public transportation, making it convenient for commuting professionals. Along 
with access to transportation, this Project provides multiple resident areas and 
open spaces for residents to gather in and make use of. 
 
3.3 
Landscape Plan 
The Proponent is proposing a project that incorporates a number of open space 
features. Currently, the lots contain existing structures, some front yard green 
space and a significant amount of paved or impervious areas for parking and 
storage. Verdant Landscape Architecture has developed an extensive 
landscape plan which includes street trees, lawn areas, a wide variety of 
plantings, planter boxes, and opportunities for future residents to congregate. 
Landscape features are proposed all around the building as well as the common

decks which will allow for future residents to take full advantage of usable outdoor 
living spaces. Verdant also conducted a tree survey which identified the general 
health and classification of the existing trees and steps to be taken to maintain as 
many of the existing trees on the property as possible. 
 
3.4 
Building Design 
The proposed development is a new multifamily residential building situated on 
the mid-block of Pratt Street. The proposed structure is six stories tall and has been 
designed to respond to the surrounding neighborhood context while maximizing 
site efficiency. The massing steps down from the rear of the site toward the street 
to reduce perceived height at the pedestrian level and better integrate with the 
adjacent, smaller scale structures. 
The ground floor hosts the primary entrance, transformer vault, and vehicular 
entrance at the front façade. The twelve foot front setback at the first three stories 
promotes active pedestrian engagement while creating a prominent, welcoming 
entry. Balconies above the primary entry highlight the entry point and respond to 
the traditional style balconies in the neighborhood that overlook the public realm. 
The building’s mass is broken down through the use of vertical material 
articulation, recessed upper floors, and a carefully composed material palette 
that reflects a contemporary interpretation of traditional masonry structures in the 
neighborhood. Street-level landscaping softens the edge of the building, creating 
a buffer between the sidewalk and ground floor. The upper three floors are 
setback 15’ from the first three floors which allows for a partial rooftop terrace to 
provide outdoor amenity space for residents. 
 
3.5 
Materials and Finishes 
The structure is designed with two distinct, but cohesive aesthetics. The front 
portion of the structure, facing Pratt Street, has a dark brick base at the first three 
stories, and fiber cement cladding at the upper three stories. The rear portion of 
the site, which acts as a front façade to the future Allston Multi-modal project & 
people’s pike, is clad with a tan brick at the first four stories, and the upper two 
floors transitions to a series of fiber cement panels in warm neutral tones that 
articulate the facade and break up the overall mass. Both portions of the structure 
are provided with generous windows provide natural light to units and are 
proportioned to complement the building’s vertical rhythm The two portions of

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact 
accessibility in Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at 
the beginning of projects, rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet 
minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment which provides equitable 
experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this 
Checklist to provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project 
plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility 
throughout Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability 
Commission staff prior to filing.

Dear Chief Jemison: 
 
 
It is my pleasure to submit this application for Small Project Review pursuant to Article 
80, Section 80E, of the Boston Zoning Code, for the KABLE D @ 352–354 Washington Street 
Mixed Use Project in Brighton. 
 
 
The proposed project is to consist of ground floor commercial space and 19 new 
residential units, primarily market rate, with 4 affordable units in accordance with the City’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy, served by 6 garage parking spaces. The project site comprises 
5,133 square feet at 352–354 Washington Street in Brighton’s historic Brighton Center 
neighborhood, and is currently occupied by a liquor store that will be rebuilt and relocated into 
this proposed project once construction is complete. 
 
 
The applicant is Kable D LLC and its principals, Brandon Dervishian and Kerri Digregorio.

2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new five-story building containing 19 residential units, 
primarily market rate, with 4 affordable units in accordance with the City of Boston’s Inclusionary 
Development Policy, situated at 352 – 354 Washington Street in Brighton. Six garage parking 
spaces will be provided, as well as bicycle storage for twenty-four spaces. The lot size is 
approximately 5,198 square feet and is currently occupied by a single-story commercial building 
operating as a liquor store. 
 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of 19 new rental units in an attractive low-rise building, including 4 
affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy; 
 

352–354 Washington Street Mixed Use Project 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
 
• the expected creation of approximately 60 construction industry jobs to complete the 
proposed project; 
 
• commitment to use local design firms, contractors, and future maintenance personnel 
for the proposed project;

5. 
Building Program Details, Massing, and Materials 
 
The project site exists within a varied urban fabric in the Brighton Center Neighborhood at the 
Washington and Market Street intersection. The area has a multitude of uses and building 
masses as well as close access to public transportation with multiple bus lines and short walks to 
both the green line and commuter rail. The existing 1 story building sits between a 1 story setback 
restaurant on the left with a parking lot along the street and the Architectural Hall building to the 
right which is one of the last remaining remnants of the former cattle business that once were 
prevalent of the area. Directly across the street are much larger masonry buildings. 
 
The proposed design looks to borrow elements from some of these surrounding elements. 
Rendered in brick, the lower 3 floors act as a base and speak to the many masonry buildings in 
the commercial area. The massing of these 3 levels also aligns with the peak of the neighboring 
Architectural Hall to create some harmony with the massing of the 2 differing building types. The 
4th floor sets back to a similar dimension of the lower roof and upper façade of the front of 
Architectural Hall to again echo the neighboring structure. The fifth floor sets back again which 
relates to the large dormers setback on the roof of Architectural Hall, again taking ques from the 
adjacent structure. These setbacks and change in materials above the 3rd floor will also work to 
make the building feel shorter along Washington and maintain a better presence in the existing 
streetscape. The proposal also looks to improve on the streetscape by adding street trees along 
the sidewalk at the front of the building.

6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The project will include 6 on-site garage parking spaces accessed via a garage entrance on 
Academy Hill Road. The location of garage entrance and its associated vehicular traffic off of 
Washington Street, making for a better and safer pedestrian environment and also reducing the 
opportunity for vehicular conflicts. Direct elevator access will be provided from the garage to all 
floors. Secure storage for twenty-four resident bicycles will be provided on the first floor, with 
direct access to Academy Hill Road. Visitor bike parking spaces will also be provided in compliance 
with the City of Boston’s requirements for new development. Additionally, the site is within short 
walking distance to the MBTA’s bus routes.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact 
accessibility in Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at 
the beginning of projects, rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet 
minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment which provides equitable 
experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this 
Checklist to provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project 
plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility 
throughout Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability 
Commission staff prior to filing.

community benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

(entrances, doors openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional 
limitations to visit

Urban Design Overview, Building Massing & Design, Materials 
 
The project site is located on Chestnut Hill Avenue in Brighton between Cleveland Circle and 
Commonwealth Avenue directly across from the Chestnut Hill Reservoir. This stretch of Chestnut 
Hill Avenue has heavy foot traffic from commuters traveling to Cleveland Circle and the Reservoir 
from the Brighton neighborhood and Boston College campus. The adjacent parcels house a 
variety of uses serving the commuters and neighborhood including, retail storefronts, 
restaurants, automotive uses, mixed commercial and multifamily housing. The site currently 
houses a three-story commercial building with retail at the street level. 
2

358 Chestnut Hill Avenue Mixed-Use Project 
The proposed project is to retain the footprint of the existing building and construct a six-story 
mixed use, transit oriented multi-family building. The retail space will be retained on the ground 
floor to maintain activity along the street and the residences will replace underutilized 
commercial office space. The proximity to multiple bus and transit lines allows for a reduction of 
existing parking for residents and creation of a communal greenspace at the rear of the site 
replacing existing impermeable surfaces. 
 
As the site is located within the Aberdeen Historic District, much care has been taken in the design 
of the building and landscape to fit within the district’s guidelines, and the design team spent 
considerable time working closely with urban design staff of the BPDA and Boston Landmarks 
Commission prior to the submission of this application. The building’s façade is organized in 
tripartite with a clear base, middle and top to the building. A strong cornice line at the fifth floor 
breaks the massing and ties into the adjacent context along Chestnut Hill Avenue. Materially, the 
use of brick respects the neighborhood context while modern detailing creates depth and texture 
to the façade. The residential entry is signified by a vertical break in the massing and material 
tying into the sixth floor which has been stepped back from the lower levels to minimize the 
perceived height of the structure. Large window openings and Juliet balconies have been 
incorporated on the front façade to take advantage of view facing the reservoir. 
 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
The proposed project includes nineteen surface motor vehicle parking spaces which will be 
located in in the rear of the property, accessed by a single existing curb cut on Chestnut Hill 
Avenue. The site is located within a new minutes’ walking distance of both the Chestnut Hill 
Avenue and Cleveland Circle stops on the MBTA’s Green Line branches B and C. The new building 
will also feature secure interior resident bicycle storage, and outside visitor post-and-ring 
assemblies, in compliance with the City of Boston’s bicycle parking requirements.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

PROJECT NARRATIVE/PROGRAM
The following Small Project Review Application (SPRA) is being submitted by The Rise At Longwood development 
team (the “Proponent”) in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). 
The combined property at 36, 40 and 44 Parker Hill Ave. (the “Site” or “Project Site”) is situated on an approximately 
25,441 square foot contiguous parcel with street direct frontage on Parker Hill Ave. The site serves as an anchor to the 
intersection of Parker Hill Ave. and Hillside St.
The project team proposes the redevelopment of an existing surface parking lot into an amenitized new construction 
multifamily housing building and associated site and streetscape improvements. The Project is comprised of a five 
(5) story building of approximately 30,861 square feet of gross floor area (“GFA”), including thirty-eight (38) residential 
rental apartments, with a mix of studios and two-bedrooms unit types. The ground floor programming accomodates 
a shared outdoor courtyard with new catenary exterior lighting, soft seating and pavers, a fitness/yoga studio, indoor/
outdoor bike storage and a modest amount of off-street parking. The project also envisions an outdoor roof deck 
amenity for residents to enjoy access to fresh air and views of the Boston skyline. 
The Proponent is also commited to providing a host of public realm and streetscape improvements including newly 
constructed public sidewalks, street trees, pavers, planters and exterior lighting. The new construction project at 36 
Parker Hill is envisioned to be a welcome addition to the neighborhood with respct to location, program and its ability 
to strenghthen the sense of community in the area. Together the buildings at 36, 40 and 44 will provide residents a full-
service residential community experince with the idea that residents from each of the three buildings can enjoy the 
cross network of amenities both within the buildings and adjacent on-site open space and off-street parking.

SITE ANALYSIS
The Project Site includes approximately 25,441 square feet of combined land area at the intersection of Parker Hill Ave. 
and Hillside St. in Mission Hill, near Brigham Circle. 
The aforementioned contigous parcel forms the project site with direct street frontage and access to light, views and 
offers an outdoor courtyard and other spaces between the buildings, most notably the space to the rear of 44 Parker 
Hill Ave. Vehicular access is achieved by way of Parker Hill Ave. to a series of surface spaces behind 40 Parker Hill Ave. 
The neighborhood is largely comprised of 3, 4, 5 and 6-story mixed-use and residential building stock, with a dense 
residential typology along Parker Hill Ave. and Hillside Streets. The project site is also located near several medical 
institutions including New England Baptist Hospital, the Brigham and Women's Hospital, cultural and religious 
organizations, educational facilities, libraries and community enrichment centers.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Dear Director Jemison, 
 
On behalf of MTK Development LLC, the proponent and development sponsor of the project, we are 
pleased to submit the enclosed application for Article 80 Small Project Review. The combined property 
at 376-384A Blue Hill Ave. in Dorchester (the “Site”) is situated on an approximately 11,480 square foot 
rectangular shaped parcel with direct street frontage on Blue Hill Avenue. The 376-384A Blue Hill Ave. 
site has been vacant as a city-owned parcel for some time and sits between adjacent multistory mixed-
use developments to the left and right of it. 
 
During the latter half of last year, the MTK Development team (MTK) responded to a City of Boston RFP 
for development on this site, administered through the Mayor’s Office of Housing (MOH). Subsequent to 
our team’s RFP response, related community meetings and presentations, MTK was awarded tentative 
designation through MOH to advance the development project through the city’s Article 80 regulatory 
permitting and approvals process. 
 
After a series of city and community conversations, the development carefully arrived at the proposal 
for a new construction 4-story mixed-use development of approximately 25,900 SF. The proposal as 
further described herein includes; 18 family-style affordable homeownership condominium units (3) 1-
bedrooms, (9) 2-bedrooms and (6) 3-bedrooms, approx. 2,000 SF of ground floor commercial retail, 
approx. 1,300 SF of community event space, (10) surface parking spaces, 1 to 1 covered bike storage and 
a series of public realm streetscape improvements. 
 
In this regard, the Proposed Project will vastly improve the long-term viability and vibrancy of the site 
and neighborhood and will revitalize this underutilized parcel with much-needed affordable 
homeownership housing, new brick and mortar commercial space and off-street parking for residents. 
Furthermore, the project will seek high performing sustainability and energy goals in support of the 
long-term resiliency of the project and its impact on our city’s carbon footprint. 
 
We have already begun to undertake extensive preliminary outreach with nearby and abutting property 
owners, area residents, business owners, local elected and appointed officials, and agency staff to seek 
and integrate input into its development program.

This Small Project Review Application is being submitted by MTK Development LLC (the “Proponent”) in 
accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). The combined 
property at 376-384A Blue Hill Avenue (the “Site” or “Project Site”) is situated on an approximately 
11,480 square foot rectangular shaped parcel with street frontage on Blue Hill Avenue. The site 
currently exists as a contiguous adjacency of five (5) city owned lots which are currently vacant and 
unoccupied. 
The MTK development team proposes a “family legacy project”, which contemplates the improvement 
and revitalization of the Site with the construction of a new, four (4) story, mixed-use development 
building of approximately 25,900 square feet of gross floor area (“GFA”), including 18 affordable 
homeownership condominium units, commercial retail and community ground floor space, off-street 
surface parking and major improvements in landscaping, pedestrian connectivity and related public 
realm improvements in and around the Site, consistent with the character and housing needs of the 
surrounding community (the “Proposed Project”). The new building will cater to families with the desire 
for long-term residency, through the programmed unit mix of majority two (2) and three (3) bedrooms 
units. 
The Proposed Project would create a mixed-use development with a contemporary aesthetic 
appropriate in scale, massing and design for Grove Hall's emerging growth and revitalization. In 
planning the building, great care was given to respecting the area’s as-built conditions. As a result, the 
proposed building has been designed and scaled to complement both of the Site’s street frontages, the 
busy thoroughfare of Blue Hill Ave. and the smaller residential side streets like Intervale and Brunswick.
The Proposed Project also includes a unique roof deck in order to provide for resident open space, 
accessible and available to all future residents, along with several additional juliet balconies at the 
upper floor of the building.

SITE DESCRIPTION
The Project Site includes approximately 11,480 square feet of combined land area along Blue Hill Avenue 
in Dorchester, comprised of the following adjacent City owned plots [Parcel ID's 1400503000, 1400504000, 
1400505000, 1400506000, and 1400507000. 
The above mentioned parcels with be consolidated to form the project site with direct street frontage 
and access to light and views. Vehicular access is achieved by way of an existing curb cut along Intervale 
Street, just east of the parcel. The site is relatively flat and currently vacant with overgrown vegetation and 
perimeter fencing. 
The neighborhood is largely comprised of 3 and 4-story mixed-use commercial retail and residential 
building stock with active storefronts at the base and punched windows at the upper floors. The project site 
is also located near a number of cultural and religious organizations, educational facilities and community 
enrichment centers.

TRAFFIC, PARKING & ACCESS
The proposed development includes 10 (off-street) on-site surface parking spaces that will be accessed from 
Intervale St. along the northeastern edge of the site. Vehicles will both enter and discharge from the surface 
parking lot onto Intervale St. via the existing curb cut. All vehicular traffic has been directed away from Blue 
Hill Avenue as not to adversely contribute to congestion along its busy thoroughfare. 
Resident bike storage and employee bike storage have been located at the ground floor of the building with 
direct access to the public realm for easy in/out operation, while several visitor bike racks will be located 
along the sidewalk at the building entry. 
All floors of the building (including the roof deck) are equipped with elevator access and direct at grade 
entrances off the street. In this way the building is compliant with MAAB 521 CMR, ADA regulations and is 
also universally accessible. Direct elevator access is also provided from the parking to all residential floors of 
the building through the interior lobby.

URBAN DESIGN NARRATIVE
The redevelopment of 376-384A Blue Hill Ave. will contribute to the on-going transformation of this area 
of Grove Hall into a vibrant mixed-use subdistrict with 18 new affordable homeownership condominiums, 
accompanying amenities, commercial retail and community space, off-street parking with site wide public realm 
improvements. The project site is prominently located between two other mixed-use multistory buildings with direct 
street frontage along Blue Hill Ave. 
This urban redevelopment project is envisioned as a community-based mixed-use affordable housing and 
commercial retail development along a critical transition between Dorchester and Roxbury. The project, aptly 
named Marzuq Plaza II pays homage to the life and legacy of the late Marzuq Muhammad who was both a 
tremendous and tireless advocate for the creation and sustainability of truly affordable housing developments 
throughout Boston’s most vulnerable inner-city neighborhoods.
MTK's project proposal is carefully designed to reflect the urban design goals expressed in the City of Boston, 
Mayors Office of Housing (MOH) RFP. As indicated in the accompanying floor plans, program documents and 
perspective images, the proposal seeks to ground the 4-story building within the adjacent and surrounding 
built context for the area. The ground floor is designed with an active commercial retail edge, new street tree 
plantings, signage bands, lighting and a new and vibrant 1,300SF flexible community space. The design of the 
ground floor incorporates both on-site covered bike storage for residents (1 space/unit), as well as (10) off-street
parking spaces at the rear. The parking spaces will be reserved for 2 and 3 bedroom units in addition to (2) of 
the spaces being designated for ride-share amongst the residents. 
The upper floors will feature a range of residential unit types from one to three-bedrooms, designed to meet to 
a very present need in the community for local residents in need of quality housing with larger families. Open 
green space has been made an essential part of the development proposal. Not only is there rear yard space 
for residents to enjoy, but there is also common roof deck above the fourth floor with potted plants and flexible 
furnishings. The residents at the fourth floor will also have private juliet balconies with the ability to hang seasonal 
plantings. 
The exterior of the building is clad in a rich toned red-brick masonry, fiber cement siding and metal cornice bands 
at the podium and attic story levels of the building. The undulating roof plane provides definition and scale to the 
building in keeping with the overall architectural character of the neighborhood. The building is further refined 
by the use of an articulated cornice along the primary roof line with secondary datum lines at lower floors. The 
building achieves façade modulation through the use of vertically organized punched windows and accent bands 
to create a dynamic visual rhythm along the building’s façade. Warm toned wood-look fiber cement cladding 
is broadly used across the façade as an accent to relate back to the residential context of neighborhood and 
breakdown the scale of the massing. Metal picket railings with a warm wood cap have been employed at fourth 
floor of the building to facilitate private juliet balconies for the units as the building edge steps back to minimize 
height from the street.

The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

ZONING COMPLIANCE AND LAND USE APPROPRIATENESS 
The project site is located within the Harvard Avenue CC-1 zoning subdistrict as 
designated under Article 51 of the Boston Zoning Code. This Community Commercial 
subdistrict designation specifically encourages mixed-use development that supports 
the pedestrian-oriented commercial character of the Harvard Avenue corridor. Allowing 
for increased density and building height above what is allowed by the circa 1991 
zoning limits will accommodate the growing demand for services and amenities in this 
transit-accessible location. 
The CC-1 subdistrict's underlying zoning philosophy aligns perfectly with the 
proposed hotel use, as it seeks to create vibrant, walkable commercial areas that serve 

393 Cambridge Street Hotel Small Project 
both local residents and the broader metropolitan region. Hotels represent an ideal 
complement to the existing retail, restaurant, and service establishments along 
Cambridge Street and Harvard Avenue, providing a customer base that supports local 
businesses while contributing to the area's economic sustainability. 
Despite the largely outdated dimensional limitations of the CC-1 subdistrict, the 
proposed seven-story hotel represents an appropriate scale of development that 
maximizes the efficient use of urban land while respecting the transitional nature of the 
surrounding built environment. The project's height and massing have been carefully 
calibrated to ensure compatibility with both existing structures and approved future 
development in the immediate vicinity. 
CONTEXTUAL COMPATIBILITY AND URBAN DESIGN 
The proposed hotel's height and overall massing demonstrate sensitivity to the 
evolving character of the Allston neighborhood, particularly in relation to other 
significant development projects that have received approvals from the Planning 
Department and the Zoning Board of Appeal. The building's scale is reflective of the 
area’s transitions between lower-scale residential areas and higher-density commercial 
and institutional uses along the major transportation corridors. 
Recent approvals for similar-scale development projects in the immediate area 
have established a precedent for mid-rise construction that enhances the urban 
character of Cambridge Street while maintaining appropriate relationships with existing 
neighborhoods. The design team has conducted extensive analysis of these precedent 
projects and has incorporated lessons learned from their design and community 
engagement processes. 
The building's façade treatment and material selection will reflect contemporary 
architectural standards while respecting the historic character of Allston's built 
environment. The development team has prioritized the creation of an active ground-
floor streetscape that will enhance pedestrian experience and contribute to the 
vibrancy of Cambridge Street as a commercial corridor. 
TRANSPORTATION AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
The proposed hotel's location offers exceptional access to multiple 
transportation modes, making it an ideal site for hospitality use that can serve visitors 
while minimizing transportation-related impacts on the surrounding community. The 
site is within walking distance of several MBTA bus routes that provide direct 
connections to Harvard Square, Central Square, and downtown Boston, and to the 
Green Line’s Harvard Avenue stop, reducing the need for guest automobile travel and 
supporting the city's sustainability objectives.
