The provision of four drop-off spaces reflects a carefully considered approach to 
balancing guest convenience with urban planning best practices that prioritize 
sustainable transportation modes. The covered valet area will ensure efficient vehicle 
circulation while screening parking activities from public view, maintaining the 
pedestrian-oriented character of the streetscape. Rideshare vehicles and taxis, as well 
as delivery vehicles, will have a convenient temporary arrival area providing direct 
access to the hotel lobby, and valet service will additionally support hotel guests who 
have private vehicles parked off site. 
The project's transportation demand management approach aligns with the 
principles established in the Boston Transportation Department's “Go Boston 2030” 
plan, which emphasizes the importance of supporting development in transit-
accessible locations while encouraging a modal shift away from single-occupancy 
vehicle travel. 
COMPLETE STREETS AND PUBLIC REALM IMPROVEMENTS 
A cornerstone of the development approach involves significant improvements 
to the public realm that will benefit not only hotel guests but all users of Cambridge 
Street. These improvements have been designed in accordance with Boston's 
Complete Streets guidelines, which prioritize the creation of safe, accessible, and 
attractive streetscapes that accommodate pedestrians, cyclists, transit users, and 
vehicles in a balanced manner. 
The site improvements will include enhanced sidewalk treatments, improved 
pedestrian lighting, on-site and public way street trees and green planting beds, public 
bike racks, and new public seating, all of which will contribute to the walkability and 
environmental quality of this section of Cambridge Street. The development team will 
continue to coordinate with the Planning Department, BTD, Public Works Department, 
and the Public Improvement Commission to ensure that these improvements 
complement planned infrastructure investments in the broader area. 
The hotel's ground-floor design will incorporate features that activate the 
streetscape, including a carefully designed entrance, transparent glazing systems, and 
landscape elements that create visual interest and support pedestrian safety. These 
improvements represent a significant private investment in public infrastructure that will 
yield benefits for the entire community. 
ALIGNMENT WITH PLANNING STUDIES AND MUNICIPAL OBJECTIVES 
The proposed project directly supports several key planning and policy 
initiatives developed by the Planning Department and other municipal departments. 
The project neatly aligns with the goals and recommendations outlined in “Imagine 
Boston 2030,” the city's comprehensive planning document, particularly in its 

393 Cambridge Street Hotel Small Project 
emphasis on creating inclusive growth, enhancing neighborhood character, and 
supporting sustainable transportation patterns. 
The Allston-Brighton neighborhood has been identified in various planning 
studies as an area with significant potential for appropriate density increases, 
particularly in locations with strong transportation access and existing commercial 
character. This hotel project represents exactly the type of thoughtful commercial 
development that can help meet the city's hospitality and economic development goals 
while respecting neighborhood character. 
The Planning Department's “Housing a Changing City: Boston 2030” report 
specifically identifies the need for increased accommodation options that can serve the 
diverse population drawn to Boston's educational institutions, healthcare facilities, and 
innovation economy. While not residential housing, this hotel will help address 
accommodation needs and reduce pressure on the residential housing market by 
providing temporary lodging for visitors who might otherwise compete for rental 
housing. 
Additionally, the project supports objectives outlined in the city's economic 
development strategies, which emphasize the importance of supporting the hospitality 
and tourism sectors as contributors to Boston's economic resilience and diversity. The 
hotel will create permanent employment opportunities in the service sector while 
generating tax revenue that supports municipal services and infrastructure 
investments.

broader Boston metropolitan area. The project will create approximately 25-30

the broader commercial ecosystem in Allston. This is particularly important for small, 
independent businesses that form the backbone of the neighborhood's commercial 
character.

employment opportunities created by both construction and operation of the hotel are 
accessible to Allston residents. 
ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE RESILIENCE 
The development team recognizes the critical importance of addressing climate 
change through responsible building design and operation. The proposed hotel will 
incorporate numerous sustainable design features and operational practices that meet 
or exceed baseline code requirements and support Boston's ambitious climate action 
goals. 
The building's design will prioritize energy efficiency through high-performance 
building envelope systems, efficient mechanical and electrical systems, and smart 
building technologies that optimize resource consumption. The team is exploring 
opportunities for on-site renewable energy generation and are committed to meeting 
certification requirements under recognized green building standards. 
Stormwater management systems will be designed to reduce runoff and support 
the city's efforts to improve water quality and reduce combined sewer overflow events. 
Landscape elements will incorporate native plant species that support urban 
biodiversity while requiring minimal irrigation and maintenance.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new five-story mixed-use building at 43 Preble Street 
in South Boston’s Andrew Square neighborhood. The new building will contain 31 
residential condominium units for sale, as well as a ground-floor commercial unit. The 
combined lot size is approximately 11,762 square feet, comprises seven parcels, and is 
currently occupied by a single-story concrete block building used as an auto repair shop, 
with the vast majority of the site being used for surface vehicle storage. The site is within 
an L-.5 zoning district under the Base Code, and is further located within Use Zone 3 
and a 60-foot density bonus height zone under PLAN: South Boston Dorchester Avenue. 
 
Total development cost is estimated at $18,200,000, with a projected commencement 
of construction in the fourth quarter of 2024 and a projected completion date of the 
second quarter of 2026. 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood 
and to the City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of 31 new dwelling units in an attractive and energy-efficient mid-
rise building, including 5 affordable units in accordance with the City of Boston’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy; 

43 Preble Street Mixed-Use Small Project 
• generation of tens of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of 
Boston once the project is completed in the form of new real property tax 
payments; and 
• the expected creation of approximately 55 construction industry jobs to 
complete the proposed project; 
• new commercial space on Preble Street to activate the site and provide new 
retail options to the local community; and 
• a community benefits package to be determined by the BPDA which will provide 
financial commitments to improving public infrastructure in the area and also to 
one or more South Boston non-profit community service organizations.

The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in

rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

1. Project Summary / Overview
1.1 Introduction
This application is being submitted on behalf of 4 Liberty Square LLC (the “Proponent”) for an office to
The proposed conversion would include 36 residential units occupying floors 2-7. The proposed ground
level Use will be restaurant/ retail as well as residential lobby.
proposed project consists of the redevelopment of the existing building, with an interior fit out for
residential. The current estimated construction cost of this project is approximately $4,920,000.
The vision of the project is to revitalize this section of the neighborhood by replacing the existing office
space with a residential building that will add new housing units to the Liberty Square neighborhood.
As part of the community benefits related to the proposed project, the existing and under utilized
building will be reused with a new residential building. The development seeks to activate the ground
level, thereby bringing more much needed retail space to the neighborhood. The addition of new
residents will activate the neighborhood during the day and the evenings.
The proposed project requires filing under Small project review regulations, pursuant to Article 80 of
the boston Zoning Code as the proposed 36 units will exceed 15 units requirement for article 80. The
proponent has also applied to participate in the Downtown Boston Office to residential conversion
Program.
Additionally, the proponent will need to go before the board of appeal for GCOD, and CFROD.
1.2 Detailed Project Description
The proposed project will be contained in the existing 7 story building on the roughly 3,800 Sq ft corner
Site. The location lies within a commercial neighborhood but also has various residential buildings and
residential is an allowed use. The neighborhood is a home to a unique mix of commercial and
Residential uses. The building has been used as an office building for many years, with the ground level
operating as a restaurant for many years. The developers are proposing a project that fits well in the
neighborhood, and are filling a large need by providing residential apartments. The Liberty Sq site is
positioned in the Broad Street protection subdistrict of the Government Center/ Markets district
(article 45). As part of the community benefits related to this project, the commercial building will be
renovated, greatly needed affordable housing will be provided and new market rate residential housing
will be developed. The proposed project will serve to invigorate this section of downtown boston and
bring residential foot traffic to the neighborhood.
The proposed project will be comprised of the redevelopment of the existing seven-story building and
a conversion to residential apartments. The building is ideally situated for commuters, steps to
multiple train stations, & bus lines. Additionally the proposed bike room with storage for 36 bikes
should allow for an environmental & economically friendly transportation option for residents. Ideally
located walking distance to multiple local restaurants, shops and retail, the additional residents
should had a positive contribution to the local economy.
The proposed project will provide a unique mix of apartment sizes, including five Two bedroom homes,
one (1) bedroom homes, and thirty studios. 7 Of these units would be affordable. A bike room will
allow for bike storage for each resident. The project is also a very short walk to multiple Train lines, as
well as MBTA bus stops.
In addition to Small Project Article 80 Review, will go before the board of appeal for GCOD and CFROD
residential use conversion development of the existing 29,587 Sq ft existing structure at 4 Liberty Sq.

2.3 Public Benefits
The proposed project will provide substantial benefits to the City of Boston and the immediate
community. The proposed project will generate both direct and indirect economic and social benefits to
the Downtown Boston neighborhood. The proposed project provides for:
●Revitalizing underutilized building and office space.
●Creating much needed market rate residential housing in the neighborhood.
●Creating six on-site affordable IDP units, which will meet the Boston Planning and
Development Agency’s affordable housing standards
●Creating one much needed Voucher unit
●Encouraging alternative modes of transportation through the use of bicycling and
walking, due to the close proximity of the bus lines and the MBTA and the high number

encourage bicycling as a mode a transportation, allowing for less vehicular traffic.

●Creating temporary construction and labor jobs.

3. Design And Sustainability_____________________________________________
3.1 Site and Surroundings
The project site is located in the Liberty Sq pocket of the Government Center/ Markets District on the
Corner of Water St & Batterymarch. . The proposed site is roughly 4400 Sq feet with an existing 7 Story
brick structure. The building's current use is office space, and currently sits as a mostly vacant
underutilized structure. The proposed development will be contained to the existing building, which fits
very well in the neighborhood, which is made up of commercial & office buildings both similar in height
and building materials as well as taller high rise buildings. For existing site pictures see Appendix B.

The proposed design is a mixed use re-development of the existing building prominently sitting on the
corner of Batterymarch and Water St. The existing office lobby will be reconfigured as the Main entry
for Both Residential and ground level retail/restaurant. The rest of the Ground level would serve as
retail/restaurant for the neighborhood, whereas floors 2-7 would be home to 36 Residential
apartments, with 6 apartments on each floor.

4 Liberty is a brick structure in excellent condition. The exterior needs little to no work. The majority of

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

The urban design of the 51 Dudley Street area reflects Roxbury's evolution, shaped 
by historical factors, existing infrastructure, and ongoing development. This blend is 
crucial for integrating history with modernism.

living. This approach benefits both current and future residents of 51 Dudley Street.

aesthetics.

abandoned building, it will revitalize the corner into a livable space with green space 
on the Dudley Street end. Promoting walkability and transit usage, 51 Dudley Street 
will advance Boston's urbanism goals, contributing to a more sustainable future.

Executive Summary: Passive to Positive 
51 Dudley Street represents a step forward in sustainable, carbon-conscious, and 
resilient multifamily housing. Designed for Passive House certification through 
Phius, this all-electric building is focused on aggressive reductions in energy use, 
greenhouse gas emissions, and long-term operational costs. While the project is still 
in design and detailed energy modeling is in progress, the design team is committed 
to achieving measurable performance targets. 
Energy & Carbon Performance: 
Energy modeling is currently underway, so specific energy modeling is not 
yet available. However, the building is being designed to meet the Passive 
House Design Standard. Based on these preliminary design assumptions, 51 
Dudley St. is expected to achieve the following energy demand savings 
compared to conventional construction: 
○
85% reduction in heating energy demand*
○
65% reduction in cooling energy demand*
*Estimated Operational Performance (Preliminary)
Systems & Strategies: 
Passive House design principles are at the foundation of the project’s 
sustainability goals. The project’s passive design prioritizes: 
o
Optimized solar orientation and shading
o
A thoughtfully insulated, air-tight envelope with thermal bridge
mitigation
o
Triple-glazed, high-performance windows and doors
o
Balanced, energy recovery ventilation
o
High-efficiency, all-electric mechanical systems
This integrated strategy supports long-term energy savings, operational carbon reductions, 
and occupant health and comfort.

Space Conditioning: 
These energy demand reductions will translate into significant operational GHG 
emissions reductions under any circumstances, thanks to its extremely efficient 
envelope. As an all-electric building, all site emissions of GHGs and other pollutants 
associated with combustion appliances will be eliminated. Ventilation will be 
provided with high-efficiency Energy Recovery Ventilators (ERVs), reducing the 
space conditioning loads associated with ventilation air by approximately 80%. High-
performance heat pumps will meet the project’s space conditioning demand even 
more efficiently. Heat pumps with coefficients of performance of ~2.5-3 for winter 
heating and 3.5-4.5 for cooling will further reduce energy demand. Heat pump 
water heating will deliver a 65% reduction in DHW energy demand, and efficient 
appliances and lighting will make it far more likely that the building’s energy 
demands will be able to be significantly offset by renewables. 
While it is difficult for a five-story building to achieve net-zero energy with PV 
production on its rooftop, decreasing demand as described, and increasing the 
production on the roof (or with nearby community solar) reduces the need for 
remote, off-site solar farms to meet its zero energy goals, which, in turn, reduces 
the threat to farmland and forested areas from solar development.* 
Carbon Emissions: 
While a full carbon model is forthcoming, we anticipate a significant reduction in 
operational emissions compared to a typical code-compliant, multifamily baseline 
(assuming IECC 2021). Recent project modeling experience suggests a 60-70% 
reduction. 
*Design consideration and review required

The team is also pursuing embodied carbon reductions as part of the project’s total 
climate impact reduction strategy. As an adaptive re-use of an existing structure, 
some degree of embodied carbon reduction is automatic. However, integrating into 
an existing building does not ensure a low carbon footprint. Materials and 
assemblies, for both retrofit and new construction, will be selected for embodied 
carbon reduction, and even carbon capture and storage. 
The Structural team will optimize structural design to reduce overbuild and any 
unnecessary concrete and steel. For the concrete that is required, the team will 
explore the use of various low-carbon concrete strategies. The team will minimize or 
eliminate the use of high-GWP foam insulation, especially on the exterior walls, 
which are the largest surface area of the building envelope. We are exploring 
several different prefabricated, bio-based, carbon-negative building assemblies that 
can deliver excellent insulating and thermal mass properties for high-performance 
operational energy goals. 
Climate Resilience: 
Baseline resilience begins with Passive House design. High-performance envelopes 
support passive survivability: buildings that can remain at habitable temperatures 
for days without power, especially in winter. 
However, as summer outages increase with climate change, dense multifamily 
buildings face the risk of overheating due to increased internal loads and solar gain. 
To address this, 51 Dudley St. will incorporate a critical load backup sub-panel 
strategy, powered by a solar + battery nano-grid.* This back-up system will: 
●
Provide critical occupant safety levels of cooling/warming refuge during

Durability and Preservation: 
Adaptive re-use and deep energy retrofits of existing buildings are essential to 
meeting climate impact reduction. Retrofitting buildings with historical character or 
cultural significance, such as 51 Dudley St., can be challenging from several different 
perspectives. Significant stabilization and repair may be necessary, yet historical 
structural systems may need to be adapted to avoid thermal bridging and the 
potential for moisture damage. Preserving the appearance of the historical façade 
requires that all insulation and air-sealing measures occur on the interior. However, 
doing so can add to the risk of moisture accumulation within the building materials 
by reducing the energy flow through the assemblies, which had historically been 
dried out by escaping energy and convection air flow. Rotting, pocketed, or masonry 
bearing wood structures, mold growth on surfaces or in interstices, and freeze-thaw 
damage of old porous brick may all result. Correspondingly, the design team is 
undertaking in-depth hygrothermal simulation of wall assemblies to ensure that 
adaptive re-use proves to be as durable as the original structures while achieving 
zero energy and low carbon objectives. 
Process: Integrated Design:
A key differentiator of this project is the early, integrated collaboration across the 
design team—Passive House consultants, architect, MEP and structural engineers, 
developer, and sustainability advisors. This approach ensures that performance and 
resilience goals are embedded from the earliest stages of concept design, reducing 
the need for re-design efforts and allowing energy-efficient strategies to take 
precedence, rather than being afterthoughts of a traditional design process. 
In conclusion, this project goes above and beyond current market and regulatory 
expectations. By incorporating deeply sustainable strategies like Passive House 
certification and all-electric design from the outset, we are exceeding the standard 
for energy efficiency, carbon reduction, and long-term resilience of affordable 
housing in Boston.

07 ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS 
 
The building envelope at 51 Dudley has been designed to offer numerous 
environmental benefits, contributing to a more sustainable and resilient built 
environment. 
Reduced Energy Consumption: 
 
Green buildings maximize energy efficiency through insulation, high-performance 
windows, and efficient heating and cooling systems. Passive solar design, 
orientation, and daylighting techniques minimize the need for artificial lighting and 
mechanical conditioning. Renewable energy sources like solar panels and 
geothermal systems further reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Green roofs can reduce 
heating and cooling costs by absorbing and storing heat, thereby reducing 
temperature fluctuations. When dry, green roofs decrease heat flow, reducing 
energy needed for heating in winter and air conditioning in summer. They also 
lower cooling costs by reducing roof surface and ambient air temperatures, 
ultimately reducing both peak and total energy demand. 
Water Conservation: 
Green construction incorporates strategies to reduce water usage, both indoors and 
outdoors. High-efficiency plumbing fixtures like low-flow toilets and faucets 
minimize indoor water consumption. Rainwater harvesting systems collect and store 
rainwater for irrigation and other non-potable uses. Landscaping with drought-
tolerant plants and efficient irrigation systems reduces outdoor water demand. 
 
Improved Materials and Resource Efficiency: 
 
Green building prioritizes sustainable materials with lower environmental impacts, 
utilizing recycled and reclaimed materials to reduce demand for virgin resources. 
Rapidly renewable materials like bamboo and cork are favored for sustainability, 
and locally sourced materials minimize transportation emissions.

Waste Reduction: 
 
Green construction minimizes waste generation throughout the building's lifecycle. 
Strategies like prefabrication and modular construction reduce on-site waste during 
construction. Design for deconstruction allows for easier disassembly and material 
reuse or recycling at the end of the building's life. 
 
Enhanced Biodiversity and Ecosystems: 
 
Green building practices consider the impact on the surrounding environment, 
striving to protect and enhance biodiversity. Green roofs and living walls provide 
habitats for plants and animals, supporting local ecosystems. Sustainable site 
development practices minimize disruption to natural habitats and preserve green 
spaces. 
 
Reduced Greenhouse Gas Emissions: 
 
By reducing energy consumption and utilizing sustainable materials, green 
construction plays a crucial role in mitigating climate change. Energy-efficient 
buildings require less energy to operate, leading to lower greenhouse gas emissions 
from electricity generation. The use of materials with lower embodied carbon, such 
as wood, further reduces the building’s carbon footprint 
 
Improved Air Quality: 
 
Green buildings enhance both indoor and outdoor air quality. Reduced energy 
consumption directly translates to less pollution from power plants.

Passive House Construction Principles and Benefits: 
 
Passive house construction is a rigorous standard for energy efficiency that builds 
upon general green construction principles. 
 
Super Insulation and Airtightness: 
 
Thick, continuous insulation and meticulous airtightness dramatically reduce 
heat loss and gain. This results in drastically reduced energy consumption 
(often up to 90% less than conventional buildings), directly decreasing fossil 
fuel demand and environmental impact. This also leads to significantly 
lower greenhouse gas emissions, a major contributor to climate change. 
 
High-Performance Windows: 
 
Advanced window technology, including triple glazing and specialized 
coatings, minimizes heat transfer, enhancing energy efficiency and reducing 
heating and cooling needs. 
 
Balanced Ventilation with Heat Recovery: 
 
Mechanical ventilation systems with highly efficient heat recovery provide a 
continuous supply of fresh, filtered air while recovering heat from outgoing 
stale air. This ensures excellent indoor air quality while minimizing energy 
losses.

In summary, green construction provides a comprehensive approach to minimizing

3. DRAINAGE: THE LANDSCAPE CONTRACTOR SHALL INSURE BEFORE AND AFTER THE SPREADING OF LOAM THAT ALL AREAS WILL DRAIN.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Green Roof Systems
EXTENSIVE
SYSTEM SPECIFICATIONS
• Media Depth: 6” or less
• Weight: 12 - 45 lbs/sf
SYSTEM DESCRIPTION Extensive roofs are the 
most cost-effective and lightweight options, using 6 
inches or less of growing media. Sedum can survive 
in as little as 2 inches of soil with an irrigation 
system. For a bio-diverse approach, a minimum 
of 3 inches of soil is recommended to support a 
broader selection of flowering perennials. A depth of 
3 to 6 inches accommodates a wider range of plant 
species and enhances drought tolerance.
SYSTEM CARE After installing a temporary irrigation 
system during the initial plant establishment phase, 
many extensive green roofs require minimal to no 
ongoing irrigation. Typically, these systems need 2-4 
maintenance visits per year, which include tasks like 
weeding, fertilizing, replanting, deadheading, and 
irrigation system upkeep. 
SYSTEM SPECIES Common species include: Sedum 
album, Sedum kamtschaticum, Sedum sexangulare, 
Sedum spurium. Bio-diverse options include: Allium, 
Asclepias tuberosa, Phemeranthus calycinus, Dianthus, 
Phlox, Coreopsis lanceolata.

2. PROPOSED PROJECT SUMMARY 
The site is located at 521 Cambridge Street in the Allston-Brighton Neighborhood of Boston 
just west of the intersection of Cambridge Street and North Beacon Street. The site spans 
across two separate lots and two separate zoning sub-districts, a 1F-3000 and a CC-1 sub-
district. The total site area once the lots are merged will be 9,045 square feet. 
The project includes demolition of an existing 2-story structure presently used for office space, 
demolition of an existing one-story repair and service garage and the termination of use of a 
used car lot that spans across the majority of the property. New construction will include the 
creation of a new 6-story 33 unit residential building. The project includes (9) Studios, (17) 1-
Bedroom Units, (6) 2-Bedroom Units and (1) 3-Bedroom Unit. 
The development will feature a significant increase in landscaped / pervious area with the 
introduction of green space fronting on Cambridge Street and along the western edge of the 
site. Presently, the entire lot is impervious. The proposed building conforms with the required 
front yard setback in the 1F-3000 district and, for the most part, holds this same setback 
dimensions in the CC-1 sub-district where no setback is actually required. 
 
3. COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
The proposed project will provide many benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
• 
Replacement of used car dealership with 33 units of new rental housing, in furtherance 
of the City’s housing production goals; 
 
• 
Creation of five (5) new affordable housing units, including one 3-bedroom unit; 
 
• 
Generation of thousands of dollars in annual revenue to the City in the form of new 
real property tax payments upon completion; 
 
• 
Creation of numerous construction period jobs; 
 
• 
Elimination of two existing curb cuts on Cambridge Street to improve safety and the 
pedestrian environment; 
 

• 
Improvements to the public realm through robust urban landscaping plan, including 
planting 2 new trees; and 
 
• 
Incorporation of significant sustainability measures, including all-electric systems and 
efficient building envelope. 
 
4. BUILDING PROGRAM DETAILS, MASSING, AND MATERIALS 
The site is located in the Allston neighborhood of Boston just west of Union Square and just west 
of the confluence of Cambridge Street, North Beacon Street and Brighton Avenue. The site 
spans across two different zoning sub-districts each with varying front and side yard setbacks. 
Following its neighbor at 531 Cambridge Street (which is located within the 1F-300 sub-district), 
the proposed project maintains the street wall established by 531 Cambridge across the 
majority of the site even beyond the limits where such a setback is required. Within the CC-1 
sub-district portion of the site (which does not require a front yard setback), the massing of the 
building shifts towards the street to provide better definition of the entrance while maintaining 
a 10’-0” setback. By maintaining the required side yard setback on the west side, the proposed 
design allows for significant landscaping and the introduction of private terraces for those 
ground floor units. As the building rises in height, that setback is increased by approximately 
another 10’-0” feet. 
Responding to the massing materials of the adjacent 531 Cambridge, the height of the brick 
and the height of metal panels bays of the proposed building align with the prominent mass of 
531 Cambridge at the 4th Floor roof line. The ground floor of the proposed building is clad 
with cast stone elements with articulation around windows and doors and capped by a strong 
horizontal band at the second floor line. The brick volume rises above that line and is capped 
by a two-story volume clad in fiber cement siding beginning at the fifth floor line. This 
articulation and mixture of materials is prevalent on all faces since the building has prominent 
exposure on many faces from the surrounding public streets. 
The proposed design includes approximately two-thousand square feet of outdoor open 
space. Areas include ground floor private terraces, the amenity terrace located at grade, the 
common roof deck located at level 6 and various balconies serving individual dwelling units. 
 
 
 
 
 

5. TRAFFIC, PARKING, AND ACCESS 
The proposed project will reinstate the street curb line by eliminating a large extent of curb 
cuts along the site. The absence of parking in the project will eliminate the frequent vehicular 
crossings of the sidewalk that have been typical with the used car lot that occupies the 
property presently. 
Bicycle parking spaces are provided in the building and are accessed from a walkway that 
connects to Cambridge Street. Space is provided for 34 bicycles in conformance with the 
City of Boston’s Bike Parking Guidelines. In addition, visitor bicycle parking is provided at 
the front of the building, for an additional 6 spaces. 
 
6. ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS 
Each unit will be heated and cooled with individual heat pumps. Domestic hot water will be 
provided with electric hot water heaters and all appliances within each unit will be electric. 
As was noted above, the project will not be providing parking. In addition to deterring 
dependence on cars within the city, this has several beneficial aspects to the building itself. To 
begin with, there will be significantly less building materials used to create what would 
otherwise be an entire story of the building dedicated to housing parking spaces. In addition, 
the lack of a garage within the building will save a significant amount of energy both 
ventilating the garage as well as keeping the floor of the residential units above warm.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

Project Summary

Project Summary
Project Summary
The Proposed Project consists of the redevelopment of a 9000 square-foot lot at 555 Talbot Ave 
located at Peabody Sq in the Ashmont Hill neighborhood of Dorchester (the “Proposed Project”). 
The Proposed Project is a mixed-use development consisting of a 6 story building containing 34 
residential units, approximately 4,000 square feet of ground ﬂoor commercial space, a semi-public 
landscaped retail plaza space and 46 bike storage spaces. The Proposed Project is a true Transit 
Oriented Development in the direct vicinity of the Ashmont T Station and adjacent to multiple MBTA 
bus routes within Peabody Sq.
The project design strives to respect the character and scale of Peabody Sq to the south and east 
of the site and Ashmont Hill neighborhoods directly uphill and to the west. As a result, the Proposed 
Project has been designed to emphasize a bold 6 story gesture fronting Peabody Sq and Dorchester 
Ave. Setback and folds create a series of welcoming spaces that engage with and activate the 
square.
The southern and western edges approaching residential neighborhoods on Ashmont Hill setback in 
height and reduce the massing of the building with balconies and smaller building proportions more 
appropriate to abutting residential scale.
Community Beneﬁts
The Proposed Project will oﬀer many public beneﬁts to the neighborhood and the City of Boston, 
including the following:
• The creation of 34 new residential units. The Project will meet the income-restricted units 
required under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
• The creation of approximately 700 square feet of landscaped semi public open space along 
Dorchester Ave, enhancing the width and sidewalks of Peabody Sq and enlarging the plaza 
space for an improved pedestrian experience adjacent to both the new commercial space and 
residential entries. 
• Creating a more pedestrian friendly Dorchester Ave by enhancing the street scape with 
improved sidewalks and landscaping.
• The addition of new commercial space in the heart of a vibrant commercial corridor.
• The reduction of traﬃc congestion through maximizing utilization of public transit.
• The future generation of hundreds of thousands of dollars in new property and sales tax revenue 
annually to the City of Boston.

Design Approach
The proposed Project will consist of a new six story mixed use residential building. The Project 
site, extending east-west from Peabody Sq towards Ashmont Hill, interacts with a variety of 
urban contexts: a busy commercial corridor on the east along Dorchester Ave and Peabody Sq 
transitions to residential scale made up of single and multifamily homes in the abutting Ashmont 
Hill neighborhood to the west and north. The Project responds to surrounding context with a 
forward looking design, reactive it its surrounding, employing high quality materials. A 6 story urban 
gesture creates a focal point on the Square and the site plan activates the street scape with a new 
restaurant use and an adjacent public plaza enlarging the existing open space. 
 
The lobby and residential bike room will be at-grade, fully accessible, and accessed via an entry at 
the front of the building. The remainder of the ground ﬂoor area is dedicated to the restaurant use. 
The basement contains additional restaurant support space, utility rooms and area for residential 
storage. Floors two through six will contain 34 residential units with a mix of one-and two-bedroom 
units. A roofdeck area is provided on the east side of the roof exclusive for the residential tenants use.

617 Dorchester Avenue Residential Project 
2. 
Proposed Project Summary 
 
The proposed project consists of a new four-story residential building situated on a through lot 
fronting on both Dorchester Avenue and Boston Street. The project is located on a vacant 6,135 
square foot parcel and proposes the construction of eighteen residential condominium units, 
with a residential lobby, bike parking room, trash area, community room, and a spacious common 
roof deck. The main entrance is provided at-grade and accessed on Dorchester Avenue. The 
building also includes an accessible basement, providing private storage rooms for each unit. 
There are accessible paths that run parallel along the entire site, allowing for passage to either 
Dorchester Avenue or Boston Street, installed with privacy gates to ensure the security and 
privacy of the residents. Residential units are located on every level, although units on the first 
floor have been raised above the SLR-BFE. Owing to proximity to the MBTA’s Andrew Station on 
the Red Line, no on-site motor vehicle parking is proposed. 
 
3. 
Community Benefits 
 
The proposed project will offer many public benefits to the surrounding neighborhood and to the 
City of Boston, including: 
 
• the creation of eighteen new condominium units in an attractive low-rise building, 
including three affordable units in accordance with the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy; 
 
• generation of thousands of dollars in revenue annually to the City of Boston once the 
project is completed in the form of new real property tax payments; 
 
• the expected creation of approximately forty-five construction industry jobs to 
complete the proposed project; 
 
• contribution in an amount TBD to the Boston Parks & Recreation Department to 
support public open space improvements. 
 
• a bikeshare contribution in an amount TBD to the Boston Transportation Department, 
in accordance with Boston’s Bike Parking Guidelines. 
 
4. 
Project Financing and Developer Pro Forma 
 
The principals of the developer, 20 Boston Street LLC, Mark Little and Jack Ordway, possess a 
record of development success in Boston, enjoy a strong working relationship with several local 
lenders, and intend to finance the project using traditional institutional financing. 
 
Total Development Cost (soft/hard costs): $7,000,000

5. 
Planning Context 
 
The surrounding neighborhood features a mix of residential and commercial uses, with the site 
being within a B-1 general business zoning district under the 1964 Base Code. This area has been 
undergoing a residential transformation in recent years and is located within the area of PLAN: 
South Boston Dorchester Avenue. Specifically, it is located within a sixty-foot density bonus 
height zone, and with Zone 1 of the PLAN, which provides for 100% lot coverage area, with 
appropriate ground level setbacks to allow for the meeting of Complete Street guidelines. The 
SLR-Base Flood Elevation at the site is 20 feet, and the proposed building has been designed to 
be fully compliant with the requirements of Article 25A. 
 
The site meets the street both on Dorchester Avenue and on Boston Street, which converge at a 
busy six-way intersection less than 0.1 mile away in Andrew Square. Several restaurants, eateries, 
and local businesses are accessible within a short walking distance. For a greater variety of 
options, an eight-minute walk takes one to South Bay Center, a shopping center which includes 
a large supermarket. A twelve-minute walk from the project site are Moakley Park and Carson 
Beach, offering a wide range of outdoor amenities and open recreational spaces. 
 
6. 
Urban Design Approach 
 
The proposed project will be building out an underutilized site, to fit contextually at an urban 
scale with its abutters and surrounding neighborhood. Overall, the building is designed with a 
modern aesthetic; however, small design decisions, including the use of cornices, building mass 
setbacks, and careful considerations to material and color, all contribute towards a more visually 
cohesive streetscape. The site is visible along the Southeast Expressway (Interstate 93) and 
among commercial and residential roads which will serve to enliven and enhance the surrounding 
context. 
 
The proposed project will complement other projects approved in the area, including at 603 
Dorchester Avenue and at 400 Dorchester Street. A blend of brick, and various tones of smooth 
and horizontal fiber cement panels, are being proposed, along with large windows and Juliet 
balconies to populate the front facades. A recessed entry on Dorchester Avenue offers residents 
greater privacy, providing access to pedestal mailboxes, bike parking, and the transformer vault 
directly underground. The building sits back from the property line on both street faces to 
support larger pedestrian sidewalks and a furnishing zone that can accommodate community 
amenities such as street trees and post-and-ring bike spaces. On the upper three floors, the 
building pulls back along the façade helping it to break down its mass in a more visually enticing 
manner. At the roof level, an 1,853 square foot common roof deck with elevator access offers a 
large open space that can be enjoyed by all the building’s residents. 
 
 
3

617 Dorchester Avenue Residential Project 
6. 
Traffic, Parking, and Access 
 
Utilizing no on-site motor vehicle parking, the proposed project is a true transit-oriented 
development, being approximately 0.1 mile from the MBTA’s Andrew Station, providing direct 
access to the Red Line and bus routes, CT3, 9, 10, 16, 17, 18, and 171, and .8 mile from the 
Newmarket Commuter Rail stop. The building will feature secure interior resident bicycle storage, 
and outside visitor post-and-ring assemblies, in compliance with the City of Boston’s bicycle 
parking requirements.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes
and communities
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Dear Director Jemison: 
 
This firm represents Shanti Acquisition LLC (the “Applicant”), the owner and developer of 66 
Geneva Avenue, Boston, MA 02121 (the “Property”) in connection with its Small Project 
Review Application pursuant to Article 80, Section 80-E-2 of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”). 
The Property consists of approximately 19,673 square feet of land and is currently improved by 
an existing one-story, approximately 17,200 sq. ft., building operating as New Faith Missionary 
Baptist Church. The Applicant is proposing to construct a new five-story (5) residential building 
consisting of approximately forty-nine thousand, five hundred and six (49,506) square feet of 
living space divided into fifty (50) units ranging from studio units to three (3) bedroom units (the 
“Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project will exceed the City’s Inclusionary Development 
Policy minimum by designating eight (8) units as affordable. The Proposed Project will also 
provide seventeen (17) parking spaces, fifty (50) indoor bicycle spaces, and ten (10) outdoor 
visitor bicycle spaces. The goal is to create 50 newly constructed units of homeownership 
opportunity for area residents. The development team will be closely monitoring the market to 
determine the feasibility of homeownership. 
In planning the Proposed Project, a great deal of care and attention was paid to the 
existing and proposed densities and massing in the surrounding area. The Proposed 
Project has been specifically designed to reflect the architecture of the surrounding 
community, such as larger-scale multi-family structures, inset porches, and double 
and triple hung windows, while still relating to the larger-scale three-family 
structures to the right of the Property. The Proposed Project prioritizes open space 
along the main pedestrian corridor on Geneva Avenue, including an area for 
commuters to wait for MBTA bus access. 

 
 
 
Prior to submitting this Article 80 Application for Small Project Review, the Applicant 
conducted initial community outreach with Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and the 
Neighborhood Development Corporation of Grove Hall (the “NDC”), as this particular area does 
not have a neighborhood association. The Applicant anticipates the support of both organizations 
with respect to the Proposed Project. As a community benefit, the Applicant has offered to 
partner with the NDC to provide first time homebuyer classes to area residents. Additionally, the 
Applicant has met with District 4 City Councilor, Brian Worrell, which resulted in the increased 
number of family sized units to be included in the Proposed Project. The Applicant looks 
forward to continued outreach with local organizations, elected officials, and residents as the 
process advances. 
Thank you for your consideration and please do not hesitate to contact me with any comments or 
questions.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
 
The Property consists of approximately 19,673 square feet of land and is currently improved by 
an existing one-story, approximately 17,200 sq. ft., building operating as New Faith Missionary 
Baptist Church. 
The Property fronts along Geneva Avenue and is directly across the street from the Jeremiah E. 
Burke High School and the Grove Hall Community Center and Library. This portion of Geneva 
Avenue is populated with a mixture of multifamily structures, some three (3) family structures, 
underutilized and/or vacant lots, and commercial uses. Bishop Joe L. Smith Way, which runs 
perpendicular to this portion of Geneva Avenue and is visible from the Property, consists of four 
(4) story multi-family structures. Additionally, the Property is located directly next to a bus stop 
along bus Route 19 and is approximately 0.27 miles from the Four Corners/Geneva MBTA 
station, which provides access to the Fairmount Line and transfers to the Route 16 bus. 
The Applicant proposes to incorporate the existing one-story building into a new five (5) story 
residential building in order to reuse and preserve the existing structure. The Proposed Project 
consists of approximately forty-nine thousand, five hundred and six (49,506) square feet of 
living space divided into approximately twenty (20) one-bedroom units, twenty (20) two-
bedroom units, six (6) three-bedroom units, and four (4) studio units. There will be 
approximately seventeen (17) parking spaces, fifty (50) indoor bicycle spaces, and ten (10) 
outdoor visitor bicycle spaces. The first floor of the Proposed Project will offer residents 
amenities such as a common area, an exercise room, and a bicycle repair area and storage space. 
In addition to each unit having a private balcony, the Proposed Project will provide 
approximately four-thousand, eight-hundred and sixty-one (4,861) square feet of shared outdoor 
space for residents along the roof deck on the second floor. 
The Proposed Project will consist of approximately eight (8) designated affordable units, as such 
the Proposed Project exceeds the required Inclusionary Development Policy minimum by 
reaching sixteen percent (16%) affordability. 
The Proposed Project has been specifically designed to reflect the architecture of the surrounding 
community, such as larger-scale multi-family structures, inset porches, and double and triple 
hung windows, while still relating to the larger-scale three-family structures to the right of the 
Property. Parking access has been moved to the rear of the Property in order to prioritize open 
space along the main pedestrian corridor along the front of the Property, including an area for 
commuters to wait for MBTA bus access. The Proposed Project seeks to meet the massing of 
Geneva Avenue, namely, to reflect the larger buildings of the Jeremiah E. Burke High School 
and the Grove Hall Community Center and Library. 
The Proposed Project has been modified from its originally proposed plans and has gradually 
been reduced in size through the community process. The most recent plan change increased the 
number of family-sized units within the Proposed Project.

The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of Geneva Avenue by creating approximately 
fifty (50) newly constructed units of homeownership opportunity for area residents. In keeping with the 
mayor’s initiative to bring additional market rate housing to the city, the Proposed Project is not designed 
to be luxury apartments but rather market priced units, approximately eight (8) of which will be 
designated as affordable. The Proposed Project will increase the number of residential units available in 
the city, and in part offer relief from the affordable housing crisis currently challenging the City of 
Boston, in a manner that is consistent and complimentary to the surrounding neighborhood. 
 
In addition to the creation of market rate and affordable housing units, the Proposed Project will create 
upwards of two hundred (200) construction jobs and will result in approximately six (6) full-time jobs. 
 
 
COMMUNITY OUTREACH AND ENGAGEMENT 
The Applicant has engaged the local community through meetings with the Neighborhood Development 
Corporation of Grove Hall (the “NDC”) and the Greater Grove Hall Main Streets, as this area is not 
served by a neighborhood association. 
The Applicant initially met with the Executive Board of the NDC on November 15, 2021. Since then, the 
design plans for Proposed Project have undergone numerous iterations, which have all been presented to 
the NDC. The Applicant regularly updates the NDC with respect to the Proposed Project, with the most 
recent meeting being held on May 21, 2022. 
The Applicant first met with Greater Grove Hall Main Streets on February 8, 2022. The Applicant hosted 
a subsequent meeting with Greater Grove Hall Main Streets on April 10, 2022, to present updated design 
plans, which were amended to reflect concerns raised at the February 8th meeting. 
Additionally, the Applicant met with District 4 City Councilor, Brian Worrell, which resulted in the 
increase in the number of family sized units to be included in the Proposed Project 
As a community benefit, the Applicant has offered to partner with the NDC to provide first time 
homebuyer classes to area residents. The Applicant looks forward to continued outreach with local 
organizations, elected officials, and residents as the process advances. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

9 
 
TRAFFIC, PARKING, PUBLIC TRANSIT, AND VEHICULAR AND PEDESTRIAN ACCESS 
 
The Proposed Project will provide an opportunity for accessible, transit-oriented housing as it is located 
directly next to a Route 19 bus stop and is approximately 0.27 miles from the Four Corners/Geneva MBTA 
station. The Proposed Project will also be developed and designed to provide proper public safety and 
functionality. 
As aforementioned, the Proposed Project fronts along Geneva Avenue and proposes to use Geneva 
Avenue as the primary vehicular and pedestrian access to the building. Parking access has been 
moved to the rear of the Property in order to prioritize open space along the main pedestrian 
corridor along the front of the Property, including an area for commuters to wait for MBTA bus 
access.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

GROUP 1 DWELLING UNITS 
In multiple dwellings, for which building permits for new construction are issued on or 
after September 1, 1996, that are for rent, hire, lease or sale and that are equipped 
with an elevator, all dwelling units must be constructed as Group 1 Dwelling Units, 
except those covered in 521 CMR 9.4, Group 2 Dwelling Units. 
Group 1 units must comply with 521 CMR 9.5, and, 521 CMR 42.00: GROUP 1 
BATHROOMS; 521 CMR 43.00: GROUP 1 KITCHENS; and 521 CMR 46.00: 
GROUP 1 BEDROOMS. 
GROUP 2 DWELLING UNITS 
In multiple dwellings that are for rent, hire, or lease (but not for sale) and contain 20 
or more units, at least 5% of the dwelling units must be Group 2A units. Group 2A 
units must comply with 521 CMR 9.5, Dwelling Unit Interiors; and 521 CMR 44.00: 
GROUP 2 BATHROOMS; and 521 CMR 45.00: GROUP 2 KITCHENS; and 521 
CMR 47.00: GROUP 2 BEDROOMS.

PROJECT SUMMARY
This Small Project Review Application is being submitted by the Bonnet Family and their entity 745 River Street 
LLC (the “Proponent”) in accordance with Article 80, Section E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”). The combined property at 735-745 River Street in Hyde Park (the “Site” or “Project Site”) is situated on 
an approximately 18,020 square foot irregularly and uniquely shaped parcel with frontage on both River Street 
and Thorn Street. The 745 River Street site has been owned by Dr. Jean Bonnet for over twenty years and is the 
home of his longtime medical practice with the Hyde Park Health Associates, which brings community-based 
health services and specialists to an underserved community. The Bonnet family also recently purchased the 
adjacent site at 735 River Street to include in the overall project. 
The Bonnet family proposes a “family legacy project”, which contemplates the improvement and revitalization of 
the Site with the construction of a new, five (5) story, mixed-use development building of approximately 49,900 
square feet of gross floor area (“GFA”), including vastly improved and expanded health clinic space for Dr. Bonnet’s 
medical clinic on the first floor, 40 rental apartment units on the upper floors (including 25 combined two- and 
three-bedroom units), 26 off-street, at-grade parking spaces, and major improvements in landscaping, pedestrian 
connectivity and related public realm improvements in and around the Site, consistent with the character and 
housing needs of the surrounding community (the “Proposed Project”). In this regard, the Proposed Project will 
help the long-term viability and vibrancy of the Site and the medical clinic to remain as a fixture of much-needed 
neighborhood services for years to come. Furthermore, the Proposed Project will revitalize this vastly under-
utilized Site with a residential component of market-rate and on-site affordable housing in excess of the City’s 
current Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) requirements, with a building aesthetic appropriate in scale, 
massing, and design for this section of the Hyde Park neighborhood.
The Proposed Project would create a mixed-use development by combining a ground floor medical clinic, to be 
expanded and improved from that currently existing at the Site, along with market-rate and income restricted 
affordable housing opportunities in a contemporary aesthetic appropriate in scale, massing and design for Hyde 
Park’s emerging growth and revitalization. In planning the building, great care was given to respecting the area’s as-
built conditions. As a result, the proposed building has been designed and scaled to complement both of the Site’s 
street frontages, the busy thoroughfare of River Street and the smaller, dead-end Thorn Street, along with the area’s 
long-existing multifamily residential buildings. The Proposed Project also includes a unique second floor roof deck 
above the parking surface area at the rear of the building, safely located away from the busy River Street, in order to 
provide for resident open space, accessible and available to all future residents, along with several additional small 
private decks for second floor units. 
PROJECT NARRATIVE

COMMUNITY BENEFITS
The Proposed Project will offer many public benefits to the Hyde Park neighborhood and to the City of 
Boston, including the following:
• Replacing a vastly underutilized Project Site that includes a non-conforming single story commercial 
medical office building at 745 River Street and a non-conforming and overgrown, trash filled automobile 
repair service garage at 735 River Street, and developing it with a vastly improved and expanded health clinic 
space on the first floor along with 40 much needed and high quality rental apartment units on the upper 
floors, of which at least seven (7) will be affordable in excess of the IDP;
• Introducing new neighborhood residents who will provide support to the local community and utilize local 
businesses;
• Including a project scope and scale that is intended to further the residential policy goals of the City of 
Boston;
• Improving the safety and visual appearance of the site and immediate area by removing large curb cuts along 
both River Street and Thorn Street and reintroducing new on-street parking spaces and better pedestrian 
experience along the same;
• Coordinating with abutting property owner to review possible enhancements and improvements to private 
passageway between Site and abutting property running between River Street and Thorn Street, with potential 
new sidewalk area, landscaping, wayfinding and overall refinements; 
• Improving environmental conditions at the site, which is the longtime site of an auto-body repair garage 
surrounded by unimproved parking lots with no open or pervious space; 
 
• Exploring the planting of new street trees, widened sidewalks, and other streetscape amenities to improve 
and enhance the pedestrian landscape and experience; 
 
• Encouraging alternative modes of transportation through the use of bicycling, walking, and public 
transportation due to the walkable proximity of several bus lines along River Street and the MBTA Mattapan 
Redline Subway Station; 
• Generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in new property tax revenue annually to the City; and
• Temporarily creating approximately thirty (30) to forty (40) new construction jobs over an 18 month period.

DETAILED PROJECT INFORMATION
DESIGN APPROACH
The Project Site includes approximately 18,020 square feet of combined land area on River Street in Hyde Park, 
comprising two (2) parcels located at the corner of River Street and Thorn Street, which will be combined and 
consolidated as part of the Proposed Project. Thorn Street is a dead end street with a grade change from top 
to bottom which abuts MBTA Commuter Rail tracks for the Franklin and Fairmount lines. The City of Boston 
Assessor’s Parcel Numbers for the Project Site are 1801552000 and 1801551000, which are located in Ward 18 of 
the City of Boston.
The development is located near the end of Thorn Street, a dead end street located just off River Street, which is 
a main thoroughfare between Mattapan and Hyde Park. The neighborhood offers several parks, restaurants and 
cafes. The building’s siting is derived from a creative response to its context and urban conditions. The partially 
below grade parking is pushed to the rear of the site, adjacent to the MBTA tracks, leaving space for the lobby and 
common area at the ground level adjacent to the street. The addition of a sidewalk where one does not currently 
exist at the vacant lot will create a pedestrian friendly experience for both residents and neighbors.
The proposed massing includes a vertical reveal at the front stair which breaks the building into two halves 
and diminishes the overall scale while creating more pleasing proportions. A palette of complementary facade 
materials creates a contemporary aesthetic that will serve as a compelling precedent for the area’s current and 
future development.
 
TRAFFIC, PARKING AND ACCESS
The proposed development includes 26 on-site surface parking spaces that will be accessed via a relocated curb 
cut along Thorn Street. Vehicles will both enter and discharge from the garage onto Thorn Street via this relocated 
curb cut in order to provide a better entering/exit experience versus garage access off the busier thoroughfare of 
River Street. Direct elevator access is provided from the parking to all residential floors of the building through 
the interior lobby. Secure and covered bike storage will be provided adjacent to the parking with direct access 
to River Street as well as access via the residential lobby, while several visitor bike racks will be located near the 
sidewalk at the building entry.
