DETAILED PROJECT INFORMATION
In support of the required Article 80 Small Project Review process and prior to submission of this application, 
the Proponent conducted extensive preliminary outreach with abutting and nearby property owners, residents, 
businesses, and the Belnel Family Neighborhood Association (“BFNA”), as well as related discussions with local 
elected and appointed officials from the area, including but not limited to, the Mayor’s Office of Neighborhood 
Services Hyde Park Liaison and District City Councilor Arroyo’s Office. In particular, the Proponent appeared 
and presented the Proposed Project by hosting its own initial abutter meeting (virtually) on November 10, 2021, 
with members of the immediate neighborhood, and presenting at meetings with the Belnel Family Neighborhood 
Association (December 16, 2021, and September 22, 2022, respectively), in order to obtain feedback from those 
in the direct vicinity of the Site. Additionally, the Proponent met and discussed the Proposed Project several 
times with its direct abutting property owners of 731-733 River Street, 10 Thorn Street and 20 Thorn Street, and 
720 River Street directly across the street (GBM Portfolio Owner LLC). Feedback from this extensive preliminary 
outreach was then incorporated into the resulting Proposed Project and this application. 
Finally, the Proponent has also processed the Proposed Project as part of the BPDA’s pre-file review prior to 
filing this Application, in order to identify and respond to certain issues of concern and advance its design. The 
Proponent will continue to meet with City agencies, the BFNA, local business organizations, abutting and nearby 
property owners and other interested parties as part of the Article 80 public review process.

URBAN DESIGN OVERVIEW
DETAILED PROJECT INFORMATION
The redevelopment of 735-745 River Street will contribute to the on-going transformation of this area of Hyde 
Park into a vibrant mixed-use subdistrict with 40 new residential rental apartments, accompanying amenities, 
medical office and retail space and off-street parking with site wide improvements. The project site is prominently 
located on a corner lot at the intersection of River and Thorn Street. The site offers multi-sided street frontage 
and is adjacent to a series of four and five story multifamily residential buildings, retail uses, parking and open 
spaces. Currently, access to the site is provided on both River and Thorn Streets, both of which will undergo 
comprehensive improvements to enhance access and the larger public realm as a result.
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
735-745 River is proposed as a five-story building which encompasses a ground level podium and adjacent 
surface parking and perimeter green space/site improvements. The unit mix will include spacious one, two 
and three bedroom units with the intent of catering to family-style living. The ground floor is activated by an 
outpatient medical clinic, surface parking, retail and residential lobby uses along with covered and street post and 
ring bike racks.
 
 	 	
	
	
	
	
 	
	
 
The proposed building is grounded with an iron-spot brick veneer to create a durable base, complemented by 
spaces for art murals along the street wall. The building is further refined by the use of an articulated cornice 
along the primary roof line with secondary datum lines at lower floors. The building achieves façade modulation 
through the use of vertically organized three story bays with large picture windows, while also providing a 
dynamic visual rhythm along the building’s façade. Warm toned wood-look fiber cement cladding is broadly 
used across the façade to relate back to the residential context of neighborhood and breakdown the scale of the 
massing. Metal picket railings with a warm wood cap have been employed at fifth floor of the building to facilitate 
private terraces for the units as the building edge steps back to minimize height from the street. 
 	
	
	
	
	
 	
	
 
The landscape and hardscape design for the proposed building and site complements the architecture as well 
as the developments to each side of this proposed building. On the Thorn Street and passageway sides of the 
building, the plantings are compact and scaled to soften the space, but not overwhelm it. The streetscape along 
River and Thorn includes street trees, small growth plantings and new curbs and sidewalks. As part of the 
development’s community benefits package the project will include the enhancement of the adjacent vehicular 
passageway to the east of the property. Improvements as shown on the plans herein will include a newly paved 
roadway surface to accommodate one lane of directional traffic, parallel parking for (7) vehicles, new sidewalks 
with benches, native plantings and LED street lighting. The landscape and hardscape design will include street 
trees in a 3’ furnishing zone, and a city standard concrete sidewalk at 5’, meeting the existing curb. Street trees 
will frame the building façade and be consistent with Boston Complete Streets guidelines.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in Boston’s 
built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, rather than after 
a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a 
built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly.
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth by 
MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth by 
MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes and 
communities 
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4

PROJECT SUMMARY 
 
Introduction 
The Applicant respectfully submits this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”) in accordance with 
the requirements of Article 80E of Chapter 665 of the Acts of 1956 for the development of 819 Cummins 
Highway, Boston, MA 02126. 
The project is led by Sathuan Sa the Principal of EJS Investment Inc., a privately held and minority 
owned development and investment firm with over twenty (20) years of experience in delivering the 
highest quality residential and commercial projects. EJS has partnered with Eric Zachrison of Context, a 
collaborative architectural workshop that believes in cultivating deep relationships with community 
stakeholders and centering the community in its designs. Additionally, EJS has paired with TJD 
Construction Services LLC, a Black woman owned Boston based construction firm to serve as the 
Project’s general contractor. 
 
Existing Conditions 
The Proposed Project is located within the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Zoning District and the 
Gateway Development Area Overlay District, along an evolving section of Cummins Highway and within 
walking distance of Mattapan Square. The Property consists of four (4) existing parcels under common 
ownership comprising a total of approximately 19,491 square feet of vacant land. 
This area is populated with a mixture of two (2) and three (3) family homes along Hollingsworth Street 
and Cummins Highway, and the recently constructed Cote Village Apartments, which transformed the 
former Cote Ford Dealership into a four (4) story, fifty-two (52) unit affordable residential building. 
 
Project Description 
The Proposed Project consists of approximately forty-six thousand, nine hundred and ninety-six (46,996) 
square feet of livable area divided into forty-two (42) units ranging between studio, one-bedroom and 
two-bedroom units. One- and two-bedroom units are needed in this section of Boston, as illustrated in the 
City of Boston Planning and Development Agency’s Housing and Household Composition Community 
Profile tool, 57.4% of households in the project area contain one or two persons; however, the project area 
has only 49% housing stock as studios, one-bedrooms, or two-bedrooms, as compared to 66.3% citywide. 

 
In other words, the project area needs additional one- and two-bedroom units. Seven (7) of the units will 
be designated as affordable, giving the project an affordability rate of 16.7 %. Additionally, there will be 
twenty-five (25) parking spaces, and forty-six (46) bicycle parking spaces. The ground level will offer 
residents amenities such as a bicycle parking area, community room, and fitness center. The retail space 
at the corner of the corner of Cummins Highway and Hollingsworth Street will be an amenity for the 
broader community, prominently demarcating the Proposed Project. 
The Proposed Project has been specifically designed to reflect the architecture of the surrounding 
community, particularly the larger scale multi-family structures in the vicinity. The massing of the 
Proposed Project blends in with that of the surrounding community as it provides a balance between the 
smaller two and three-family and the larger Cote Village Apartments. The design team has intentionally 
activated the pedestrian walkway along the building’s periphery on Cummins Highway by allowing for a 
substantial setback, prioritizing landscaping and green space, and moving the parking entrance to the side 
of the building on Hollingsworth Street. 
The Proposed Project has been modified from its originally proposed plans and has gradually been 
reduced in size and enhanced through the community process. The most recent plans reflect that the 
proposed structure is drawn back from the street in order to enlarge the sidewalk along Cummins 
Highway, a reduction in the building’s massing along Hollingsworth Street, and the relocation of the 
retail space from fronting along Cummins Highway to the corner of Cummins Highway and 
Hollingsworth Street, which further activates the pedestrian area on Cummins Highway providing 
additional outdoor space for residents and neighbors alike. In addition, after meeting with the MBTA, the 
proposed project has been modified to include a 10 ft setback from the property line of the MBTA Right 
of Way (ROW).

Public Benefit: Affordable Homeownership and Job Creation 
In the face of Boston’s rising real estate prices and the well documented wealth gap, the Applicant 
recognizes the importance of homeownership as a tool to build wealth and seeks to increase the number 
of homeownership opportunities available to middle and low-income individuals and families. According 
to the City of Boston Planning and Development Agency’s Housing and Household Composition 
Community Profile, 64.1% of housing units in the Proposed Project area are renter occupied. As such, 
the Proposed Project will further contribute to the ongoing revitalization of Cummins Highway by 
creating forty-two (42) condominium units for homeownership. 
In keeping with the mayor’s initiative to bring additional market rate housing to the city, the Applicant 
has designated seven (7) of the units as affordable, giving the project a 16.7% affordability rate. The 
Proposed Project will increase the number of residential units available in the city, and in part offer relief 
from the affordable housing crisis currently challenging the City of Boston, in a manner that is consistent 
and complimentary to the surrounding neighborhood. 
Additionally, the Proposed Project will create upwards of one hundred (100) construction jobs and result 
in approximately seven (7) to ten (10) full-time jobs. 
 
PLAN: Mattapan 
The Proposed Project is located along the Cummins Highway corridor and surrounded by a rich 
residential fabric, bringing it within the boundaries of PLAN: Mattapan (the “Plan”). The massing and 
site plan meet the goals of the PLAN’s recommendations for both corridors and residential fabric. 
Mattapan’s corridors are prime locations for transit-oriented development (TOD) and larger mixed-use 
projects that can pair increased height and density with benefits such as affordability, improved public 
realm, and ground floor amenities. 
The Proposed Project achieves this objective as it is located across the street from the MBTA Commuter 
Rail at Blue Hill Avenue and, as a result, will make transit a more attractive and feasible travel option. 
Moreover, the inclusion of 2,143 sq. ft. of retail on the ground floor that leads out to a spacious pedestrian 
area with seating along Cummins Highway will activate the public realm at this key intersection. There 
are also plans for a raised crosswalk at this intersection which will improve overall accessibility to the 
Property while reducing crossing pedestrians’ exposure to conflicts with cars. Additionally, the ground 
floor includes a community room that will enable Mattapan residents to connect. Finally, the Proposed 

 
Project increases the urban canopy, an important environmental justice goal of the Plan, by including 
trees within the three (3) ft wide green zone along both Cummins Highway and Hollingsworth Street. 
The Proposed Project also remains in keeping with the surrounding residential fabric. Most importantly, 
the Proposed Project introduces forty-two (42) new homeownership units to Mattapan, promoting an 
essential goal of the Plan to build wealth and encourage neighborhood stability. The inclusion of a 
pedestrian zone along Cummins Highway and Hollingsworth Street promotes safer mobility for residents 
to reach neighborhood destinations on foot. 
Community Outreach and Engagement 
As of the date of this Application, the Applicant has engaged the local community through meetings with 
elected officials and community leaders to introduce and discuss the project. 
The Applicant held its initial Boston Planning and Development Agency (the “BPDA”) prefile meeting 
regarding this project on October 24, 2022, the Applicant took the BPDA’s recommendations into 
consideration and incorporated them into the design and presented the same at its second BPDA prefile 
meeting on March 2, 2023. Additionally, the Applicant met with community stakeholders in May of 
2022, with City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo on November 3, 2022, and with the MBTA on multiple 
occasions. 
The Applicant looks forward to continued outreach with local organizations, elected officials, and 
residents as the process advances.

PROJECT COMPONENTS: 
 
Traffic and Parking Management 
Due to its proximity to public transportation, the Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to 
minimize vehicular traffic by encouraging and accommodating alternate modes of transportation, such as 
public transportation, transportation services, bicycles, and pedestrian traffic. 
As previously mentioned, the Project site is located along the MBTA Commuter Rail at the Blue Hill 
Avenue Station and is within walking distance of the Mattapan Trolley Station in Mattapan Square. The 
area is also accessed by the MBTA Bus Routes #28, #29, and #31. This area is easily accessed on foot 
and via bicycle. Additionally, the Proposed Project offers twenty-five (25) off-street parking spaces for 
residents, and forty-six (46) resident bicycle spaces located on the ground floor. 
 
Construction Management 
 
The Applicant will engage a professional traffic engineer to provide the required Construction 
Management Plan that shall be submitted to the City. 
 
Project Impact and Mitigation, Monitoring 
The Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to minimize the impact to the surrounding 
neighborhood and community before, during and after construction. The Applicant has intentionally 
incorporated into the Proposed Project’s design to minimize the Proposed Project’s impact. The Applicant 
will have a dedicated staff person who will establish consistent, ongoing procedures for evaluating and re-
evaluating the effectiveness of any and all mitigation measures related to the Proposed Project, including, 
but not limited to construction management, traffic management, parking management, and post-
construction aspects. The Applicant will work with the City and the community to regularly intake 
feedback and recommendations to improve upon and revise any and all mitigation measures.

DESIGN 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of this portion of Cummins Highway by 
transforming four (4) vacant lots into a mixed- use residential building that will match the surrounding 
neighborhood at an urban scale. Although the Proposed Project has been designed with a modern 
aesthetic, the building’s massing, setbacks, and carefully curated landscaping all lends towards a 
streetscape that is both cohesive with the existing architecture and welcoming to pedestrians. 
The Proposed Project will complement the recently constructed Cote Apartments and the existing 
buildings in the immediate vicinity. The Proposed project will be a primarily wood framed construction 
over a concrete podium with a variety of fiber cement panels for the exterior façade. Many units will 
feature a private balcony, with additional open space accessed by the common decks on levels two (2) and 
five (5). 
The building is prominently located at the intersection of Cummins Highway and Hollingsworth Street. 
The design team revised the plans so that the building was stepped back along the front yard in order to be 
more in keeping with the modality, alignment and conformity of the abutting buildings along Cummins 
Highway. The ground level retail space and community room are located along Cummins Highway, 
activating that portion of the sidewalk in addition to a furnishing zone that offers benefits such as robust 
landscaping and guest bicycle racks.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

PROJECT SUMMARY 
 
Introduction 
The Applicant respectfully submits this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”) in accordance with 
the requirements of Article 80E of Chapter 665 of the Acts of 1956 for the development of 81 Hancock 
Street, Boston, MA 02125. 
The project is led by Huy Nguyen the owner of 81 Hancock Street has partnered with J. Peter Vanko of 
Vanko Studio, a multi-faceted Boston based architectural design firm to serve as the architect, and Vargas 
DaSilveria of DaSilveria Builders, a minority owned construction company with over thirty (30) years’ 
experience in the construction industry, to serve as the general contractor. 
 
Existing Conditions 
The Proposed Project is located within the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning District, at the intersection 
of Trull and Hancock Streets, and is within walking distance of the Uphams Corner Arts and Innovation 
District. The Property consists of approximately 14,994 square feet of land currently improved by a liquor 
store, pizzeria, and laundromat. The front of the project will be on Hancock Street. 
This area is populated with a mixture of three (3) family dwellings, four (4) story multifamily dwellings, 
and commercial uses along Hancock Street. The surrounding area is undergoing a significant 
transformation with the recent approval, and proposal of various mixed-use and other residential 
developments, as well as the construction of the Conservatory Lab Charter School at 395 Columbia Road. 
The Proposed Project will be similar in height and massing to these newer developments, while 
complimenting the existing structures. 
 
Project Description 
The Proposed Project consists of an approximately thirty-two thousand three hundred and nine (32,309) 
square feet building divided into thirty-nine (39) residential dwelling units- twenty-four (24) studio units, 
three (3) one-bedroom units, six (6) two-bedroom units, and six (6) three-bedroom units. Six (6) of the 
units will be designated as affordable, giving the project an affordability rate of 15.4%. Additionally, 
there will be fourteen (14) parking spaces, and forty (40) bicycle parking spaces. The ground level will 
provide public access to the community serving retail establishments, as well as resident access to the 
lobby. 

The Proposed Project has been specifically designed to complement the surrounding community, 
particularly the larger scale multi-family structures in the vicinity. The massing of the Proposed Project 
blends in with that of the surrounding community as it provides a balance between the smaller three-
family and the larger multi-family residential buildings. 
The Proposed Project has been modified from its originally proposed plans and has gradually been 
reduced in size through the community process. 
The Proposed Project has been designed to reflect the extensive community planning led by the BPDA as 
referenced in the BPDA Fairmount Indigo Planning Initiative for the Upham’s Corner Station area. In 
particular, the Proposed Project will enhance neighborhood safety through well-lit pedestrian-oriented 
streets and the activation of thriving ground floor uses.

Public Benefit: Affordable Homeownership and Job Creation 
The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of this portion of Hancock Street by creating 
thirty-nine (39) newly constructed units of residential rental units, six (6) of which will be designated as 
affordable. The Proposed Project will increase the number of residential units available in the city, and in 
part offer relief from the affordable housing crisis currently challenging the City of Boston, in a manner 
that is consistent and complimentary to the surrounding neighborhood. 
Additionally, the Proposed Project will create approximately ten (10) construction jobs and result in 
approximately seven (7) to ten (10) full-time jobs, while preserving existing retail. 
Community Outreach and Engagement 

As of the date of this Application, the Applicant has engaged the local community through meetings with 
elected officials and community leaders to introduce and discuss the project. 
The Applicant held its initial Boston Planning and Development Agency (the “BPDA”) prefile meeting 
regarding this project on October 17, 2022, the Applicant took the BPDA’s recommendations into 
consideration and incorporated them into the design and presented the same at its second BPDA prefile 
meeting on November 16, 2022; with its third BPDA prefile meeting held on March 29, 2023. 
Additionally, the Applicant met with the Hancock Street Civic Association on March 1, 2022; April 5, 
2022; and September 6, 2022, and with City Councilor Frank Baker on January 24, 2023. 
The Applicant looks forward to continued outreach with local organizations, elected officials, and 
residents as the process advances.

PROJECT COMPONENTS 
 
Traffic and Parking Management 
Due to its proximity to public transportation, the Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to 
minimize vehicular traffic by encouraging and accommodating alternate modes of transportation, such as 
public transportation, transportation services, bicycles, and pedestrian traffic. 
As previously mentioned, the Project site is easily accessible by bicycle and public transportation, as it is 
located along MBTA Routes #15 and #17 and is 0.8 miles from the MBTA Red Line via Savin Hill 
MBTA Station and the MBTA Silverline and 1.7 miles from the MBTA Silver Line and additional bus 
routes via Nubian Station. This area is easily accessed on foot and bicycle via Columbia Road. 
Additionally, the Proposed Project offers fourteen (14) off-street parking spaces for residents, and forty 
(40) resident bicycle spaces located on the ground floor. 
 
Construction Management 
 
The Applicant will engage a professional traffic engineer to provide the required Construction 
Management Plan that shall be submitted to the City. 

 
 
Project Impact and Mitigation, Monitoring 
The Proposed Project has been thoughtfully designed to minimize the impact to the surrounding 
neighborhood and community before, during and after construction. The Applicant has intentionally 
incorporated into the Proposed Project’s design to minimize the Proposed Project’s impact. The Applicant 
will have a dedicated staff person who will establish consistent, ongoing procedures for evaluating and re-
evaluating the effectiveness of any and all mitigation measures related to the Proposed Project, including, 
but not limited to construction management, traffic management, parking management, and post-
construction aspects. The Applicant will work with the City and the community to regularly intake 
feedback and recommendations to improve upon and revise any and all mitigation measures. 
 
DESIGN 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of this portion of Hancock Street by 
transforming the existing one (1) story commercial property, consisting of three (3) storefronts, into a 
mixed- use residential building that will match the surrounding neighborhood at an urban scale. Although 
the Proposed Project has been designed with a modern aesthetic, the building’s massing, setbacks, and 
carefully curated landscaping all lends towards a streetscape that is both cohesive with the existing 
architecture and welcoming to pedestrians. 
The building is prominently located at the intersection of Trull and Hancock Streets. In response to 
community feedback, the design team is proposing the elimination of an existing curb cut on Trull Street 
and revised the plans to increase the amount of green and increased the number of three-bedroom units, 
from four (4) to six (6) to better suit the needs of the community. Additionally, the ground level has been 
reconfigured to provide better access to the resident bicycle parking area.

Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects,

but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

(4) story multi-family structures. Two larger structures, the Jerimah E. Burke High School and the Grove 
Hall Community Center sit directly across the street from the Proposed Project. 
 
Project Description 
The Proposed Project consists of approximately thirty-two thousand, four hundred and thirty-nine 
(32,439) square feet of livable area divided into thirty-three (33) one-bedroom/one-bathroom units, and 
six (6) two-bedroom/two-bathroom units. One- and two- bedroom units are needed in this section of 

 
 
Boston, as illustrated in the City of Boston Planning and Development Agency’s Housing and Household 
Composition Community Profile tool, 52.1% of households in the project area contain one or two 
persons; however, the project area has only 48.9% housing stock as studios, one-bedrooms, or two-
bedrooms, as compared to 66.3% citywide. In other words, the project area needs additional one- and 
two-bedroom units. Six (6) of the units will be designated as affordable, giving the project an 
affordability rate of over fifteen percent (15%). Additionally, there will be twenty-four (24) parking 
spaces, and forty-two (42) resident bicycle parking spaces. The ground floor level will offer residents 
amenities such as an enclosed bicycle parking area, gym, and community room. In addition, a publicly 
accessible café will also be sited on the ground floor level. 
The Proposed Project has been specifically designed to reflect the architecture of the surrounding 
community, particularly the larger scale multi-family structures and institutional buildings in the vicinity. 
The massing of the Proposed Project blends in with that of the surrounding community as it provides a 
balance between the smaller three-family and multi-family residential buildings and the larger school, 
community center, and library. The design team has intentionally activated the pedestrian walkway along 
the building’s periphery on Geneva Avenue by prioritizing landscaping and green space and moving the 
parking entrance to the rear of the building on Oldfields Road. Furthermore, the path along the paper 
street, Winder Street, will be developed to provide pedestrian access between Oldfields Road and Geneva 
Avenue. 
The Proposed Project has been modified from its originally proposed plans and has gradually been 
reduced in size and enhanced through the community process. The most recent plans create a step-down 
along the left side of the building, the side that abuts a four (4) story, three (3) family development, on the 
right side the building steps up to relate to future development of the city owned lot. These heights are 
consistent with each other.

Public Benefit: Affordable Homeownership and Job Creation 
In the face of Boston’s rising real estate prices and the well documented wealth gap, the Applicant 
recognizes the importance of homeownership as a tool to build wealth and seeks to increase the number 
of homeownership opportunities available to middle and low-income individuals and families. According

Community Profile, 83.4% of housing units in the Proposed Project area are renter occupied. As such, the 
Proposed Project will further contribute to the ongoing revitalization of Geneva Avenue by creating 
thirty-nine (39) condominium units for homeownership. 
In keeping with the mayor’s initiative to bring additional market rate housing to the city, the Applicant 
has designated six (6) of the units as affordable, giving the project an affordability rate of over fifteen 
percent (15%). The Proposed Project will increase the number of residential units available in the city, 
and in part offer relief from the affordable housing crisis currently challenging the City of Boston, in a 
manner that is consistent and complimentary to the surrounding neighborhood.

approximately seven (7) to ten (10) full-time jobs.

Traffic and Parking Management

DESIGN 
 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will contribute to the revitalization of this portion of Geneva Avenue by 
transforming two vacant lots into a mixed- use residential building that will match the surrounding 
neighborhood at an urban scale. Although the Proposed Project has been designed with a modern 
aesthetic, the building’s massing, setbacks, and carefully curated landscaping all lends towards a 
streetscape that is both cohesive with the existing architecture and welcoming to pedestrians. 
The Proposed Project will complement the recently approved project at 66 Geneva Avenue and the 
existing larger scale buildings in the immediate vicinity. The Proposed project will be a primarily wood 
framed construction over a concrete podium with a variety of fiber cement panels for the exterior façade. 
Each unit will feature a private balcony, with additional open space accessed by the common roof deck as 
described below. The building will sit back from the property line on both Geneva Avenue and Oldfields 
Road allowing for a furnishing zone that offers benefits such as robust landscaping and eight (8) guest 
bicycle racks, which will accommodate up to sixteen (16) bicycles. The recessed entry on Geneva Avenue 
provides a welcoming combination of landscaping and hardscaping between the building and sidewalk 
that offers residents greater privacy and pedestrians a visually stimulating sidewalk. Additionally, the path 
along the paper street, Winder Street, will be developed to provide pedestrian access between Oldfields 
Road and Geneva Avenue. 
The upper level of the building’s east elevation is designed to pull back along the façade in order to break 
down its mass in a more visually appealing manner. At roof level, a 1,645 square foot common green roof 
deck with elevator access, a seating area, and outdoor gas grill area, offers a large open space that can be 
enjoyed by the building’s residents.

3 Future Conditions 
This section describes the future conditions of the site, including site access locations, parking and loading 
layout, and trip generation. 
3.1. Site Access 
Vehicular access to the site will be provided via a driveway along Oldfields Road on the northeast side of 
the site. The driveway will provide access to a parking area that will contain 25 vehicle parking spaces. 
Main pedestrian access for the residential units will be from both Geneva Avenue and Oldfields Road, with 
access to the coffee shop located along Geneva Avenue. Access to the bicycle parking will be directly from 
Geneva Avenue. Figure 3 shows the first-floor site plan, which shows the location of the vehicle parking, 
bicycle parking, and the access points to the building. 
3.2. Parking and Loading 
There will be vehicle parking on-site in a covered area on the first floor. There will be a total of 25 vehicle 
parking spaces, including 15 standard spaces, nine (9) compact spaces, and one (1) accessible space. 
Vehicle loading will take place along either Geneva Avenue or Oldfields Road, as there is parking available 
along both roadways. The proposed parking area is shown in Figure 3. 
3.3. Sight Distance Analysis 
Sight distance measurements and calculations were conducted at the location of the proposed site driveway 
along Oldfields Road. An analysis of intersection sight distance (ISD) confirms that adequate sight distance 
is provided along Oldfields Road to allow safe maneuvers to and from the site driveway. The calculations 
were based on a speed limit of 25mph and compared to recommended distances set forth by the American 
Association of State Highway Transportation Officials (AASHTO). Due to the location of the proposed 
driveway, as well as Oldfields Road being a dead-end, the driveway will be a left-turn exit only. 
From the proposed site driveway location, a driver will have sight lines of approximately 300 feet towards 
the intersection of Oldfields Road at Normandy Street, which is in excess of the recommended minimum 
of 240 feet. Based on this analysis, there is sufficient sight distance for safe maneuvers from the proposed 
site driveway. 
3.4. Trip Generation 
This section describes the proposed trip generation for the site. As the site is currently unoccupied, there 
are zero (0) vehicle-trips being generated. 
 
The trip generation estimates were calculated based on calculations utilizing the number of proposed 
residential dwelling units and the square footage of the proposed coffee shop, combined with the rates for 
LUC 220 – Multifamily Housing (Low-Rise) and LUC 936 – Coffee/Donut Shop without Drive-Through, 
respectively. The rates were gathered from the Trip Generation Manual, 11th Edition produced by the 
Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) in 2021. The proposed Project will contain 40 residential 
dwelling units and an approximate 468 square foot coffee shop. 
To estimate the anticipated mode split, BSC referenced Go Boston 2030 produced by the City of Boston, 
which provides mode split data for each of the neighborhoods in Boston. The mode split data provided was 
gathered from the 2013 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Since the publication of Go 
Boston 2030, newer ACS 5-year data has been published, most recently in 2021. As such, BSC has gathered 
the 2021 ACS 5-year estimates for mode split for each of the zip codes of Dorchester and has applied the 
percentages to the initial trip generation calculations. Table 2 shows the estimated number of proposed

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

PROJECT OVERVIEW 
1.1 
Introduction 
TCB 900 Morrissey (the “Proponent”), an affiliate of The Community Builders, Inc. (TCB), in 
partnership with Pine Street Inn, Inc. (PSI) as a supportive service provider, proposes to change 
the use of the existing building located at 900 Morrissey Boulevard from hotel to multi-family 
residential use with ground floor commercial office space (the “Project”). The proposed use will 
provide housing for formerly homeless individuals, as well as associated amenity spaces located 
throughout the building, outdoor community spaces for use by residents, and a limited amount 
of ground-floor office space. In total, the Project will result in the creation of approximately 104 
new residential units, 100% of which will be affordable to individuals earning less than 30% of the 
Area Median Income (AMI). Pine Street Inn will provide supportive services to tenants living in the 
building, enabling formerly homeless individuals to continue leading stable lives in permanent, 
leased housing. The existing surface parking will be reduced to approximately 33 parking spaces 
and landscaping improvements will be made that significantly increase green space on-site. 
About The Community Builders, Inc. 
TCB is one of America's leading nonprofit housing organizations. Its mission is to build and sustain 
strong communities where people of all incomes can achieve their full potential. This mission is 
realized by developing, financing, and operating residential communities, neighborhood 
amenities and resident opportunity programs. Since 1964, TCB has constructed or preserved 
hundreds of affordable and mixed-income housing developments and pioneered the Community 
Life model for resident success. Over the last 50 years, TCB has completed or preserved over 
30,000 homes. Today, anchored by offices in Boston, Chicago, Cincinnati, New York and 
Washington, D.C., TCB owns or manages 14,000+ apartment homes in more than 14 states and 
Washington D.C., serving 25,000+ residents. TCB is the sole member of TCB 900 Morrissey LLC, 
and will be the property owner, developer, and long-term operator and property manager of the 
site. 
About Pine Street Inn, Inc. 
Founded in 1969, PSI is the largest homeless services provider in New England, offering a 
comprehensive range of services to nearly 2,000 men and women each day, including permanent 
housing, workforce development, emergency shelter and street outreach. PSI’s goal is to end 
homelessness by making permanent housing a reality for all, by supporting men and women in 
moving off the streets, out of shelter into a permanent home, reconnecting with the community 
and reaching their highest level of independence. PSI has been developing, managing, and 
providing supportive services in permanent housing since 1984. 
Today, PSI supports more men and women in housing than in shelter, with over 850 tenants in 40 
locations across Boston and in Brookline. PSI has housed thousands of men and women over the 
last 35 years. With a 90+% retention rate in housing, PSI helps tenants become and remain stable.

Project Overview 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
PSI will provide supportive services to the tenants living in the Project through a contract with the 
property owner that will ensure tenants have access to daily case workers on-site, with the goal 
of keeping people living stable lives in their apartment homes long-term. 
This Small Project Review application is being submitted to initiative review under Article 80E of 
the Boston Zoning Code (Zoning Code). 
1.2 
Project Description 
1.2.1 
Project Site 
The approximately 57,106 square foot (sf) Project site is bounded by Morrissey Boulevard to the 
north and west, Conley Street to the south, and Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority 
(MBTA) railway tracks to the east. At the northwest corner of the site, a pedestrian bridge lands 
to provide a safe crossing over Morrisey Boulevard. The site is currently improved by a five-story 
hotel building and approximately 96 surface parking spaces. In the Project vicinity, there are 
restaurants, a supermarket, and numerous recreational facilities such as Tenean Beach, Garvey 
Playground, and Joseph Finnegan Park. See Figure 1-1 for an aerial locus map and Figure 1-2 shows 
existing site conditions photographs. Appendix A includes a site survey. 
1.2.2 
Project Program 
As described above and shown in Table 1-1, the Project comprises the renovation of the existing 
hotel building into approximately 104 residential units, associated amenity space, office space, 
and commercial space. The Project will also reduce the number of parking spaces from 96 spaces 
to approximately 33 spaces. See Figure 1-3 for a view of the Project. Appendix B includes floor 
plans, sections, elevations, and unit details.

1.2.3 
Transportation, Parking and Loading 
Because the Project provides 100% affordable housing, no parking is required to serve the 
residents of the building. Two spaces per 1,000 gross floor area (GFA) will be required per Zoning 
for the limited office/commercial space, or approximately 9 parking spaces total. The proposed 
33 parking spaces at the Project site will satisfy the required parking for the commercial/office 
users, on-site staff who will provide social and building services, and the limited number of 
tenants who own a vehicle. The Project will also provide bicycle parking for building tenants and 
commercial office users. The designated loading area will be located at the rear of the building, 
which will be gated. 
1.2.4 
Site Access 
Primary vehicular access will be from Conley Street. The existing access driveway from Morrissey 
Boulevard will be removed and replaced with greenery and an updated sidewalk based on 
approval from DCR and the Boston Fire Department. The proposed new landscaping will provide 
attractive and effective screening from Morrissey Boulevard for the benefit of both tenants and 
public users of Morrissey Boulevard. 
Pedestrians may access the Project site via the sidewalk that connects Morrissey Boulevard and 
Conley Street as well as the raised pedestrian bridge that crosses Morrissey Boulevard. The 
primary entrance to the building will remain in its current location. Updated signage will be 
located onsite to direct tenants and visitors. 
1.3 
Public Benefits 
The Project will provide multiple benefits to the City of Boston (the City) as a result of converting 
the existing hotel into a permanent apartment community that will house extremely low-income 
individuals who have been chronically homeless. 
The Project will improve urban design improvements on this part of Morrissey Boulevard, will 
improve pedestrian connections to the Port Norfolk neighborhood and waterfront amenities at 
the rear of the site, will create jobs, and will increase economic activity. 
Affordable Housing 
The Project will transform a hotel that temporarily houses a transient population into apartments 
that will permanently house approximately 104 chronically homeless individuals. The City’s 
affordable housing stock will be increased by approximately 104 units as a result of this Project, 
and the individuals will be placed into stable housing, reducing the number of people who are 
living in shelters. The site will be well managed, with professional property management provided 
by TCB’s experienced staff, including 24/7 security provided by a third-party security company. 
Comprehensive supportive services will be provided by PSI through daily case management 
activities, which will help tenants develop life skills to remain in stable housing, connect them 
with health and behavioral health services, and job training. 

6749/900 Morrissey Boulevard 
1-7 
Project Overview 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
There are no existing residences at the Project site and therefore there will be no displacement 
as a result of the Project. 
Increased Employment 
The Project will result in the creation of approximately 100 construction jobs and approximately 
25 permanent jobs once it is occupied and in operation. 
Site Improvements 
The Project will significantly reduce impervious surfaces on the site by replacing approximately 
10,000 sf hardscaped surfaces with landscaping. Existing parking spaces will be reduced from 96 
to 33 spaces, and the former parking spaces will be converted to a planted recreation area for 
tenants to use, in addition to community garden plots for building tenants. In addition, the 
Proponent proposes to close both of the curb cuts on Morrissey Boulevard, improving safety for 
vehicles entering and existing the site, as well as pedestrians and bicyclists along the Morrissey 
Boulevard edge of the site. Pending approval from DCR, which owns the land fronting Morrissey 
Boulevard that is outside of the property boundary, the curb cuts will be replaced with 
landscaping. 
Transportation 
The Project is consistent with ongoing transit improvement plans to the surrounding roadway 
network, especially given the significant reduction in travel demand to and from the site. The 
Project will generate considerably less travel demand than the existing hotel use. Based on the 
Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE) Trip Generation, 11th Edition, calculations the Project 
will generate only half of the travel demand than the existing use, including less travel during the 
AM peak and PM peak travel periods. The Proponent will operate a shuttle service for tenants to 
access nearby transit facilities, medical and shopping centers, and places of employment. The 
Proponent commits to providing a spot for Blue Bike Stations. 
1.4 
Zoning and Regulatory Controls 
1.4.1 
Zoning Overview 
The Project site is located within the Community Commercial (CC) Subdistrict in the Dorchester 
Neighborhood of Boston. 
1.4.2 
Boston Zoning Code – Use and Dimensional Requirements 
The Project will involve a change in use from hotel to Multifamily Dwelling Residential Use within 
the existing building on the Project site. Multifamily residential is a conditional use at this location. 
Office and retail uses are allowed by right at the site. The Project does not propose any 
dimensional changes to the existing building. As a 100% affordable housing project, the parking

requirement for residential use on this site is zero. For the proposed ground floor 
office/commercial space, a ratio of two parking spaces per 1,000 sf is required, or 9 spaces 
required. The 33 parking spaces proposed for the site comply with this minimum requirement. 
1.4.3 
Article 25A Compliance 
A portion of the Project is within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District (CFROD) per the 
BPDA Sea Level Rise – Flood Hazard Area Map and is therefore subject to Article 25A of the Boston 
Zoning Code. The areas of the Project within this overlay district have an existing elevation of 
approximately 15.25 (BCB) [8.78 (NAVD88)] to 18.46 (BCB) [12.0 (NAVD88)]. Using the BPDA Sea 
Level Rise – Flood Hazard Area map, the Sea Level Rise Base Flood Elevation (BFE) is 19.5 (BCB). 
The “Commercial Use” Sea Level Rise Design Flood Elevation (DFE) based on this information is 
equal to 20.5 (SLRBFE + 12 inches). The “Residential Use” Sea Level Rise Design Flood Elevation 
DFE based on this information is equal to 21.5 (SLRBFE + 24 inches). 
To comply with Article 25A, the Proponent proposes the following: 
1. There are no residential uses on the first floor. None of the residential living units will 
have a DFE below 21.5 feet. 
2. The first floor will contain lobby space, office commercial uses, and storage and 
maintenance space. These uses are permitted below the DFE. Approximately 4,393 SF of 
ground floor space will be designed as office commercial space, which is an allowed use. 
3. The building areas within the CFROD will be designed with guidance from the City’s 
Coastal Flood Zoning Design Guidelines as well as Article 25A. See Appendix C for 
floodproofing approaches.

the site is mainly paved, while a landscaped area between the site and Morrissey Boulevard

additional landscaping and the closure of two curb cuts subject to DCR approvals. This landscaping 
will screen portions of the site from Morrissey Boulevard. The Project will comply with GPOD 
standards.

DESIGN COMPONENT 
The proposed Project is largely an interior renovation and rehabilitation of an existing hotel 
building to change the use to a multifamily residential property. As such, the Project involves 
interior improvements including the addition of kitchenettes, amenity spaces, office space, and 
other spaces to convert what is currently a hotel building into an apartment building to house 
low-income, formerly homeless individuals. Additional site improvements will include 
landscaping, improved site circulation and access, and placemaking. The design of the Project will 
meet 2020 Enterprise Green Communities standards. 
As described in Chapter 1, the Project will greatly reduce the impervious spaces on the site. The 
existing vehicular curb cuts on Morrissey Boulevard are proposed to be removed and replaced 
with greenery and an updated sidewalk. The existing 96 surface parking spaces will be reduced to 
33 spaces, which will allow for these formerly impervious surfaces to be converted into green 
space, including open lawn area that may be utilized for future event programming for the Project. 
The existing parking spaces adjacent to Morrissey Boulevard will be transformed with additional 
trees and plantings along the sidewalk, providing new greenery and screening for pedestrians 
walking along Morrissey Boulevard and Conley Street. The sidewalk along Conley Street will be 
rebuilt following Boston City Guidelines, enhancing the pedestrian experience. The Project will 
enhance the entryway with exterior lighting and signage to foster a more welcoming experience. 
See Figures 2-1 to 2-3 for views of the Project and Figure 2-4 for the landscape plan. 
The entrance to the building will remain in its current location and will be improved with an 
updated entryway/canopy. The Project’s interior renovations will greatly improve the experience 
for the building’s occupants by converting hotel rooms into studio apartments through the 
addition of kitchenettes in each hotel room. Each studio on levels two through five will receive 
new appliances, finishes, flooring, lighting, and additional mechanical upgrades in their 
conversion to studio apartments with associated laundry, trash, recycling, and common area 
amenity spaces. As a result of this renovation, the existing hotel will be converted to a pleasant 
apartment community with sufficient amenities to serve residents and commercial office users 
both inside and outside the building. As seen in Table 2-1 below, the upper floors of the building 
will provide sufficient amenity space to meet compact living guidelines. Residents will have access

3.0 
CLIMATE CHANGE RESILIENCE 
3.1 
Introduction 
Climate change conditions considered by the Project team include higher maximum and mean 
temperatures, more frequent and longer extreme heat events, more heavy rainfall events and sea 
level rise, and more frequent and longer droughts. 
3.2 
Extreme Heat Events 
The Climate Ready Boston report predicts that in Boston, there may be between 25 to 90 days 
with temperatures over 90 degrees by 2070, compared to an average of 11 days per year over 90 
degrees between 1971 and 2000. The Project site design will include measures to adapt to these 
conditions, including the reduction of impermeable surfaces on-site and additional greenspace 
and landscaping to reduce heat island effect. The mechanical systems will be modular in nature 
with an ability to expand heating and cooling capacities in the future. 
3.3 
Precipitation and Sea Level Rise 
As a result of climate change, the northeast is expected to experience more frequent and intense 
storms. To mitigate this, the Proponent will take measures to minimize stormwater runoff and 
protect the Project’s mechanical equipment, as necessary. The existing Project site is nearly 
entirely impervious and the Project will result in a reduced amount of impervious area which will 
be expected to reduce the existing peak rates and volumes of stormwater runoff from the Project 
site, and promote runoff recharge to the greatest extent practicable. Discussion of the Project’s 
compliance with Article 25A of the Zoning Code is included in Appendix C. 
3.4 
Drought Conditions 
Although more intense rain storms are predicted, extended periods of drought are also predicted 
due to climate change. Under the high emissions scenario, the occurrence of droughts lasting one 
to three months could go up by as much as 75% over existing conditions by the end of the century. 
To minimize the Project’s susceptibility to drought conditions, the landscape design is anticipated 
to incorporate native and adaptive plant materials and high efficiency irrigation systems will be 
installed.

Floodproofing Overview 
The existing building presents several challenges, making in-situ dry floodproofing of the building’s exterior 
difficult, leading to our decision to propose the building be primarily dry floodproofed, protected by 
deployable barriers up to the commercial use SLFBFE+24” of 21.5’. Where feasible, portions of the building 
that are currently constructed of load-bearing CMU/EIFS materials are to be sealed, windows raised, and 
reinforced to function as dry floodproof barriers. The two CMU egress stairwells on either corner are being 
evaluated for wet floodproofing measures per the diagram below, adding flood gates, flood doors, and 
strengthened walls for resisting hydrostatic pressure. Panel deployment and evacuation procedures will be 
outlined in an Emergency Action Plan. 
Dry Floodproofing 
• 
Provide temporary flood barriers on site to deploy around the perimeter of the building and around 
ground-mounted electrical, switch gear, and condensers as part of an emergency action plan. 
(~500’ of 6’ tall AquaFence or equal). 
• 
Install small concrete barrier walls to transition from areas of dry floodproofing to wet floodproofing 
at existing CMU walls that can be easily modified to be wet floodproofing barriers. 
• 
Adjust design of new curbs to accommodate barrier layout. 
• 
Provide on-site storage for barriers. 
Wet Floodproofing at Stairwells: 
• 
Replace first floor stairwell wall finishes with tile and similar durable materials. 
• 
Provide flood hatches into the exterior wall to permit equalization of hydrostatic pressure and flood 
water recession. 
• 
Apply waterproof barriers to the floor and interior walls surfaces inside the stair up to 5’-3”. 
• 
Install flood proof door into a new engineered interior wall at corridor to separate the dry and wet 
floodproofed areas.

ii. 
Proposed Project 
The proposed 90 Allandale development will be constructed upon the 87,162 square 
foot lot located at 90 Allandale Street, Jamaica Plain, MA 02130. The lot is currently 
occupied by a single-family dwelling, which will be razed and replaced with the 
proposed development. The Proposal is to Construct a new four (4) phase residential 
development comprised of four (4) two and a half story townhouses each containing 
two (2) single-family dwelling units, for a total of eight (8) home ownership 
condominiums on the northerly portion of the lot. Each condo will be two and a half 
stories and contain 3 bedrooms. The southerly portion of the lot will be protected from 
future development with the recording of a deed restriction. 
iii. 
Design Process 
The design of the proposed development has been shaped by prefiling input from the 
BPDA. During the prefiling process, meetings were held on May 4, 2023, September 19, 
2023, and March 12, 2024. The meetings were attended by the project team and 
representatives of the BPDA. 
iv.

The Proposed Project is located on Allandale Street. The area surrounding the site on 
Allandale Street has uses mostly comprised of one-family residential, along with Senior 
Living facilities, Urban Wild Open Space, and Hospital facilities. Directly abutting the 
project site are two (2) single-family dwellings and one multi-building lot holding three 
(3) single-family dwellings. To the rear of the site is the Allandale Woods, an Urban 
Wild Open Space. Directly across the street are a number of single-family homes. This 
project will fit within the residential context in the area, providing eight (8) home 
ownership condominiums in townhouse design. 
Located in the Southwest corridor of the City of Boston, the proposed project provides 
access to the downtown area by train (Needham Line inbound to Back Bay via 
Roslindale Village Commuter Rail Station). The Project Site is relatively distanced from 
public transportation provided by the Massachusetts Bay Transport Authority 
(“MBTA”). The closest means of public transit are MBTA 35 and 38 Buses, which have 
inbound and outbound stops 0.3 miles from the Project Site. The nearest MBTA Subway 
Station is the Forrest Hills Station (Orange Line), which is approximately 1.2 miles from 
the Project Site, a twenty-six (26) minute walk. The nearest MBTA Commuter Rail 
Station is the aforementioned Roslindale Village Station, which is approximately a mile 
from the Project Site; this would be about a twenty-eight (28) minute walk from the 
Project Site. 
In addition to being distanced from public transit, the surrounding neighborhood lacks 
in basic amenities within a reasonable walking distance, aside from healthcare facilities 
with Brigham & Women’s Faulkner Hospital located just 0.3 miles from the Project Site; 
this would be a six (6) minute walk. The nearest pharmacy is CVS Pharmacy on 
Washington Street, approximately 1.6 miles and a thirty (30) minute walk from the 
Project Site. The nearest Supermarket is Roche Brothers, 1.4 miles from the Project Site; 
this would be a thirty-seven (37) minute walk. The nearest library is the Public Library 
of Brookline, approximately a mile and a twenty-three (23) minute walk from the 
Project Site. The distance from these amenities and others, as well as the distance from 
most public transit, informed the Developer’s decision to provide each unit with two (2) 
vehicle parking spaces. 
v. 
Development Context 
The Proposed Project will contain eight (8) dwelling units, with units ranging in size 
from 2,736 to 3,694 square feet, averaging approximately 3,127 square feet per unit. The 
total gross floor area across the four (4) buildings is 25,021 square feet.

Per Map 11B of the West Roxbury Neighborhood District, the Proposed Project is 
located within a 1F-8000 subdistrict. Based on a zoning analysis, the Proposed Project 
requires zoning relief and will be seeking variances from the City of Boston’s Zoning 
Board of Appeals. 
vi. 
Urban Design 
The Proposed Project will replace a single-family dwelling with a multi-family 
residential development. The project site is located within a 1F-8000 subdistrict and 
abuts both an Open Space Urban Wild subdistrict and a Conservation Protection 
subdistrict. The Proposed Project will serve to update and enhance the residential 
subdistrict by adding eight (8) single-family home ownership units on a large lot that 
can accommodate such a proposal. 
vii. 
Building Design 
The proposed 8 units are divided into 4- duplex buildings to allow for natural light and 
views for each side-by-side arrangement. The site is also a steep grade from Allandale 
Street at the top sloping southerly downhill toward the vast open space of Allandale 
Woods. The stepping of the site allows for picturesque views from the 2 rows of units 
and maximum opportunity for passive solar exposure for each owner to partake in 
energy conservation. 
The buildings are designed to mimic the neighboring single-family residence in mass 
while having articulated roof lines to accent the natural setting among the existing 
woodland setting. Each unit will include patios or balconies to interact with the natural 
setting and all residents will have common access to the ample open site and serene 
setting of the intermittent stream that crosses the development. 
Each unit is planned as a generous family-style home with spacious open living spaces, 
full kitchens and ample bedrooms and bathrooms. The intent is for long-term resident 
ownership that feels like country living yet only minutes from the recently expanded 
Faulkner Hospital and the Arnold Arboretum. The exterior materials chosen for the 
facades express the natural setting while being carbon sensitive and low maintenance to 
enhance the aesthetic of this small community and conserve future energy and 
environmental impacts of the construction of these homes

viii. 
Site Design 
The site is very dramatic with a steep south facing slope from Allandale Street down to 
the Allandale Woods Conservation Area. The duplex building are set into the hillside 
in a terraced arrangement to blend into the landscape and allow for the preservation of 
most of the existing large trees that enhance this setting. The existing driveway will be 
raised with fill to lessen the steepness and also provide for an intermittent storm water 
drainage base. The buildings have been situated to allow for as much undisturbed view 
as possible from the north uphill balconies over or in between the southerly downhill 
units. As Allandale Street is very narrow and several vertical feet above the unit 
entrances, each unit will have 2 garaged parking spaces and visitor parking will be 
accommodated in common hardscape areas that will also accommodate the 
maneuvering of firetrucks should the need arise. 
ix. 
Landscape Design 
 
This stunning site offers a unique opportunity to provide 8 new Boston residences 
within a rare Urban Wild context and Allandale neighborhood. The proposed landscape 
design includes the following primary goals: 
 
- 
support residential living on site 
- 
restore the riparian resource area of the intermittent stream 
 
The residential landscape is mainly limited to the upper half of the site along Allandale 
Road. The shared driveway and unit paved pedestrian walkways are proposed to re-
use the existing curb cut and existing driveway location to limit site impacts. The shared 
circulation is designed through the center of the residences, with separate access to each 
of the two-car garages located within the footprint of the architecture. Welcoming 
entries at each of the private units will be distinguished by large-format bluestone 
pavers and a layered approach to planting design including native ornamental trees, 
shrubs and perennials. Each unit also includes private rear porches with views to 
existing wooded areas and new plantings. An overlook and central stairway is 
proposed in the center of the site to provide access to the restoration area. A sloped path 
along the right sideyard will allow barrier-free access to the rear. Reuse of the existing 
stone patio to limit disturbance near the intermittent stream and an informal mown 
path over the existing culvert will provide a way to access a small mown lawn area and

new patio for the enjoyment of the residents. This new outdoor amenity area is 
proposed outside the 50’ resource boundary. 
 
Preservation of many of the existing trees, restoration of the existing rear yard lawn to a 
native meadow, and a plant palette of only Massachusetts native plants will ensure a 
resilient, ecologically-focused site design. The maintenance regime of the rear area will 
include invasive species removal, 1x yearly mowing at the meadow areas, and no 
fertilization nor irrigation. The restoration of the area is intended to support 
biodiversity and increase ecological function of this important natural resource. 
 
x. 
Traffic and Parking 
Vehicular trip generation from the eight (8) units is expected to be consistent with 
recent suburban land use guidance from the Institute of Transportation Engineers (ITE). 
The opportunity to reduce trip counts is minimal, as the closest MBTA bus route (Bus 
38) is 1,600 feet away at the Wren Street-Forest Hills Station (opposite Faulkner 
Hospital) on Centre Street; and the closest subway station is 4,800 feet away at the 
Forest Hills Station (Orange Line), walking through the Arnold Arboretum. Either 
public transit mode would likely be accessed on foot, as bicycle and other alternative 
transport options would be dangerous along the narrow and busy corridor of Allandale 
Street. 
As a result of the expected mixture of residential and light commercial vehicles entering 
and leaving the site, and the need to plateau the driveway at the entrance for public 
safety (that allows vehicles to identify pedestrians walking along the Allandale Street 
sidewalk and properly identify busy vehicular traffic along the public way), the upper 
portion of the shared driveway at the intersection with Allandale Street is 24 feet wide. 
The width allows safe two-way traffic at the entrance. The driveway width transitions 
to 18 feet wide within the site. 
Resident and guest parking space allocations for each unit are consistent with ITE 
guidance on parking demand for the suburban setting.

minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built environment which provides equitable 
experiences for all people, regardless ofage or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Planmodifications, must complete this 
Checklist to provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project 
plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility 
throughout Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability 
Commission staff prior to filing.

1.0 
Introduction 
This Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (IMPNF) is being submitted to the Boston 
Planning and Development Agency (BPDA) by Harvard University (Harvard). This document is 
being submitted in accordance with Article 80A-2 and Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
Zoning Code), for purposes of amending the current Institutional Master Plan (IMP) for Harvard 
University’s Campus in Allston. As described in more detail in Section 6, this document is being 
submitted in accordance with Section 80D-9(2)(b), Projects Qualifying for Expedited Amendment 
Procedure. 
This IMPNF considers one project: the renovation of the existing building at 92 Seattle Street (the 
Project) to accommodate institutional uses. 
92 Seattle Street and 38 Travis Street are attached buildings located on an approximately 56,200 
square foot site located in between the corners of Travis and Rena Streets and Academic Way and 
Science Drive. Together, the buildings have a Gross Floor Area (as defined in the Boston Zoning 
Code) of approximately 31,000 square feet of Gross Floor Area (GFA). This document refers to 
the property and buildings together as “92 Seattle.” 
This IMPNF does not propose to add any additional land to the existing Harvard IMP area in 
Allston. The Project site is already part of the Harvard IMP area; the proposed institutional use 
requires approval under the IMP requirements of Section 80D of the Zoning Code. 
Figure 1 depicts the Project site within the Harvard University IMP Area. 
2.0 
Status of the Institutional Master Plan for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston 
2.1 
IMP Amendments 
Harvard has been filing Institutional Master Plans for its Allston campus since 1989. Most 
recently, Harvard’s IMP for its campus in Allston was approved by the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (BRA) Board in October 2013 and by the Boston Zoning Commission in November 2013. 
Since that time, Harvard has filed four amendments to its 2013 IMP: 
1. The First Amendment described changes to Harvard’s Allston Science Complex, now referred 
to as the Science and Engineering Complex (SEC). This First Amendment and the revised SEC 
project were approved at the May 2016 BPDA Board Meeting. 
2. The Second Amendment described the proposed Life Lab, a new facility located on Western 
Avenue which provides wet laboratory/co-working space for small Harvard-related scientific 
start-ups. This Second Amendment and the Life Lab project were approved at the March 2017 
BPDA Board Meeting.

Under Section 51-29(6) of the Zoning Code, colleges and universities in Allston/Brighton are 
required to renew their Institutional Master Plans every four years. By way of this IMPNF, Harvard 
seeks to renew its current IMP; except for the Project described in the IMPNF, the IMP renewal 
contemplates no changes to the current IMP. In addition, Harvard intends to start the process of 
preparing a new IMP pursuant to Section 80D-8 of the Code in 2023.
