Description of the Proposed Institutional Project 
4.1 
Project Need and Vision 
The 92 Seattle Street project focuses on renovation of an existing warehouse structure located on 
Harvard University’s Campus in Allston, in order to provide new institutional program space for 
use by Harvard programs, including the athletics department and studio/office space for the 
Department of Art, Film, and Visual Studies. 
As part of the overall effort, the existing single-story structure will be retained and will receive 
various upgrades, including new windows, two new accessible entries, improved exterior 
envelope and insulation, updated infrastructure systems, and a full interior fit-out to support new 
program uses. As a whole, the Project provides much needed program space for University 
tenants, but also seeks to convert an existing warehouse program use to a more suitable, 
community friendly use consistent with the goals of the University’s IMP, and the development 
of the Allston Campus. In addition, one of the design benefits of the Project is to remove the 
loading dock function from the east façade, an area that is adjacent to a future section of the 
Greenway. 
Figure 2 depicts an aerial photo of the site, and Figures 3 and 4 depict existing ground level 
photographs of the existing building and site. 
4.2 
Proposed Project 
As noted previously, this document refers to the property and buildings at 92 Seattle Street and 
38 Travis Street together as “92 Seattle.” The building currently includes an area leased to an 
auto body shop, as well as storage and office space. 
92 Seattle was added to the Harvard IMP Overlay Area in 2013, in connection with the Fifth 
Amendment to the 1998 IMP for Harvard’s Campus in Allston (the Fifth Amendment), dated 
December 14, 2012. (Note that the Fifth Amendment referred to the building as “90 Seattle 
Street.”) The BRA Board approved the Fifth Amendment on March 14, 2013. As set forth in the 
Fifth Amendment and the 2013 Board Memorandum, the occupancy of 26,800 square feet of 
storage and warehouse space at 90 Seattle was part of a Proposed Institutional Project called the 
“28 Travis Street Project,” which also included the renovation and occupancy of 28 Travis Street 
and the construction of a new fleet management building between them.

5.0 
Project Impacts 
The following sections describe the key environmental impacts from the Project. 
5.1 
Transportation 
As the Project represents a relocation of existing uses from other locations on Harvard’s campus 
and an introduction of low density uses, it is expected to result in a minimal impact to the overall 
transportation network. The primary access to the building is located on the eastern edge of the 
site, adjacent to the intersection of Academic Way and Science Drive. The site’s proximity to the 
SEC and Western Avenue affords it good access to local and regional transportation services and 
assets, including the Mobility Hub at the SEC. 
Walking 
The Project is located on a major pedestrian route between Harvard’s Cambridge campus and the 
new SEC building on Western Avenue. Pedestrian access to the Project will be located at the 
eastern edge of the building adjacent to Academic Way. Pedestrian crosswalks with rectangular 
rapid flash beacons are located at the intersections of Academic way with Western Avenue and 
at the crossing of North Harvard Street. Additionally, pedestrian access to the Site will come 
from the west through Ray Mellone Park to Rena Path. 
Bicycle 
The Project is conveniently located near existing and future bicycle facilities that connect with the 
Allston and Cambridge campuses as well as the local and regional bicycle network. Bicycle lanes 
are located on North Harvard Street and there are buffered and separated bicycle facilities east

Western Avenue. There will be bicycle parking spaces created on-site as part of the Project. In 
addition, there are 630 total bike parking spaces and bicycle repair stand associated with the SEC 
project (this includes the Mobility Hub) all within 1,000 feet of the Project. Of these, 354 are 
covered and secure requiring HUID access, and 276 are open access. Shared bicycle service is

Vehicle Access, Parking, and Loading 
No new parking will be constructed as part of this Project. Instead, Harvard faculty, students, 
staff, and affiliates will have access to Harvard’s institutional parking facilities, the most proximate 
facility being 2 Hague Street. This facility has sufficient capacity for the Project’s Harvard users 
and is also one of Harvard Transportation’s Flexible Parking Locations which enables visitors to 
park there as well. Loading is provided on the western side of the site via the 28 Travis Street 
parking lot. 
Car sharing service ZipCar has vehicles located adjacent to the Project site at 28 Travis Street and 
at the 2 Hague parking facility, approximately 700 feet from the Project. 
MBTA Transit 
MBTA bus route 66 stops on North Harvard Street approximately 750 feet from the site (adjacent 
to the Honan-Allston Library) and Routes 86, 70 and 70A stop in Barry’s corner approximately 
1,000 feet from the site. Routes 66 and 86 provide connections to Harvard Square and operate 
on 10-minute and approximately 10-20 minute headways respectively. Routes 70 and 70A 
connect with Central Square and operate on approximately 15-30 minute and 30-60 minute 
headways. 
Shuttle Transit 
The existing Harvard University shuttle service – which is open to the public – will connect the 
Project site with Harvard Square and Harvard’s Cambridge campus. Harvard currently operates 
two bus routes in Allston: the Quad-SEC Direct and the Allston Loop. The Project site is best 
serviced by the SEC bus stop, a short walk from the building. 
The Quad-SEC Direct provides transportation from the Radcliffe Quadrangle and Harvard Yard in 
Cambridge to the Stadium Complex and the new SEC building and back. The route operates 
roughly every 20 minutes from 7:00 AM until 7:40 PM Monday - Friday. 
The Allston Loop route is a one way loop around the perimeter of the Allston and Cambridge 
campuses. During the academic year, buses depart from the Allston campus approximately every

5.2 
Project Sustainability 
The Project has been developed to align with the Harvard Sustainability Plan, including the 
University’s goals for environmental stewardship and sustainability, and incorporates various 
features in support of these goals. The design reuses and renews an existing building located on 
campus, rather than demolishing and replacing it. In addition, the Project will implement a series 
of improvements to maintain and upgrade the structure, as well as to improve the 
uninsulated/unreinforced building envelope, incorporating new windows and insulation to 
minimize energy loss. 
The Project will also deploy new all-electric HVAC systems, eliminating the use of fossil fuels in 
the operation of the building, and providing greater efficiency in the building systems. With the 
addition of new windows on all sides, the Project aims to increase the availability of natural light 
on the interior of the building. The Project includes material selections to reduce impervious 
surfaces and lower the heat island effect of the building. The building will also incorporate healthy 
building materials in the interior finishes, helping reduce the overall use of harmful or hazardous 
materials in the construction of campus buildings. 
5.3 
Project Utilities 
The Project will utilize existing water and sewer connections to the building, but will expand the 
current use through with additional toilet rooms, sinks, and a shower room. Existing stormwater 
structures will be maintained on site, and the Project will work with the ongoing development of 
the Rena Path extension to incorporate additional stormwater features, if feasible, as part of the 
entry development, and overall district development plan. 
The Project will cap the existing gas service to the building as it will no longer be required, and 
will upgrade the existing electrical service currently provided to the building, including updating 
equipment internal to the building and specifying energy efficient infrastructure systems. 
5.4 
Construction Logistics 
A Construction Management Plan (CMP) in compliance with the City’s Construction Management 
Program and consistent with the University’s program-wide construction guidelines will be 
submitted to the Boston Transportation Department.

Developer Background 
 
Thibeault Development, managed by William J. Thibeault is a privately held, multi-platform real estate 
company. It operates throughout New England, with a strong presence in downtown Boston. Thibeault 
Development develops, operates, manages and owns residential, retail, industrial and mixed use 
properties. Residential properties include re-developed downtown Boston buildings, urban ring apartment 
complexes and suburban subdivisions and residential communities. Retail projects have included big box 
retail development and storefront Boston sites. Thibeault Development’s industrial properties are both 
operating heavy industrial sites, smaller light industrial rentals and commercial storage and warehouse 
facilities. 
 
Project Summary 
 
The Proposed Project consists of the re-development and adaptive re-use of an existing four (4) 
story, 33,000 +/- square-foot industrial building situated on the edge of the Eagle Hill 
neighborhood at 98-100 Condor Street, East Boston. The Proposed Project would reprogram the 
entire existing structure from a vacant industrial/commercial use to 35 new residential rental units. 
In connection with the Proposed Project, there will be seven (7) accessory off-street surface parking 
spaces, which complies with the Boston Transportation Department’s maximum off street parking 
guidelines based on the Premises’ mobility score. In addition, Project Amenities will include an on 
site fitness room, bike storage for 44 bikes, building gathering space, laundry room, bike storage 
room, and storage lockers, in addition to other measures to meet the City of Boston’s Transportation 
Demand Management (TDM) strategies. 
 
The Proposed Project will take the existing non-ADA compliant building and create an accessible 
main entry as well as provide a new elevator creating access to all floors for those who are disabled 
while providing an additional residential development along the emerging Condor Street Corridor 
– an area that has seen significant interest in residential re-development. 
 
The Proposed Project will create and additional 35 market-rate housing opportunities while 
preserving and maintaining an existing structure. The site is less than a three minute walk to the 
MBTA’s Bus Line servicing routes 114, 116, and 117 with access to Maverick Station. The Project 
Site is located more than .5 miles from the MBTA’s Blue Line Airport Station. (See Exhibit ___).

Civic Association indicating support for the proposal. (See Exhibit ___). 
 
Site Background 
 
The existing 4 story structure, is an early 20th century reinforced concrete industrial building that 
served as the headquarters for the Boston and Lockport Block Company, which manufactured wood 
and steel tackle block, pumps, differential hoists, and other handling equipment. The original 
buildings on this site were framed structures and replaced in the early 20th century by the structures 
presently on the site. In 1930, the company employed nearly 200 people until it was absorbed by 
Brewer-Titchener of New York, the company left the site in 1973, wherein the building was used for 
smaller businesses through the late 1980s and early 1990s. The building has been identified in 
the Boston Landmarks Commission comprehensive survey of significant building in East Boston and 
is considered a significant example of industrial buildings in the Eagle Hill Study Area associated 
with a business that was a major employer for over 80 years and which includes re-use possibilities 
in connection with preservation considerations. (See Exhibit ____). 
 
Although the Project Site is located within a Designated Port Area (“DPA”), the main structure is not 
located within the jurisdiction regulated by Chapter 91, and is therefore not subject to DPA 
regulations prohibiting residential use. (See Exhibit ____)

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

To Whom it May Concern: 
 
I write in support of the proposed project at 98-100 Condor Street in East Boston. This project will
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
renovate an existing industrial space, long left vacant and previously utilized for warehouse and
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
manufacturing purposes, and convert the building to 39 residential units, of which five would be
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
affordable under the IDP program. 
 
It is my understanding that the Eagle Hill Civic Association voted to support this project at their July
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
meeting. Community members supported the conversion to residential units, feeling that commercial use
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
no longer suited this property, located directly on a street and abutting a local daycare and residences.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
They also supported the creation of parking, storage, and a common green roof. However, some residents
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
did express concern at the density of the project, whose units are compact. Residents also advocated for a
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
more activated first floor and increased green space on the property. Additionally, there was emphasis that
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
the included IDP units would be truly affordable at a lower band of AMI consistent with East Boston’s
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
population, and that some of these units could be larger, with additional bedrooms, to support families. It
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
is my expectation that the developers will commit to addressing these requests where feasible. With that
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
understanding, I am satisfied that the community stands behind this proposal. 
 
Moreover, I think it is important to note that despite being located within the DPA, this building has no
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
direct access to the water. While we want to preserve some of this use along our waterfront, the main
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
access for manufacturing or commercial uses at this site would be via Condor Street, an already congested
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
corridor. I feel that the proposed re-use of the structure for residential and possible ground floor retail is
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
more consistent with the changing landscape along this section of Condor Street and the immediate
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
neighborhood context. Finally, since this building is vacant, its redevelopment would result in no
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
displacement of existing tenants.

concerns, and support in evaluating approval for the variances required for this project. I stand with the
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
neighborhood in supporting this proposal, and I ask that the variances to complete this project be granted.

Dear Director Jemmison: 
It is my pleasure to submit this application for Small Project Review pursuant to Article 
80, Section 80E-2 of the Boston Zoning Code, for the 9 Geneva Street Small Project in East 
Boston. 
The proposed project is to consist of twenty eight (28) new residential units, primarily 
market rate, with five (5) income restricted units (17.85%), which exceeds the requirements 
under the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”). The project site is currently occupied 
by a one story auto body and single family home, both of which will be razed in connection with 
the proposed project. 
The applicant is Geneva Street, LLC, led by Mr. Nicholas Yebba, who has completed 
numerous projects in the Boston area, including several in the East Boston neighborhood where 
this project is located. Architectural services are being provided by David O’Sullivan and civil 
engineering services by PJF Associates. 
Situated on seven (7) parcels of land containing approximately combined 14,869 square 
feet of industrial and residential land in a predominantly residential section of the East Boston 
neighborhood, the project site consists of an existing non-conforming automotive repair garage 
and an adjacent single family home (the “Site” or “Project Site”). The Proponent proposes to 
revitalize the Project Site with a new multi-family development that is more consistent with 
character and context of the surrounding community. In particular, the proposed project would 
replace the existing non-conforming structures and upgrade this distressed Project Site with a 
new five-story, 28 unit residential development that includes 16 on-site garaged parking spaces, 
new sidewalk, pedestrian access, landscaping, open space and overall site improvements (the 
“Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project also address the shortage of market-rate and

Gove Street (the “Site” or “Project Site”). It is bounded by Geneva Street to the 
northwest, residential building abutters on the south side and across the street, and a 
public park abutting the north side of the proposed building. The Project Site is also 
relatively flat in topography. For several decades, it has been occupied by the industrial 
operations of American National Auto Body and Repairs, which includes an existing 
concrete garage building, a smaller, wood-frame garage, and an un-improved asphalt

(7) separate parcels including 9 and 15 Geneva Street, Ward 01, Boston, Suffolk 
County, Massachusetts. While the single family residence at 15 Geneva conforms to 
current zoning, 9 Geneva Street maintains an assessing classification code of 0332 
(Commercial Property / Repair / Service Garage). The existing uses and structure at 
9 Geneva are non-conforming under the current requirements of the Zoning Code 
(collectively, the “Existing Conditions at the Premises”). The Site is mostly 
surrounded by other multi-family residential buildings, and the immediate area

including 28 units of rental apartments on the upper floors (2-5), above a main level

Maverick Street, while also including dedicated bicycle parking spaces for the 
residents of the building with direct access to both the exterior and vehicle garage.

 Design Concept 
The Proposed Project’s urban design goal is to significantly enhance this ‘missing tooth’ 
element along Geneva Street, with a well-designed building using high quality, modern 
building materials typical to a residential building and found within the neighborhood. A 
widened public sidewalk with proposed street trees, and a building courtyard at the main 
residential entry with a mix of hardscapes and landscaping, will help to provide a much 
more pedestrian friendly environment. 
 
The building is fronted by a large residential lobby on one end with the entry courtyard, a 
secondary building entry for building residents along the left side, and a centrally located 
bicycle room to activate the streetfront with approximately ten (10) foot high ceilings for 
this floor. Brick masonry exterior finish and full height aluminum and glass storefront 
windows along the length of the wall along the ground floor will give the building a 
residential feel for its frontage. A building canopy and lighter colored finishes demarcate 
the main building entry for residents and guests. 
 
The materials used on the building are reminiscent of typical residential buildings in the 
Northeast, Boston, and East Boston respectively. At the base along the front of the building, 
brick masonry is utilized, while at the upper floors a mix of lap and panel siding is used to 
complement the brick and help break down the scale of the buidling. The use of paneling 
also complements the typical brick and siding materials, and help demarcate the main entry 
of the building. 
 Height and Massing 
The massing and height of the building has been designed to respond to the unique land 
conditions and contraints of the Project Site, and to fit in with the contextual height and 
scale of many existing and new buildings on the street, including future proposed 
development. The building proposes to match the height of several nearby buildings. Along 
the front of the building at the fifth residential floor, the building has been pulled back an 
additional +/- four (4’) feet (+/- 9’-3” total from the property line) to help further reduce 
the appearance and massing of the building. The use of recessed bays along the street and 
balconies further help reduce the scale of the building on all sides.

 Façade Design, Fenestration, and Building Materials 
The proposed façade utilizes typical residential building design elements, but incorporated 
in a contemporary way. The ground level, common areas of the building utilizes larger 
storefront windows and frequency, while the upper residential levels employ a more typical 
residential fenestration pattern translating the bedroom and living room spaces on the 
interior to the exterior. Additional fenesetration elements, such as window pairing, help 
reinforce the residential nature of the building. Also, all fenestration is designed to be black 
with a contemporary muntin pattern to further the contemporary feel to the building 
façade. 
 
The Proponent has worked with the BPDA on initial design review during the pre-file 
process and will continue to do so throughout through the more formal approval process 
for the Proposed Project. 
 Exterior Signage and Lighting 
The Proposed Project will not have any signage on the front façade of the building except 
the address at the main entry, and any required signage by Boston Fire Department to 
locate life safety system. Exterior lighting, where used, will be indirect LED lighting to 
illuminate building entrances, ground surfaces, and pedestrian pathways as required by 
building code. Additionally, lighting at private unit balconies will be provided, however, all 
exterior lighting will utilize cut-off shields as part of their design to limit light spill outside 
the building. 
 Site Design and Dimensional Constraints 
The new building has been situated on the Project Site and scaled to respond to its unique 
land conditions and related constraints, and to specifically address and respond to privacy 
and noise concerns by its directly abutting residences. Again, the Site is relatively flat across 
its whole area. 
Other than the auto repair, there currently is no pedestrian level activity uses on Site or 
along the street, contrary to the residential buildings located on either side which both have 
visible ground floor pedestrian friendly activity. Therefore, in contrast with the Site’s 
current condition, the Proposed Project will provide a much-needed urban revitalization to 
better fit within its neighborhood context. 
The Proposed Project is located approximately 0.4 miles from the MBTA’s Maverick Station, 
0.6 miles from the Airport Station, and is in very close proximity (350 ft) to the 120 MBTA 
bus line. The Proposed Project is also located within close proximity (0.5 miles) to the Lewis

existing non-conforming structure and an unimproved asphalt surface lot with a

The Proposed Project is being designed in accordance with the City’s Complete 
Streets Design Guidelines, which will greatly improve upon the existing pedestrian

Dear Director Jemison,
231 Maverick LLC is pleased to submit this application for Small Project Review under Article 80, of the 
Boston Zoning Code, with respect to the proposed development at 9 McKay Place in the Jeffries Point 
neighborhood of East Boston. 
The proponent’s project contemplates the construction of 41 condominium units (five of which would 
be subject to the inclusionary development policy), on-site parking for 36 cars, and has a gross square 
footage of approximately 43,460 square feet. The site contains four vacant existing structures - three 2- 
and 3-family buildings and the clubhouse for a fraternal organization. These are slated to be demolished 
and be replaced with a five-story residential building with a ground-floor commercial space that will be 
used by the local nonprofit Eastie Farm. 
This project is transit oriented, with close proximity to the Blue Line Maverick Station as well as being 
along several bus lines and proximate to BlueBikes docking stations. The site is adjacent to BPS’ Donald 
McKay K-8 School and serves as a gateway to it from the Jeffries Point neighborhood. It sits along Mav-
erick Street, which is quickly developing into a local commercial and service corridor. The surrounding 
area is a mix of multi-family residential buildings and small commercial uses.
 
This proposal consists of the team members, project summary, Zoning Analysis, proposed plans and 
elevations for the project, and supplemental views and information on how the proposed design has 
changed over time. The proposed development is a reflection of feedback and input from several pre-
filing meetings with the BPDA, meeting with City Councilor Lydia Edwards, the Gove Street Neighbor-
hood Association, the Donald McKay School, and with Eastie Farm and Tree Eastie.

Project Summary
Site Information
The project site comprises six parcels - Parcel # 0103993010 - 232-234 Maverick St, Parcel # 
0103995000 - 230 Maverick St, Parcel # 0103996000 - 228 Maverick St, Parcel # 0103997000 - 226 
Maverick St, Parcel # 0103998000 - McKay Place, and Parcel # 0103999000 - 9 McKay Place - and cov-
ers a total of approximately 15,751 sf. As a part of this development the four existing wood framed resi-
dential and commercial structures contained on the site will be demolished. 
Project Cost and Financing
The estimated total cost of this project is $12,000,000. It will be financed through a construction loan 
from Needham Bank
Proposed Project
The proposed project will house 41 Residential Condominiums. The existing four structures will be 
demolished and a single 5 story structure will be erected in their place The first level will contain a com-
mercial retail unit along with the residential lobby and 36 on-grade parking spaces contained within the 
building footprint. The four levels above will be a mix of 1 bedroom, 2 bedroom and 3 bedroom units. 
Great care has been taken to break up the building mass along both Maverick and McKay streets and to 
step back the top floor of the building to make it compatible in scale and massing with the surrounding 
neighborhood. As a result, the project will enhance the urban fabric along Maverick Street and contribute 
to the growing vibrancy of pedestrian activity in Jeffries Point.
Community Benefits
The proposed project will offer substantial public benefits to its neighborhood and to the City of Boston, 
including the following:
• 
The creation of a substantial landscaped pocket park at the corner of McKay and Maverick streets, 
complete with trees, bushes, benches, and quality hardscaping, giving a place for locals to gather, pe-
destrians to pause, and local kids to play and relax.
• 
A 1,200 sf commercial space to activate the local streetscape, provide a landmark for locals, and 
to provide jobs for local residents. This will be an IDP-supported commercial space used by the lo-
cal non-profit Eastie Farm as their office and central distribution point for CSAs, urban farming and 
cooking classes, and potential farmers markets in the adjacent pocket park. Eastie Farms will use this 
permanent space to expand their outreach efforts to the community and to connect with students at 
local schools.
• 
The creation of 41 new residential units, a majority of which will be 2- and 3-bedroom units. This is a 
higher proportion than is typical of similar projects in East Boston and will allow for families with chil-
dren to settle in or stay in the neighborhood as they outgrow other housing stock. The variety of unit 
sizes will allow for upsizing, downsizing, or ageing in place as family sizes and needs change.
• 
All units will be wheelchair accessible and be designed to accommodate residents with a variety of 
needs, providing a convenient alternative for East Boston residents if they are having difficulty living 
in existing buildings with stoops and internal stairs.
• 
The creation of 5 affordable residential units under the BPDA inclusive development program, All af-
fordable units for this project will be on-site and will be distributed throughout the building to create 
an integrated and inclusive place to live.
• 
Enhancing the streetscape for local pedestrians by widening the sidewalks and providing ample space 
for outdoor dining, additional bicycle parking, and new trash receptacles and street furniture.
• 
Preserving an existing 3’ diameter street tree and planting seven more street trees along Maverick 
and McKay, providing a green oasis in an area sorely lacking in park space and helping combat the 
urban heat island effect.
• 
Giving the majority of residential units their own exterior space in the forms of balconies and roof 
decks.
• 
Including an amenity suite, common roof deck, and rooftop garden with sensational harbor and sky-
line views of Boston for all building occupants and guests to enjoy.
• 
Encouraging alternative modes of transportation by increasing residential density in proximity to the 
Maverick T station, supplying bicycle parking for all units, and supplying bicycle parking for visitors 
and commercial users along the sidewalk.
• 
Create permanent jobs for local residents in the commercial space and construction jobs over the 
18-month erection of the building.

Building Statistics
Traffic and Parking Analysis
The proposed project includes 36 parking spaces. They are contained within the footprint of the building 
and are accessed from McKay Place to minimize traffic on Maverick Street. 44 bicycle parking spaces will 
be provided within the garage area with an additional 16 bicycle spaces available along the sidewalk. The 
garage entrance for the project is located on McKay Place to reduce any additional congestion on Maver-
ick Street. No street parking spaces will be affected by the erection of this building.
The site is a transit-oriented development, located a third of a mile from the Maverick Blue Line T Sta-
tion, along the 120 Bus Line, and within two blocks of two BlueBikes docks.
Fostering an Inclusive and Welcoming Community
Our project at 9 McKay has been designed to be a support to the community. The existing buildings on-
site were empty since 2019, and all occupants moved out upon termination of their leases prior to sale of 
the property. No families were displaced as a result of this project. 
We see our new building at 9 McKay Place as an urban oasis where the local community can gather 
and that Eastie families can move into when existing triple deckers and row houses no longer work for 
them. Whether then need more space for a growing family, a smaller unit for empty nesters, or a space 
with greater accessibility as they age, our building provides units that can work for them. Our marketing 
will focus on East Boston to draw in homeowners from the local community. We will give preference to 
first-time home buyers and provide marketing materials in Spanish to best serve current residents of the 
neighborhood.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1.
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2.
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3.
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4.
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5.
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6.
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7.
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8.
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9.
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10.
Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Project Description 
Harrison Lenox, LLC, a joint venture between Related Beal, LLC and DREAM Development, LLC 
(collectively, the “Proponent”), is pleased to submit this Small Project Review Application (“SPRA”), to 
initiate review by the Boston Redevelopment Authority d/b/a the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency (the “BPDA”) under Article 80E of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) for the 
proposed construction of an approximately 44,000 square foot (SF) of Gross Floor Area (as such term 
is used in the definition of “Floor Area Ratio” in the Code, “GFA”), six-story residential building that 
will be no greater than 67 feet in building height (as such term is defined in the Code) (the “Project”) 
at East Lenox Street in the Roxbury neighborhood of Boston (the “Project Site”). Refer to Figure 1.1 
for the Site Location Map. 
This SPRA only includes details on the construction of the first phase of the proposed redevelopment 
of the Boston Water and Sewer Commission (“BWSC”) Lots (“Building 1”), which the BPDA awarded 
tentative designation to Related Beal and DREAM Development in April 2024. Building 1 will benefit 
from federal American Rescue Plan Act (“ARPA”) funds that must be designated by year-end 2024. 
The future phases, and planned Buildings 2-5 will be designed and permitted at a later date, 
following a land transfer from BWSC to the City of Boston. 
1.1 Project History and Background 
On February 28, 2024, the Proponent responded to the City’s Request for Proposals (“RFP”) for the 
redevelopment of the Boston Water and Sewer Commission parking lots in the Nubian Square area 
of Roxbury. The five parking lots, directly across Harrison Street from the BWSC headquarters, consist 
of approximately 190,000 square feet of vacant land. The Proponent’s response aimed to redevelop 
the existing parking lots to deliver affordable and workforce housing expeditiously and provide 
creative solutions for homeownership for families, as well as for seniors. The BPDA awarded a 
tentative designation to the Proponent for the redevelopment of the BWSC parcels and a handful of 
associated, small BPDA-owned parcels at the April 11, 2024, BPDA Board Meeting. This designation is 
in direct response to the Boston’s 2022 Citywide Land Audit which identified the RFP area as a high-
priority opportunity site for community planning and development. The April 11, 2024, BPDA Board 
Memo outlined that the BWSC parcels associated with the land area necessary to deliver Building 1 
(ID: 0801854010 and 0801846000) would be transferred on or before July 1, 2024, with the remainder 
of the parcels to be transferred by 2030. 
The Building 1 Project Site can also be referred to as the parking lot surrounded by Newcomb Street 
to the West, Reed Street to the South, and E Lenox Street to the East, and sits at a critical intersection 
of Roxbury, in between Lower Roxbury and the South End. The historic buildings on the Project Site

were razed after the development of the 1975 General Plan for the City of Boston and Regional Core

The Proponent is committed to the creation of sustainable careers and business opportunities for

strong relationships and partnerships with local organizations and intends to expand economic

1.2 Site Context and Existing Conditions 
1.2.1 Neighborhood Context 
The Project builds upon and will comply with two important neighborhood planning initiatives: the 
Roxbury Strategy Master Plan (2004) and PLAN: Nubian Square (2019). The Project follows the goals 
of both plans by creating inviting new housing and open space within a cohesive framework that 
weaves itself into the fabric of the neighborhood, enriching civic and cultural life for all. 
The five blocks of BWSC parking lots are underutilized in a once-thriving, contiguous neighborhood. 
Building 1 will be located along Reed Street between Newcomb and East Lenox Streets, occupying 
the southern half of this block. To the north, existing buildings include Grant A.M.E. Church and four-
story brick walk-up residential units along Newcomb, a two-story mixed-use building and a seven-
story apartment building along Washington, and a four-story and a newer six-story apartment 
building along East Lenox. Throughout the neighborhood, the urban form is dominated by 
traditional massing, brick facades, and strong ground-floor emphasis with prominent entries, 
architectural detailing, and generously proportioned retail windows. 
The immediate neighborhood has a shortage of green, inviting open spaces. Most existing open 
spaces within a 10-minute walk, including Ramsay Park located two blocks from Building 1, are active 
sports fields. Few passive and informal community-accessible open spaces exist within a 10 to 15 
minute walk except for a few small community gardens and Blackstone and Franklin Squares toward 
the South End, which are located about 0.5 miles east of the Project Site. The heart of the RFP area, 
along Reed Street, is nearly devoid of trees, and ambient temperatures are high in warmer months. 
As accessibility is key, Building 1 is intended to be part of a larger redevelopment plan designed to 
improve alternative transportation options by creating a walkable and bikeable environment with 
direct and safe connections to the Melnea Cass Bike Path. Vehicular parking will be downplayed and 
hidden from view of the most important pedestrian routes and spaces, in favor of other travel modes. 
Limited possible, on-street parking will be maintained along certain streets (such as Newcomb Street 
next to Building 1) as convenient short-term spaces for visitors and as a supplement to off-street 
parking areas for neighborhood residents. Transit accessibility is high in this area, with bus stops for 
many lines, including the cross-town and Silver Line routes. Refer to Figure 1.2 for Site Context plan.

1.2.2 Existing Site Conditions 
The block planned for Building 1 includes zero setback and four- to six-story residential buildings to 
the north. Across East Lenox Street, brick apartment buildings are set further back from the street 
and delineated by wrought iron fences. The existing BWSC parking lots on this block are surrounded 
by low chain link fences, and driveway access to both is from Reed Street. Sidewalks bounding the 
parking lot are in good condition, but are very narrow, and devoid of any trees or landscaping. The 
block is fairly level and occupies the highest ground relative to the larger context of the surrounding 
BWSC parking lot blocks. On-street parking is permitted only along the side of Newcomb Street 
bounding the block. Refer to Figure 1.3 for Existing Conditions Site Plan, and Figure 1.4 for Existing 
Site Photos. 
1.3 Overview of Project 
1.3.1 Proposed Development Program 
The Building 1 Project Site is approximately 32,930 SF, includes the rear courtyard, parking lot, and 
associated landscaped areas. This Project area extends up to property lines, including all required 
dedicated setback areas along public rights-of-way. The proposed development program is provided 
in Table 1-1 below.

Building 1’s footprint is approximately 8,000 SF. The Project will have 6 floors and be no greater than 
67 feet in height, with a total GFA of approximately 44,000 SF. Project Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is 1.43. 
Building 1 will provide 45 condominium ownership units across the six floors. The unit mix will 
include 16 studios, 12 one-bedroom, 12 two-bedroom, and 5 three-bedroom units. Unit sizes range 
from around 500 SF for a studio to 1,200 SF for the largest three-bedroom unit. An approximately 
1,400-SF residential amenity space is provided at the ground floor to the rear of the building. An 
approximately 600-SF bike room within the building will provide space for the required 54 resident 
and visitor bike parking spaces (including two-tiered, ground-level, and extra wide spaces), with 
direct access off of Newcomb Street. Generous window glazing and a comfortable seating area will 
make the approximately 900-SF entry lobby a welcoming entry point for residents and provide 
activity on the street. The rear parking lot will provide 32 spaces, for a parking ratio of 0.71 spaces 
per unit. Refer to Figure 1.5 for Proposed Conditions Site / Landscape Plan.

Project Description 
1.3.2 Proposed Design Approach 
Building 1 will serve as a catalyst for the revitalization of the Harrison Avenue neighborhood, 
beginning the transformation of the parking lot-dominated landscape and reintroducing a vibrant 
urban character to the area. It will enhance and set a precedent for the existing street grid by 
creating a more inviting public realm, featuring wider sidewalks, bike lanes, green spaces, and a 
canopy of shade-providing street trees. The building’s main entry lobby, located at the corner of 
Reed and Newcomb Streets, will offer convenient access to the surrounding neighborhood. 
The vision for Building 1 is to cultivate a quieter, more residential atmosphere along Reed Street that 
will seamlessly integrate with future open spaces and community amenities. Building 1 will 
memorialize the western portion of Reed Street as a car-free, bike- and pedestrian-friendly space 
that connects to the Melnea Cass Bike Path, while the eastern section will link the development to 
the adjacent Grant Manor residences. By delivering thoughtfully designed housing, Building 1 will set 
the standard for the neighborhood’s growth and future development. 
1.3.3 Project Phasing and Schedule 
This SPRA is being filed for the approval to develop Building 1, which will provide 100% low- and 
moderate-income ownership housing. The timeline for future buildings is unknown until the BPDA 
obtains land control of the remaining parcels associated with the BWSC lots. In the interim, a portion 
of the Building 1 lot behind the proposed building will be used for temporary parking to support the 
residents of Building 1. This will ensure adequate parking in the interim prior to the development of 
supplementary parking in a future phase. Once supplementary parking is built in a future phase, the 
rear lot behind Building 1 will be developed into another residential homeownership building, further 
contributing to the overall housing goals of the Project. 
It is anticipated that the Project construction will commence during the 2nd or 3rd quarter of 2025 and 
completion is expected by the 4th quarter of 2026 (to align with the American Rescue Plan Act 
expenditure timeline requirements). 
1.4 Overall Sustainability & Resiliency Approach 
The Proponent is committed to implementing measures aimed at reducing energy and water 
consumption, enhancing the efficiency and longevity of building systems and infrastructure, and 
lessening the impact of buildings on the environment, city services, and public health. In line with 
these goals, the Project will be designed to comply with the Massachusetts Opt-In Specialized Code 
and will pursue Passive House (PHIUS) and LEED Platinum certifications. Additionally, the Project will 
implement sustainable strategies to address existing environmental justice issues impacting the 
neighborhood and its surroundings. These strategies include mitigating heat island effects, 
minimizing noise and light pollution from the Project Site and adjacent commercial areas, addressing 
potential soil contamination, and enhancing access to green spaces for the community. Refer to 
Figure 1.6 for the LEED Scorecard. 
1.4.1 Proposed Sustainability Goals/Design Elements 
The project team comprises a skilled group of professionals, including LEED Accredited Professionals 
and consultants, with extensive experience in designing and developing high-performance buildings

and sustainable and resilient built environments. This expertise spans across various disciplines and is 
geared towards achieving ambitious sustainability goals. 
To ensure the Project's success, the design team engaged in an early-design charrette facilitated by 
enviENERGY Studio. This collaborative session aimed to define the Project's energy and sustainability 
objectives and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) fostering synergy between disciplines and building 
systems to realize high-performance buildings and an energy-positive community. 
The Project's sustainability goals encompass four key categories: Energy and Carbon, Water, 
Resiliency, and Health and Wellbeing. Through quantitative and qualitative metric tracking, the team 
will identify opportunities to reduce operational and embodied carbon, minimize water consumption, 
enhance the lifespan of building systems and infrastructure, and reduce burdens on city services, the 
environment, and public health. 
1.4.1.1 
Energy and Carbon 
The Proponent is committed to the development of a high-performance building and will implement 
several energy conservation and carbon reduction measures to reduce the building's operational and 
embodied carbon footprint. In line with the City of Boston's carbon neutrality goals and the Opt-In 
Specialized Energy Code, the building envelope will adhere to Passive House standards, significantly 
reducing space heating and cooling demands. The implementation of high-efficiency LED lighting 
fixtures, Energy Star appliances, and an advanced HVAC system equipped with central energy 
recovery ventilators will further decrease the building's energy consumption and greenhouse gas 
emissions. To effectively address operational emissions, the Project will eliminate reliance on fossil 
fuels for space heating and service water heating. 
To ensure alignment with the carbon emissions and energy consumption targets established by the 
Mayor's Office of Housing (MOH) Zero Emissions Buildings standards, this Project will target a 
projected Energy Use Intensity (pEUI) of 25 or less and a Carbon Emissions Intensity (pCEI) of 1.4 or 
less. Tenants and occupants will also be encouraged to opt for Boston Community Choice 100, 
ensuring 100% carbon neutrality and further advancing the Project's sustainability efforts. 
Regarding embodied carbon, the Project will prioritize reducing GHG emissions associated with 
construction materials and processes. Emphasizing adaptability and longevity in its design, the 
Project aims to minimize the need for frequent renovations and demolitions, thus reducing waste 
and emissions over time. To ensure well-informed decision-making in the early stages of design, a 
comprehensive Whole Building Life Cycle Analysis will be conducted by the sustainability consultant 
in collaboration with architectural and structural teams. This analysis will provide crucial insights into 
the environmental impact of design choices, guiding the Project toward its sustainability objectives. 
1.4.1.2 
Water 
The Proponent is dedicated to implementing a comprehensive water efficiency strategy to improve 
and promote water efficiency. All residential units will be equipped with low-flow and low-flush 
plumbing fixtures, with the aim of reducing indoor potable water usage by at least 35 percent. This 
initiative will significantly contribute to water conservation efforts and minimize unnecessary water 
consumption. In addition to efficient plumbing fixtures, water-saving appliances such as Energy Star 
Certified washing machines and dishwashers will be installed throughout the building. These

appliances are designed to minimize water usage while maintaining optimal performance, further 
reducing water waste. 
Furthermore, the landscaping design will predominantly feature native and adopted plants, 
complemented by a drip irrigation system where feasible. This approach aims to reduce outdoor 
water usage by at least 50 percent compared to the EPA Water Budget baseline, ensuring responsible 
water management in outdoor spaces. 
1.4.2 Resiliency Approach 
The Project will adhere to the City of Boston resiliency guidelines and LEED v4 standard as the 
foundation for implementing strategies aimed at mitigating the negative environmental impacts 
associated with new constructions. Transforming an existing parking lot into a more sustainable and 
resilient community, the Project will include green open spaces with native plant species that will 
help to combat the heat island effect and reduce stormwater runoff. 
The Project will integrate tree canopies throughout the Project Site and along the boundaries to 
provide shade, mitigate the urban heat island effect, act as natural buffers, and slow down rainwater, 
thus reducing flooding and erosion. These green spaces will also enhance air quality, add aesthetic 
appeal, support biodiversity, and offer social and economic benefits. 
Due to the Project Site’s vulnerability to coastal storm events, all residential occupied spaces will 
feature finished floors elevated at or above the Sea Level Rise – Design Flood Elevation (SLR-DFE) 
and Boston City Base (BCB) of 20.5 feet, ensuring resilience against potential flooding. Additionally, 
the Project proposes landscaped areas around the Project Site perimeter, serving both as stormwater 
management solutions and potential soft barriers. 
To manage stormwater effectively, the Project will employ green infrastructure and infiltration 
systems to retain 1.25 inches of rainfall at the Project Site. Critical utilities will be strategically 
elevated above the SLR-DFE, and the Project will prioritize strategies for managing rainwater flow 
during severe weather events and will implement technologies to delay and reduce outflow, rather 
than focusing solely on coastal flood and tide surge defenses. 
1.4.2.1 
Health and Wellbeing 
Ensuring healthy indoor environments plays a crucial role in enhancing the health and wellbeing of 
residents. By reducing respiratory issues linked to poor ventilation, allergens, and pollutants, 
preventing Sick Building Syndrome, minimizing chemical exposure (particularly VOCs) and improving 
sleep quality, the Project will help its residents to enjoy a higher quality of life. 
In line with the Project’s health and wellbeing objectives, the Proponent will implement strategies to 
identify and eliminate potential sources of indoor air pollutants, provide adequate ventilation, and 
maintain a healthy indoor environment. Each residential unit will feature operable windows and 
mechanical ventilation facilitated by a central energy recovery ventilator equipped with at least 
Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value (MERV) 13 filters. The building envelope will be designed to 
ensure proper drainage to safeguard surfaces against moisture damage. 
To further promote indoor air quality, the Project will pursue LEED Enhanced Indoor Air Quality 
Management standards. This includes implementing 10-foot-long entryway systems, ensuring 
adequate exhaust in chemical storage areas such as janitor closets, utilizing high-efficiency filters,

1.5 Proposed Resiliency Measures 
1.5.1 Transportation Options 
Building 1 is the first phase of a larger redevelopment plan intended to improve alternative travel 
options by creating a bikeable environment with direct and safe connections to the Melnea Cass Bike 
Path. At Building 1, vehicular parking is placed to the north and rear, away from Reed Street, helping 
to create a more inviting environment for walking. A future building and associated green, open 
space is currently envisioned to replace this surface parking lot, and the parking for Building 1 will 
move to a structured garage elsewhere within the wider project. Parking ratios are low, in keeping 
with the City’s policies to reduce automobile usage. The Project is also providing a bike room with 54 
long-term bike parking spaces for residents and their visitors. 
1.5.2 Reducing Urban Heat Island Impacts 
The Project will have tree-lined streets that provide shade during hot summer months, reducing the 
urban heat island impact. Light-color and porous paving, landscaped areas, and high albedo 
reflective roofing will further reflect heat and reduce ambient temperatures. Building 1’s rooftop will 
include areas available for PV arrays, with location and size to be determined. 
The building design will consider additional features, such as overhangs, awnings, and 
sunshades/brise-soleils, that could contribute further to increased shading and reduced energy use 
during summers. 
1.5.3 Sustainable Water Management Features 
Water management strategies are integrated into desirable outdoor amenities to enhance the value 
of the neighborhood. Drought tolerant, native plantings will reduce water usage. 
Groundwater recharge is an important part of any healthy watershed and even more important in 
urban environments. The Project prioritizes strategies for managing rainwater flow during severe 
weather events. Project Site drainage will minimize impervious surfaces, and combined with grading, 
will allow for infiltration of stormwater. Landscape design will incorporate bioretention plant beds to 
encourage onsite infiltration. 
1.5.4 Floodproofing and Raising Critical Infrastructure 
As required, the building will feature finished floors elevated at or above the SLR-DFE based on BCB 
20.5 feet, ensuring resilience against potential flooding. Based on the survey provided with the City 
RFP, existing site grades are close to 23 feet at East Lenox / Reed Street and farther north. The site 
grade for Building 1 will be raised as needed so that building entries and finished floors will comply 
with City of Boston flood requirements. Additionally, the Project includes landscaped areas around 
the Project Site perimeter, serving both as stormwater management solutions and potential soft 
barriers.

1.5.5 Building Design and Greenhouse Gas Reduction 
The Proponent is committed to the development of high-performance building and will implement 
several energy conservation measures to reduce the building’s operational carbon footprint and 
eliminate its dependence on fossil fuels. Aligned with the City of Boston’s commitment to carbon 
neutrality and following the recently enacted Specialized Opt-In Code, Building 1 will employ electric 
heating, cooling, and DHW systems and is anticipated to be designed and constructed to not only 
meet the Mayor’s Office of Housing (MOH) Zero Emissions Buildings requirements but also achieve 
Passive House certification, leveraging meticulous attention to detail and cutting-edge technologies. 
To effectively address operational emissions, the Project will entirely eliminate reliance on fossil fuels 
for space heating and service water heating. This will be achieved through the implementation of 
energy-efficient design and construction strategies. These strategies include optimizing building 
envelope performance, ensuring airtightness, minimizing thermal bridging, and utilizing high- 
efficiency heating and cooling systems. Additionally, a central ventilation system equipped with a 
high-efficiency energy recovery wheel will be employed. The integration of an on-site solar 
Photovoltaic (PV) array will significantly reduce operational GHG emissions. 
All-electric design leads to a future of net zero/positive energy consumption and aligns the Project 
with Architecture 2030 goals of net-zero buildings. As natural gas heating is expected to become 
more expensive than electric as soon as 2030, an all-electric design ensures future affordability of 
building energy needs. Demand response and load-shifting of energy needs via building 
management systems create less stress on the electric grid. Resident manuals and training help 
residents form new climate-friendly habits with the timing of their activities. 
Hydrofluoroolefin (HFO) or natural refrigerants will be used for heating/cooling to reduce the global 
warming potential of the systems by over 99 percent. 
Regarding embodied carbon, the Project will prioritize reducing GHG emissions associated with 
construction materials and processes. Emphasizing adaptability and longevity in its design, the 
Project aims to minimize the need for frequent renovations and demolitions, thus reducing waste 
and emissions over time. To ensure well- informed decision-making in the early stages of design, a 
comprehensive Whole Building Life Cycle Analysis will be conducted by sustainability consultants in 
collaboration with architectural and structural teams. This analysis will provide crucial insights into 
the environmental impact of design choices, guiding the Project toward its sustainability objectives. 
1.6 Summary of Public Benefits 
The proposed Project will offer many public benefits to the Lower Roxbury neighborhood and the 
City of Boston, including the following. 
› 
Creation of 45 new, affordable, residential homeownership units. All units will be income-
restricted to 80% or 100% of AMI, and will support the City’s housing production goals; 
› 
Significant improvements to the streetscape along Reed Street, East Lenox Street, and Newcomb 
Street, including a robust urban landscaping plan, which will help activate the public realm and 
transform the Project Site; 
› 
Improved safety and visual appearance of the Project Site and surrounding neighborhood by 
replacing an underutilized and currently vacant property in the community;

2.2.2 Local Zoning Compliance/Approach 
The Project is generally consistent with the underlying planning goals and approved neighborhood 
concepts. Under the Code’s current use and dimensional constraints, the Project would not be 
allowed. The Project would exceed maximum building height, maximum floor area ratio, and perhaps 
other dimensional requirements. Zoning overlays at the Project Site include Restricted Parking 
District and Groundwater Conservation Overlay District. 
The Project is also located within the South End Urban Renewal Plan Subdistrict. The Proponent 
anticipates the BPDA will request a Minor Modification to the Urban Renewal Plan, which will be used 
instead of traditional zoning. The Minor Modification would only apply to the Project Site, and not 
the remaining BWSC parcels.

3-1 
Urban Design 
3 
Urban Design 
This chapter discusses the planning principles and design goals for the Project, including the 
proposed urban design characteristics (e.g., height and massing) and public realm and streetscape 
improvements. 
3.1 Key Commitments and Urban Design Benefits 
Major objectives for the Project include: 
› 
Provide 45 much needed affordable homeownership units; 
› 
Develop an underutilized parking lot, healing gaps in the neighborhood fabric; 
› 
Establish an active and inviting street frontage along the primary pedestrian route, Reed Street, 
that helps bring back a human-scaled, walkable character to the area; and 
› 
Provide space for a more generous streetscape and public realm, with wider sidewalks and shade 
trees, by setting the building and parking lot back from the public rights-of-way. 
3.2 Site Design Approach/Considerations 
Building 1 is situated at the corner of Reed, Newcomb, and East Lenox Streets. The building’s 
footprint and associated parking areas are set back from property lines / public rights-of-way by 16.5 
feet along Reed Street, 18.5’ along Newcomb Street, and 16 feet along East Lenox Street to create a 
generously proportioned public realm with sidewalks and landscaping areas that complies with the 
City of Boston’s Complete Streets standards. Building 1’s massing and articulation are oriented to 
place the greatest visual interest along Reed Street, the neighborhood pedestrian spine for the larger 
area. The entry lobby will face Reed Street at Newcomb Street to enliven the public sidewalk along 
the important Reed Street corridor. An amenity room for building residents is provided at the rear of 
the building, where the exterior terrace can provide additional gathering space for spillover events. 
The rear parking lot will have access only from a single, existing curb cut along East Lenox Street. The 
parking lot frontage along Newcomb Street will have a deeper planted buffer to help screen cars and 
echo the deeper, planted setback of existing apartment buildings across East Lenox Street. Trash, 
back-of-house, and MEP facilities for Building 1 will be located in the north, rear portion of building, 
facing the parking lot. Resident move in/move out will be possible from the front lobby or from a 
rear entry off the parking lot.

3.3 Building Design Concept and Development 
3.3.1 Height and Massing 
Building 1 is six-stories, with five stories of wood (“stick”) construction over a one-story concrete 
podium. The building mass of each facade will be broken visually into smaller bay volumes, indicated 
by different materials and setbacks providing a change in plane extending vertically down the 
building and horizontally between the fourth, fifth, and/or sixth floors to create more light and air on 
the street level and visually reduce the height of the building. These changes will help emphasize a 
lower four- to five-story datum line, harmonizing with the lower neighborhood scale and with future 
buildings envisioned for Reed Street. Larger bay volumes will be further reduced visually through 
vertical fenestration and material patterns that echo rowhouse-proportions. Through these, a 
modern interpretation of bay windows will help provide visual interest and dimensionality to the 
façades. Refer to Figure 3.2 for Building Massing, Figure 3.3a-d for Building Floorplans, and Figure 
3.4a-c for Building Elevations, and Figure 3.5a-b for Building Sections. 
3.3.2 Architectural Style & Articulation 
The design of Building 1 draws from the character of South End brownstones and traditional brick 
buildings in Lower Roxbury, updated with a modern interpretation that allows for energy efficiency 
and continued pedestrian-scale design. For Building 1, brick cladding will marry the existing context 
into the new. Building 1 materials will include brick echoing the historic vernacular, textured fiber 
cement panels, and textured metal panels that recall existing concrete façades and buildings in the 
area. 
The main entry to Building 1, at the corner of Reed and Newcomb Streets, includes a high proportion 
of glazing to visually connect to the future open space envisioned to replace BWSC’s adjacent 
parking lots. The entry lobby will be highlighted via architectural features, including a flat canopy and 
a generous expanse of windows providing transparency into the lobby/lounge area (a 
meeting/gathering place for residents). All façades will have architectural emphasis and detailing at 
the ground floor, with horizontal banding between the ground floor and second floor to emphasize a 
pedestrian scale. Residential units on the ground floor of Building 1 will have smaller windows with 
higher sill heights and landscape screening to balance the need for residential privacy while 
maintaining a friendly street presence. On all floors, residential windows will include framing detailing 
to create shadow lines for interest in façade. Refer to Figure 3.6a-c for Project Renderings 
3.4 Public Realm/Streetscape Improvements 
Building 1 will be set back from public rights-of-way to create wider sidewalks and public realm 
areas. Existing curblines on Newcomb, East Lenox, and Reed Streets are relatively new. Per the 
BPDA’s request, curbs will remain in their current locations to align with existing property curbs. 
Building 1’s entry lobby will face the corner of Newcomb and Reed Streets. In front of this lobby, a 
decorative, paved hardscape will highlight the entryway. To the northeast along Reed Street, a 
landscaped buffer will provide some separation between the public sidewalk and ground-floor units. 
At the rear of Building 1, an exterior terrace will be provided adjacent to the ground-floor resident 
amenity room. A landscaped buffer will be provided between the parking lot and the terrace. A

pedestrian pathway will link the terrace over to East Lenox Street, with buffered landscaping 
providing privacy to ground-floor residential units in this area. 
Stands of mature trees separate the existing BWSC and the BPDA parking lots and line the back 
(north end) of the BWSC parking lot. A few of these trees must be removed to construct Building 1 
and its rear terrace, as well as to make modifications to the existing rear parking lot. However, the 
Project team is endeavoring to maintain the existing trees towards the back / north end of the 
Project Site during Phase 1, while providing parking spaces to meet resident needs Further study will 
be needed to determine how the future building planned to replace this temporary parking lot will 
affect the ability to retain these existing trees. 
Reed Street will follow complete streets guidelines for a Neighborhood connector. The green 
furnishings zone with be 5’ wide inclusive of the curb. The existing City of Boston light infrastructure 
will remain. Street trees, bike racks, and a porous paver band will establish a new standard for Reed 
Street. The pedestrian zone will be a consistent 8 feet wide and will connect smoothly with the 
crossing zones to the existing accessible routes in this neighborhood block. Where feasible within the 
frontage zone, we will add trees and other native plantings within the area between back of sidewalk 
and Phase 1 building façade. Grade also will be gradually sloping to provide protection and privacy 
to ground floor units. 
East Lenox Street and Newcomb Street will also maintain existing City of Boston Street lighting and 
existing infrastructure. In keeping with the Neighborhood Connector guideline, the pedestrian zone 
will be a consistent 8 feet wide from back of sidewalk. The remaining frontage zone will include some 
trees where room allows, as well as a richly diverse shrub and groundcover layer. West of the 
development, each of these sidewalks will transition to 4 or 5 feet wide to blend into the existing 
sidewalks off our parcel boundary. Refer to Figure 3.7 for Public Realm/Streetscape Improvement 
Plan. 
3.5 Accessibility 
All ground-floor units in Building 1 will be accessible at-grade through the building entry at the 
public sidewalk. Upper-floor units will be accessible via an elevator and stairways. Of Building 1’s 45 
new units, three units (over 6%) will be built out per MAAB requirements for group 2 units. One unit 
will be ADA/MAAB sensory complaint. Accessible parking will be provided within the temporary 
parking site provided during the construction of the Project. Existing pedestrian ramps and sidewalks 
have been identified as MAAB Compliant. Refer to Figure 3.8 for the Pedestrian Access and 
Circulation Plan. Additional detailed information is provided in the BPDA Accessibility Checklist 
included in Appendix A.

Infrastructure 
This chapter describes the existing infrastructure systems surrounding the Project Site and discusses 
the Project’s anticipated utility requirements and potential utility impacts. The following utilities are 
discussed: sewer, domestic water, fire protection, storm drainage, electrical and telecommunications, 
and natural gas. 
4.1 Overview of Utility Services 
This section provides a description of the existing utility systems in the vicinity of the Project Site and 
evaluates potential impacts to those systems. The existing infrastructure surrounding the Project Site 
appears sufficient to service the needs of the proposed Project. The proposed Project is in the early 
design phases and as a more definitive design evolves, the proponent will coordinate with the 
various utility companies to ensure full service for the new residential facility. For the above 
referenced utility systems, appropriate mitigation measures are discussed to address project related 
impacts. 
As indicated on the Site Utility Plan (Figure 4.2), there are existing utilities located within Reed Street, 
Newcomb Street, and East Lenox Street which will service this site. Utilities in Reed Street include 2 
water mains (low service, high service), a storm drain, 2 gas mains, underground telecommunications 
conduits, and underground electric conduits. Utilities in Newcomb Street include a water main (low 
service), a storm drain, a gas main, and underground electric conduits. Utilities in East Lenox Street 
include a water main (low service), a sanitary sewer, a storm drain, 2 gas mains, underground 
telecommunications conduits, and underground electric conduits. 
The water, drain, and sewer lines are all Boston Water and Sewer Commission (BWSC) utilities, with 
other utilities being privately owned by their respective utility companies. 
Permits and approvals for the proposed Project may include approvals from the Boston Water and 
Sewer Commission (BWSC) and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Boston Water and 
Sewer Commission (BWSC) Site Plan Approval and General Service Application will be required for 
the proposed new water and sewer connections, and the stormwater management system will be 
designed in conformance with BWSC’s design standards. The gas, electric and telecommunications 
utilities will be coordinated with their respective companies.

within East Lenox Street, there is a 12” sanitary sewer line owned by the BWSC, which flows in a 
southerly direction. Figure 4.1 depicts the existing sewer lines.

this Project.

The proposed Project is in the preliminary design stages and a detailed plan of the proposed site 
utilities is still being developed. However, it is anticipated that the proposed Project will connect to

4.2.4 Wastewater Flow Mitigation 
To help conserve water and reduce the amount of generated wastewater, the proposed Project will 
include water conservation measures such as low flow toilets, restricted flow aerators in faucets and 
showerheads and water saving appliances.

4.3 Water Supply System 
4.3.1 Existing Water Supply 
BWSC owns, operates, and maintains the water distribution system in the vicinity of the proposed 
Project (see Figure 4-1). According to record plans, there is a 12” high service water main located in 
front of the proposed Project within Reed Street, which feeds a sidewalk fire hydrant located mid-
block in front of our site. Reed Street also contains a 12” low service water main. 
There is also a fire hydrant located mid-block within the East Lenox Street sidewalk on our side of the 
street, which is fed from the 12” low service waterline in East Lenox Street. 
In addition, there is a fire hydrant located mid-block within the Newcomb Street sidewalk on the 
opposite side of the street, which is fed from the 12” low service waterline in Newcomb Street. 
4.3.2 Estimated proposed Project Water Consumption 
The estimated water consumption for this Project is 8,107 gpd. This estimate is based on MassDEP’s 
Standard wastewater generation plus 10% or 110% of the wastewater generation identified above. 
There are no known water capacity issues in the vicinity of the proposed Project. This will be 
confirmed later in the design process when fire flow tests are conducted. Water demand and 
availability will be coordinated with BWSC during the Site Plan Review process to ensure the 
proposed Project’s needs are met, while maintaining adequate water flows to the surrounding 
neighborhood. 
4.3.3 Water Service Connections 
The proposed Project is in the preliminary design stages and a detailed plan of the proposed site 
utilities is being developed. However, it is anticipated that the proposed Project’s domestic water 
service will connect to the 12” low service water main located within Reed Street. Also, the proposed 
Project’s fire suppression service will connect to the 12” high service water main located on the 
opposite side of Reed Street. 
The proposed Project’s impacts to the existing water system will be reviewed as part of the BWSC’s 
Site Plan Review process. The domestic and fire protection water service connections required for the 
Project will meet the applicable City and State codes and standards, including cross-connection 
backflow prevention. Compliance with the standards for the domestic water system service 
connection will be reviewed as part of BWSC’s Site Plan Review Process. This review will include sizing 
of domestic water and fire protection services, calculation of meter sizing, backflow prevention 
design, and location of hydrants and Siamese connections that conform to BWSC and Boston Fire 
Department requirements. 
Efforts to reduce water consumption will be made. Aeration fixtures and appliances will be chosen for 
water conservation qualities. New water services will be installed in accordance with the latest local,
