4.4 Storm Drainage System 
4.4.1 Existing Storm Drainage System 
BWSC owns, operates, and maintains the roadway storm drain system in the vicinity of the proposed 
Project (see Figure 6-1). The entire Project Site is virtually a 100% parking lot impervious surface. All 
parking lot stormwater is collected within a series of catch basins and drains into the local roadway 
drainage system. 
4.4.2 Proposed Storm Drainage System 
The following sections summarize the approach to addressing the City of Boston’s Smart Utilities 
Policy as applicable within the Project. 
The Project is expected to reduce the volume of stormwater runoff leaving the site and substantially 
improve the water quality. Because the Project is located within the City of Boston Groundwater 
Conservation Overlay District, the proposed Project will exceed BWSC standards for stormwater 
management by mitigating 1.25-inches of stormwater runoff generated by proposed impervious 
surfaces. 
The volume of stormwater runoff leaving the site will be reduced as a result of the construction of 
on-site subsurface infiltration/ detention systems. It is expected that rooftop runoff from the 
proposed building areas and driveway, measuring 9,758 square feet of on-site impervious surface, 
will be collected and conveyed to subsurface infiltration systems (refer to Figure 4.2, Site Utility Plan). 
The infiltration systems will have overflows tied into the BWSC drain system into Newcomb Street. It 
is anticipated that the equivalent of 1.25-inches over the site’s impervious roof surface area can be 
recharged as prescribed in BPDA’s Smart Utilities design criteria, which will also satisfy BWSC’s Site 
Plan Review requirements. 
To mitigate the amount of impervious surfaces, the proposed Project envisions utilizing porous 
pavers for all pedestrian travel ways and hardscapes within private property. For instances where 
stormwater discharges into the drainage system is subject to petroleum laden runoff, discharges will 
be treated through the use of water quality treatment units. 
Erosion and sediment controls will be used during construction to protect adjacent properties, the 
municipal storm drain system, and the on-site storm drain system. A Stormwater Pollution Prevention 
Plan (SWPPP) will be prepared for use during construction including during demolition activity. As 
part of the SWPPP, an operation and maintenance plan will be developed to support the long-term 
functionality of the proposed stormwater management system. 
4.4.3 Stormwater Measures During Construction 
The Project will not affect the water quality of nearby water bodies. Erosion and sediment control 
measures will be implemented during construction to minimize the transport of site soils to off-site

areas and BWSC storm drain systems. During construction, existing catch basins will be protected 
with filter fabric, straw bales and/or crushed stone, to provide for sediment removal from runoff. 
These controls will be inspected and maintained throughout the construction phase until the areas of

All necessary dewatering will be conducted in accordance with applicable MWRA and BWSC

4.4.4 MassDEP Stormwater Management Policy Standards 
In March 1997, MassDEP adopted a Stormwater Management Policy to address non-point source 
discharges and published the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook as guidance on the Stormwater 
Policy, which was revised in February 2008. The Policy prescribes specific stormwater management 
standards for development projects, including urban pollutant removal criteria for projects that may 
impact environmental resource areas. Compliance is achieved through the implementation of Best 
Management Practices (BMPs) in the stormwater management design. The Policy is administered 
locally pursuant to the state Wetlands Protection Act, MGL Ch. 131, s. 40. 
A brief explanation of each Policy Standard and the system compliance is provided below: 
Standard #1: No new stormwater conveyances (e.g., outfalls) may discharge untreated stormwater 
directly to or cause erosion in wetlands or waters of the Commonwealth. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. The design will incorporate the appropriate 
stormwater treatment and no new untreated stormwater will be directly discharged to, nor will 
erosion be caused to, wetlands or waters of the Commonwealth as a result of stormwater discharges 
related to the Project. 
Standard #2: Stormwater management systems shall be designed so that post-development peak 
discharge rates do not exceed pre-development peak discharge rates. This Standard may be waived 
for discharges to land subject to coastal storm flowage as defined in 310 CMR. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. The existing discharge rate will be met or 
decreased by the improvements associated with the Project. 
Standard #3: Loss of annual recharge to groundwater shall be eliminated or minimized through the 
use of infiltration measures including environmental sensitive site design, low impact development 
techniques, stormwater best management practices, and good operation and maintenance. At a 
minimum, the annual recharge from the post-development site shall approximate the annual 
recharge from pre-development conditions based on soil type. This Standard is met when the 
stormwater management system is designed to infiltrate the required recharge volume as 
determined in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard to the maximum extent practicable. 
Standard #4: Stormwater management systems shall be designed to remove 80% of the average 
annual post-construction load of Total Suspended Solids (TSS). This Standard is met when: 
a. Suitable practices for source control and pollution prevention are identified in a long-term 
pollution prevention plan, and thereafter are implemented and maintained;

b. Structural stormwater best management practices are sized to capture the required water quality 
volume determined in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook; and 
c. Pretreatment is provided in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. Within the Project’s limit of work, there will 
be mostly building roof, paved sidewalk, parking, and driveway areas. Runoff from paved areas that 
would contribute unwanted sediments or pollutants to the existing storm drain system will be 
collected by deep sump, hooded catch basins and conveyed through water quality units before 
discharging into the BWSC system. 
Standard #5: For land uses with higher potential pollutant loads, source control and pollution 
prevention shall be implemented in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook to 
eliminate or reduce the discharge of stormwater runoff from such land uses to the maximum extent 
practicable. If through source control and/or pollution prevention all land uses with higher potential 
pollutant loads cannot be completely protected from exposure to rain, snow, snow melt, and 
stormwater runoff, the proponent shall use the specific structural stormwater BMPs determined by 
the Department to be suitable for such uses as provided in the Massachusetts Stormwater 
Handbook. Stormwater discharges from land uses with higher potential pollutant loads shall also 
comply with the requirements of the Massachusetts Clean Waters Act, M.G.L. c. 21, §§ 26-53 and the 
regulations promulgated thereunder at 314 CMR 3.00, 314 CMR 4.00 and 314 CMR 5.00. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. The Project is not associated with Higher 
Potential Pollutant Loads (per the Policy, Volume I, page 1-6). 
Standard #6: Stormwater discharges within the Zone II or Interim Wellhead Protection Area of a 
public water supply, and stormwater discharges near or to any other critical area, require the use of 
the specific source control and pollution prevention measures and the specific structural stormwater 
best management practices determined by the Department to be suitable for managing discharges 
to such areas, as provided in the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. A discharge is near a critical 
area if there is a strong likelihood of a significant impact occurring to said area, taking into account 
site-specific factors. Stormwater discharges to Outstanding Resource Waters and Special Resource 
Waters shall be removed and set back from the receiving water or wetland and receive the highest 
and best practical method of treatment. A “storm water discharge” as defined in 314 CMR 3.04(2)(a)1 
or (b) to an Outstanding Resource Water or Special Resource Water shall comply with 314 CMR 3.00 
and 314 CMR 4.00. Stormwater discharges to a Zone I or Zone A are prohibited unless essential to 
the operation of a public water supply. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. The Project will not discharge untreated 
stormwater to a sensitive area or any other area. There are no Zone II or Interim Wellhead Protection 
Areas in the vicinity of the Project Site. 
Standard #7: A redevelopment project is required to meet the following Stormwater Management 
Standards only to the maximum extent practicable: Standard 2, Standard 3, and the pretreatment and 
structural stormwater best management practice requirements of Standards 4, 5, and 6. Existing 
stormwater discharges shall comply with Standard 1 only to the maximum extent practicable. A 
redevelopment project shall also comply with all other requirements of the Stormwater Management 
Standards and improve existing conditions. 
Compliance: The Project is a new development and thus this Standard is not applicable.

Standard #8: A plan to control construction-related impacts including erosion, sedimentation and 
other pollutant sources during construction and land disturbance activities (construction period 
erosion, sedimentation, and pollution prevention plan) shall be developed and implemented. 
Compliance: The Project will comply with this Standard. Sedimentation and erosion controls will be 
incorporated as part of the design of the Project and employed during construction. A Stormwater 
Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) will be prepared for use during construction as well as during 
demolition activities. 
Standard #9: A Long-Term Operation and Maintenance (O&M) Plan shall be developed and

Standard #10: All illicit discharges to the stormwater management system are prohibited.

4.5 Other Utilities 
4.5.1 Electrical Service 
 
The Proponent will work with Eversource to identify where proposed building electrical services will 
connect and to confirm adequate system capacity as the design is finalized. 
4.5.2 Telecommunications Services 
 
Telecommunication services will be coordinated with the telecommunication providers. 
4.5.3 Natural Gas Systems 
 
National Grid owns and maintains the existing gas mains adjacent to the Site. Since the Project is 
anticipated to be all electric, a proposed natural gas service is not required. 
4.5.4 Utility Protection During Construction 
 
The contractor will notify the utility companies and will contact “Dig Safe” prior to any excavation 
associated with the proposed Project. During construction, the infrastructure will be protected using 
sheeting and shoring, temporary relocations and construction staging as required. The contractor will

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4

Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in

Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community

1.1 Introduction 
This development package is being submitted on behalf of DND Homes (the “Proponent”) for a 
residential development that is approximately 49,000 square feet in size and includes forty-two 
rental units and a subsurface parking garage with thirty-four parking spaces. 
 
The project site contains approximately 25,941 square feet of land. (See Figure 1: Project Locus). 
The Development Team is seeking to combine 25, 29, and 37 Dighton Street lots and redevelop 
the site with a residential building which is conducive to this neighborhood. The project site has 
approximately 248.29 feet of frontage along Dighton Street. (See Figure 1: 25 Dighton Street 
BPDA Zoning Map, Figure 2: 29 Dighton Street BPDA Zoning Map, and Figure 3: 37 Dighton Street 
BPDA Zoning Map). There is a strong residential presence in the area, including Mount Vernon 
Street and the abutting Washington Street and Chestnut Hill Avenue and throughout this section 
of Brighton. The proposed project includes a revitalization of the site by razing the existing three 
buildings and replacing them with a new residential building. The Proponent is looking to 
reinvigorate the existing site and substantially invest in this community. The current estimated 
cost of this project, based upon the most recent plans, is approximately $12,551,000. 
 
The Proponent’s goal when conceptualizing this project was to revitalize this section of Dighton 
Street by replacing the existing outdated residential buildings with a new residential building, as 
well as replace the extensive black top with greenery and landscaping. This development project 
will add new housing units and will replace the paved exterior space with new usable green space 
and landscaping. This project will add new residential housing opportunities to the popular 
Brighton community and allow for new residents to move into the neighborhood. 
 
The Proposed Project will exceed the 20,000 square foot total build-out threshold for a project in 
a Boston neighborhood, and therefore requires the preparation of filing(s) under the Small Project 
Review regulations pursuant to Article 80 of the Boston Zoning Code. The Proponent will also 
seek dimensional variances from the Boston Zoning Board of Appeal related to lot area minimum 
per unit, FAR, building height stories, building height feet, rear yard, usable open space, loading, 
and off-street parking.

1.2 Project Description 
The proposed project site consists of three parcels and is approximately 25,941 square foot in 
total which runs along Dighton Street and abuts Washington Street and Eastburn Street in the 
Brighton section of the Allston-Brighton neighborhood. The project site is located within a Three-
Family Residential Subdistrict; however, the site is surrounded by a variety of housing types, 
including two-family and multi-family residential structures along Dighton Street, Washington 
Street, and Eastburn Street. The project site directly abuts a two-family residence and a church 
on Dighton Street. Additionally, across the street from the project site on Dighton Street are 
several residential structures, including two two-family buildings, a three-family, and a multifamily 
building. The project site currently contains three separate multi-family structures. As part of this 
project, the existing buildings will be razed, and new housing will be erected. The proposed 
project will fit the character of the neighborhood and provide needed housing units for the 
community, while creating green space and affordable on-site units. 
 
The proposed project will be constructed as a four-story residential structure with a subsurface 
parking garage and will offer a variety of different bedroom and unit sizes, along with usable open 
space. The proposed project is ideally situated approximately 0.8 miles to the South Street, 
Chestnut Hill Avenue, and Chiswick Road MBTA Green Line stations, as well as within walking 
distance to several MBTA bus stops including the 57, 51, 86, 65, and 501 routes. The development 
team is proposing a project that would include some parking options for future residents but will 
also be located in close proximity to public transportation and would include bike storage for 
residents. 
 
The project is approximately 49,000 square feet in size and will include forty-two units with thirty-
four parking spaces. The building will incorporate a mix of one-bedroom, two-bedroom, and 
three-bedroom units to accommodate a variety of renters. The project will include ample usable 
green space for residents to enjoy and each of the units will contain private decks which will add 
additional light and air to each unit. There is approximately 380 square feet of usable open space 
per unit. Finally, the developer is proposing a private subsurface interior bike room in the parking 
garage and an exterior Bluebike Station to encourage alternative means of transportation. The 
project is 0.6 miles to the nearest MBTA Green Line and less than 1,000 feet to several bus lines. 
Additionally, the focus on bicycle storage and bike sharing will minimize community impact from 
resident parking from the proposed project. 
 
The proposed project is subject to Small Project Review under Article 80E of the Boston Zoning 
Code. In parallel with this application, the proposed project will seek zoning relief from the Boston 
Zoning Code at the Boston Zoning Board of Appeal related to lot area minimum per unit, FAR, 
building height stories, building height feet, rear yard, usable open space, loading, and off-street 
parking.

2.4 Compliance with Boston Zoning Code (Use and Dimensional 
Requirements) 
The Site is located in a Three-Family Residential Subdistrict (3F-4000) in the Allston-Brighton 
Neighborhood, Article 51 of the Boston Zoning Code. (See Table 3: Zoning Compliance). 
 
As part of the permitting and approval process, this project would be required to appear before 
the Boston Zoning Board of Appeal to obtain certain variances. Under Article 51, Table A of the 
Boston Zoning Code, multi-family dwellings are not an allowed use. Therefore, a Use Variance 
would need to be obtained from the Boston Zoning Board of Appeal. The proposed project will 
also seek relief from several requirements of the existing Boston Zoning Code outlined in Article 
51, Table D which governs dimensional regulations in a residential neighborhood. The proposed 
structure exceeds the maximum allowable floor area ratio and the maximum allowable building 
height for number of stories and feet. Additionally, the proposed project will also require 
variances for minimum lot area per unit, minimum usable open space per unit, and minimum rear 
yard depth. Lastly, the project will also seek variances for off-street parking and loading 
requirements, which are governed by Article 51, Tables J and K. 
 
The project site is located in an area that contains a mix of residential housing, including several 
multi-family residential buildings. The design team feels that given this location and the structures 
influencing the design, as well as comparable developments in the neighborhood, the proposed 
building’s height, mass, and scale are appropriate for this location and conducive to the Brighton 
neighborhood.

3 Urban Design and Sustainability 
 
3.1 Site and Surroundings 
The proposed project site encompasses three parcels containing approximately 25,941 square 
feet along Dighton Street in the Brighton section of Allston-Brighton. The project site is located 
within a Three-Family Residential Subdistrict, however the site is surrounded by a variety of 
housing types, including two-family and multi-family residential buildings, as well as commercial 
buildings, on Dighton Street and Washington Street. The site directly abuts a residential multi-
family building to the right and a church to the left on Dighton Street, a paved lot to the rear, and 
several residential buildings across the street, including two two-family residential buildings, a 
three-family residential building, and an apartment building. 
 
The project site currently contains three, dated multi-family buildings which are identified by the 
Boston Assessor as four-six family buildings. These buildings are surrounded by black top 
pavement. The development team is seeking to redevelop the site with a new residential building 
which is conducive to the neighborhood and will provide affordable units. Additionally, the team 
is seeking to remove the black top and replace it with new green space and landscaping to 
reinvigorate the site. 
 
For existing site pictures see Appendix B. 
 
3.2 Urban Design Concept 
The proposed project is a multi-family building located on Dighton Street, in the Brighton 
neighborhood of Allston-Brighton. The sloped topography along Dighton Street provides the 
opportunity for a garage partially sunken into the ground to house thirty-four parking spaces and 
a dedicated bike room, as well as the opportunity for a tiered landscaping design to abut the 
sidewalk. Both the parking and the bike room will be accessible off Dighton Street through a 
garage door. Elevator access to each floor gives tenants handicap accessibility to the generously 
sized units designed to accommodate both young professionals as well as families. The unit mix 
consists of one-, two-, and three-bedroom units with the units having direct outdoor access to a 
private deck. 
 
The proposed design offers a clean, modern design with a contemporary roofline and exterior 
detailing. The stone-covered garage level blends with the tiered landscaping structure to create 
a balanced contrast with the other exterior surfaces. 
 
For renderings of the Proposed Project see Appendix C. 
 
3.3 Materials and Finishes 
The proposed development is located in a neighborhood of mixed construction types and styles. 
We have designed a building with many angles and setbacks that respond to the site. Dighton

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

Project Summary
The proposed project sits on two lots with a combined area of 9,232 square 
feet. The site is at 39-45 Dudley Street and 51 Dudley Street. The project 
includes constructing a three-story building containing 22 residential units and 
approximately 2,200 SF commercial space. For accessibility and fire safety 
purposes, three separate buildings are proposed on the combined lot. Each 
building will have the resident entrances on 49 Dudley Street, 23 Kenilworth 
Street, and 27-29 Kenilworth Street. Commercial space visitors will have 
separate access on 27-29 Kenilworth Street.
The project will create three (3) affordable units at 80%-100% AMI and is 
close to the Roxbury Crossing MBTA orange line stop and the Nubian Station 
MBTA grey line stop. The project includes an expansion of the sidewalk and 
public realm. These public realm improvements intend to increase green 
space and make the nearby road crossings safer for tenants, neighbors, and 
the community.
The project’s urban massing repeats the scale of the adjacent residential 
typologies. The massing is further sculpted through specific energy model 
calculations, optimizing its solar gain to achieve passive house standards. 
As a community benefit, the project proposes to extend the sidewalk at the 
intersection of Dudley Street and Kenilworth Street. The extended sidewalk 
would create additional open space with new trees and landscapes to 
improve the pedestrian experience. A community gathering space will face the 
new green space that will provide opportunities for vibrant activities to happen 
in the area.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors 
openings, hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit

1.3 Community Benefits 
The proposed project offers the following benefits: 
• 
PROVIDES NEW HOUSING UNITS – Roxbury, has seen an influx of new people moving 
in because of its close proximity to Downtown Boston, and accessible public transportation, and 
therefore there is a strong need for new market rate residential housing. The Project will create 16 
affordable units of housing. 
• 
PROVIDES AFFORDABLE HOUSING - As Dorchester apartment prices continue to rise 
there is a strong need to keep longtime residents, and new families from being out priced. This 
Project will create affordable units that will meet the Boston Planning & Development Agency 
requirement. 
• 
REVITALIZATION OF SITE - The Project will revitalize an abandoned land provide new 
infrastructure and landscaping. 
• 
ON-SITE PARKING - This Project will create 46 on-site parking spaces for residents of 
the building. The Project is also within walking distance to public transportation, which will 
encourage less need for vehicular travel. 
• 
GREENSPACE - The Project will create green space with an exterior courtyard located in 
the west side of the Property for the exclusive use of the residents. The front and rear of building 
will be beautified with planters and grass area. 
• 
ELIMINATE BLIGHT - Over the years the parcel of land has deteriorated, and it is uneven 
and overgrown with weeds. This Project will clean up this parcel and create a visually aesthetic 
building and landscape that will complement the surrounding residential community. 
• 
JOB CREATION - This Project will create temporary construction and labor jobs during 
the development process. It will also create permanent jobs in the form of property management 
of the building and grounds.

PROJECT OVERVIEW 
1.1 
Introduction 
Harvard Street Neighborhood Health Center (“HSNHC” or the “Proponent”) proposes to 
redevelop the underutilized parcels located at 8 Old Road, 14 Ellington Street, and 16 Ellington 
Street in Boston (the “Project site”, or “site”) with the construction of a new approximately 42,300 
square foot (“sf”) health center with clinical, laboratory and pharmacy sub-uses (the “Project”). 
In 2016, the Department of Neighborhood Development (now the Mayor’s Office of Housing 
[“MOH”]) issued a Request for Proposals ("RFP") for the redevelopment of the 8 Old Road and 14 
Ellington Street parcels. On March 14, 2018, MOH certified the tentative designation and intent 
to sell the two parcels to HSNHC; the certification has been extended since that time, most 
recently in March 2023. The Project site includes these two parcels, as well as the 16 Ellington 
Street parcel which is owned by HSNHC. 
The Project described herein aligns with the RFP’s development goals for the site, which identified 
the preferred use as an institutional or commercial building, and sought a development that 
would “activate the street, create jobs, create a community destination/connection and promote 
pedestrian access.” The existing health center located at 632 Blue Hill Avenue has been in its 
current building for approximately 40 years; the current building itself no longer meets the 
community’s needs or accessibility standards, having been constructed in the early 1900s. By 
redeveloping the Project site, the Project will improve the public realm, activate the street, and 
enhance the important services that HSNHC provides to the community. 
About Harvard Street Neighborhood Health Center 
HSNHC is a prominent health resource for the Boston community and provides the delivery of 
comprehensive patient-centered medical care. HSNHC first opened in 1969 at 895 Blue Hill 
Avenue as part of the Boston Department of Health and Hospitals. In 1976, HSNHC became an 
independent not-for-profit institution and relocated its main service location to the current 
location at 632 Blue Hill Avenue. Designated as a Federally Qualified Health Center (“FQHC”), 
HSNHC continues to provide a comprehensive system of care that is responsive to the 
community’s health care needs. The proposed health center described herein will bolster 
HSNHC’s mission to provide quality care to the community. 
This Small Project Review application is being submitted to initiative review under Article 80E of 
the Boston Zoning Code (“Zoning Code”).

Project Description 
1.2.1 
Project Site 
The Project site has a total area of approximately 19,428 sf and comprises three parcels located 
at 8 Old Road, 14 Ellington Street, and 16 Ellington Street. The site is currently occupied by two 
single-story garages and surface parking and is bounded by Old Road to the north, Michigan 
Avenue to the east, Ellington Street to the west, and residential properties to the south. 
Figure 1-1 shows the existing conditions on the Project site and Appendix A includes a site survey. 
1.2.2 
Neighborhood Context 
The neighborhood to the south, east and west of the Project site includes residential properties 
that range from one- to three-stories, and surface parking. Directly across the street on Old Road, 
there is a five-story commercial building. To the north, there are existing commercial properties 
along Blue Hill Avenue. Public recreational facilities in the vicinity of the Project site include 
Franklin Park to the northwest, and Erie-Ellington Playground to the south. There are several 
Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (“MBTA”) bus stops in the area, including the 
existing Old Road at Ellington Street bus stop adjacent to the Project site. See Figure 1-2 for views 
of the surrounding neighborhood. 
The neighborhood is a low-income, minority-majority area with a range of socio-economic 
challenges; residents experience lower life expectancy rates compared to other areas in the City, 
and there is also a high proportion of low-wage jobs. HSNHC recognizes the importance of the 
site’s prominent location in the neighborhood and aims to leverage it to enhance its mission of 
providing accessible healthcare to the community. 
1.2.3 
Project Program 
As described above, the Project proposes the redevelopment of the Project site to construct a 
new three-story, approximately 40-foot-tall community health center with clinical, laboratory and 
pharmacy sub-uses. The pharmacy space is not retail pharmacy, but instead will provide 
prescription services to HSNHC patients. Additionally, there will be a community space that will 
be used for temporary programs, services, and/or events. 
The Project will be built to the property line on Old Road, consistent with the other residential 
and commercial uses on Old Road, and with landscaped setbacks to complement the residential 
properties on Michigan Avenue and Ellington Street. Public realm improvements include sidewalk 
modifications and new street trees to create an engaging streetscape. See Figure 1-3 for the 
proposed site plan and Figure 1-4 for a view of the Project. Appendix B includes floor plans and 
elevations. The exterior material palette will be refined over time and in dialogue with the BPDA. 
Materiality and colors shown in the accompanying visuals are conceptual and subject to revisions 
as the design process progresses.

and departing from the Project, are anticipated to be created through the City’s proposed plans 
for the redesign of Old Road. The Proponent will continue to coordinate with the City regarding 
the Old Road redesign, and the Project’s design will not preclude the City’s proposed redesign. 
1.3 
Public Benefits 
The Project will provide multiple benefits to the City as a result of converting the Project site into 
an expanded neighborhood health center. The new facility will primarily offer healthcare services 
for low-income people of color, who make up a vast majority of the population in this area. 
The Project will significantly expand HSNHC’s operational capacity, reinforce HSNHC’s mission of 
offering high-quality affordable services to at-risk populations, generate savings for City and State 
healthcare systems, create jobs, and capitalize on urban design improvements occurring along 
Blue Hill Avenue and Columbia Road. 
Public Health Benefits 
The Proponent provides vital care for thousands of patients annually. HSNHC’s service offerings 
are comprehensive, including family care, behavioral health, dentistry, obstetrics and gynecology, 
and eye care, plus an on-site laboratory and pharmacy. The Proponent runs numerous programs, 
including a food pantry, veterans center, and a Women’s, Infants, & Children’s Program to support 
maternal and early life health outcomes. HSNHC is also part of the Grove Hall Trauma Team, a 
City of Boston-sponsored group that supports residents with mental health care following 
traumatic events. 
In 2022, the health center saw over 7,600 unique patients across more than 35,000 visits – most 
of which were in-person at clinic locations. Over 95% of HSNHC patients in 2022 were people of 
color, predominantly Black. A vast majority of patients had incomes at or below the poverty line, 
and most patients relied on Medicare, Medicaid, or were uninsured. Throughout the COVID-19 
pandemic, the health center has given more than 20,000 tests and over 15,000 vaccines, primarily 
to racial and ethnic minorities. 
The Proponent serves some of the most racially and economically vulnerable populations in the 
City. The Project will expand HSNHC’s capacity to serve these patients both by increasing the 
facility space and allowing for more health services, including behavioral care, to be concentrated 
in one location. This Project would provide public health benefits in such a way that supports the 
City’s targets of promoting racial justice and equity.

3.0 
CLIMATE CHANGE RESILIENCE 
3.1 
Introduction 
Climate change conditions considered by the Project team include higher maximum and mean 
temperatures, more frequent and longer extreme heat events, more heavy precipitation events, 
and more frequent and longer droughts. 
3.2 
Extreme Heat Events 
The Climate Ready Boston report predicts that in Boston, there may be between 25 to 90 days 
with temperatures over 90 degrees by 2070, compared to an average of 11 days per year over 90 
degrees between 1971 and 2000. The Project site design will include measures to adapt to these 
conditions, including the reduction of impermeable surfaces on-site and additional greenspace 
and landscaping to reduce the heat island effect. The mechanical systems will be modular in 
nature with an ability to expand heating and cooling capacities in the future. 
3.3 
Precipitation Events 
As a result of climate change, the Northeastern region of the country is expected to experience 
more frequent and intense storms. To mitigate this, the Proponent will take measures to minimize 
stormwater runoff and protect the Project’s mechanical equipment, as necessary. The existing 
Project site is nearly entirely impervious; the Project will result in a reduced amount of impervious 
area which will be expected to reduce the existing peak rates and volumes of stormwater runoff 
from the Project site and promote runoff recharge to the greatest extent practicable. 
As described in Section 2.2.3, stormwater will be collected and directed to an oil/water separator 
prior to discharging into an underground detention and infiltration system located under the 
proposed parking spaces, with an overflow to Ellington Street. The system will be designed in 
compliance with MassDEP stormwater standards. 
3.4 
Drought Conditions 
Although more intense rainstorms are predicted, extended periods of drought are also predicted 
due to climate change. Under the high emissions scenario, the occurrence of droughts lasting one 
to three months could increase by as much as 75% over existing conditions by the end of the 
century. To minimize the Project’s susceptibility to drought conditions, the landscape design is 
anticipated to incorporate native and adaptive plant materials, and high efficiency irrigation 
systems will be installed. Aeration fixtures and appliances will be chosen for water conservation 
qualities, thereby conserving potable water supplies.

3.5 
Sustainable Design 
The Project will be designed to attain design excellence across multiple facets of sustainability and 
resiliency. The Project will reduce exposure to climate hazards by minimizing contributions to 
climate change at every opportunity. The Project expects to meet building and energy codes 
aligned with Passive House standards. 
The Project will utilize an all-electric, high efficiency mechanical system, coupled with an 
optimized building envelope to achieve an ultra-low Energy Use Intensity (“EUI”). To further 
decrease the Project’s energy demand, the Proponent is evaluating the incorporation of an on-
site, roof-mounted solar photovoltaic (“PV”) array. Additionally, the potential climate change 
impacts associated with the extraction, transportation, and construction of all building materials 
will be tracked and lowered through a Lifecycle Analysis (“LCA”). 
The Project benefits the surrounding neighborhood context by improving climate resiliency on 
the site through mitigating urban heat island effect and responsibly managing stormwater. As 
described above in Section 3.3, the Project will reduce exposure to flood events caused by 
extreme precipitation by responsibly managing rainwater captured on the site. Additionally, the 
Project will include a white roof membrane, and is evaluating the incorporation of a solar PV array. 
In addition to its environmental stewardship, the Project will prioritize the health and wellness of 
the HSNHC staff and greater Boston community through its health center services. The Project’s 
mechanical systems, ventilation, and materials will be selected to improve indoor air quality to

Project Overview
Project Summary
The Proposed Project, “New Madinah,” seeks to provide expansion to the Society for Islamic 
Brotherhood and their religious and social services through the redevelopment of their current building 
and adjacent under-utilized land.
As long term community leaders, the Society for Islamic Brotherhood has served Lower Roxbury for 
many decades. Through their Islamic Multi-Services Organization, they operate a food pantry bi-weekly, 
serving an estimated 2,000 residents in need. They offer college and career prep courses to high school 
students and learning adults, and help to organize professional training and certification courses. They 
help local residents secure stable housing, and connect them with counseling services. Additionally, as 
the Mosque for Praising Allah, they provide a welcoming house of worship for 300 local residents. All of 
these services are currently operated from the single existing 3-story structure at the corner of 
Shawmut Avenue and Williams Street.
Located along Shawmut Avenue in Roxbury, in the Boulevard Planning District Overlay, the project site 
is a significant gateway to Roxbury’s culturally rich neighborhoods. Occupying the length of Shawmut 
Avenue between Williams Street and Gary Street, the site is long, relatively flat, and very narrow in 
several locations. It is comprised of 6 lots, totaling approximately 10,609 sf, most of which is currently 
serving as paved parking for the existing structure.
The proposed project would raze the existing structure and surface parking to allow for the complete 
redevelopment of the site. As a mixed-use development, the project proposes over 14,000 sf of new 
cultural, commercial, and services space, along with 38 new low-income tax credit subsudized 
Affordable housing units (DND and DHCD compliant), and a common roof deck and green roof. The 
ground floor is generally dedicated to public, commercial, and cultural uses; including a multi-purpose 
event space, cultural cafe and bookstore, and access to the mosque and educational spaces above. 
Towards the southwest end of the site is the residential entry, bike storage access, and surface 
parking underneath the residential floors above. The frontages along both Shawmut Avenue and 
Williams Street would include a new colonnade of street trees and other amenities to align with the 
city’s Complete Streets Guidelines.

Community Benefits
Project Summary
The “New Madinah” project, in keeping with the organization’s goals of expanding opportunity and supporting 
advancement of local residents, offers many community benefits to Lower Roxbury and the City of Boston. They 
include:
- Increased service capacity for the Islamic Multi-Services Organization’s (IMSO’s) food pantry, ensuring greater 
food security for local residents in need. They currently feed over 2,000 residents bi-weekly. This number is grow­
ing.
- Expanded educational and classroom space for the IMSO’s college and career prep courses, empowering youth 
and learning adults to pursue greater opportunities and goals. Many local residents are immigrants for whom En­
glish is a second language. They face greater challenges in securing the same opportunities as other residents.
- Easier access to housing and social services for the local community, helping to connect local residents to the 
city’s programs through dedicated administrative and office space.
- New religious worship spaces to meet the growing demands of the congregation and worshiping community. 
Currently over 300 people would like to worship with the mosque, but the current space allows for less than half 
of that.
- Opportunity for community conversations and cultural events, through the event space for community gather­
ings. Opportunity for local businesses to start, stabilize, and grow through the cafe and bookstore. This will help 
to activate the public space along Shawmut Avenue.
- Creation of 38 new low-income tax credit subsudized Affordable housing units (DND and DHCD compliant), 
providing some relief to a strained housing market, and overburdened population seeking housing in the area.

Design Approach
Detailed Project Information
The proposed project, “The New Madinah,” takes its name from the old city of Madinah; one of the 
holiest cities in Islam. As an economic, cultural, and residential center, the city is and was regarded as 
a sort of social crossroads; encouraging the exchange of ideas, commerce, and people with streets of 
dwellings overlooking commercial bazaars and markets. The New Madinah project aims to continue 
that spirit.
The ground floor of the project acts as a “bazaar,” with its many public uses overlapping and blending 
together. They build and organize towards more formal religious and educational uses on the upper 
floors, totaling approximately 14,000 sf of Cultural and Commercial space. This organization of increas­
ing formality is expressed architecturally as a colonnade of metallic folded “curtains” around the north 
eastern mass of the building. Pulling queues from Islamic concepts of layered screening and privacy, 
these “curtains” build a rhythm of openings; ribbons of filtered/obscured light.
This expression of privacy filtering continues up the building, in the form of perforated metal balconies, 
tucked between the residential masses above. The 38 units (~34,000 sf) of residential program above 
is broken down into smaller proportions of massing, with a separate circulation and egress system.
The building’s footprint is set back 2’ along Shawmut Avenue on the ground floor to provide a wider 
sidewalk along the project site. At the south western end of the site the building mass overhead pro­
vides shelter for the parking area, and access to building service areas at the rear.

Parking and Access
Detailed Project Information
Shawmut Avenue is a one-way Neighborhood Connector street, with 2 lanes of travel and parking on 
both sides along this segment of the street. Vehicular access to the site, its 4 surface parking spac­
es, and the rear building service area are all from Gary Street, the small shared dead-end street on the 
south western end of the site. This access leads directly to the covered area under the building, which 
shelters the parking and building services spaces. These spaces will all be screened from the front and 
rear with landscaping and architectural building elements. The exit from the site occurs at the rear, onto 
Dade Street, which immediately turns onto Williams Street.

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in Boston’s 
built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, rather than after a 
design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ADA requirements, but that they create a built 
environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to provide 
specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout Boston's 
built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

 https://www.usgbc.org/articles/social-equity-pilot-credits-added-leed-nd-and-leed-om 
 
Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth by 
MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth by MAAB 
521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes and 
communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the specific 
functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in the City. 
For more information visit: http://www.bostonplans.org/housing/overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https://www.boston.gov/pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community benefits, 
particularly for persons with disabilities 
10. Visitability – A structure that is designed intentionally with no architectural barriers in its common spaces (entrances, doors openings, 
hallways, bathrooms), thereby allowing persons with disabilities who have functional limitations to visit
